en: Preface to the Compendium of Essential Rules for Laypeople:
One becomes a human being by grasping the ultimate quintessence of the "two fives" (the ten virtues). One should contemplate how to remain complete as a human being;

only then will one have no cause for shame before Heaven. Each person receives this completeness from Heaven, yet from the highest sages down to the lowest, none can avoid being obscured by their human limitations.

When desire arises, one's original nature daily becomes diluted and one's innate truth daily lost. One must urgently seek a means to rescue it, just as when a mirror is cleansed of its grime, its radiance returns as before;
or as when water is free from wind, its waves naturally subside. This is not an increase of something new, but merely the non-diminution of what was originally there.
Regarding the method for restoring nature and returning to truth, the sacred teachings speak of "overcoming and clarifying" (*kémíng*) and "daily renewal" (*rìxīn*), leading to ultimate goodness.
This region is what is called the original face of the Buddha-dharma. To lose that original [nature] is to change one’s face;
to maintain this face is to return to one’s original state. Without adding or subtracting, neither identical nor separate, one attains the Supreme Vehicle, which is equivalent to ultimate sincerity.
At the very moment of self-illumination and sincerity, there must necessarily be the power of cultivation and practice.

He disciplines them with the Three Precepts and molds them with the Five Constant Virtues. When human affairs are complete, the mind of Heaven is restored. To overcome self in a single day, the whole world returns to benevolence.
The *I Ching* says: "Returning before it is far, there will be no cause for great regret. Is this not what is meant? The scholar aspires to the worthy;
the worthy aspire to the sage; the sage aspires to Heaven. Man is the most spiritual among all things; all can become a Yao or a Shun, provided their character is not...
To remain stationary is to distance oneself from the sages; to flow into depravity and excess leads further to self-destruction, which is truly unavoidable.

Since the Way lies in acting early, one must ensure that every person knows to loathe the heterodox and honor the orthodox, returning to the root and the source to roam together in the vast and bright heavens of peace—what limit could there be to such joy?
Among Buddhists, the *bhikṣu* is honored; among Confucians, the *jūshì* (lay practitioner) is esteemed. As for the *jūshì*, they are *chǔshì* (recluses).

Furthermore, a scholar should be like a maiden in seclusion, valuing the gravity of his initial conduct. How could one who does not rely on the teachings of the Name (Confucianism) be entitled to the title of "Dweller in the Land" (a Buddhist lay follower)?
The Buddha’s regulation to depart from the three poisons is precisely the Confucian school’s Three Precepts of removing lust, strife, and gain.

Receiving the five precepts is equivalent to upholding the Five Constant Virtues of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and trustworthiness. To refrain from lust is to be free from greed; to refrain from strife is to—

Free from anger, one attains the precept of non-delusion; thus one abandons evil and follows the good. Benevolence means not killing or harming; righteousness means not stealing; propriety means not engaging in sexual misconduct;
wisdom means not drinking intoxicants; and faith means not speaking falsehoods. Being free from desire, one manifests steadfastness.

One should further advance by generating the bodhicitta and upholding the Bodhisattva precepts, ensuring that every aspect of conduct, whether major or minor, is pure. Thus all people shall return to the path.
Its nature is such that one does not flow toward dissipation and desire; this is what constitutes attaining it.

Now, when a layperson at home wishes to receive the five precepts, they must first take the three refuges—meaning to turn back from delusion to return to truth, and to depart from evil to rely upon goodness.

One who receives the three refuges is called an *upāsaka* in Sanskrit, which translates as "lay follower" (*jìnshì nán*). This means to draw near to the Triple Gem and extensively cultivate all manner of wholesome deeds.
This is followed by the five precepts, which are called *śikṣāpada* (points of training), for they are that which a lay male (*upāsaka*) should study.

They are also called the "tracks of training" (*śikṣā-vartman*), for by treading upon these, one attains great wisdom. They are further termed the "pathway," for all other forms of discipline (*vinaya*) may enter into them.
They are again designated as the "root of training" (*śikṣā-mūla*), for they constitute the foundation of everything that is to be studied. One should maintain these...

Only through the precepts does one truly attain the name of an upāsaka. In our city of Hangzhou, there was a great bhikṣu, Master Yuanhong, who gave rise to a profound and earnest mind of compassionate protection and great compassion.
He compiled and edited the *Expanded Collection of Essential Vinaya Rules* (Lüyào guǎngjí), which was originally the aspiration of Mr.
Chen Zixi, and published it so that laypeople might cherish it and have a standard to follow, while the five classes of renunciants could likewise be unified.
Adhering to the Brahma-net Sūtra, the Way is realized together through the Three Vehicles; the Dharma is equally ascended upon the Five Divisions. The primordial goodness resides entirely therein.
I, [Qian], being of dull wit, have received this compilation and respectfully offer these humble words as fodder for the wise. This is from one who currently manifests in the body of a layperson.
Do not mistake these words of mine for idle chatter. Written on the day of the winter solstice in the second month of winter in the fourth year of the Daoguang era,
by Shen Qiqian of Zhentang, a disciple of Renhe who received the Bodhisattva Upāsaka precepts as a former sixth-grade military officer of Shaanxi,
and who has examined his own life, prostrating in reverence.
The Essentials of the Vinaya for Laypeople was compiled by the Great Master Ouyi of Lingfeng.

Out of compassion, the Master, having already compiled the essential Vinaya rules for the sons of the Śākya to bequeath as a gift to later students, further considered that while the two groups of lay followers were willing to follow these precepts, they found it difficult to seek them out.
He therefore further compiled the Essentials of the Vinaya for Laypeople, along with various annotations, so that...
As for those who uphold [the Dharma]: they interpret the meaning according to the text and collect their minds according to the meaning; thus, the grace of their gift of the Dharma is also vast.

Now, the Vinaya texts are extensive and the meanings of the Vinaya are profound and subtle; therefore, we disciples of Śākyamuni should reverently uphold the *vinaya* and devote our minds to its study and recitation.
It is already difficult to obtain even a single good edition for the purpose of investigating and practicing its contents, let alone for those living as householders.
For a person who has only recently resolved to attain enlightenment, this book is truly indispensable, as it concerns matters they have never previously practiced.

It is a pity that the woodblocks have decayed over time and copies are extremely rare; consequently, contemporary practitioners possess little more than a superficial understanding of the principles of what is maintained and what is transgressed.
There was a work titled *Jingjie* (Essential Explanations). He [the author] was asked what constitutes the precepts of return (*guījiè*) and what constitutes the permitted and prohibited (*kāizhē*).

He was likewise at a loss for how to respond. This truly caused Master Chén to feel deep regret; he wished to augment the original collection with further materials and have it reprinted, seeking my advice.
I immediately encouraged him. After several months, the Master commissioned me to collate and edit the *Guǎngjí* (Extended Collection), yet upon seeing that it contained no meaning...
All dharmas are gathered and nothing is left unprepared; yet within their sequential order, there exists a profound logic.

Beginning with the origins of the four-part *śīla* (precepts) for returning to the refuges, and concluding with the ultimate destination of the heavy and light offenses of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, this work briefly demonstrates the ritual procedures for receiving the three refuges and the five precepts therein.
It introduces the ultimate truth through the *Sūtra on the Merits of Renunciation and Detachment*, and the *Sūtra on Protecting the Body*, as well as the *Sūtra on the Path of Ten Wholesome Actions*.
The *Sūtra on the Precepts for Eliminating Calamities* uses both protection and encouragement to clarify their benefits.

The *Sūtra on the Characteristics of the Five Precepts* provides a detailed explanation of the characteristics of correctly and erroneously observing the five precepts. The *Eightfold Restraint and Fasting Precepts* reiterate the rituals for honoring the proper time and receiving empowerment.

These aforementioned precepts, rooted in the Vinaya discipline, appear to be comprehensive. Next, one enters the sublime precepts of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva, such as those in the *Cittabhūmi-parivarta Sūtra*.
The *Anātma-artha-sūtra* first establishes the bodhicitta precepts as the essence of the precepts (*śīla*).

The *Śīla-grahaṇa-varga* and the *Ācāra-sūtra* subsequently demonstrate the various characteristics of the precepts through their specific articles. Following the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, the ritual for repentance (*pāpadeśanā-vidhi*) is appended;

this is because sentient beings of the Dharma-ending age have deep obstructions and shallow wisdom, making it difficult to maintain and easy to transgress the precepts. Thus, this one method was established to enable them [to succeed].
That which was deficient is made whole again; that which was lost is recovered. It is hoped that those who have been bitter in their abandonment may find a path toward self-renewal;
such a collection is indeed indispensable. As for this compilation, it consists entirely of the golden rules and jade statutes of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
Mr. Chen has not added a single word of his own, nor would I dare to append even a single phrase of my own. It is only in the matter of its compilation and selection...
Following the sequence of its arrangement, I shall here set forth the subtle intentions of the Master for public revelation.

From this day forward, let those who receive the lay precepts each be provided with a copy to study at their leisure; likewise, our monastic disciples should also keep it at hand to prepare for inquiries and debates.

Truly, this may be called a resource for all seven classes of followers and a universal benefit for those of the three faculties. Therefore, I have gladly commissioned it for printing, and have further added...
Its title is "Extensive Collection.

It was respectfully prefaced on the anniversary of Amitābha’s birth, during the second month of winter in the fourth year of the Daoguang era (the Jiashen year), by the bhikṣu Yirun Yuanhong of Zhenji Temple.

*The Four-Part Vinaya Piṭaka* (Excerpted from the Tripitaka, Ji-zi Case, Volumes 31–32; Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of the Yao Qin Dynasty together with Zhu Fonian). Chen’s Additions.
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. In that kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a son of noble family named Yaśoda.
His parents had only this one son; they cherished and watched over him, never letting him out of their sight.
His parents provided him with palaces for the three seasons—spring, summer, and winter—so that their son might constantly play within them and enjoy the pleasures of the five senses. At that time...
"O youth, having indulged excessively in the pleasures of the five senses, you became utterly exhausted and fell asleep. When you awoke from sleep, you beheld the first palace.
You saw the various female musicians with their musical instruments scattered and strewn about in disorder;

they lay propped against one another like pillows, their hair disheveled, snoring as they lay on their backs, grinding their teeth and muttering in their sleep. Having seen this, you were struck with terror, and the hairs on your body stood on end."
The youth immediately conceived a sense of weary detachment and had no desire to join the assembly. "This is suffering indeed! What is there to crave?
he thought, and he abandoned the palace where he resided and proceeded to the middle palace. Upon arriving there, he observed that the halls and the female attendants were no different from before.
His terror doubled, and the hairs on his body stood on end. He immediately conceived a sense of weary detachment and had no desire to meet with them, thinking, "This is suffering!
What is there to crave? He then departed and went to the third hall. What he saw there was also as described above;
his terror doubled, the hairs on his body stood on end, and he conceived a heart of weary detachment, having no desire to meet with them, just as before. He then returned and went out.
The Prince went to the gate of the city of Śikhā. At that time, the deity guarding the gate of Śikhā saw the youth approaching from afar;
having seen him, he thought to himself: "This youth comes because he surely wishes to see the Tathāgata, and by no other path. I shall open the gate so that he may pass."
He immediately opened the gate for him. Once the youth had exited the city gate of Śiśumāragiri, he went to the banks of the Bārāṇasī River.
Having arrived, he took off his golden sandals on the riverbank and crossed the Bārāṇasī River. He then proceeded to the Deer Park of the Seers (Ṛṣipatana).
At that time, the World-Honored One was walking back and forth in the open air; seeing the youth coming from afar, he spread out a seat and sat down. This is the constant custom of all Buddhas.
A halo of light shone everywhere. The youth Yaśas saw the Tathāgata from afar; his countenance was upright and serene, and he felt a heart full of joy.
He approached the World-Honored One, and having arrived, he said: "I am now in distress and have no one to turn to for refuge; I pray that you will save me.
The Buddha told the youth: "Come! This place is unconditioned; this place is free from distress; this place is peaceful and secure. Desiring—
"Those who seek eternal tranquility and the unconditioned desire the extinction of craving—the nirvana of total cessation.
At that time, the youth Yaśas, having paid homage to the World-Honored One, sat to one side. The World-Honored One gradually preached the Dharma to him, exhorting him to give rise to a heart of joy.
The Dharma he taught consisted of the teachings on generosity, ethical discipline, and rebirth in heaven; he censured the impurity of sensual desires and praised [the virtues of renunciation].
"Renunciation is bliss. At that very seat, all his defilements were exhausted, and he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.

He saw the Dharma, grasped the Dharma, and became established in the Dharma; he realized the fruit for himself. He then addressed the Buddha, saying, "I wish to practice the pure holy life under the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said, "Come, Bhikṣu! In my Dharma, you shall find great joy and practice the holy life until its end."
At that time, Yaśoda received full ordination. When the first palace chamber was completely awakened by its attendants and female musicians, they searched for Yaśoda but did not see him;
they went to the middle palace to search for him, but did not see him there either.
He went again to the third palace chamber to search for him, but once more he did not see him.
Then the palace ladies and courtesans went to his mother and said, "Madam, we do not know where Yaśodharā is now.
At that, the mother immediately hurried to her husband's place and asked, "Do you know? I do not know where my son is now. At that time, the father was...
In the courtyard before that palace, he bathed and combed his hair; then, quickly inspecting his locks, he commanded those about him, saying:
"Block all the side streets in the city of Vārāṇasī. [Search] from the city gate of Mukhavisoka until you reach the banks of the Varuṇā River.
There he saw his son’s golden sandals by the river's edge and thought to himself: "My son must have crossed the river. He then followed the tracks across the river.
He went to the Deer Park of the Rishis. At that time, the Tathāgata saw Yaśodharā’s father approaching from afar;
he immediately employed his supernormal power so that Yaśodharā’s father could see the Buddha but not see his son. Upon reaching the Buddha’s presence, he addressed him, saying, "Great Śramaṇa!"
“Have you seen my son, Yaśoda? The Buddha said, “Sit for a moment; perhaps you shall see your son.
Yaśoda’s father thought to himself, “This Great Śramaṇa is truly marvelous and extraordinary, for he even offers such consolation.”
Then Yaśoda’s father, having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side. The World-Honored One gradually preached the Dharma to him, causing his heart to give rise to joy.
He censured the impurity of desire and praised the renunciation of it as bliss. Thereupon, while still on his seat, all defilements were exhausted and he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, and mastered the Dharma, he personally verified his attainment of the fruit of realization.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying: "I now take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, and I take refuge in the Saṃgha.
I pray only that the World-Honored One will grant me the status of an upāsaka. From this day forth, for as long as life lasts, I shall not kill living beings, and so on, up to not drinking alcohol.

This constitutes the original threefold refuge of an upāsaka (since the prohibitions against killing and drinking alcohol are already present here, the five precepts must likewise be understood to originate from this). Is it not so?
With Yaśas’s father as the leader, the World-Honored One then preached the Dharma for Yaśas’s father.

At that time, Yaśas attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), his mind was liberated, and he attained the liberation of unimpeded knowledge (*anāvaraṇajñāna-vimukti*). At that moment, there were seven arhats in the world:
six disciples (at that time, Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the other five bhikṣus had already been delivered, making six with Yaśas) and the Buddha as the seventh. Then, the World-Honored One...
Having mastered the bases of psychic power, he caused Yaśoda’s father to see his son sitting not far from the Buddha.
He went directly to Yaśoda and said to him, "Your mother is behind you; she lost sight of you and does not know where you are. She is overcome with such grief that she intends to take her own life.
You should go to visit her and prevent her from harming herself. At that time, Yaśoda gazed upon the countenance of the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One addressed Yaśoda’s father, saying: "How is it, noble son? By training in knowledge and training in the path, all defilements are exhausted and the pure Dharma-eye is attained.
Having made such an observation, the mind with outflows is liberated from attachment. How is this so, householder?"
“Have you already abandoned sensual desire? Could you ever return to practicing it again? He replied, “No, sir.
“In this way, Yaśas, son of good family, having trained in knowledge and trained in the path, with all defilements exhausted, has attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Having made such an observation, his mind was liberated from the outflows; he will never again practice sensual desire as he did when he was formerly a layman. Now...
“Yaśaska, son of good family, has well attained great benefit. Having studied wisdom and studied the Path, his mind is liberated from outflows;

all defilements are exhausted, and he has attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. Having performed this contemplation, his mind is liberated from outflows. We pray only that the World-Honored One [will grant us further instruction].”
"Now accept my invitation, as well as that of Yaśoda and his attendant bhikṣu. At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

However, Yaśoda was unwilling to accept separate invitations, saying, "The Buddha has not yet permitted me to accept separate invitations. The Buddha said, "From this day forward, I permit you to accept separate invitations.
There are two kinds of invitations: the sequential invitation for the Saṃgha and the separate invitation. At that time, Yaśoda...
Knowing that the Tathāgata had accepted his invitation by remaining silent, Śuklodana rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and departed.
He spoke to Yaśodharā and her former co-wife, saying: "Do you know now? Yaśodhara is practicing the holy life (brahmacarya) under the Great Śramaṇa.
Today I have invited the Great Śramaṇa, and Yaśodharā shall follow as his attendant."

“You know the time has come; you may now prepare what is required. Yaśodharā’s mother and her foster-mother immediately prepared various kinds of food and drink as needed, and having done so, went to inform him that the time had arrived. Then, when it was time, the World-Honored One put on his robes and took his bowl.
Yaśodhara attended him as he entered, and the two of them went to his father’s house. Upon arrival, they took their seats.
Then Yaśodharā’s mother and her former co-wife offered various kinds of food and drink required by the World-Honored One.

When he had finished eating and set aside his bowl, they took another small seat and sat before the Tathāgata. At that time, the World-Honored One gradually taught them the subtle and wondrous Dharma, exhorting them to give rise to a heart of joy.
Thereupon, while still on their seats, all defilements were exhausted and they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.

Having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, and realized the various dharmas, she immediately addressed the Buddha, saying: "From this day forward, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Please accept me as a laywoman (upāsikā). From this day forward, for as long as life lasts, I shall refrain from taking life, and so on, up to refraining from drinking alcohol.
This was the first laywoman to receive the three refuges; [it was] Yaśodharā’s mother, together with her former...
With the two [wives] at their head, the World-Honored One, having preached the Dharma to Yaśodharā’s mother and her two former wives, rose from his seat and departed.
*The Vinaya Piṭaka of the Dharmaguptakas: An Abridged Extract* (End).
The Method for Receiving the Three Refuges and Five Precepts of an Upāsaka, Compiled and Explained by the Ancient Wu Bhikṣu Zhixu. Part One:
The Method for Receiving the Three Refuges (This should originally be recited by oneself; however, if one is unable, the preceptor should instruct them).

I, [Name], for as long as life lasts, take refuge in the Buddha; I take refuge in the Dharma; I take refuge in the Saṃgha (recite three times). I, [Name], for as long as life lasts, have completed taking refuge in the Buddha;
have completed taking refuge in the Dharma; have completed taking refuge in the Saṃgha (recite three times).
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: One takes the Three Jewels as one’s refuge because one desires them to provide protection and prevent oneself from being oppressed or violated.

To take refuge in the Buddha is to take refuge in the Dharma-body, which refers to the qualities of omniscience and the merits of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), accomplished through the five factors.
To take refuge in the Dharma is to take refuge in the ultimate limit of self and others; that is, the cessation of desire and the state of desirelessness, [and] extinction (*nirodha*).

One takes refuge in Nirvana as the Truth. One who takes refuge in the Sangha takes refuge in the Sangha of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*), namely the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) consisting of the virtues of the Śrāvakas, both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

(Directing the mind toward the True Teaching and overturning the return to the heterodox, there is a concluding statement: "From this day forward, I shall call the Buddha my teacher and shall no longer take refuge in celestial demons or external paths. This is the primary gateway for turning away from the heterodox and returning to the orthodox;

however, as long as one has not yet received and practiced the precepts, such a person is called a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who possesses only the three refuges. Nevertheless, once one has taken refuge in the Triple Gem, one must necessarily sever evil and cultivate good.)

"How could one permit lust, killing, theft, or falsehood, merely following old habits? According to this, it refers to turning back from former heterodoxy to return to the correct path; thus, it is called the "Three Refuges for Turning Back Heterodoxy.
Although there is no formal ritual for its reception in the Vinaya, it is fully set forth in various treatises, which we shall now follow.
Furthermore, those such as dragons, animals, ghosts, and spirits who cannot receive the five precepts may only receive the Three Refuges and the Eightfold Precepts of the Fast (Upavāsa).

Day and night. Now, these three refuges are the very source of all precepts. Upon the completion of the recitation of the three refuges, one immediately attains the unconditioned (avijñapti) essence of the five precepts, the eight precepts, and the ten precepts.

Even the bhikṣu and bodhisattva codes of discipline arise as unconditioned through taking the Three Jewels as their object; therefore, although they are introductory gates, they in fact encompass profound and esoteric meanings.

This encompasses the four teachings and subsumes the six stages of realization; it must be briefly explained. Regarding the "four teachings," they are the *śrāvaka* (Tripitaka), *pratyekabuddha* (Shared), *bodhisattva* (Distinct), and *tathāgata* (Perfect) teachings.

Each of these four teachings has its own discourse on the Three Refuges. First, regarding the *śrāvaka* teaching: [it involves] destroying prior false attachments and taking refuge in the mind within the Triple Gem—this is the Three Refuges of the *śrāvaka* teaching.
When the Buddha was in the world, he attained the Way under the Bodhi tree and became the Buddha-Gem; his preaching of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths constitutes the Dharma-Gem.

The Jewels: The five bhikṣus and others who have attained deliverance constitute the Saṅgha Jewel. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, images cast in metal or molded from clay, as well as those rendered on paper and silk with ink and colors, constitute the Buddha Jewel.
The yellow scrolls and red tablets [of the scriptures] constitute the Dharma Jewel. Those who shave their hair and dye their robes constitute the Saṅgha Jewel.
By means of images such as those of gold and clay, it represents the fivefold qualities of omniscience; by means of yellow scrolls and red tablets, it elucidates the truth of cessation and nirvāṇa;
and by means of the tonsured and dyed-robed followers, it can represent the realization of the qualities of the śrāvakas.

That which can express, that which can be cultivated, and that which is named "the Three Jewels of Sustenance" (saṃvṛti-ratnatraya). That which is signified, that which is expressed, and that which is realized, are named "the Three Jewels of Ultimate Meaning" (paramārtha-ratnatraya).
Since phenomena are not identical to principle, one must take refuge in both the two types of Three Jewels: phenomena and principle.
May all be brought under protection so that they are not oppressed or invaded by heterodox outsiders. Second, regarding the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao):

[one] realizes that the heterodox are not real and embodies the Three Jewels—this is the Three Refuges of the Shared Teaching. All physical images are identical to true emptiness; all sutras and written words are none other than liberation;
and all monastics are those in training and those beyond training, for they are illusory transformations without arising, being non-dual in nature.
To take refuge in the practice is to take refuge in the principle; since principle and practice are non-dual, one must not transgress or violate them.

Third, the Separate Teaching (consists of) overturning and destroying immeasurable false delusions and taking refuge in the immeasurable Triple Gem—this is the Three Refuges of the Separate Teaching. [It concerns] the Lotus Flower-Pedestal Treasury and the Perfectly Complete Reward Body.
The Buddha is named the Jewel of the Buddha. The twelve divisions of the scriptures, which elucidate the principle of the three truths, are named the Jewel of the Dharma.

The three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood, who benefit themselves and others, constitute the Jewel of the Sangha. By taking refuge in these Three Jewels, one is able to overturn and destroy the three delusions of views and thoughts, dust-like afflictions, and ignorance.
Thus, one will not be oppressed by the eight māras and eight inversions, whether within or beyond the realms. [The fourfold perfection...]

The teaching (observing delusive errors as the wondrous realm and awakening to the fact that the Three Jewels are fundamentally one essence—this is the Three Refuges of the Perfect Teaching) concerns the presently manifest single thought-moment of the mind capable of awakening.
That which is named the Buddha Jewel; that which is the object awakened to in the present single thought-moment is named the Dharma Jewel;
and the fact that mind and object are fundamentally non-dual is named the Sangha Jewel. One who ultimately awakens to these Three Jewels within this single thought-moment is called a Buddha.
The various means of explaining these Three Jewels within this single thought-moment are called the Dharma. To uphold the Dharma taught by the Buddha and investigate this single thought-moment—

The Three Jewels are called the Sangha. Principle completely constitutes phenomena, and phenomena are identical to principle. To mention one is to mention all three; to speak of the three is to speak of the one.

By taking refuge in this single essence of the Three Jewels of Phenomena and Principle, one is able to perfectly overturn the three delusions and perfectly encompass the demonic inversions of both the mundane and supramundane realms to perform Buddha-work, remaining unassailed by them. This is a brief explanation of the Four Teachings.

[The preceding section] concludes. Regarding the "six identities" (*liù jí*): although the principle of the six identities applies to all four teachings (*sì jiào*), the first three are provisional (*quán*) and shall be set aside for now.

Here, we consider only the Perfect Teaching (*yuán*). This means that the three—afflictions (*huò*), karma (*yè*), and suffering (*kǔ*)—of all sentient beings, in their essence, are the inconceivable secret treasury of the three virtues (*sān dé mì zàng*).
Suffering is itself the Dharma-body (*fǎ shēn*); the five aggregates (*wǔ yīn*), both physical and mental, are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha (*rúlái zàng*), the wondrous [store].

The nature of *tathatā* (suchness) is like ice being water; thus, afflictions are *prajñā* (wisdom). Views, thoughts, and ignorance originally possess no characteristics of internal, external, or intermediate.
This is like fatigue being the eye itself. Karma is *vimukti* (liberation); the fetters of outflows and attachments originally possess neither a binder nor that which is bound.
This is like a fist being the hand itself. The *dharmakāya* is the treasure of the Dharma; [it is] *prajñā*.

This is the Buddha Jewel; liberation is the Sangha Jewel. All sentient beings, down to the most minute insects, are without exception possessed of the three—delusion, karma, and suffering—and thus they are without exception possessed of the virtuous characteristics of the Three Jewels. It is only because they are separated by delusion that they do not recognize them in their daily lives.

Even though they do not yet know this, they can never transcend this principle. Therefore, this is the "principle-as-the-three-refuges" (the fact that all sentient beings fully possess the essence-nature of the Three Jewels;

though lost in delusion and unaware of it, they are nonetheless inseparable from it). If, upon hearing its name, one gives rise to understanding and knows that these three virtues of the stage of fruition are entirely realized within the rational essence of the three obstructions of sentient beings—which is truly devoid of birth or extinction, defilement or purity, increase or decrease—then...

This refers to the "Three Refuges by Name" (where one first hears the wondrous principle and resolves to settle the mind therein). With this perfect understanding, one cultivates the perfect contemplation.
When the five stages of dwelling are completely subdued, this constitutes the *observational* (or *contemplative*) Three Refuges (*nien-nian ti-hui san-te mi-tsang*;

the observational Three Refuges). Through this perfect contemplation, the six sense faculties are purified; this constitutes the *resemblance* Three Refuges (*fa-hsing li hsien, liu ken ch'ing-ching*; the resemblance Three Refuges).

Through this perfect contemplation, the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*) is manifested and the three causes are revealed; this constitutes the *partial realization* Three Refuges (*po wu-ming, hsien san-te*).

This is the partial realization of the Three Refuges. Through this perfect contemplation, one perfects the three virtues so that they accord with the fundamental nature of reality, being neither deficient nor redundant;

this constitutes the ultimate Three Refuges. Thus, when Bodhi is perfected and the self-nature of dharmas is awakened, the beginning and the end are non-dual, and wisdom and principle are as one. This is the ultimate Three Refuges. Therefore, there is no depth or shallowness in the Dharma.

"Depth and shallowness depend on the person; do not speak of a thousand li while remaining at the first step (as all subsequent chapters on the precepts contain this same meaning). Since the Three Refuges already encompass the four teachings and six stages of realization,"
One should know that this applies without exception to the five precepts, the eight precepts, and so forth; one may reflect upon this accordingly. Question:
Regarding the method of the Three Refuges alone (which is termed "the mere Three Refuges" when one has not yet received the precepts), is it permissible to take only one or two of the refuges?
Furthermore, does this dharma encompass all six realms of existence, or is it restricted only to human beings? Within the category of human beings, are there also those who should not receive it?
"No. If one commits an offense after having received [the precepts], how does one repent? Answer:

When the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he preached the Dharma for the Dragon King and two merchants, instructing them to take refuge in the Bhikṣu Saṃgha until the end of the future. Thus, one must recite the Three Refuges;
if one now stops at taking refuge in only one or two, it is not called 'taking refuge. Regarding the method of the Three Refuges, only the intense suffering of hell [is such that one cannot...]"
If one receives [the precepts] and knows how to take refuge, one shall immediately be freed from suffering. Regarding the other five destinies, there are generally no prohibitions or obstacles.

However, if one further takes refuge in malevolent spirits, demons, or heterodox teachers, this is termed "losing the three refuges. Yet, if one is subsequently able to turn away from such heterodoxy, it is likewise permitted.

This is not like receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), where re-entering a non-Buddhist path constitutes a grave offense. Question: If one receives only the Three Refuges, does one obtain the unmanifest precept (*avijñapti-śīla*)?
Furthermore, if one commits killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, or lying, would this constitute a breach of the precepts? Answer:

For those who receive the five, eight, or ten precepts, at the moment the Three Refuges are recited, they are already declared to be *upāsakas* for as long as life lasts, or for a single day and night. Thus, [the precepts are obtained].
Those who become lay followers (*upāsaka*) through pure conduct at night, or those who follow the Tathāgata in going forth from home and so forth, give rise to non-informative action (*avijñapti*).

Now, as for those who receive only the three refuges, they have originally not received the precepts; thus, there is nothing of their own that could be produced. Since they have not yet produced the precepts, there is likewise no offense of breaking the precepts.
Nevertheless, there are still worldly natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).

Next is the ritual for receiving the five precepts (*pañca-śīla*). According to the Vinaya, those who receive the five precepts all declare them themselves before a teacher; they do not receive them from the teacher, nor is there any inquiry regarding obstructing or prohibitory conditions (*antarāyika-dharma*).

The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* represents one specific path within the Mahāyāna; although Master Xuánzàng cited it, it seems inappropriate to incorporate it here. This is because heavy obstacles (*guru-antarāya*) and light prohibitions (*laghu-antarāya*) apply only to the monastic precepts, which must be inquired about because the essence of the Sangha Jewel is most venerable and thus requires greater solemnity.

If one were to inquire about these matters at the outset of the five precepts, why would one need to inquire again when receiving full ordination? Even if one wished to inquire, it would suffice to ask only about the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*), as well as whether one has personally broken the pure precepts or caused others to break their pure precepts—these seven matters are sufficient. As for the "one part," however...

Up to the point of full attainment, one may naturally accept and uphold [the precepts] according to one's own capacity. As for providing guidance at the moment, the priority lies in adapting to the individual's circumstances (*pratyaya*). The Dharma is not fixed; one should not formulate set phrases in advance that cause the teacher to merely recite the text while the listener fails to understand the meaning.

One precept constitutes a "fraction" (*aṃśa*); two precepts constitute a "small fraction" (*parīttāṃśa*); three precepts constitute a "half-fraction" (*ardhāṃśa*); four precepts constitute a "majority fraction" (*bahvaṃśa*); and five precepts constitute a "full fraction" (*pūrṇāṃśa*). One should refer to them according to what has been received; they must not be confused or conflated. The *Śīla-sūtra* states:
"If one has received the Three Refuges and upheld two precepts, yet breaks one precept, this is called 'no fraction' (*anaṃśa*)."
I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha. For as long as life lasts, I am a *pūrṇa-bhāga* upāsaka.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is my World-Honored One. (Recite this three times.)
I, [Name], have taken refuge in the Buddha; I have taken refuge in the Dharma; I have taken refuge in the Saṃgha. For as long as life lasts, I am a full-fledged upāsaka.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is my World-Honored One. (Recite this three times.)
If a virtuous woman, she is then called an upāsikā.
Just as all Buddhas refrain from taking life for the duration of their lives, so too shall I, [name], refrain from taking life for the duration of my life.
Just as all Buddhas refrain from stealing for the duration of their lives, so shall I, [name], also refrain from stealing for the duration of my life.
Just as all Buddhas refrain from sexual misconduct for the duration of their lives, so shall I, [name], also refrain from sexual misconduct for the duration of my life.
Just as all Buddhas refrain from false speech for the duration of their lives, so shall I, [name], also refrain from false speech for the duration of my life.
Just as all Buddhas refrain from drinking intoxicants for the duration of their lives, so shall I, [name], also refrain from drinking intoxicants for the duration of my life.
According to how many precepts one has received, one should speak of that many precepts; they must not be conflated or confused.

By means of the merit of receiving these precepts, one should dedicate it toward unexcelled bodhi, universally repaying the four debts of gratitude and providing equal sustenance for all beings within the three realms of existence.
May all beings together be born in the Pure Land.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha* (Sapoduo lun) states: "Upāsaka" means, in the language of Qin, "to leave evil and cultivate good," and is also called "one who draws near."
It is further stated: "Once one has completed the three refuges, one has already obtained the five precepts.

The reason for reciting the names of the five precepts is to ensure that the person before one recognizes the names of those precepts. It is also stated: "If one violates a grave precept, there is no further progress.

If one subsequently renounces the precepts and receives them again later, one will not obtain the precepts once more. (If they have not been violated, they may be renounced; once violated, there is nothing to renounce. If one renounces them [before violation], it is permissible...)"

It can be received again; however, once it is broken, it cannot be received again. This is why it is called a "limiting offense" (*antāpatti*). One is forever cast outside the ocean of the Buddha’s Dharma, which is why it is termed a "limiting offense.

Since one no longer possesses the *vinaya* precepts, one cannot obtain the dhyāna precepts or the untainted (*anāsrava*) precepts at all. Thus, should not those who receive the precepts protect and uphold the fundamental grave offenses with a profound mind? The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states:

"As for the prohibitive precepts, they are obtained in relation to everything that may be killed and everything that may not be killed—among all things that may be killed and all things that may not be killed."
It is immeasurable and boundless. The karmic fruit of the precepts is likewise immeasurable and boundless.
If anyone were to say that one can transcend birth and death apart from the five precepts, such a thing is impossible.
This path to Bodhi has the precepts as its primary foundation; they are called the "first ground. Such precepts are also called the "first ground," and are also called...
It is called the Ground of Guidance; it is also called the Level Ground, the Equal Ground, the Ground of Loving-kindness, and the Ground of Compassion.
It is also called the Footprint of the Buddha, the Root of All Meritorious Qualities, and the Field of Merit. For these reasons:
The wise should accept and uphold it without disparaging. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Precepts are the ladder for all wholesome dharmas; they are also the root of all wholesome dharmas.
Just as the earth is the basis from which all trees grow, these roots of goodness are the foremost leaders, like a caravan leader who guides others."
O merchant, the precepts are the supreme banner of all wholesome dharmas, like the victory banner erected by Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
The precepts can forever sever all evil karma and the three evil realms; they can heal the maladies of evil, just like a medicinal tree.
Precepts are the provisions for the perilous path of birth and death. Precepts are the armor and weapons for crushing the bandits of the fetters.
Precepts are the efficacious incantation for extinguishing the venomous snakes of the fetters. Precepts are the bridge for crossing over the conduct of evil karma.
Question: The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha* states that if one violates a heavy precept, there is no further spiritual progress.

However, suppose a layperson who has already received the five precepts, or the eightfold *upavāsa* fast for one day and night, experiences the manifestation of afflictions and commits an irredeemable offense (*anatyaya*).
If they later seek to leave the household life, sincerely repent, and are permitted to have their hair shaved and receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), would this be allowed?
Answer: According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*, this is the universal standard and protocol. All who receive the precepts must maintain them with single-minded diligence.
Should one commit a transgression, one immediately falls from the state of purity; how then could there be further spiritual progress?
As for repentance, there is no offense that cannot be extinguished; this is the profound, transcendent compassion of all Buddhas, which must be practiced in accordance with the sūtras and the Dharma.
One must practice the Way with the utmost sincerity before even a single thread of connection can be established; it must not be regarded as a trivial matter.
These Three Refuges and Five Precepts are recorded here in brief according to what the recipient says for themselves.

If received in the presence of a teacher, there are instances at Mount Huashan in Jinling and at Zhaokong Temple in Hangzhou where the Three Refuges are conferred upon the two groups of lay followers.
The *Zhengfan* (Model for Correct Practice) and the *Wujie Zhengfan* (Model for the Five Precepts) have been in circulation for a long time; they shall not be recorded here.
Furthermore, according to the *Zhengfan*, if one receives [the precepts] from an elder bhikṣu, one should follow the model in its entirety.
However, if it is a bhikṣu who has not yet been appointed as abbot, or one practicing with two or three companions, or one dwelling alone, or a bhikṣuṇī, or a śikṣamāṇā—[the procedure differs].

For śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs, should there happen to be faithful laypeople who resolve to receive the Three Refuges or seek to receive the Five Precepts, it is sufficient simply to provide guidance and administer the Refuges and Precepts along with the making of vows;
the remaining formalities need not be fully employed. Alternatively, one may follow this brief record. Once the Three Refuges and Five [Precepts]...
Regarding the precepts: one should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness, take pity upon sentient beings, and cultivate weariness toward the world’s lack of true joy;

therefore, one should advance them with the *Sūtra on the Merit of the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, Loving-Kindness, and Weariness*. (From the *Lóngzàng*, Section Shàn, Volume 10). Translated by Cén Zēng during the Chen Dynasty.
The translator’s name is lost; it is now appended to the Record of the Eastern Jin.
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha was teaching for the sake of the elder Anāthapiṇḍada that, in the distant past, there was a brahmin named Vīramatī who possessed abundant wealth and many treasures.
When practicing generosity, he used eighty-four thousand golden bowls filled with crushed silver;
eighty-four thousand silver bowls filled with crushed gold; furthermore, eighty-four thousand golden and silver bathing jars;
and eighty-four thousand oxen, all with horns covered in gold and silver; as well as eighty-four thousand noble women, fully adorned with ornaments.
Furthermore, he gave eighty-four thousand bedding sets, each covered with various colorful fabrics; eighty-four thousand garments;
eighty-four thousand elephants and horses, all equipped with saddles and bridles of gold and silver; and eighty-four thousand houses as alms.
Moreover, at the four city gates, he bestowed gifts upon those who came, granting them everything according to their desires.
Furthermore, suppose one were to give a single dwelling to the *caitya* Sangha; the merit of such a gift as described above would not equal that of receiving the three refuges.
Why is this so? Because one who receives the three refuges bestows fearlessness upon all sentient beings; therefore, they take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
The merit thereof is immeasurable. The merit of the aforementioned acts of giving, as well as that of receiving the Three Refuges, does not equal the merit of receiving the Five Precepts.

For one who receives the Five Precepts, their merit is complete and perfect; thus, its merit is superior. The merit of the aforementioned acts of giving, as well as that of receiving the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, does not equal the merit of contemplating all sentient beings with compassion for even the duration of a finger-snap. As above...

The merit of practicing generosity, as well as receiving the three refuges and the five precepts and cherishing sentient beings with loving-kindness, is not equal to the merit of giving rise to the perception that all worlds are unlovely.
Why is this so? Because the merit of giving rise to the perception that all worlds are unlovely [is far superior].
It can cause the practitioner to extinguish the suffering of birth and death and ultimately achieve the Buddha-way; therefore, its merit is most supreme.
At that time, the elder, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Merit of the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, Compassion, and Renunciation (End) (Note:
According to the Guanding section, the names of the deities who protect the precepts are themselves mantras; this is included within the Vinaya Piṭaka).
The Sūtra of the Consecration, the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, and the Protective Dhāraṇī to be Worn (Extracted from the *Longzang*, Volume Gong, Section on Great Consecration Divine Dhāraṇīs).
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śrīmitra of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty.
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with twelve hundred [monks].
One hundred and fifty bhikṣus, ten thousand bodhisattvas, and the eight classes of devas and nāgas all came to the assembly.

With single-minded devotion, they joined their palms and listened to the Dharma. At that time, a deer-headed brahmin from a heterodox path came to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself in greeting, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I have long heard of Gautama, whose fame has spread far and wide. Now I wish to renounce..."
Setting aside other teachings, he received the three refuges along with the dharma of the five precepts. The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, brahmin!
Since you are able to abandon other paths and take refuge in me, you should personally repent for the sins of birth and death;
its merit shall be immeasurable and beyond calculation. The brahmin replied, "Yes," and accepted the instruction. He immediately purified his body, speech, and mind, and further formed this thought:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will bestow upon me the Dharma-precepts, which I shall practice throughout my life, never daring to violate or neglect them.
The Buddha said, “This is the precept-dharma taught by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and by all Buddhas of the three periods of time.

The Buddha said, “Brahmin, listen attentively and receive it well; hold it in your mind and keep it in mind. He further said, “Brahmin, for as long as you live, take refuge in the Buddhas, the Unsurpassed Ones.”

“Venerable One, for as long as life lasts, I take refuge in the Dharma, the Honored One who is free from desire. For as long as life lasts, I take refuge in the Saṅgha, the Honored One among the assembly.
The Buddha said, “Brahmin, having completed these three refuges, you are a true disciple; you shall not be disturbed by evil or wickedness.
The Buddha told the Brahmin, “Since you have been able to receive the three refuges with a single mind, I shall [act] for you and...”
To the people of the ten directions, [the Buddha] commanded Śakra, Lord of Devas, to dispatch various spirits and deities to protect those men and women who have received the Three Refuges.
A brahmin then asked the Buddha, "Who are these? I wish to hear about them, so that they may instruct and transform all those in the ten directions who have received the Refuges.
The Buddha said, "Such are the consecrated benevolent deities; I shall now explain this briefly for you."
There are thirty-six deities.
A deity dispatched from the fourth heaven is named Mili-tou-bu-luo-po (translated as "Excellent Radiance"); he presides over illnesses.
A deity dispatched from the fourth heaven is named Mili-tou-bo-he-sa (translated as "Excellent Clarity"); he presides over headaches.
The gods from the fourth heaven dispatched a deity named Mṛḍupāla (translated here as "Good Power"), who presides over cold and heat.
The gods from the fourth heaven dispatched a deity named Mṛḍukāntāra (translated here as "Good Moon"), who presides over abdominal distension.
The gods from the fourth heaven dispatch a deity named Mṛḍudhāriśa (translated here as "Good Vision"), who presides over abscesses and swellings.
The gods from the fourth heaven dispatch a deity named Mṛḍudhāruha (translated here as "Good Offering"), who presides over insanity.
The Four Heavenly Kings dispatch a deity named Mṛḍu-kāyava-ti (which means "Good Renunciation"), who presides over ignorance.
The Four Heavenly Kings dispatch a deity named Mṛḍu-siddhi-ta (which means "Good Tranquility"), who presides over anger.
The Four Heavenly Kings dispatch a deity named Mṛḍu-bodhi (this means "Good Awakening"), who presides over lustful desires.
The Four Heavenly Kings dispatch a deity named Mṛḍu-deva (this means "Good Heaven"), who presides over malevolent spirits.
The Four Heavenly Kings dispatch a deity named Mṛḍuhāsati (translated here as "Good Abiding"), who presides over the wounded and the deceased.
The Four Heavenly Kings dispatch a deity named Mṛḍubhadra (translated here as "Good Fortune"), who presides over tombs and burial grounds.

The Four Heavenly Kings dispatched a deity named Mṛḍu-piśāca (translated here as "Skilled Artisan"), who presides over the four directions (the characters for his name are partially damaged and incomplete, but it is suspected to be "Skilled Artisan").
The gods dispatched from the fourth heaven are named Mṛḍhuka-leśa (which means "Good Sovereign"); they preside over enemies.
The gods dispatched from the fourth heaven are named Mṛḍhuka-rāja-cha (which means "Good Master"); they preside over theft.
The gods of the fourth heaven dispatch a deity named Mṛḍu-sugandha (translated here as "Good Fragrance"), who presides over creditors.
The gods of the fourth heaven also dispatch a deity named Mṛḍu-dānapa (translated here as "Good Giver"), who presides over thieves.
The gods dispatched from the fourth heaven are named Mṛdūcitta (translated here as "Good Intention"), who preside over pestilence and toxins.
The gods dispatched from the fourth heaven are named Mṛdūravaṇa (translated here as "Good Auspiciousness"), who preside over the five types of epidemics.
The deity dispatched from the fourth heaven is named Mṛḍuparvata (translated here as "Good Mountain"); he presides over the *veśī* spirits.
The deity dispatched from the fourth heaven is named Mṛḍusamada (translated here as "Good Tamer"); he presides over the *tulana* spirits.
The Four Heavenly Kings dispatch a deity named Mṛḍu-liditi (meaning "Well-Equipped"), who presides over the restoration of what has been poured out.
The Four Heavenly Kings dispatch a deity named Mṛḍu-pārita (meaning "Well-Honored"), who presides over mutual invitation.
The Four Heavenly Kings dispatch a deity named Mṛḍu-pāriṇa (which means "Well-Purified"), who presides over malevolent factions.
The Four Heavenly Kings dispatch a deity named Mṛḍu-gāndhika (which means "Good Class"), who presides over sorcery and poisons.
The gods sent from the fourth heaven are named Mṛḍhupilīṭa (translated here as "Good Bond"); they preside over terrors.
The gods sent from the fourth heaven are named Mṛḍhucittana (translated here as "Good Life"); they preside over calamities.
The gods of the fourth heaven dispatched a deity named Mṛḍhugālinma (translated here as "Well-Gone"), who presides over the production of milk.
The gods of the fourth heaven also dispatched a deity named Mṛḍhu-āryuga (translated here as "Good Vow"), who presides over local officials.
The gods of the Fourth Heaven dispatch a deity named Mṛḍuśarita (translated here as "Good Firmness"), who presides over speech.
The gods of the Fourth Heaven dispatch a deity named Mṛḍv-āgata (translated here as "Good Illumination"), who presides over sorrow and affliction.
The Heaven of the Four Great Kings dispatches a deity named Mṛḍu-Ahava (translated as "Good Birth"), who presides over illness.
The Heaven of the Four Great Kings dispatches a deity named Mṛḍu-Saṃkula (translated as "Good Arrival"), who presides over a hundred strange portents.
The gods of the fourth heaven dispatched a deity named Mṛḍhupāriṇa (which means "Good Treasury"), who presides over jealousy.
The gods of the fourth heaven also dispatched a deity named Mṛḍhughoṣaṇa (which means "Good Sound"), who presides over curses.
The Four Heavenly Kings dispatched a deity named Mili-tou-wei-da-lo (which means "Excellently Wondrous"), who presides over rites of suppression and exorcism.
The Buddha said to the Brahmin: "This is one of the thirty-six classes of divine kings.
These virtuous deities have ten thousand *koṭis* of *gaṇeśvaras* and *bhūtas*, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as their retinue. They secretly take turns in shifts to protect men and women."

"One who has received the Three Refuges should write down the names of the King of Spirits and carry them upon their person; whether walking, coming, going, or entering, they shall have nothing to fear.
They will ward off the wicked and evil, and eliminate all that is unwholesome. The Brahmin replied, "Yes, indeed; yes, indeed, O God among Gods.
The Brahmin further addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, having been granted the Dharma of the Three Refuges, the Heavenly Emperor has dispatched thirty benevolent spirits."
"The Six Great Kings protect and assist my person; having already received the compassionate salvation of the World-Honored One, I now prostrate once more and request to receive the Dharma-precepts.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, Brahmin! You should purify your body, speech, and mind, and with a sincere and earnest heart, reverently receive the Dharma-precepts.
The Buddha continued, "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions and three periods of time, the Most Honorable and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, all [attained their state] through the Three Refuges."
One obtains them through the five precepts. The Buddha said: "Brahmin, for as long as life lasts, do not kill living beings, nor teach others to kill.
Can you uphold this precept? If you can uphold it, there will be five divine kings who follow and protect your body, ensuring that malevolent spirits and evil ghosts find no opportunity to harm you.
Brahmin, for as long as life lasts, do not steal the wealth and treasures of others, nor teach others [to do so]..."
"Committing theft. Can you uphold this precept? If you can uphold it, five benevolent divine kings will follow and protect your person.
Brahmin, for as long as life lasts, do not engage in sexual misconduct. Can you uphold this precept? If you can uphold it, five divine kings will follow and protect your person;
none of the Māras shall find an opportunity against you. Brahmin, for as long as life lasts, do not speak falsely..."
He said: "As for frivolous speech, double-tongued speech, and inciting strife—can you maintain these precepts? If you can maintain them, five divine kings will follow and protect your person.

Ghosts, spirits, and rākṣasas will ultimately never harass those who are near. Even if one enters the home of a practitioner of sorcery, they shall be unable to cause harm.

[He] hid [it]. He did not harm others. The Buddha told the brahmin: "Long ago, in the great kingdom of Kālaṇa, there was a son of a brāhmaṇa named Dhāraṇī.

The holy Sangha guides and transforms all beings so that they may attain wealth, nobility, long life, and peace.
Furthermore, it enables them to transcend birth, old age, sickness, and death, receiving the Dharma without end. In both this life and future lives, they shall not fall into the three evil realms.
Holding these thoughts, the Elder abandoned other paths and resolved to revere the Triple Gem; he then went to the Buddha and prostrated himself, touching his head to the ground.

The man of the earth prostrated himself before the Buddha, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I was originally ignorant and lacked understanding.

"Universally saving all under heaven, I now wish to abandon other paths and take refuge in the Buddha.
I pray only that the World-Honored One will have compassion for us, allowing us to receive the Dharma-precepts and become lay devotees. The Buddha said, "You have deliberated well.

"Are you one who has escaped from all hardships? He, named Dhṛti, addressed the Buddha, saying: "Now, because that which I previously served was not true, I take refuge in the Buddha.

The Buddha said: "First, do not kill; second, do not steal; third, do not engage in sexual misconduct; fourth, do not engage in double-tongued speech, harsh speech, lying, or frivolous chatter;

The Buddha said to the elder, "If you can uphold these precepts of taking refuge, wherever you travel, there shall be nothing to fear.
Twenty-five deities of the precepts and thirty-six deities of the refuge will constantly follow and protect you; no evil spirits from without will dare to oppose you.

After the elder had received the precepts of taking refuge in the Buddha, the Buddha preached the Dharma for him. The elder rejoiced, attained faith and understanding, and prostrated before the Buddha.
He departed. Thereafter, the elder traveled to other countries. He saw people killing living beings and stealing others' property;
seeing women of beautiful appearance, he became greedily attached to them; seeing people's likes and dislikes, he would immediately engage in idle gossip;
seeing those who drank alcohol, he desired to follow after them. His mind was thus unsettled at all times. Then he thought to himself: "I regret having followed the Buddha."
Having received the dharma of the three refuges and the five precepts with solemn vows, he formed this thought: "I shall return the dharma of the three refuges and the five precepts to the Buddha.
He immediately went to where the Buddha was and addressed him, saying: "The dharma of the three refuges and the five precepts previously received imposes many prohibitions;
I am no longer able to act according to my original intentions. Now, reflecting upon myself, I wish to cease [the practice], yet I cannot serve the Buddha."
"Is this permissible? For what reason? The Buddha-dharma is revered; it is not something for ordinary beings to handle. Should you not return it to the Dharma and the precepts?
The Buddha remained silent and did not respond. Before his words had even ceased, a natural spirit spontaneously appeared from within his mouth.
There were spirits who struck the elder’s head with iron mallets; there were spirits who stripped away his garments;
there were spirits who used iron hooks to pull out his tongue from within his mouth; there was a ghost of a courtesan who probed and cut off his genitals with a knife;
and there were other spirits who poured molten copper into his mouth—[all occurring] before, behind, to the left, and to the right.
Various spirits and ghosts vied with one another to come and tear him apart, seizing his flesh and blood to devour it.
The elder, gripped by terror, trembled violently; he had nowhere to turn for refuge, and his face turned the color of ash. Furthermore, a spontaneous fire broke out, burning his body;
he could not seek life, nor could he seek death. The host of spirits and ghosts seized the elder urgently, not allowing him—
He was able to move. When the Buddha saw this, he felt compassion for him and asked the elder, "What do you intend to do now?
The elder’s mouth was clenched; he could not speak again, but could only raise his hand and strike himself. He sought mercy from the Buddha.

The Buddha then used his majestic spiritual power to rescue the elder. When the various ghost kings and spirits saw the World-Honored One using his majestic spiritual power to rescue the elder, they each withdrew and stood to one side. Thereupon, the elder recovered slightly;
he rose, prostrated himself, and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying: "Within my body there are these five thieves who seize me and drag me into the three evil realms."

[He was] sitting [there], intending to commit a transgression and thus violating what he had received. He prayed, "May the Buddha have compassion for me. The Buddha said, "As for what you have done with your own mind and mouth, whom should you blame?
The elder addressed the Buddha: "From this day forward, I shall reform my past ways and cultivate myself for the future.

I shall respectfully receive the Three Refuges and the Dharma of the Five Precepts; I shall observe the six fast days of each month and the three long fasts of each year, burning incense, scattering flowers, and hanging various banners."
"Indeed, as you serve the Triple Gem, from this day forward, do not again commit such violations of the precepts for returning [to the faith].
The Buddha said: 'What you have just spoken is most excellent. What you now see with your eyes and experience with your body is what you have created and obtained yourself;
it was not bestowed by heaven. The Buddha addressed the householder: 'Now that you have received these Three Refuges and Five Precepts, do not again act as you did.'"

This was the method for previously receiving the precepts of taking refuge. To violate these precepts of refuge is called a "second offense. If one commits a third offense, one falls into the hands of the Five Officials.

The summoning of spirits and the recording of life-spans all proceed according to one's original offenses. For this reason, I speak these words to encourage faithful men and women to receive the precepts of taking refuge.

I praise these laymen and laywomen of pure faith. At the time of their death, the Buddha will manifest emanations of his body to go and welcome them, ensuring that men and women who uphold the precepts do not fall into the evil realms.
If their observance of the precepts has weakened, they should further cultivate merit and virtue.
By practicing generosity, maintaining the precepts, cultivating patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, and wisdom;

by lighting lamps and burning incense, scattering flowers of various colors, hanging silk banners and canopies, singing hymns of praise, paying respectful homage, and further observing the fasts and precepts, one shall likewise attain transcendence.
If one cannot practice such meritorious virtues as described above, and furthermore fails to maintain the precepts completely, seeking blessings and protection through various heterodox paths,
then the three refuges, the five precepts, and the billions upon billions of ghost kings and spirit kings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, will each abandon them.
Evil spirits frequently come to harass those who draw near; consequently, they bring about decline, illness, and disorder within their households.

This is an opportunity for the Ten Kings of Spirits to act; it is no longer an opportunity for external māras. These spirits and ghosts observe the good and evil of people.

At that time, out of compassion, Śakra, the Lord of the Gods, went to where Cūḷamāṇava was and said to him: "O noble son, why is it that you..."
He rolled upon the ground, weeping in sorrow and recounting his various sufferings, moving all who saw him to pity.
At that time, Jāmbūnada suddenly heard these words; he rose from the ground, adjusted his robes, assumed a solemn countenance, and stood with palms joined, addressing Śakra, saying:
"Lord of Devas, my life now remains for only seven days. After my death, I shall fall into the world of Jambudvīpa as a king."
"Having abandoned the great city, due to past karma, he has received the body of a pig.

"I take refuge in the Dharma, the Honored One who has transcended desire. I take refuge in the Saṅgha, the Most Honored among the multitudes.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, observed where that devaputra had been reborn; he saw that he had been born as a king in Rājagṛha, in Jambudvīpa.
"Does the city receive the body of a pig, or does it not receive the body of a pig? He exhausted his divine eye to observe it, yet he did not see it.
He further observed the realms of animals and hungry ghosts, yet again he did not see it. He further observed the human world within the Sahā universe, yet again he did not see it.
He observed as far as the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, yet he could not see him at all.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having failed to see him, felt doubt and uncertainty in his mind.

Thereupon, Śakra went to the Jeta Grove, approached the World-Honored One, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, that [being]..."

The devaputra Vaṇamañjarī was on the verge of death; the five signs of decay had appeared before him, and with only seven days remaining in his life, he rolled upon the ground, weeping in sorrow and lamenting his various sufferings, moving all who saw him to grief. At that time, I went to him, and having witnessed this scene, I asked him:
"Why, O worthy one, do you weep so piteously and lament, appearing so haggard and distressed? Then, sighing for Vaṇamañjarī, I addressed him:
I said, "My life now remains for only seven days. After my life ends, I shall fall into Jambudvīpa and be born in Rājagṛha to receive the body of a pig.
For many years, I shall feed upon various kinds of filth and excrement.
When I heard these words, my heart was filled with extreme compassion, and I told him: "Now, O worthy one, if you wish to escape this suffering, you must take refuge..."

He addressed the Three Jewels, speaking these words: "I take refuge in the Buddha, the Honored One among two-legged beings; I take refuge in the Dharma, the Honored One who is free from desire; I take refuge in the Saṅgha, the Honored One among assemblies.
At that time, Jāmbālaka, out of fear of death and dread of rebirth as an animal, said to me:

"O World-Honored One, after Cāmaradhara had completed receiving the three refuges, he passed away.

"Kauśika, the devaputra Cāmaradhara has already been born in Tuṣita Heaven, where he enjoys the five [divine pleasures]."
[Desiring joy. At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having heard the Buddha’s words, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness;
his mind was refreshed and his faculties were perfected. He then spoke these verses before the Buddha:
If one takes refuge in the Buddha, one will not fall into the evil realms; having cast off this human body, one shall obtain a celestial body.
If one takes refuge in the Dharma, one will not fall into the evil realms; having cast off this human body, one shall obtain a celestial body.
If one takes refuge in the Saṅgha, one will not fall into the evil realms; having cast off this human body, one shall obtain a celestial body.
Furthermore, he spoke these verses:
With a sincere heart, one takes refuge in the Buddha; whatever that person shall obtain, whether by day or by night, the mind of the Buddha will constantly be mindful of them.
With a sincere heart, one takes refuge in the Dharma; whatever that person shall obtain, whether by day or by night, the power of the Dharma will constantly sustain them.
"Those who with sincere heart take refuge in the Saṅgha shall always be protected by the majesty of the Saṅgha, whether by day or by night.
When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had spoken these verses, the World-Honored One confirmed them, saying: "So it is, so it is."
"I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; I shall certainly not fall into the evil realms. Having cast off this human body, I shall surely obtain a celestial body.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
If the two syllables "Buddha" reach one's tongue, it is equivalent to taking refuge; one’s life will not have been spent in vain.
If the two syllables "Dharma" reach one's tongue, it is equivalent to taking refuge; one’s life will not have been spent in vain.
If the two syllables "Saṃgha" reach one's tongue, equaling [the merit of] taking refuge and so forth, one’s life will not have been spent in vain.
Furthermore, a verse says:
"If one does not know the names of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha, that person is most base and shall not attain [liberation]; they will wander through saṃsāra for a long time."
It is like a kāśī flower abiding in space.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the assembly of bhikṣus, Śakra, Lord of Devas, and the entire great multitude rejoiced,
accepted it with faith, prostrated, and withdrew.
