translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of India during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty;
annotated with essential points by the Śramaṇa Ouyi Zhixu of Ancient Wu.

The First Precept on Killing (Note: According to the logical sequence of the treatise, the four characters "The First Precept on Killing" should appear later in the text—after "Wishful to Hear" and before "The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus.

However, as they are listed here in the original text, perhaps due to the translator’s oversight, I have not dared to change them arbitrarily; I have merely provided this note so that when reading or reciting, the structure remains clear).
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kapilavastu. At that time, King Śuddhodana came to visit the Buddha.
He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I wish to make a request for my own deliverance;
I pray only that the World-Honored One will compassionately grant my desire. The Buddha said: "This wish may be granted;

it shall be according to what the King requests. The King addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, you have already established light precepts for the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs."
We respectfully pray that the Tathāgata will also, for our sake as upāsakas, distinguish between those of the five precepts that may be confessed and those that cannot,
so that we may recognize the characteristics of each precept and be free from doubt.
Kāpilavastu is the name of a kingdom in Central India; it is the birthplace of the World-Honored One. King Śuddhodana was the father of the World-Honored One.
Taking the father king as the primary interlocutor (*yathābhavya*), he requested the formal characteristics of the five precepts (*pañca-śīla*).
This precisely demonstrates that these five precepts are the father of all Buddhas of the three periods of time. Relying upon the five precepts, the ten [virtuous paths] are born.
How could one possibly disregard all the Buddhas of the three periods of time?
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent! Kautama, it has been my long-standing intention to distinguish the five precepts for lay followers (*upāsaka*).
If there is a son of good family who receives and upholds them without violation, by this causal condition, he shall attain the Way of the Buddha."
If one commits an offense and does not repent, they will constantly remain within the three miserable realms;

therefore, [the Buddha] accords with the intent of the Buddhas above and accords with the capacities of sentient beings below, and thus twice exclaims, "Excellent! *Kauṭumba* is the same as *Gautama*, which is the king's clan name.
In the Western Regions, it is customary to use the clan name as a mark of respect. If one receives and upholds [this precept] without violating it, then one shall surely achieve [enlightenment].

The Buddha said: "If one commits transgressions and does not repent, one will fall into the three miserable realms (*trāya*). The five precepts constitute the dharma-realm; all ten dharma-realms ultimately converge within these five precepts.
There is no convergence that exceeds them. Question: "If one receives and upholds [the precepts] without violating them, one shall attain the Buddha-way.

But as for those who receive them and yet violate them—will they also attain Buddhahood? If one violates them and does not repent, one will constantly remain in the three miserable realms. What of one who violates them but repents?"
"Will those who fall into the three miserable realms [thereby lose their potential]? He replied: "Even those who receive the precepts but then violate them shall attain Buddhahood.

Only those who do not receive the precepts will forever lack the causes and conditions for attaining Buddhahood. As for those who violate the precepts but repent, they shall not fall into the three miserable realms.

However, violations are distinguished into three grades—superior, middling, and inferior—and repentance likewise differs according to three methods: the ritual method (*zuo-fa*), the method of taking signs (*qu-xiang*), and the method of non-arising (*wu-sheng*). In principle, one must..."
Each of these precepts has been explained in detail; they cannot be fully exhausted in a single word.
At that time, after the Buddha had taught King Śuddhodana in various ways, the king, having heard the Dharma, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him, and departed.
On account of this incident, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "I now wish to [establish] the precepts for the upāsakas."
Regarding the explanation of the gravity of transgressions against the precepts—whether they are expiable or inexpiable—the bhikṣus all said: "Indeed, we wish to hear it with joy.
[The Teacher] asked: "The bhikṣu-vinaya is the dharma of the Great Saṃgha; for this reason, it is not permitted for laypeople to hear it. Now, as for the characteristics of the five precepts..."
"This is what a lay follower (upāsaka) studies. For what reason did he not speak to the king, but instead wait until after the king had departed before informing the bhikṣu of these circumstances?

The answer is: "The precepts and laws for the seven classes of disciples were all established by the Tathāgata within the community of bhikṣus precisely because the bhikṣu is the most honored among the seven classes. The Buddha-dharma relies upon the Jewel of the Saṃgha to be established."
Therefore, it is said that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, all bhikṣuṇīs should learn the precepts from the great assembly of monks (bhikṣusaṃgha).
If even the bhikṣuṇī precepts are subordinate to those of the bhikṣus, how much more so must the five precepts not be subordinate to them?
Thus, by now declaring these five precepts before the bhikṣusaṃgha, the intention is precisely to cause the upāsakas to likewise learn from the bhikṣus.

The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "There are three ways of committing the offense of killing that take human life. First, doing it oneself; second, commanding another; and third, dispatching an agent.
'Doing it oneself' means taking the life of another with one's own body. 'Commanding another' means instructing another person, saying:
'Seize this person, bind them, and take their life. 'Dispatching an agent' means saying to another person: 'Do you know so-and-so?'"
"No. If you seize this person, bind them, and take their life, then at the moment that messenger takes his life according to your command, the upāsaka commits an unforgivable offense."
The precept against killing is established as an unforgivable offense through five conditions: first, it must be a human being (meaning the victim is a person, not an animal or the like);

second, there must be the perception of a human; third, there must be the intent to kill; fourth, there must be the undertaking of the means; and fifth, the life of that person must be terminated prior to death.
Whether one acts personally, instructs another, or dispatches a messenger, all involve the undertaking of the means with the intent to kill; therefore, at the moment that life is taken...
This constitutes the commission of an unforgivable offense (*anatikramaṇīya-āpatti*). Regarding what is unforgivable:

at the time one first receives the *upāsaka* precepts, once the Three Refuges have been completed, one immediately attains the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) precept-substance (*śīla-skandha*). Now, by committing the sin of killing a human being, one loses this unmanifest precept-substance and no longer remains an *upāsaka*.
Therefore, it is not possible to perform a formal ritual confession (*vidhi-pratideśana*). Since it is impossible...
If one repents, one is forever cast outside the shores of the Buddha-ocean; this is called a "limiting offense" (*antāpatti*).

One may not again receive the five precepts, nor may one receive the eightfold fast-precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*) for a day and a night, nor may one receive the śrāmaṇera precepts or the bhikṣu precepts, nor may one receive the Bodhisattva Great Precepts. One may only rely upon the Mahāyāna Dharma to practice and attain realization.

Regarding the repentance through signs: once one has seen auspicious signs, one is then permitted to receive the Bodhisattva precepts, as well as to receive again the full precepts, the ten precepts, the eight precepts, the five precepts, and so forth.
At that time, although the offense of breaking the precepts is extinguished through this repentance by means of taking signs, [the merit of the precepts is still obtained].
Although one does not fall into the three miserable realms, the nature of worldly transgressions remains;

therefore, when the conditions and causes meet, one must still repay former debts. Only by entering *nirvāṇa* or being born in the Western Land can one escape them and avoid receiving retribution. How can one not exercise caution?
Furthermore, there are three ways of taking human life: first, by means of internal form; second, by means of non-internal form; and third, by means of both internal and non-internal form.

Regarding "internal form": if an upāsaka strikes another with his hand, or with his foot, or with any other part of his body, with the intention, "May he die because of this," and that person dies as a result, this constitutes an offense of irreparable transgression (pārājika).
If one does not die immediately, but dies later as a result of this, it is likewise an offense of non-confession (āpatti-ānantarya).
If one does not die immediately, nor dies later as a result of this, it is an offense of confession (sāvadya-vinaya). Regarding the use of non-internal matter:

if a person, with wood, tiles, stones, knives, spears, bows and arrows, or lumps of white tin or lead, hurls them from afar at another person with the intention, "May he die because of this," and that person [dies] because of it...

If one dies after committing an offense of irreparable transgression (*āpatti-ānantarya*), one commits that irreparable transgression; even if one does not die immediately, but later dies as a result of this [offense], one likewise commits that irreparable transgression.
If one does not die immediately, nor later as a result of it, the offense therein is one that can be confessed. This applies to both internal and non-internal forms.

If one takes hold of wood, a tile, a stone, a sword, a spear, a bow and arrow, a piece of white tin, a piece of lead or pewter, or a piece of wood, and strikes another with it while forming the thought, "May he die because of this," and that person dies as a result, this is an offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).

If they do not die immediately, but later die as a result of this, it is likewise an offense of immediate retribution. If they do not die immediately, nor later die as a result of this, it is... [an offense of wrong-doing].
These middle-grade offenses are subject to repentance.
These three types are likewise all methods of killing, namely, the employment of skillful means. Hands, feet, and bodily parts are what ordinary sentient beings grasp and maintain;
therefore, they are called "internal matter" (*adhyātma-rūpa*). Wood, tiles, stones, and so forth are not grasped by ordinary sentient beings.
That which is received is called "non-internal form. It may also be called "external form" depending on the context.

Because one uses that internal form to seize that external form, it is referred to as the dual application of both internal and non-internal form. One dies by means of this stratagem, whether death occurs immediately or subsequently;
in all cases, the intent to kill has been fulfilled. Therefore, from the moment the life of the previous person was severed, the [karmic] bond is established.
Regarding offenses that can be expiated through repentance: if one does not subsequently die [as a result], there is only the offense of having initiated the means for killing;

since the intent to kill was not fulfilled, the essence of the precept has not yet been lost. It can still be diligently repented of and eliminated; this is called a "middling offense expiable through repentance."
Furthermore, there are those who, for the purpose of killing a person, compound various poisons— neither by means of internal matter, nor by means of non-internal matter,
nor by means of both internal and non-internal matter— and apply them to the eyes, ears, nose, body, or open sores, or place them within various foods.
If one is on a mat or in a carriage and forms such a thought, "May he die because of this," and he dies because of that, one commits an offense of non-atonement (*āpatti-ānantarya*).
If he does not die immediately, but later dies as a result of this, one likewise commits an offense of non-atonement.
If he does not die immediately, nor does he later die as a result of this, it is an intermediate offense that may be atoned for.

This refers to using poison as a means of killing. Since neither the hands, feet, and so forth are employed, nor wood, stones, swords, staves, and the like, it is said that "neither by internal nor non-internal form" [the person's life is ended]; yet the result is the same.
In such cases, the sin is likewise not subject to repentance.

Furthermore, there are those who kill others by means of smokeless fire-pits, by crushing, by snares, by pits, by striking, by *vīdara* (mechanical contrivances), by causing abortion, by pressing on the abdomen, or by pushing them into water, into fire, or into pits. If...
He was sent away and died along the way. This extends even to the moment in the womb when the two faculties—the body faculty (*kāyendriya*) and the life faculty (*jīvitendriya*)—are first received.
Within that state, one employs means to kill [the fetus], such as using snares (*vāgurā*)—meaning wooden traps used for deception—or projectiles (*kṣepaṇa*), such as those from a crossbow.
This further elaborates upon various means of killing. The pitfall, the snare, and the lever are all instruments of killing.
*Vetāla* refers to the sorcery of raising the dead, which will be explained in the text below. The rest may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the pit of smokeless fire for killing: if a lay follower (upāsaka) knows that a person is coming by this path and, prior to their arrival, constructs a pit of smokeless fire and covers it with sand and soil; and if he says aloud, "Because this person is coming by this path, I have made this pit";
and if that person dies as a result of this, he commits an offense of non-expiation (ānantarya). If not...

If [the victim] dies immediately, or dies later as a result of this, one commits an inexpiable offense (ānantarya). If [the victim] does not die immediately, nor dies later as a result of this, it is a grave offense that can be expiated.
If one creates a pit of smokeless fire for a human being and the person dies, it is an inexpiable offense.

If a non-human being dies, it is a grave offense that can be expiated. (From the side of a human, one incurs the preparatory offense; from the side of a non-human, one does not incur the full offense of killing, because there is no intent to kill with respect to non-humans. [The same applies to] animals.

If the victim is a human, it is a minor offense (*āpatti*) that may be confessed (the character "xia" [minor] here is likely an error; according to all Vinaya sections, this is also a medium offense. Furthermore, one incurs the preparatory offense (*prayoga-āpatti*) from the side of the human, but does not incur the full offense of killing from the side of an animal, because there is no intent to kill with respect to an animal).
If one digs a pit for a non-human (*amanuṣya*) and a non-human dies, it is a medium offense that may be confessed (non-humans refer to devas, asuras, ghosts, and spirits;

since their capacity for the Way is weak, one who kills them has not lost the essence of the precept and it can still be removed through confession). If a human dies, it is a minor offense that may be confessed. If an animal...

Regarding "birth and death": if one commits a minor offense that requires confession (pāyattika), it is likewise incurred from a non-human being (amanuṣya) through the preparatory act (prayoga); however, the crime of killing is not incurred from humans or animals, because there was originally no intent to kill them.

If one digs a pit for an animal and the animal dies, this is a minor offense requiring confession (because animals are inferior to devas and spirits, the offense for killing them is somewhat lighter).
If a human falls into it and dies, or if a non-human being falls into it and dies, in both cases one commits a minor offense.

This is a transgression that can be expiated (for one has incurred the offense of preparatory action from the side of animals). If an upāsaka does not specifically construct a pit for a single purpose, but intends for all who come to fall and die therein:
if a human dies, it is an inexpiable offense; if a non-human dies, it is a middling offense that can be expiated;
if an animal dies, it is a minor offense that can be expiated; if no one dies at all, one incurs three offenses of preparatory action that can be expiated.
This is called "killing by a pit of smokeless fire.

This detailed explanation of killing another by means of a pit of smokeless fire serves as a model for examining other forms of killing, such as killing with a trap, killing with a snare, killing by a pitfall, and killing by a blow;
there is none that is not so. Question: One must not intentionally kill any living being. Those who do so are not disciples of the Buddha.

“Son, for what reason is it that killing devas, nāgas, ghosts, or spirits results only in a middle-grade offense, while killing an animal results only in a lower-grade offense, such that one does not lose the precepts and does not fall [into hell]?
He replied: “In general, when discussing the loss of the precepts, it must involve the violation of the four root grave offenses (*catur-uttara-pārājika*):
namely, killing a human being, stealing five *māṣaka* coins, sexual misconduct, and great falsehood. Among these four grave offenses, whichever...”
If one commits even a single type [of offense], it certainly cannot be expiated through ritual procedures (*dharma-karman*).

For instance, in cases such as killing non-humans or animals, although the offense is grave by nature (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), it remains relatively light in comparison to the violation of the unmanifest offense (*avijñapti-āpatti*).

When it is now stated that "middle-grade offenses may be repented" and "minor offenses may be repented," this refers to repenting and eliminating the violation of the unmanifest offense so as to avoid falling into the three miserable realms; it does not mean [that the nature-offense itself is removed].
This also excludes natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). For one who takes a single life, one must necessarily repay with a single life.

Thus, for intentional killing, one must certainly repay intentionally; for accidental killing, one must likewise repay accidentally. Even for those who have not received the precepts, there will inevitably be sin.
Therefore, the *Mahābuddhatoṣaṇī Sūtra* (The Great Buddha-Topknot Sūtra) states: "If, in the interim, one kills another's life or eats their flesh, it is thus..."

Even for as long as it takes to pass through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, they devour one another and slaughter one another like a turning wheel, rising and falling in alternation without rest.
It was for this reason that the Buddha established the precept against killing. By receiving and upholding it without violation, one may bring an end to the cycle of saṃsāra forever.
Even if one should happen to violate it, by repenting with a sincere heart and vowing never to commit it again, one may likewise avoid falling into the three [evil realms].

Because it is smeared [with defilement], it is called "middling repentance" or "inferior repentance. Even if one does not practice mindfulness of the Buddha to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, by what means could one ever escape the suffering of retribution?

Regarding the *vettāla*: if an upāsaka, on the twenty-ninth day of the lunar month, seeks out the corpse of a person who has died with their body intact, summons a spirit through incantations to raise the corpse, washes it, clothes it, and causes it to hold a sword in its hand;

and if he then thinks in his mind and speaks aloud, "For the sake of so-and-so, I am making this *vettāla*," and recites the sorcery mantras—if he intends to harm or kill someone, he commits an offense.

Regarding offenses that can be confessed: if the victim has entered various *samādhis*, or is protected by a celestial deity, or is rescued and released by a great master of mantras, the act of killing is not accomplished;
one incurs an intermediate offense that can be confessed. This is called "Vetāla-killing.

As for "half-Vetāla," it refers to a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who, on the twenty-ninth day of the month, constructs an iron chariot; having constructed the iron chariot, he then constructs an iron man.
One summons the spirits with a mantra to cause an iron man to rise. Water is sprinkled upon his clothing, causing the iron man to grasp a sword in his hand.
If one thinks in the mind and speaks aloud, "I am reciting this mantra for the sake of [so-and-so]," and if that person dies, one commits an unforgivable offense (*āpatti-ānantarya*).
However, if the person has entered various *samādhis*, is protected by various devas, or is rescued and released by the mantra-master, death will not occur.
This is a transgression that may be repented of; it is called "half-Vetāla-killing. Regarding the taking of life:
on the twenty-ninth day, smear the ground with cow dung, place wine and food therein, and having lit a fire, immediately cast [the victim] into the water.

If one then mentally intends and verbally recites the words of a mantra, saying, "May he be extinguished as fire is extinguished by water," then at the moment the fire is extinguished, his life shall likewise be extinguished. Furthermore...
Again, for twenty-nine days, one should smear the ground with cow dung and place wine and food upon it. There, one should paint an image of the person one intends to kill.
Having made the image, one should immediately erase it while reciting the words of the incantation and thinking in one's mind:

"As this image is extinguished, so too shall his life be extinguished; when the image perishes, his life shall perish accordingly. Furthermore, for another twenty-nine days, one should smear [the ground] with cow dung...
Place wine and food inside the ground. Insert a needle into the corner of a garment, then immediately pull it out. Mentally contemplate and verbally recite the words of a mantra, saying:
"As this needle comes out, so shall his life depart. This is called taking life. If one causes death by means of various such mantras, one commits an offense of non-expiation (*ānantarya*).
If the person does not die, it is an intermediate offense that may be expiated.
The three types of incantations that sever life are all termed "killing through malevolent sorcery" (*abhicāra*); they are all varieties of *vaidhṛta*.
Furthermore, regarding those who cause abortion: they administer emetics or purgatives to a pregnant woman, or apply drugs to all parts of her body;
or they pierce her blood vessels, even to the point of administering drugs to induce tears. With the thought, "By these causes and conditions, may this woman die," [they act].

Regarding the deceased: if one commits an offense of irreparable transgression (*āpatti-ānantarya*), should they not die immediately but later die as a result of this [act], one likewise commits an offense of irreparable transgression.
If they do not die immediately and later do not die as a result of this, it is an offense of intermediate gravity that may be confessed.

If, for the purpose of killing the mother, one causes an abortion, if the mother dies, one commits an offense of irreparable transgression; if the fetus dies, this offense may be confessed (though one remains liable toward the mother).

One incurs the offense of the means employed; one does not incur the offense regarding the fetus itself, because there was no intention to kill the fetus. If both [mother and fetus] die, this offense cannot be expiated.
If neither dies, it is a middling offense that can be expiated. If, for the purpose of killing the fetus, one performs a method to cause an abortion and the fetus dies...
If one commits an unforgivable offense (*ānantarya*), and the fetus does not die, it is a medium offense that may be expiated;

if the mother dies, it is a medium offense that may be expiated (yet one still incurs the offense of preparatory action regarding the fetus). If both die, this constitutes an unforgivable offense. This is called the method of killing by causing an abortion.
As for pressing the abdomen, one causes a pregnant woman to perform heavy labor, carry heavy loads, or instruct her to run in front of a vehicle.
If one causes [a woman] to ascend a steep bank and thinks, "May this woman die," and she dies, it constitutes an offense of non-remorse (ānantarya).
If she does not die immediately, but later dies as a result of this, the offense is likewise one of non-remorse. If she does not die because of this, it is a middling offense that can be remedied.
If she is pregnant, it is as explained above; this is called killing by pressing the abdomen. If one dispatches her to die on the road, [the same applies].
Knowing that there are hungry wild beasts within this path, one dispatches [the victim] to go into that evil path. One forms the thought:
"May those who die in that evil path commit an irreparable offense (ānantarya), and may the others likewise commit it. This is as explained above; this is called killing in an evil path.
This continues until [the embryo] has first acquired two faculties within the mother’s womb: the body faculty (kāyendriya) and the life faculty (jīvitendriya). [This applies to] the kalala...
At the time of the *kalala*, if one employs a means with the intent to kill, desiring to cause death, one commits an offense of irreparable transgression (*āpatti-ānantarya*).
Other offenses are as explained above.
*Kalala* is also called *ghana* (or *kalala*), or *kalala*; this translates as "coagulated slime. It is also translated as... [text ends]
It is a mixture of impurities, appearing like congealed butter; this is the state during the first seven days within the womb.

There are three types of persons whose killing is praised: first, those with evil precepts; second, those with virtuous precepts; and third, the elderly and the sick. Regarding those with evil precepts:
they slaughter oxen and sheep, raise chickens and pigs, release hawks to catch fish, and include hunters who surround rabbits and shoot them.
If one encounters such people as those who hunt deer and other wild animals, thieves, executioners, those who cast spells upon dragons, or jailers, and says to them:
"You people of evil precepts, why do you persist in committing sins? It would be better for you to die soon.
If these people die because of this, the sin cannot be expiated; if they do not die because of it, the middling sin can be expiated. If an evil person acts in this manner...
He said, "I did not intend for this person to die; it was not because of my words that he died. I have committed a middling offense requiring confession.
If, however, he had praised that person to the point of causing death and subsequently felt remorse, thinking, "Why did I instruct this person to die? and returned to say, "You wicked people!
It is perhaps through the influence of a virtuous friend that you have drawn near to a good person and been able to hear the sublime Dharma," [he would be cleared of the offense].
Through right reflection, one attains freedom from evil transgressions. You must not commit suicide. If that person accepts these words and does not die, the offense therein may be confessed.
Those who possess virtuous precepts are the fourfold assembly of the Tathāgata. If one goes before such virtuous persons and speaks thus:
"You uphold the virtuous precepts; you are a person of merit. If you were to die, you would immediately receive celestial blessings. Why [do you wish to die]?"
If one takes one's own life, that person commits an offense of non-confession (*āpatti-āvaśeṣa*). If one does not take one's own life, it is a middling offense that can be confessed.
If a person of virtuous precepts thinks, "Why should I take my own life based on another's words? and does not die, this offense can be confessed.
If, after instructing another to die, one feels regret in one's heart and says, "It was not right of me... [the offense can be confessed].
Having instructed this good person to die, one returns and says to them: "O good person, remain as long as your lifespan lasts;
because your merit is increasingly great, you shall receive increasing blessings. Do not take your own life. If you do not die [as a result of this], the offense therein can be confessed."

Regarding those who are old and sick, whose four elements are in a state of increase or decrease and who undergo various sufferings and afflictions: one goes to such a person and says, "Why do you endure this suffering for so long?
Why do you not take your own life? If death results from this, the offense is irredeemable;
if death does not result from it, it is a middling offense that can be confessed. If the sick person thinks, "For what reason should I follow this person's words? and [proceeds to act...].
If one has told a sick person [to commit suicide] and subsequently feels regret, thinking, "I was wrong; why did I tell this sick person to take their own life?

and goes back to say, "You who are sick, perhaps you will obtain excellent medicine and have a skilled caregiver who provides you with appropriate food and drink according to the medicine, so that your illness may be cured;
do not take your own life," then if the person does not die as a result, the offense therein is repentable.
These three types of praising killing are all not found in the broad exposition (uddeśa); nevertheless, they may be understood according to the text.
As for the remaining seven types of killing mentioned above, their classification as an offense or a non-offense is identical to that of the fire pit discussed previously.
There are seven types: pointing out, broad indication, marking the core, using a snare, a pitfall, a shovel, and pushing someone into water, fire, or a pit.
If one kills a human being while perceiving them as a human, this offense is irredeemable. If one kills a non-human being while perceiving them as a human, [the result] arises within the human realm.

If one kills out of doubt, it constitutes an offense of non-remorse (anantarya). If one kills without the perception that the victim is a human, or if one kills while harboring doubt as to whether the victim is a human, these are offenses of intermediate gravity that can be remedied.

According to other schools, either the single phrase "perceiving [the victim] as a human" constitutes a grave offense, or both phrases—"perceiving [the victim] as a human" and "doubting [whether they are] a human"—constitute a grave offense.
"Severe. Now, all three phrases conclude with "severe. Judging by the underlying principle, there should only be two phrases concluding with "severe":

namely, [acting toward] a person while perceiving them as a person—this is not subject to repentance; and [acting toward] a person while doubting whether they are a person—this also is not subject to repentance.

The remaining four phrases conclude with "repentable": namely, acting toward a person while perceiving them as a non-person—this is repentable; acting toward a non-person while perceiving them as a person—this is also repentable. [The other cases follow similarly. Non-...

If one suspects that a person is not a human being, it is an offense of medium confession (*dukkaṭa*). If one perceives a non-human being as a non-human being, it is likewise an offense of medium confession.
Furthermore, there was a man whose hands and feet had been severed and placed within the moat of a city; then, a multitude of women entered the city.

Hearing this sound of weeping, they went to investigate and said to one another, "If anyone could give this person a medicinal potion to drink so that she dies at once, she would not have to suffer for long.
Among them was a simple-minded woman who then gave her the medicinal potion, and she died immediately.
The other women said, "You have committed a transgression of the precepts that cannot be atoned for," and they reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "You gave her the potion..."
Regarding those who die while receiving medicinal gruel: this constitutes an offense for which there is no confession.
This passage from the *Saṃgīti* school cites a case to clarify the determination of the offense, yet the text is overly concise.

According to other Vinaya sections, if one engages in such deliberation, one commits a minor offense requiring confession (*duṣkṛta*). If, however, with a single mind, one causes another to seek medicine [for the patient], [the offense is different].
If one commits the same offense of an irredeemable transgression (*āpatti-āvaśeṣa*), and if one knows [of it] yet does not prevent it, one also commits a middling redeemable transgression.

If a layperson (*gṛhapati*) employs the means (*upāya*) intending to kill his mother, but kills someone who is not his mother, this is a middling redeemable transgression (yet he incurs the offense of the preparatory act toward his mother;

he does not incur an offense toward the one who is not his mother, because this was a killing by mistake and he originally lacked the intent to kill). If a layperson intends to kill someone who is not his mother, but [kills his own mother instead]...

Killing one's mother is an offense of intermediate gravity that may be confessed; it is not a *ānantarya* (immediate) transgression. (Furthermore, if one employs the means toward someone who is not one's mother, one incurs the offense of preparatory action; one does not incur the full offense of killing with respect to the mother.

If a layperson (*gṛhapati*) employs the means intending to kill a human being, but kills a non-human (*amanuṣya*), this is an offense of intermediate gravity that may be confessed (but one incurs only the offense of preparatory action with respect to the human).
If a layperson employs the means intending to kill a non-human, but kills a human being, he commits a minor offense that may be confessed (but only with respect to the non-human).

[This constitutes] the offense of preparatory effort (*prayoga*). If a person conceives the fetus of an animal and causes that fetus to miscarry, one commits a minor offense requiring confession (*duskṛta*).
If an animal conceives the fetus of a human and that fetus dies upon being caused to miscarry, one commits an offense not requiring confession (*anāpatti*).

If a layperson (*gṛhapati*) makes a preparatory effort to kill a person, and the layperson dies first, and subsequently another person dies [as a result], this offense is one requiring confession. (Prior to the death, one has committed only the offense of preparatory effort.)
At the time of their death, the essence of their precepts perishes along with them; therefore, those who die later do not incur the grave offense of breaking the precepts.

If a layperson intends to kill their parents and feels doubt as to whether they are indeed their parents or not, yet definitively knows they are their parents, then killing them constitutes a parricidal crime (ānantarya) that cannot be expiated.
This must also be analyzed through six propositions: [1] one's own parents; [2] the perception that they are one's parents; [3] doubt regarding them being one's parents.

These three propositions constitute the offense of parricide when directed toward one's parents despite the lack of the perception that they are one's parents, as well as the case where they are not one's parents. In all these cases, one commits an irredeemable offense (*ānantarya*), though it does not constitute the specific crime of parricide.

If a layperson harbors doubt as to whether this person is human or non-human, yet their mind determines with certainty that it is human, the one who kills commits an offense of non-confession (anāpatti-āpatti).

[This should also be analyzed according to six permutations: two cases of non-confession and four cases of confession, as clarified previously. If a person seizes a thief intending to kill him, but the thief manages to escape;

If an upāsaka uses water containing living beings, or kills insects within plants and trees, he commits an offense. If there are living beings but he perceives them as non-existent, using the water still constitutes an offense.
If there are no living beings but he perceives them as existing, using the water likewise constitutes an offense.
This should also be analyzed according to six cases: 1. There are insects, and one perceives them as such; 2. There are insects, but one suspects there are insects.
These two cases result in a fundamental minor offense of regret (*duṣkṛta*). 3. There are no insects, but one perceives them as such; 4. There are no insects, but one suspects there are none.
These two cases result in a preparatory minor offense of regret. 5. There are insects, but one perceives them as being none; 6. There are none... [text truncated]
If there are insects but one perceives them as being without insects, these two cases constitute no offense.

As for the present statement that even perceiving no insects when there are insects constitutes an offense, it is intended to cause people to examine and observe with careful scrutiny, so that they do not recklessly and lightly use water, plants, or wood.
There was a householder who built a new residence and stayed atop the roof. He dropped a beam from his hand, which fell upon the head of a carpenter, killing him instantly.
The householder became doubtful and asked the Buddha, "Is this offense one that can be expiated? The Buddha said, "There is no offense, for there was originally no intent to kill."

The householder immediately became suspicious [of the Buddha’s teaching]. The Buddha said, "There is no fault. Terrified, he leaped down and fell upon a carpenter, killing him instantly. The householder again became suspicious. The Buddha said, "There is no fault. From this day forward, apply yourself with care and do not let anyone be killed."
A lay devotee (gṛhapati) became doubtful. The Buddha said, "There is no offense. From this day forward, you must apply your mind with care when working; do not cause anyone to be killed.

The Second Precept on Stealing:
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus and upāsakas: "One commits an offense that cannot be remedied by taking another's property of significant value through three ways:

first, by means of the mind; second, by means of the body; and third, by removing it from its original place. 'By means of the mind' refers to initiating a thought and reflecting with the desire [to steal]."

Regarding theft: as for "using the body," it means taking another's property by means of one's own body or its parts; "removing from its original location" means, according to where the object was situated, lifting it and placing it in another place.
The precept against stealing is established as an unforgivable offense through six conditions: first, another’s property; second, the perception that it is another’s property;
third, the intent to steal; fourth, the undertaking of the means to take it; fifth, the value being five *māṣakas* (one large coin of the Western Regions is worth sixteen small coins of this region;

thus five coins equal eighty small coins. The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: five *māṣakas*; each *māṣaka* is eighty cowries, which equals four hundred cowries. In Yunnan, five cowries are equivalent to one *cili* of silver, which is also eight-tenths of a silver coin); sixth, [the completion of the act].
Leaving its original place—this is now called "taking another's heavy object," which constitutes the object itself; the perception that it is another's property is the third condition;
the application of the mind is the intention to steal; the application of the body is the undertaking of the means to take it;
leaving the original place is the sixth condition. When these six conditions are fully met, one loses the non-informative (avijñapti) precept-body.

Furthermore, there are three ways of taking another's property that constitute an offense of irreparable transgression (*āpatti-āvaśeṣa*): first, taking it oneself; second, commanding another to take it;

and third, sending a messenger to take it. Regarding "taking it oneself": this means lifting it with one's own hand and moving it from its original location. Regarding "commanding another to take it":

if a lay follower (*upāsaka*) instructs someone, saying, "Steal another's property," and that person takes it at will, the moment it is moved from its original location, [the offense is incurred]. Sending a messenger...
The messenger says to the agent: "Do you know the location of that valuable object? He replies, "I know its location. The messenger then dispatches him to steal it.
When this person, following these instructions, takes the object and removes it from its original place—
These three types of taking all distinguish the different means employed; they alike constitute a grave offense through six conditions.
Furthermore, there are five ways of taking another’s property that constitute an irredeemable offense (*anapatrāpya*): first, taking by means of harsh coercion; second, taking with contempt;
third, taking by falsely assuming another’s name; fourth, taking by forceful seizure; and fifth, taking what has been entrusted to one.
These five types of taking are also different in their methods, yet they are all equally grave offenses due to six conditions.
Regarding the "heavy object": if it is five coins, or an object worth five coins, one commits an offense that cannot be remedied.
This correctly explains that anything valued at five *kārsāpaṇas* or more is termed a "heavy object.

Regardless of the specific item, if its value at the original location is equivalent to eight units of silver, the moment it is taken away from that place, one commits an offense of non-confession (*pārājika*).
If a layperson knows that another has the five kinds of precious objects or their equivalents, and with a thieving mind selects them while they have not yet been moved from their place,

he commits an offense entailing confession (having not fulfilled the six conditions, he incurs an offense of preliminary preparation). If, after having selected them, he takes them and moves them from their original place, and their value is five *kārsāpaṇas* or more,
he commits an offense entailing irreparable loss (having fulfilled the six conditions, he loses the essence of his precepts, regardless of whether the items were subsequently used or not).
The "five treasures" refer to the five metals: namely, gold, silver, copper, iron, and tin. "Resemblances" (sì) means images or imitations.

Various utensils fashioned from gold, silver, and so forth are called "resemblance treasures" (sìbǎo). If the gold, silver, and other materials have not yet been formed into utensils, they are called "raw treasures" (shēngbǎo).
Therefore, it is said: "raw and image gold, silver, and precious objects. This refers to: first, raw gold and silver precious objects.
The second refers to images made of gold, silver, or precious objects. Alternatively, it may be said that the seven treasures can be understood by analogy.

Regarding "leaving one's original location": in the case of woven cloth, different threads are called different locations; in the case of leather or clothing, if they are of a single color, they are called one location, and if they are of different colors, they are called different locations.
In the case of clothing, leather, or beds, if they are of a single color, they are called one location, and if they are of different colors, they are called different locations.
Regarding a woolen rug: if the wool is not doubled over, it is called one place; a single color is called one place; different colors are called different places. These are what are termed "places.
When a householder carries goods for another, if he shifts them from his left shoulder to his right shoulder, or from his right hand to his left hand, such bodily parts are termed "different places.
As for a cart, there are the wheels, axle, pole, and yoke; as for a boat, [there are the planks, etc.]...
On both sides, front and back, as well as the beams, rafters, purlins, and eaves of the roof, and the four corners and the innermost recess—all these are called distinct locations.
To move an object with the intent to steal and place it in any of these distinct locations constitutes an offense that cannot be remedied.
For example, regarding a woolen rug: suppose one places one's own items on one layer and another's items on a second layer;

or perhaps one places one's own items on one color and another's items on a different color. Now, if one takes the other's items, removes them from those two layers and places them within one's own layer, or removes them from that different color and places them within one's own color, this causes the other person to form the perception that they have lost their property.

Therefore, it constitutes a breach of the place [of restraint] and fulfills the six conditions for a further offense that cannot be rectified. This applies by analogy to the left shoulder, the right shoulder, and so forth.
If there is no intention to steal, then even if one shifts them back and forth many times, how could there be any offense?
*Héng*: A horizontal wooden beam at the front of the shafts, used for yoking horses. *É*: A horizontal wooden beam at the front of the shafts, used for yoking oxen.

*Xián* (pronounced *xián*): The edge of a boat. The beam that supports the ridgepole is called a *liáng*. The ridgepole itself is called the *dòng*. *Chuán* and *jué* (pronounced *chuán* and *jué*): The rafters.
These are all rafters from a house.
As for those who steal things from the water: if a person, a raft, or timber is carried downstream by the current, and a householder takes them with the intent to steal, [it constitutes theft].

One commits an offense of irreparable transgression (*āpatti pārājika*). If, with the intent to steal, one seizes a piece of wood and holds it stationary, such that it subsequently drifts toward the upstream limit (this is termed "separation from its place"), or if, with the intent to steal, one submerges it to the bottom of the water (this is also termed "separation from its place"), or if one lifts it out of the water (this is also termed "separation from its place"), in all these cases one commits an offense of irreparable transgression.
Furthermore, suppose there are birds being raised in a pond belonging to a master, and a layperson, with the intent to steal, presses them down into the water of the pond.

If one lifts [a bird] from a pond while still within that place, one commits an offense of expiation (*pāyattika*); however, if one lifts it out of the water so as to leave that place, one commits an offense of non-expiation (*anantarya*).

If a domestic bird kept by a householder flies into a wild pond, and one with the intent to steal lifts it out of the water (this constitutes leaving the place), or sinks it to the bottom of the water (this is also called leaving the place), in all such cases, one commits an offense of non-expiation.
Furthermore, if there are articles of internal and external adornment belonging to a householder located on a multi-storied pavilion...
Above. If a bird possessing a master takes this object away, one who seizes it from that bird with a thieving mind commits an offense of non-expiation (because the six conditions are fulfilled).
If one sees a bird flying while carrying a treasure and, with a thieving mind, waits for it from a distance, one commits an offense of intermediate expiation.
(This is a transgression of expedient means. If one uses the power of mantras to cause a bird to go wherever it desires, one commits an irreparable offense (because the six conditions are fulfilled).
If one goes to another location, it constitutes an offense of intermediate confession (also an offense of preliminary preparation).

If a wild bird picks up a jewel and flies away, and a householder seizes it from the bird with a thieving mind, it constitutes an offense of intermediate confession (although the object has no owner, the offense is incurred through the thieving intention). While waiting for the wild bird...

One commits a minor offense requiring confession (*dukkaṭa*). Furthermore, when various wild birds carry away jewels, and various birds possessing owners seize them from the wild birds, if a layperson (*gṛhapati*) seizes them from the birds possessing owners with a mind of theft, he commits an offense of non-confession (*pārājika*). (This is because six conditions are fulfilled; one incurs the offense against the owner of the birds.

If one waits for the bird [to leave], one commits a middling offense requiring confession (*sthūlātyaya*), which is an offense of preliminary effort (*prayoga*). The rest is as explained above. Moreover, there are cases where a bird possessing an owner carries away a precious object.

It departs and is seized by a wild bird (as it has no owner). If a layperson seizes it from the wild bird with a thieving mind, they commit an offense of the middle grade that requires confession (the offense is also established based on the thieving mind).

If they wait for the bird [to leave], they likewise commit an offense of the middle grade that requires confession (according to the above, this should be an offense of the minor grade; the character "middle" is likely an error, otherwise the former case should also be called an offense of the middle grade).
The rest is as above. If a layperson plays at dice and, with a thieving mind, shifts the dice to defeat another and win, [he commits an offense].
Regarding "five coins": to commit this offense is unforgivable.
Using money for gambling is called *chupapu* (backgammon), or *shuanglu* (double-six), also known as *liubo* (six-gambling).

The pieces used by gamblers—such as the horse-men, the surrounding chessmen, the chessmen of *xiangqi*, and the dice—are all termed *chi* (teeth). To move these *chi* is what is meant by "turning the teeth."
This refers to stealing by exchanging moves in a game of chess, or even using drugs or loaded dice and the like.

According to the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* and the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, activities such as gambling also constitute minor offenses (*āpatti*). For those who currently receive only the five precepts, it may be possible not to commit them;
however, altering the teeth to gain an advantage over others is entirely an act of a thieving mind, and therefore constitutes a grave offense.
If there is a layperson who steals a relic with a thieving mind, they commit an offense that is repentable (since its value cannot be calculated).
If, however, one takes it with a reverent mind, thinking, "The Buddha is also my teacher," and does so with a pure mind, it constitutes an offense.

If a layperson takes a scripture with a thieving mind, they commit an offense that is not repentable; the gravity of the offense depends on the calculated value (if the stolen scripture is worth five coins or more, then...).
It is a *pāyattika* (an offense requiring confession). If it is less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *dukkaṭa* (a minor offense). Now, regarding the theft of fields, there are two causes:

first, seizing another's field by means of verbal dispute (that is, filing a lawsuit with the government); second, seizing it by means of establishing physical markers (that is, setting up boundary signs).

If a layperson, for the sake of land, wins a case against another, or if they obtain land beyond their share by means of fraudulent markers, and the value reaches five *kārsāpaṇas*, it constitutes an *anantarya* (an offense of immediate retribution). There is.
O householders, if one owes customs duty and fails to pay it, when the amount reaches five *kārsāpaṇas*, one commits an offense of non-expiation (*pārājika*).
Furthermore, if there is a householder who, at a customs post, says to other householders, "Pass these goods for me;

I will give you half the tax as a fee for carrying them through," and they thus evade the tax by five *kārsāpaṇas*, they commit an offense of non-expiation. If a householder shows another person a different route...
If one causes the loss of taxable goods worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, it constitutes a middling offense that requires confession.

However, there is no offense if, at a customs post, there are thieves, wild beasts, or famine, and one intentionally shows a different route to avoid such harm. Furthermore, there is the case of a householder who conspires with a thief.
They plundered various villages and divided the goods among themselves. If the value [of the stolen item] was five *kārsāpaṇas*, one committed an offense of non-expiation (*āpatti pārājika*).

Regarding the theft of legless sentient beings—such as leeches (the character for "leech" is pronounced *zhì*; they are aquatic insects) and *yutuo* worms (not yet translated)—if a person takes them up and places them in a vessel...
If a layperson takes [an item] from a vessel, they commit an offense of non-confession (*apatideśanīya*). The selection [of items] is as stated above.

Regarding the theft of two-legged or three-legged sentient beings—such as humans, geese, wild ducks, parrots, and other such birds—if one takes them with a thieving mind while they are confined within a cage or enclosure, they commit an offense of non-confession.
The rest is as explained above. There are two ways of stealing a person: first, carrying them away.

Second is the case of a common agreement. If a layperson, with a thieving mind, places another person upon their shoulder and both of that person's feet leave the ground, they commit an offense of irreparable transgression (*pārājika*).
If they have made a common agreement to travel together and exceed two double-steps, they commit an offense of irreparable transgression. All other cases are as explained above.
Regarding the theft of four-footed creatures—namely elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep—if a person has them tied by a rope in one place and [takes them] with a thieving mind...
If one leads [the animal] away and passes four double-paces, one commits an offense of non-confession (*anantarya*).
If [the animal] is lying in one place and one drives it up with a thieving mind, passing four double-paces, one commits an offense of non-confession. This is the same for multi-legged animals.

If [the animal] is within a wall, a fence, or a screen, and one drives it out with a thieving mind, passing four double-paces beyond the herd, one commits an offense of non-confession. The rest is as explained above. If...

1. Temporary use. 2. Knowing it has an owner. 3. Not being insane. 4. Not being mentally deranged. 5. Not having a mind impaired by illness.

Taking a heavy object with these seven conditions constitutes an offense of non-expiation (*anivārya*). Taking a light object (four *kārsāpaṇas* or less) under these conditions constitutes a middling expiable offense (*pāyattika*).

Furthermore, there are seven other [conditions]: 1. Thinking it is one’s own (*svakīya-saṃjñā*)—meaning one considers it to be one's own property. 2. Consent (*anumati*)—having been previously intimate, when one hears that they are using it, their heart rejoices. 3. Temporary...
(The items shall be used for a short time and then returned to their original owners). Fourth, that which has no owner (meaning it is unknown whether anyone has rightful possession of this object).

Fifth, one who is insane. Sixth, one whose mind is deranged. Seventh, one whose mind is impaired by illness. Taking objects under these seven conditions constitutes no offense. There was a householder who planted radishes.

At that time, there was a man tilling the soil within the Jeta Grove; he had removed his clothes and laid them on one side of the field. A householder, seeing no one in the four directions, then took those clothes.

As he was leaving, a plowman saw him from afar and said to the householder, "Do not take my garment. The householder did not hear him and, thinking there was no owner, continued to take the garment with him.

If one conceives the intention to steal but has not yet taken it, one commits a minor offense requiring confession.

If one takes it but the value is less than five *māṣaka* coins, one commits a middling offense requiring confession. If one takes it and the value reaches five *māṣaka* coins, one commits an irreparable offense (*anivārya*).

If one intends to steal but has not yet taken it, this is a distant preparatory act (*dūre-prayoga*) and is subject to confession. If one has taken it but it has not yet left its place, this is a proximate preparatory act (*āsanne-prayoga*) and is subject to confession.

Regarding the third precept on celibacy, the Buddha told the bhikṣus and upāsakas: "One should not give rise to thoughts of desire or sensual perceptions; one should not even give rise to such a mind."
How much more so for the arising of desire—the root of the fetters of hatred and delusion, and of impure, evil karma.
To establish conventional designations (*nāma-paññatti*) regarding the objects of desire is called "perception of desire" (*kāmasaññā*).

To suddenly give rise to seeking within the objects of desire is called "thought of desire" (*kāmavitakka*). Because desire is not fulfilled, one gives rise to hatred; both desire and hatred depend upon the same basis.
Regarding delusion: once the three poisons are fully present, they become the root of all fetters and bonds.
They contravene pure conduct and are capable of summoning the retribution of suffering in both this life and future lives; therefore, they are called impure and evil karma.
In this regard, there are four objects for the commission of sexual misconduct: a male, a female, a *paṇḍaka*, and one with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*).

As for the "female," she may be a human female, a non-human female, or a female animal. As for the "male," he may be a human male, a non-human male, or a male animal; *paṇḍakas* and those with both organs are likewise included in these same categories.

Sexual misconduct constitutes an offense of irreparable transgression (*anantarya*). If one engages in sexual intercourse with a human male, a non-human male, a male animal, a eunuch, or a hermaphrodite—specifically through two locations—it constitutes an offense of irreparable transgression.
If one forms the intention to engage in sexual intercourse but the act has not yet been consummated, it constitutes a minor offense of transgression (*duskṛta*).

(This refers to the distant preliminary action. If two bodies come together but one refrains from sexual intercourse, it constitutes a transgression that is subject to confession (this refers to the proximate preliminary action).
The precept against sexual misconduct is established as an irredeemable offense through three conditions:

first, the lustful mind—meaning, for example, being like one who obtains food when hungry or a drink when thirsty, rather than like hot iron entering the body or a foul corpse tied around one's neck; second, the [appropriate] passage, which is explained below.
The three points clarified are as follows: the three matters are thus established. That is to say, if one enters [a woman] even to the extent of a sesame seed, one immediately loses the precepts.
If an upāsaka engages in sexual misconduct with a female servant who has already married and has a husband, he commits an offense that cannot be rectified.

Other minor offenses are as explained above. Regarding the "three places": the mouth, the anus, and the urinary tract. Engaging in sexual desire at any location other than these three may be expiated through confession.
If a lay follower (*upāsaka*) engages in non-penetrative sexual intercourse with a female servant who has not yet been married, he commits an offense that can be confessed;
however, the retribution for the resulting karma in future lives will be heavy.

If a maidservant has not yet been married and thus has no other master, one who wishes to take her into their care should do so according to the Dharma, establishing her status through proper rites as either a concubine or a wife;

in these cases, there is nothing improper. However, if one engages in sexual misconduct contrary to the Way, thereby destroying her integrity and causing this woman to lose her virtue and chastity, then although one does not forfeit the essence of the precepts, one will incur retribution for the subsequent offense.
This is grave. What is called the impairment of hidden virtue (*guṇa*) is that which is deeply detested in the realm of the unseen.
If a lay follower (*upāsaka*) engages in sexual misconduct with a male servant, a slave, or an attendant, he commits an offense of non-expiation (*āpatti-ānantarya*) in both parties.
Other minor offenses are as explained above. If a lay follower engages in sexual misconduct with a courtesan who has not [given her consent]...
Regarding "the upright": committing sexual misconduct with one who is upright is an unforgivable offense; with one who is not upright, there is no offense.

If a person has died—even down to an animal—and their physical faculties have not yet decayed, to engage in sexual misconduct with them constitutes an unforgivable offense for a woman in three places.

Minor offenses are as explained above. If an upāsaka has personally undertaken the eightfold precepts (i.e., the eight prohibitions for one day and one night) and engages in sexual intercourse, he commits an offense.
Regarding the eightfold precepts that cannot be transgressed, there is no longer a distinction between wrong and right; one has violated them all.

If an upāsaka, even though he has not received any precepts at all, violates a person who observes the pure precepts of the Buddha’s disciples, then although he incurs no formal offense against the precepts, he shall never thereafter be able to receive the five precepts, nor even go forth to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The disciples of the Buddha who maintain pure precepts are the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
This applies even to one’s own wife on the day she receives the eightfold precepts; one must not violate her.
To violate her is likewise termed "destroying another's holy life" (brahmacarya). Question: Violating another's pure conduct is certainly called a grave offense.
Question: Suppose there is one who is instead seduced by the person receiving the precepts; would this constitute a formal obstacle (*antarāyika-dharma*)?
Or, if one commits an offense through ignorance and later feels regret, confessing with a sincere heart and requesting to receive the five precepts or to go forth—would this be permitted? Answer:

If one knows that the other person has already received the precepts, one ought not to follow their seduction. However, since one has already been seduced, the transgression will certainly be somewhat [lightened].
If one commits an offense through ignorance, the principle remains the same. However, the method for repentance is by no means a simple matter;
one must consult those of great virtue, esteemed reputation, and profound mastery of the Vinaya, for only then can this transgression be extinguished.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "I have two bodies: the birth-body and the precept-body.

If a son of good family were to erect a stupa made of the seven treasures for my birth-body as high as the Brahma-heaven, yet someone were to damage it, the sin of that person could still be repented.
But to damage my precept-body, the sin is immeasurable; one will undergo retribution like that of the Naga King Elāpattra."
This note indicates that pure precepts must not be deficient or transgressed. The body of precepts is the Dharma-body;

for the Buddha takes precept, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation as his Dharma-body. By means of this dharma of precepts, it has been transmitted from teacher to teacher.
This is precisely the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, which is eternally abiding and indestructible.
Should one personally violate the Brahma-faring or cause others to violate the Brahma-faring, this constitutes the destruction of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body;

therefore, it is a far more grievous offense than destroying a stupa containing relics of the physical body. The Dragon King Elāpattra is fully called Elāpattra, and is also known as I... [text ends].
*Rāva* and *Elā* are names of trees; the former means "foul odor" (*pūtigandha*) and the latter means "extreme.
This refers to the Dragon King who, in the past during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, was a bhikṣu who, out of a mind of anger, violated the precept against damaging plants and trees.
Because he did not know how to repent, this foul-smelling tree grew upon his head, causing him immeasurable suffering and torment. How much more so for one who commits killing?
How could one violate the fundamental and grave precepts against stealing, sexual misconduct, and false speech?

Now, regarding the two precepts against killing and stealing, those who possess even a slight degree of compassion or integrity and humility are generally unwilling to transgress them. Yet, this precept against sexual misconduct is the one most easily violated by people;
therefore, it is specifically addressed here with detailed instruction. Furthermore, since the sin of violating these precepts is heavier than that of destroying a stupa, one must uphold them.
...the merit [of this]. Is it not more weighty than erecting a stūpa? May the disciples of the Buddha reflect upon this.
The Fourth Precept on False Speech:
The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "I have, in various ways, rebuked false speech and praised those who do not speak falsely," and so forth.
Even in jest, one should not speak falsely; how much less so when speaking falsely intentionally. Regarding the offenses herein:

if an upāsaka, having neither known nor seen the supramundane noble dharmas, claims for himself, "I am an arhat" (one who has exhausted all afflictions of the three realms), or speaks toward those who are arhats (those who have nearly exhausted the conceptual afflictions of the formless realm), he commits an offense that cannot be rectified. If he says, "I am an anāgāmin" (one who has exhausted all afflictions of the desire realm)....

The Sakṛdāgāmin (who has abandoned six grades of afflictions of the desire realm); the Srotāpanna (who has exhausted all afflictions of the views); even up to the candidate for Srotāpanna (at the final moment of the "supreme mundane dharma," possessing the eight patiences with wisdom lacking one part);

if one attains the first dhyāna (associated with the fivefold qualities of joy and bliss born of seclusion); the second dhyāna (associated with the fourfold qualities of joy and bliss born of concentration);

the third dhyāna (associated with the fivefold qualities of sublime bliss free from joy); the fourth dhyāna (associated with the fourfold qualities of purity of equanimity and mindfulness); or if one attains loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

The immeasurable minds of compassion, joy, and equanimity; or if one attains the four formless absorptions—namely, the absorption of infinite space, the absorption of infinite consciousness, the absorption of nothingness, and the absorption of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; or if one attains the contemplation of impurity or ānāpāna (mindfulness of breathing).

Mindfulness—[herein referred to as "sending away and sending forth," which refers to inhalation and exhalation]. These two contemplations are the two nectar-gates of the Buddha-dharma; one should simply practice them, and one should not speak of "attaining" them.

Various devas come to my presence, as do various nāgas, yakṣas (swift-moving spirits), pretas (also called *pīlīta*, translated here as "ancestral ghosts"), and piśācas (spirits that devour vital essence).
The kumbhāṇḍas (jar-shaped malevolent spirits) and rākṣasas (terrifying demons) came to where I was; they questioned me, and I answered them.
I questioned him, and he answered me; both [of us] committed an offense of non-confession. This is a great falsehood.
It is established as an offense of non-confession by five conditions: first, the person to whom it is directed; second, the perception that the person is such [a person].
Third, having a deceptive mind. Fourth, speaking of grave requisites, such as saying that an Arhat or even a rākṣasa has come to one's presence.

Fifth, the listener understanding the meaning. If one speaks to a deaf person, a foolish person, or someone who does not understand the language, or if one speaks to non-humans, animals, and so forth, these all belong to the category of offenses requiring confession (deśanīya-āpatti).
If one originally intended to say "Arhat" but mistakenly said "Anāgāmin," it constitutes a middling offense requiring confession (deśanā-garhya), as it was not the intended meaning.
The same applies to other cases. If a lay follower (*upāsaka*) is asked, "Have you attained the Path?

and either remains silent or indicates it through physical gestures, this constitutes a middling offense requiring confession, as the matter has not been clearly expressed. This extends even to saying, "A whirlwind, an earth-spirit, or a ghost has come to me."

Regarding "those [offenses]": among the offenses that can be confessed (as per the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: claiming to have attained the general mindfulness of external ordinary persons when one has not; falsely claiming one's precepts are pure when they are not;

falsely claiming to have recited the scriptures when one has never done so), these constitute offenses that can be confessed. If an upāsaka actually hears but says he did not hear, actually sees but says he did not see, suspects something exists but says it does not, or says something exists when it does not—such false speech constitutes an offense in all cases.

[These offenses] are expiable (furthermore, double-tongued speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech all constitute transgressions; however, because the precepts are not lost, they are said to be "expiable. This does not mean that they lack the nature of natural offenses).

If one generates the intention to speak falsely but has not yet spoken, one commits a minor expiable offense (the distant preparatory stage). If one speaks but does not express the full intent, one commits a middling expiable offense.
(Whether spoken erroneously or indistinctly, it is merely termed a minor preparatory offense. If one says to another that one has attained the Way, one commits an irreversible offense.
If one is insane, mentally deranged, or speaking unconsciously, there is no offense.
The Fifth Precept on Alcohol.
The Buddha was staying in the country of Ceti at the town of Bhadravatī (the translation of which has not yet been seen).

In that place there was a wicked dragon named Ambatittha (the translation of which has not yet been seen), who was fierce, violent, and harmful; no one could reach that place, not even elephants, horses, oxen, or sheep.
Donkeys, mules, and camels could not approach him; even the birds could not fly over him. When the autumn grain ripened, he would destroy the crops.

The Elder Śāṇakavāsin (also known as Pāṇḍaka or Paṇḍa, translated here as "Born by the Side of a Small Road" or "Successor to the Path") had formerly been stingy with the Dharma and fond of drinking wine;

consequently, he was born dull-witted in this life, unable to recite a single verse in a hundred days. The Buddha ordered him to practice self-restraint, whereupon he realized arhatship. He then traveled through the country of Caitya and gradually arrived at...
Bhadrapāla, when that night had passed, rose at dawn, dressed in his robes and took up his bowl to enter the village for alms.
While begging for food, he heard that in this town there was a malevolent nāga named Āmrapālīta, who was fierce, violent, and harmful;
neither people nor birds and beasts could go to his dwelling place. When the autumn grain ripened, he would destroy it all. Having heard this, he continued his alms-round.
Having finished, he arrived at the dwelling place of the dragon Āmrapālī, beneath a tree by a spring. He spread out his sitting mat and sat down cross-legged.
When the dragon smelled the scent of his robes, it immediately gave rise to anger and emitted smoke from its body. The Elder Śāgata then entered into meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
By means of his supernormal powers, Śāgata’s body also emitted smoke. The dragon became even more enraged, and fire issued from its body.
Śāgata again entered the *tejodhātu-samādhi* (fire-element samādhi), and his body also emitted fire. The dragon then rained down hail;
Śāgata immediately transformed the hail into *śikṣu-pūpa*, *majjū-pūpa*, and *pāpara-pūpa*. The dragon then released a thunderbolt; Śāgata immediately transformed it.
He prepared various kinds of *modaka* cakes. The dragon again rained down arrows, bows, swords, and spears.
Śāgata immediately transformed them into *utpala* flowers (translated as "blue lotuses"), *padma* flowers (translated as "red lotuses"), and *kumuda* flowers (translated as "yellow lotuses").
At that time, the dragon again rained down venomous snakes, centipedes, earth-vipers, and millipedes. Śāgata immediately transformed them into *utpala* flowers.
Garlands: garlands of *campaka* flowers, garlands of *vārṣika* flowers, and garlands of *atimuktaka* flowers (*campaka* means "yellow flower";

*vārṣika* means "summer-born flower," also translated as "rain-flower" because it blooms only during the rainy season; *atimuktaka* was formerly called "shansi-i flower," or translated as "dragon-sweet flower").
All such powers possessed by the nāgas were manifested before Śāgata. Having thus displayed these virtues, [the nāgas] were unable to...
Because he was victorious, the dragon’s power and radiance were immediately lost.

Knowing that the dragon’s strength was exhausted and that it could no longer move, the Elder Śāgata transformed his body into a minute form, entered through both of the dragon’s ears, and emerged from its two eyes.
Having emerged from its eyes, he entered through its nostrils and emerged from its mouth; he then walked back and forth upon the dragon’s head, traversing its length without harming its body.
At that time, when the nāga saw these things, his heart was greatly startled; he was terrified and his hair stood on end.
Joining his palms, he addressed the Elder Śāgata, saying, "I take refuge in you. Śāgata replied, "Do not take refuge in me. You should take refuge in my teacher; take refuge in the Buddha.
The nāga said, "From this day forward, I take refuge in the Triple Gem. Know that for as long as I live, I shall serve the Buddha."
"Upāsaka, once this dragon had received the three refuges and become a disciple of the Buddha, he no longer committed such violent and evil deeds as before.
People and birds and beasts were all able to reach his abode; when the autumn grain ripened, he no longer damaged it.
Thus his fame spread throughout the various kingdoms: 'The Elder Śāgata is able to subdue evil dragons and bring them under control.'"
It was well. Humans, birds, and beasts were able to reach the dragon palace, and when the autumn grain ripened, it was no longer damaged.
Because of the Elder Śāṇakavāsin, his fame spread abroad; everyone prepared food and sent invitations to him.
Among them was a poor woman who possessed faith and reverence; she invited the Elder Śāṇakavāsin, and Śāṇakavāsin accepted her invitation in silence.

The woman prepared a milk gruel mixed with ghee and honey for him; he accepted it and ate it. The woman thought to herself, "If this śramaṇa eats this gruel of ghee and honey, his cold-natured constitution may be provoked.
She then took some wine that resembled water in color and gave it to him. Śākyamuni did not notice it and drank it.
After she had preached the Dharma to him, he departed and proceeded toward the monastery. At that moment, the effects of the wine began to take hold.

He immediately set out and fell to the ground near the temple gate. His *saṃghāṭī* robe and other items—the water filter, bowl, staff, oil bag, leather sandals, and needle case—were each lying in one place, while his body lay in another; being intoxicated, he was unconscious of anything.

At that time, the Buddha, together with Ānanda (here translated as "Joy," the Buddha's cousin born when the Buddha attained enlightenment and who served as his attendant; also translated as "Rejoicing" or "Untainted"), was wandering and arrived at this spot.
The Buddha saw this bhikṣu and, though he already knew, asked Ānanda intentionally: "Who is this person? He replied:
"World-Honored One, this is the Elder Śāgata. The Buddha then said to Ānanda: "Prepare a seat for me in this place and provide water."

He convened the community of monks. Ānanda, having received the instruction, immediately prepared the seating mats, arranged the water, and once the assembly was gathered, went to inform the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, I have already prepared the mats and arranged the water, and the assembly is gathered; the Buddha himself knows the proper time. The Buddha then washed his feet and sat down, asking the bhikṣus:
"Have you ever seen or heard of a dragon named Ambaḍa who is fierce, violent, and harmful, such as has never existed before?"
When people arrived at his dwelling, neither elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, donkeys, mules, nor camels could reach it;
even the birds dared not fly above it. When the autumn grain ripened, he would destroy all the crops. Good son, Śagata was able to subdue them and bring them to goodness.
Now that humans, birds, and beasts are able to reach the spring-fed lands, those among the multitude who saw this—
[The Buddha said: "He who sees, says 'I see,' O World-Honored One; he who hears, says 'I hear,' O World-Honored One. The Buddha spoke to the bhikṣu: "What do you think?
Is this son of good family, Śāgata, able now to subdue a frog? He replied: "He is not able, World-Honored One."
The Buddha said, "If even a noble person incurs such loss by drinking alcohol, how much more so for an ordinary worldly person?

Such faults and transgressions, or even those exceeding them, all arise from drinking alcohol. Therefore, from this day forward, if you say, 'I am a disciple of the Buddha,' you must not drink alcohol—not even a single drop on the tip of a blade of grass.
You must not drink it. Thus, the Buddha reprimanded the drinking of alcohol in various ways.
