Having finished speaking on the faults of alcohol, he addressed the bhikṣus: "There are two kinds of intoxicants that lay followers (upāsakas) must not drink:

grain-based liquor and wood-based liquor. Grain-based liquor is as you know. As for wood-based liquor, it is made by using various roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits, as well as various seeds and medicinal herbs, to produce a fermented liquid possessing the color, fragrance, and taste of wine, which when drunk can intoxicate a person; this is what is called 'wine. If..."
For an upāsaka, even swallowing [the dregs] is termed "drinking" and constitutes an offense. If one drinks grain-based liquor (surā), one commits an offense with every swallow.
If one drinks fermented vinegar-based liquor (maireya), one commits an offense with every swallow. If one drinks sweet wine (madhu), one commits an offense with every swallow.

If one eats yeast that can cause intoxication, one commits an offense with every swallow. If one eats drops of dregs, one commits an offense with every swallow. If one drinks the sediment of wine, one commits an offense with every swallow.

Regarding the offense of swallowing: if one drinks that which resembles liquor—possessing the color, fragrance, and taste of liquor—and is capable of intoxicating a person, there is an offense for every swallow.
If it merely has the color of liquor but lacks its fragrance and taste, and is incapable of intoxicating a person, as well as other such drinks, there is no offense.
"Vinegar" refers to that which is sour in taste. However, if its consumption can cause intoxication, it constitutes an offense regardless of whether the taste is sour or sweet.

"Fermenting agent" (*maku*) refers to the medicinal substance used to make wine. "Distilled dregs" (*teikō*) refers to what is now known as *shōchū* (burnt liquor). "Wine lees" (*shōtei*) refers to the dregs and sediment of wine;

the character for "lees" (*tei*) is pronounced *den*, and the character for "sediment" (*sui*) is pronounced *in*. "That which resembles wine" refers to fruit juices and the like that have fermented and matured to the point where they can also cause intoxication.
O person. This precept against intoxicants is a prohibitive offense (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) established for the purpose of preventing transgressions;

it is regulated in the same manner as the four preceding root precepts. An offense is committed through three conditions: first, it must be an intoxicant—meaning that which, when drunk, causes intoxication; second, there must be the perception of it as such—meaning one knows it is an intoxicant or it is mixed with intoxicants;
third, eight mouthfuls. With each swallow, a confessable offense (*duskṛta*) is incurred. If [it is consumed] within food...
If one knows that there is wine, or something boiled with wine, from which the nature of wine has already been lost and which cannot intoxicate a person,
in all such cases there is no offense. This is from the *Buddhabhāṣita-upāsaka-śīla-lakṣaṇa-sūtra*.

Question: In the original compilation, the *Sangīti* was categorized under the "Explanations of the Refuges and Precepts" and placed after this sutra. Why is it now appended before it? Answer: The original compilation was concise;
for the sake of convenience, this was appended there. Now that the present work is an extensive and complete collection, it should be placed at the beginning.
This is because regarding the Three Refuges and Five Precepts, when the Buddha first attained enlightenment, Yaśodharā’s parents were the very first [to receive them].

For the sake of the laymen (*upāsaka*) and laywomen (*upāsikā*) who have taken refuge in the precepts, there were at that time bhikṣus, as well as the three groups of lay followers—laymen, laywomen, and the three groups of novices (*śrāmaṇera*, *śrāmaṇerī*, and *śikṣamāṇā*).
At this point, before the bhikṣuṇīs had yet appeared, he preached this *Upāsaka-pañca-śīla-lakṣaṇa-sūtra*. Now that the six groups of disciples are complete, how much more so for King Śuddhodana!

Regarding this request: the Tathāgata’s teaching clarifies only the five precepts—those that may be expiated and those that cannot—in order to enable one to recognize the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*) and thereby be free from doubt.

Since the meaning of the Three Refuges (*tri-śaraṇa*) has not yet been addressed in the questions and answers, it is appropriate that the "Categorization and Explanation of the Refuges and Precepts" (*Śaraṇagamana-śīla-varga-vyākhyā*) should come first.
Furthermore, according to the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*, in the chapter on receiving the precepts (*upasaṃpadā-skandha*), there are the six fast days (*ṣaṭ-poṣadha*).
Question: Receiving the eight precepts daily is included within the six grave and twenty-eight light offenses of the Bodhisattva Precepts, which is to say, the Brahma Net Sūtra.
Why, then, is the precept against disrespecting auspicious times placed after this present sūtra? Answer:
The Buddha established the observance of the Eightfold Precepts of the Upavāsa fast. It is not restricted to lay followers (*upāsaka*);

whether Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, on fast days, on the Buddha’s birthday, on the anniversaries of the birth or death of one's parents or elders, on one's own birthday, or on days when performing various recitations and meritorious acts, one should always observe the Eightfold Precepts of the Upavāsa. As for what is called "fasting" (*upoṣadha*), it means...
Abstaining from food at noon constitutes the essence of the *upavāsa* (fasting). The eight precepts (*aṣṭāṅga*) close off evil and assist in the fulfillment of the fast.

This is because there is nothing like sexual desire that is a primary cause for birth and death, and nothing like food and drink that serves as a contributing condition for increasing birth and death.

However, since lay followers (*avadātavasana-upāsaka*) cannot permanently renounce their kin and family, they observe the five precepts for the duration of their lives, with the sole exception of abstaining from sexual misconduct.

If one receives the Eight Precepts of the Fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa-saṃvara), which are observed for only one day and one night, one strictly prohibits eating after noon as well as thoughts of sexual desire. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"On the six days of fasting, those who definitely receive the eight precepts and cultivate merit [should know that] on these days, evil spirits pursue people, causing them misfortune; therefore..."
At the beginning of the kalpa, the sages taught people to observe the fast (*upavāsa*), cultivate goodness, and perform meritorious deeds in order to avoid misfortune and decline;
they simply defined the fast as abstaining from food for one day. Later, when the Buddha appeared in the world, he said:
"You should observe the eight precepts for one day and one night, just as the Buddhas do, and not eat past midday. By this merit, you will not only be free from calamities..."

[This] is horizontal. In truth, it can accomplish supramundane nirvāṇa. Furthermore, in the *Tiwai jing* (Tiwei jing), it clarifies that one receives the eight precepts on the days of the Eight Kings.

As for what are called the "Eight Kings," they refer to the eight days of the commencement of spring, the spring equinox, the commencement of summer, the summer solstice, the commencement of autumn, the autumn equinox, the commencement of winter, and the winter solstice. On these days, the various deities of heaven and earth preside as yin and yang alternate.

This is why one receives the precepts. On all days of fasting and purification, one must not whip or strike sentient beings, nor should one engage in any conduct of body or speech that lacks dignified decorum, as explained in the *Vinaya-viniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā-sūtra*. One must not give rise to covetous desire or ill will.
Regarding the false perceptions such as afflictions (*kleśa*), one must further cultivate the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*).

As for the aforementioned four prohibitions, if one commits an offense against them, although the fast-precepts (*upavāsa-śīla*) are not technically broken, the fast-precepts are nonetheless impure. This is fully explained in the *Upavāsa Sūtra*.
It is said that there is a commentary (*vṛtti*) on this sūtra in one fascicle; I have now excerpted it here.
The Sūtra on the Fasting Observance Spoken by the Buddha (Extracted from the Mingzang, Yuanzi Case; i.e., the *Cīvarika-sūtra* from the Madhyama Āgama).
Translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty].
Annotated by the Śramaṇa Ouyi Zhixu of the Ming [Dynasty].
The Essential Summary of the Seventh Light Precept on Recent Events by the Upāsaka Chen Xiyuan of Ancient Hangzhou.
Regarding the six days of fasting each month, both groups of lay practitioners (upāsakas and upāsikās) should observe the fast.
As for the method of observing the fast: one may either go to a monastic community (saṃghārāma) or invite a teacher to one's own home.
At home. One may now receive it at home. Furthermore, for an upāsaka receiving the *poṣadha*, it is convenient to go to the monastery;
for an upāsikā receiving the *poṣadha*, it is convenient to remain at home. Moreover, in the Western Regions, there is no restriction regarding lay practitioners (*avadātavasana*).
In all practices of recitation and the cultivation of merit, one should observe the eightfold precepts of the fast.
It was heard thus: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the palace of the Prime Minister’s residence in the eastern part of Śrāvastī.

The Prime Minister’s mother, named Viśākhā, rose early in the morning, bathed, and dressed in colorful garments. Together with her sons’ wives, she went forth, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
[The Buddha] sat. The Buddha asked Vija: "Why have you bathed so early? He replied: "I wish to receive the upavāsa precepts together with my wives.

[He continued: "Colorful garments are the ordinary clothes worn at home; since they do not interfere with the eight branches [of the precepts], there is no specific rule requiring them to be dyed [in the prescribed monastic color].
If one has already received the bodhisattva upāsaka precepts and possesses the three seamless robes (*tricīvara*), one should be permitted to wear them on the day of receiving the upavāsa."
[The Buddha] spoke of it.
The Buddha said, "There are three grades of fasts (*upavāsa*). Which fast do you prefer? Vaira, kneeling with his right knee on the ground, said, "I wish to hear what is meant by the three fasts.
The Buddha said, "The first is the cowherd's fast; the second is the Nirgrantha's fast; the third is the Buddhist fast."

Relying on craving is like being a cowherd; relying on views is like being a Nirgrantha. To cultivate the eightfold path and the five mindfulnesses while eliminating both craving and views is called the Buddha-dharma.
The "Cowherd’s Fast" (gopālaka-upavāsa) is like a cowherd who seeks out fine water and grass to feed his cattle; at evening, upon returning home, he reflects:
"In which field is there such abundance? When dawn breaks, I must go back there. It is the same for members of a clan, whether men or women, who have already received the fast-precepts.
If one’s intent lies in the desires for wealth and industry within the household, or in thoughts of fine food and drink for nourishing the body, this is like the intention of that cowherd;
such a person shall not obtain great merit, nor is it the Great Illumination.
This is analogous to one who, although receiving the fast according to the Buddha-dharma, does not maintain the eightfold mental precepts nor practice the five recollections,
but instead fixates their thoughts on the five desires of the following day— just as a cowherd anticipates the water and grass for tomorrow. By extension,
this applies to those who observe the Buddhist precepts in this life while longing for the pleasures of humans and devas in future lives.

All are like cowherds; they cannot attain the great merit that transcends the world because they lack the great wisdom-light that transcends the world, which causes their aspirations for the mind to be so base and inferior.
Therefore, the concluding judgment states: "This is not the Great Illumination."
As for the Nigaṇṭha fast: on the fifteenth day of the month, at the time of the fast, one prostrates on the ground to receive the precepts.
One bows to the various deities within ten *yojanas* and says: "Today I observe the fast; I dare not commit evil. I am no longer called 'one who has a home. There is no kinship between you and me.
Wife, children, and servants do not belong to me, nor am I their master. However, their doctrine values literary form and disparages substance.

Substance. One who lacks a correct mind may reach the name of the next day [of the fast], as in the aforementioned case; yet one who observes the fast in such a manner shall not obtain great merit, nor is it true illumination.
*Nirgrantha* (尼犍) means "one who has severed ties" (*niḥsambandha*); it is the name for a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*). *Yojana* (由延), also called *yojana*, is forty *li*.
They prostrate toward various deities but do not know how to take refuge in the Triple Gem. They do not dare to commit evil;

although they do not fully enumerate the eight branches [of the precepts], their general intent is similar to the Buddhist precepts. They are not called "householders"; they have no kinship between self and others, nor...

Their precepts are largely identical to those of the Buddha; yet they are referred to merely as "Nirgrantha fasts" (ni-jian-zhai) not only because they do not know to take refuge in the Triple Gem, but because their teachings value outward form while disparaging inner substance, and thus lack a correct mind.

To "value outward form" means to apply elaborate ornamentation to the exterior in an attempt to please the eyes and ears of others. To "disparage inner substance" means to be ignorant of true cultivation and reality.
"To 'go' (詣) means to return to the root and revert to the source. To contemplate directly into True Suchness (Tathatā) is called 'rectifying the mind.

Not to be freed from the net of views is called 'lacking a rectified mind. Since the delusions of view remain entangled and the habitual tendencies of craving persist, it was as before when the next day arrived.
Although you now take refuge in the Triple Gem, you do not plan for the essential way of deliverance; you continue to value the literary and disparage the substantial."
Know that they are the same as those externalists, the Nirgranthas; by analogy, one may infer this.

Those who receive the precepts prize the reputation of being upholders of the Vinaya, yet their nature may not necessarily be pure in its subtle details regarding the prohibition of all karmic actions.

Those who expound the teachings prize the reputation of being great propagators of the Dharma, yet their essential path of cultivation and realization may not necessarily be precise, thorough, and clear. Those who practice Chan prize the reputation of having spiritual capacity...
They employ the names [of these practices], yet as for the matters within their own persons, they have not necessarily exhausted the source or reached the bottom.

Those who cultivate repentance value the names of vocal sounds and ritual protocols, yet regarding the precepts, principles, and contemplation, they have not necessarily mastered them through deep understanding or diligent practice;
they are all merely of the same sort as the Nirgranthas.
Regarding those who observe the Buddhist fast (*buddhadharma-upavāsa*): these are the disciples of the Way (*daodizi*). On the days of the six monthly fasts, they receive the eight precepts.
"Disciples of the Way" refers to lay disciples who have inherited the Buddha’s Way;

from those who merely take the Three Refuges up to those who receive the Bodhisattva Precepts, both groups of the lay community may bear this title. As for the six monthly fast days, they are the eighth day [of the lunar month].
The fourteenth day, the fifteenth day, the twenty-third day, the twenty-ninth day, and the thirtieth day.
If the month is short, the twenty-eighth day is taken to complete the count. These six days are the days when the Four Heavenly Kings, along with their princes and messengers, patrol the world.
Receiving the precepts and cultivating merit on these days yields twice the benefit compared to other times; it need not be said further.
Regarding the three months of the annual *zhāizāi* (fasting): monthly fasting is somewhat difficult and may be undertaken according to one's capacity;

daily fasting is easiest and should especially be observed. The three months of the year are the first, fifth, and ninth months. During these, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa presides over and guards the Southern Continent (*Jambudvīpa*);
one should likewise observe the fast and cultivate merit. The eight precepts are detailed as follows, or [the rule regarding] incense may be relaxed.
Flowers, songs, and dances constitute two [of these prohibitions]. Thus, the ninth day is not considered "inappropriate time"; it alone receives the name of a *zhāi* (fast/observance).
Although they differ in their expansion and contraction, there is no distinction in their essential meaning. Someone may ask: "To cultivate good and eliminate evil, one ought to do so continuously.

Why are only six days prescribed, waiting for the celestial deities to conduct their inspections before cultivating goodness? The answer is: Those who observe the six *zhāis* are not referring to ordinary days.

One may then easily fall into evil. As for the Great Precepts and the Five Precepts, they are to be upheld throughout one’s life; as for the Eightfold Precept Fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa), it is observed on six days [of the month].
This is like the feudal lords of the various states: how could they ever fail to cultivate their governance and spread their virtue during ordinary times?

How could the scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants ever fail to be diligent in their duties and occupations during ordinary times? It is only upon the occasions of imperial tours of inspection or the periods of provincial examinations that [they manifest their excellence].
One must also redouble one's vigilance and self-restraint. Thus, the Brahmajāla Sūtra contains the precept against disrespecting auspicious times.
It should be understood that this constitutes a superior merit for a bodhisattva and serves as a proximate cause for the supramundane for lay followers (*upāsaka*).

Furthermore, it is intended incidentally for a certain class of sentient beings with many transgressions; even if they are unable to cultivate wholesome deeds continuously, it causes them to temporarily distance themselves from evil.

As for karma: if one allows it to become habitual, its sprouts and shoots will gradually grow. If cattle and sheep are not tended, who knows that they might not eventually flourish as the fine trees of Mount Niu?
The first precept is to maintain a mind like that of a true person throughout the entire day and night, harboring no intent to kill, but instead maintaining thoughts of compassion.
Sentient beings must not harm or injure even the most minute crawling creatures; they must not take life with blades. With the intent to bring them benefit and peace, they must refrain from killing.
Thus, one should practice the pure precepts with a single-minded focus.

Throughout the entire day and night—meaning one must not hold this mind for only half a day or for only the middle watch of the night—one should maintain the mind as that of a "True Person" (*zhēnrén*).
"Arhat" is translated as "The Unattached," also as "The Unborn," also as "The Worthy of Offerings," and also as "The True One.
Here it is translated as "True Person. This refers to the supramundane fruit of sainthood; one should maintain the mind in accordance with it, compassionately mindful of all sentient beings.

To mindfully desire to bring benefit and peace to others is the excellence of active virtue (*pravṛtti-kuśala*). Not to commit acts of theft or harm, and not to engage in killing and so forth, is the excellence of cessation (*nivṛtti-kuśala*).
These two virtues—active and cessative—are called the pure precepts of all Buddhas; now, one should cultivate them with a single-minded focus.
Regarding the second precept: for the duration of one full day and night, maintain the mind like that of a true person (*satpuruṣa*). Be free from the intent of greedy grasping;
contemplate giving. One should give with joy, give with one's own hand, give with purity, give with respect, give without expectation, and give by overcoming stinginess and greed.
Practice this according to the pure precepts with a single-minded focus.
The intention is to be free from grasping. First, the goodness of cessation (*śamatha*) is clarified through the contemplation of giving and so forth;

next, the goodness of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is clarified through the phrase "not hoping for. This refers to practicing cessation: that is, giving at the proper time without a mind that expects either present or future rewards.
The four phrases on "rejoicing" serve to counteract stinginess; the phrase "not hoping for [reciprocal] giving" serves to counteract greed.
The third precept: for one day and one night, maintain the mind as that of a true person; be free from lustful intent and do not think of the chamber.
Cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and do not engage in perverse desires. Let the mind not covet forms, practicing with single-mindedness according to the pure precepts.

The two phrases concerning "the absence of lustful intent" first clarify the goodness of cessation (*śamatha*), which is the cultivation of the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). The subsequent two phrases concerning "not engaging in perverse desires" clarify the goodness of application (*pragraha*).
The two phrases on "the absence of lustful intent" again clarify the goodness of cessation. As for "pure conduct," it refers to the four dhyānas and the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*).
The fourth precept: For one day and one night, maintain the mind as that of a true person. Be free from the intent to speak falsely;

contemplate with utmost sincerity, speak calmly and deliberately, and do not engage in hypocrisy or deception. Let the mind and mouth correspond, observing the pure precepts by practicing them with single-minded devotion.

There is no intention to speak falsely; this collectively indicates permanent departure from the four transgressions. With sincere mindfulness, one is free from the fault of claiming to have attained what one has not.
Being composed, one avoids frivolous speech. Speaking slowly, one avoids harsh speech. One does not practice deceit or hypocrisy.

That is, one refrains from divisive speech, so that mind and mouth are in accord; one refrains from false speech. Both [the first four precepts] contain the intent of the two virtues of restraint (*saṃvara*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
As for the fifth precept: for one day and one night, one maintains the mind like that of a true person (*satpuruṣa*), neither drinking alcohol, nor becoming intoxicated, nor becoming deluded.
"Chaos. Not losing one's resolve. Removing the mind of heedlessness. Like pure precepts, practice with a single mind.

Regarding the phrase "not drinking alcohol," this serves as a general heading for abandoning all faults. Intoxication, delusion, confusion, and the like are all transgressions that inevitably follow from drinking alcohol.
The sixth precept: for one day and one night, maintain the mind like that of a true person;
do not seek comfort, do not wear fragrant flowers, do not apply cosmetics or rouge, and do not engage in singing, dancing, or entertainment. Practice this with single-mindedness as a pure precept.
Forms, sounds, fragrances, tactile objects, and other sensory realms are the domains where the six sense faculties find rest; therefore, it is said that one should have no desire for such rest.
The seventh precept is to maintain the mind as that of a true person for one day and one night, having no desire for rest.

One does not lie upon a fine bed, but uses a low bed, grass mats, or straw mats, abandoning sleep and reclining to contemplate the Way of the Sūtras with a single-minded focus, as in the pure precepts.
To practice [this]:
a bed that is high, wide, and beautifully adorned is called a "fine bed. To indulge in sleep is no different from a minor death.
Now, to renounce and eliminate sleeping and reclining is the goodness of cessation (*śamatha*); to contemplate the Way of the Sūtras is the goodness of cultivation (*vipaśyanā*).
The eighth precept: for one day and one night, maintain the mind as that of a true person (*satpuruṣa*). Honor the Dharma by eating only at the proper time; eat sparingly to moderate the body.
After the sun has passed its zenith, do not eat again. Practice this with a single-minded focus, as is the pure precept.

Eating at the proper time accords with the teachings of all Buddhas; it sustains the body to accomplish the Path, ensuring that the body is free from the suffering of illness and the mind attains peace and leisure.
It eliminates the fault of craving and indulgence at the tip of the tongue and the vexation of frequent management.

Eating at midday symbolizes the Middle Way; beyond the Middle Way, nothing further is required. This implicitly reveals the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Furthermore, regarding the sense faculties and their objects...
Relatively speaking, all [the sense faculties] possess the meaning of "nutriment" (*āhāra*). For example, the eye takes form as its nutriment, the ear takes sound as its nutriment, and so forth.

If one falls into the trap of mere auditory acuity or visual clarity, one becomes ensnared in the net of the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). If one pursues sounds and chases after forms, one will once again drift through the river of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Now, to speak of "eating at the proper time" means to rely solely upon direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); furthermore, to speak of "eating sparingly" means to be free from greed.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is explained that there are five types of dhūta practices regarding food. The third is not drinking liquids after midday;
the fifth is moderation in eating.
The Buddha told Vyeṣṭha: "On the day one observes the upavāsa fast, one should practice five reflections. What are these five?"

First, one should practice mindfulness of the Buddha. The Buddha is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, the Sugata, the Father of the World, the Anuttara, the Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, and the Buddha.

For one who practices this mindfulness of the Buddha, ignorance, evil intentions, and the habit of anger are all eliminated; a virtuous mind arises spontaneously, and one contemplates with joy the deeds of the Buddha. It is, for example, like...
When one washes the head with sesame oil and cleansing powder, impurities and grime are removed. For those who maintain the fast and recite the Buddha’s name, their purity is likewise such.
When others see this, none fail to believe and admire it.
In Sanskrit, *Tathāgata* is translated here as "Thus-Come One" (*Rúlái*). Because there is nowhere from which he comes and nowhere to which he goes, he is named "Thus-Come.

He emerges from the two truths by way of the Middle Way; thus, there is no coming or going. Having realized the Middle Way, he delivers sentient beings through this—therefore, he is the Thus-Come One.
In Sanskrit, *Arhat* is translated here as "Worthy of Offerings" (*Yìnggòng*), and it is also translated as "Worthy of Truth" (*Yìngzhēn*).

Now, translated as "Ultimate Truth" (Zhizhen): because he serves as a field of merit for the world, he is named "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat); because he is in profound accord with his own true nature, he is named "Ultimate Truth.
In the Sanskrit language, this is *Samyak-saṃbuddha*, which is translated here as "Perfectly Enlightened One" (Deng Zhengjue). "Perfectly" (*Samyak*) has the meaning of "universally" (*saṃ*);
it refers to being fully clear regarding the gates of differentiated phenomena, which is termed "perfect" (*samyak*). It refers to profoundly knowing the non-differentiated nature.

He is called "Right" (*samyak*) because he knows the two truths equally and correctly knows the middle truth; thus, he is the "Equally and Rightly Awakened One" (*Samyaksambuddha*). Furthermore, because the ultimate is not different from the conventional, it is "equal" (*sama*);
because the conventional is not different from the ultimate, it is "right" (*samyak*). He is "Illustrious" (*vidvat*) because he is endowed with the three types of knowledge (*tisro vidyāḥ*).

He is called "Well-Gone" (*Sugata*) because his conduct is perfect and he has wondrously transcended the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*). Since he dwells within the three realms of existence yet is not attached to them, he is the Well-Gone.

Furthermore, there are three kinds of lands, all of which are none other than the Land of Peaceful Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*). As the Sugata, the Father of the World, he is also called the Knower of the World (*lokavid*).
Having himself attained liberation, he is able to liberate the world—just as a wealthy elder emerges from a burning house and is able to lead his children out of that burning house.
His rank is the ultimate *samyaksaṃbodhi*, beyond which there is nothing higher; thus he is named the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara*). This is the Dharma of the Sūtras.

He is called the "Charioteer" (Śāstṛ), also known as the "Tamer of Men" (Puruṣadamyasārathi). Possessing the qualities of a great man, he is able to preach the sūtras to tame and guide sentient beings.
He expounds the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*) to elucidate immeasurable principles and to tame and guide sentient beings;

thus, he serves as the "Charioteer of the Dharma. Among the six realms of existence, humans and devas are the most excellent. Furthermore, the noble assemblies of the three vehicles all reside within the human and celestial realms. Therefore, the Buddha is [the preeminent being] among the devas.
The Teacher of Humans and Devas: that is, one who is equally embraced by the teachings and instructions of the nine realms;

because he has awakened himself and awakened others, and his awakening and practice are perfected, he is titled "Buddha. As for not saying "World-Honored One," since he is fully endowed with the ten titles, he is the most honored in the world;
this is to mention the specific while omitting the general. Recollecting the Dharma-gate can eliminate ignorance and delusion; recollecting the true mark can eliminate evil intentions.

To contemplate the marks and signs [of the Buddha] can eliminate the habit-energy of anger; when the habit-energy of ignorance, evil intent, and anger is entirely removed, this is the goodness of cessation (*śamatha*).

A virtuous mind arises spontaneously, and one contemplates with joy the deeds of the Buddha; this is the goodness of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). By means of the Tathāgata’s ten epithets, one can generate various roots of goodness, both mundane and supramundane.
Furthermore, the majestic power of these ten epithets can cause those who hear them to break through narrow-mindedness.
It subdues the inferior mind and destroys arrogance; through reverence and awe, one dares not harbor evil intentions.
Just as sesame oil and cleansing powder remove filth, mindfulness and wisdom are the instruments for eliminating delusions. One relies upon the Triple Gem in its essential unity.
Therein lies the abiding Three Jewels. Among these Three Jewels, the Buddha Jewel is the most honored; it is likened to the head.
Once defilements are removed, the head becomes pure; when the merit of mindfulness of the Buddha is perfected, the Buddha-nature manifests.
Second, one should contemplate the Dharma. One should reflect upon and never forget the Dharma taught by the Buddha—the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—which are complete and unimpaired.

One should know that this Dharma is the illumination for the world. For one who contemplates the Dharma, ignorance, evil intent, and the habituation of anger are all eliminated, and a virtuous mind arises spontaneously.
By employing the practice of delighting in the Dharma, it is like bathing the body with sesame oil and cleansing powder; impurities are thereby removed.

Excluding [other practices], those who contemplate the Dharma during the fast find its purity to be thus. When the multitude sees this, there is none who does not respond with faith. The Buddha-dharma is immeasurable;

however, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ*) fully encompass the path of cultivation and realization from beginning to end, and are therefore singled out for exposition.

They are divided into seven categories. First, the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), namely: body (*kāya*), sensation (*vedanā*), mind (*citta*), and phenomena (*dharma*), which serve as the objects of contemplation.

1. Contemplating the impurity of the body; 2. Contemplating that sensation is suffering; 3. Contemplating that the mind is impermanent; 4. Contemplating that phenomena are non-self—these constitute the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*). 2. The four right efforts (*catvāri samyakprahāṇāni*):

By means of the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness, one ensures that unarisen evil does not arise, eliminates evil that has already arisen, brings about the arising of unarisen good, and increases good that has already arisen.

3. The four bases of psychic power (*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*), namely: desire (*chanda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), exertion (*vīrya*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). [Regarding "desire": it is the longing, yearning, and aspiration for those dharmas. One-pointedness of mind...

Abiding correctly upon that object is mindfulness (*smṛti*); cultivating diligence without interruption is energy (*vīrya*); and the mind not being distracted through reflection is wisdom (*prajñā*). That all one's aspirations are attained constitutes the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

Among these, reflection leads to concentration; reflection leads to abandonment; and one is thus well able to accomplish the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Fourth, the five faculties (*indriya*), namely: faith, energy, mindfulness, [concentration, and wisdom].

Concentration and Wisdom (1. The faculty of faith: believing in the Right Path; 2. The faculty of diligence: seeking with tireless effort; 3. The faculty of mindfulness: contemplating with single-minded focus; 4. The faculty of concentration:

abiding in one-pointed stillness; 5. The faculty of wisdom: the internal nature illuminating itself). These constitute the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*). Five. The five powers (*bala*) are named as the faculties;

that is, when faith and the others have increased, they are able to destroy the five hindrances (the power of faith counters afflictions; the power of diligence removes laziness; the power of mindfulness destroys false conceptions; the power of concentration destroys discursive thoughts; the power of wisdom destroys all heterodox views). Six. The seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).

The factors (*aṅga*) are: mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, diligence, joy, pliancy, concentration, and equanimity. By regulating the mind so that it is neither sunken nor agitated, one enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

(Mindfulness refers to recollective thought; that is, when practicing the various path-factors, one should maintain mindfulness so that concentration and wisdom are balanced. Investigation, diligence, and joy belong to wisdom; pliancy, concentration, and equanimity belong to concentration. Seven.

The Eightfold Noble Path consists of right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right effort, right concentration, right mindfulness, and right livelihood—walking securely along this path (not proceeding by way of partiality or deviation is called the "Noble Path").
Regarding right livelihood: it means sustaining oneself by begging for alms, remaining free from the food of wrong livelihood.
These thirty-seven factors are able to transport sentient beings of the three lands to the three types of nirvana; therefore, they are [the factors of enlightenment].

The illumination of the three worlds should be fully possessed and never violated; contemplate it and do not forget it. (Regarding the three nirvāṇas: first, *prakṛti-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa*, which refers solely to the nature;

second, *pariśuddha-nirvāṇa*, where wisdom is perfected and delusions are exhausted; third, *upāya-śuddhi-nirvāṇa*, wherein this birth is not birth and the mind is eternally quiescent, and this extinction is not extinction, yet its application is ever-arising).

When receiving the precepts, one takes the Dharma as the body; thus, the body is used as a metaphor for the Dharma. To be ignorant of this is because the nature of the Dharmakāya is fundamentally pure.
Purity. When the turbidity of the three delusions is produced through illusion, and that turbidity is removed, the Dharma-body is revealed.

Third, one should mindfully attend to the assembly, showing respect and drawing close to them, relying upon and receiving their wise teachings. Among the Buddha’s disciples, there are those who have attained the stage of *srotāpanna* (stream-entry).

Those who have received the realization of the Once-returner may attain the realization of the Non-returner; those who have received the realization of the Non-returner may attain the realization of the Arhat;
those who have received the realization of the Arhat—these constitute the four pairs and eight classes of noble persons.

All of them are perfected in morality, perfected in concentration, perfected in wisdom, and perfected in the knowledge and vision of liberation; they possess noble virtue and are fully endowed with practice. They should...
One should join one's palms in reverence. Among those worthy of offerings in the heavens above and the world below, this is the assembly of the Sangha.

When one contemplates the Sangha, ignorance, evil intentions, and the habit of anger are all eliminated, and a heart of joy arises spontaneously. This is the work of delighting in the Sangha; it is like washing a garment with pure ash, whereby stains and impurities are removed.
For one who observes the fast and contemplates the Sangha, their virtue is thus. When people see them, there is none who does not respond with faith and affection.

The Sanskrit term *saṃgha* is translated here as "harmonious assembly. According to the Vinaya, there are four types of saṃghas: first, the shameless saṃgha, referring to those who have broken the precepts;
second, the mute-sheep saṃgha, referring to those who, though not having broken the precepts, are ignorant of the rules and laws;

third, the pure saṃgha, referring to the seven types of noble persons (ariyapuggala) both internal and external, as well as ordinary worldlings who uphold the precepts; and fourth, the true saṃgha, referring to the four pairs [of noble ones].

The eight types of noble ones. Now, one is made to contemplate the true Saṃgha: through reverence, one restrains the mind; through intimacy, one restrains the body; and through receiving the teachings, one restrains the mouth.
With the fulfillment of the sixteen moments of mind, one first ascends to the stage of the noble ones, which is called "attaining the stream" (srotāpanna), also known as "entering the stream.

This is the fruit of Srotāpanna. Having fully perfected the eight patiences (kṣānti) while the wisdom is lacking by one part, this is called "the recipient who has realized the stream. That is to say:
One who is without interval will necessarily realize the stage of the Stream-enterer (srotāpanna-pratipannaka).

Having abandoned six grades of the afflictions of the desire realm, one is called a Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), also described as "one who goes once and returns once," which is the fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin. This occurs at the time when five grades [of afflictions] have been abandoned.
One who is called a "candidate for the realization of the Once-returner" (sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka) is one who has exhausted the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm;

this is named "attainment of the Non-returner" (anāgāmin), which is also termed "not returning. This refers to the fruit of the Non-returner (anāgāmi-phala). When the eight grades [of afflictions] have been severed, one is called a "candidate for the realization of the Non-returner" (anāgāmi-pratipannaka);
this refers to the stage of the Non-returner. When the delusions of the three realms are completely severed, one is named "attainment of the Arhat" (arhat), meaning that one is...

Because it is in constant union with the ultimate truth (satya), it is the fruit of Arhatship (*arhattva-phala*). Progressing further to sever the volitions (*cetanā*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), one is called a "recipient of the true realization" (*sākṣātkārin*), which refers to the stage of the candidate for Arhatship (*arhattvaphalapratipannaka*).

Together, these constitute four pairs and eight classes (*aṣṭau puruṣapudgalāḥ*). Because they are fully endowed with wisdom (*prajñā*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*), they are called "Great Beings" (*puruṣa*).
Their nature is characterized by both positive and negative purity; being unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) and indestructible in essence, it is called "precept" (*śīla*).

The accomplishment of the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, and so forth, is called the accomplishment of concentration (*samādhi*). Seeing the four noble truths is called the accomplishment of wisdom (*prajñā*).

Attaining liberation from all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) is called the accomplishment of deliverance (*niryāṇa*). [In the text,] the two characters for "accomplishment of deliverance" are missing.

To discern the causes and effects of liberation without error is called the accomplishment of the knowledge and vision of deliverance (*nairyāṇika-jñāna-darśana*). Possessing the practice of wisdom, one enters the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
One who possesses noble virtue is called "Holy Virtue" (Āryaguṇa). One who is fully endowed with the practice of conduct is called "Endowed with Practice" (Caryāsaṃpanna). To state it briefly:
the three fruits and the four stages of the path (catur-yoga) constitute the partial realization of the fivefold Dharma-body (pañca-dharmakāya);
the fruit of Arhatship is the complete realization of the fivefold Dharma-body. One should join the palms and form the mudrā of mindfulness; by raising the joined palms, one gathers [the mind].

The three karmas [of body, speech, and mind] are directed toward the World-Honored One, the Field of Merit (puṇyakṣetra) above and below heaven. This constitutes the fulfillment of one's intention; by citing the Field of Merit, his virtuous conduct is manifested.

Nevertheless, when a lay bodhisattva observes the fast and directs their mindfulness toward the Saṃgha, they ought to apply themselves diligently with the three karmas toward the *tathatā-saṃgha* (the true Saṃgha), and they should likewise pay homage and make offerings to the *viśuddha-saṃgha* (the pure Saṃgha). As for those who are like "dumb sheep" or lack a sense of shame...

One must especially not treat the Saṃgha with contempt or dishonor. Just as even the elephant kings and rākṣasas respectfully submit to those wearing the *kāṣāya*—neither harming nor devouring them—how much more so for one who has taken refuge in the Triple Gem and calls themselves a lay follower (*upāsaka*) and a pure practitioner?
A joyful mind is itself a virtuous mind; "pure ash" is also a metaphor for mindfulness and wisdom. Since the Jewel of the Saṃgha belongs to the virtue of liberation, it is compared to clothing.
This is what is called the "garment of liberation. It is also the adornment of shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*), and it is the supreme patience of quiescence (*śānti-kṣānti*).

It is the nature-endowed Sangha-jewel, just as the body must necessarily have clothing. When mindfulness and wisdom remove defilements, then liberation is pure, adorned with all virtues, gentle, and compliant.

Fourth is the mindfulness of precepts. Having received the Buddha’s precepts with the body, one upholds them with a single mind—without deficiency, without transgression, without wavering, and without forgetfulness.

One establishes them well and guards them with care, so as to be praised by the wise; later, there shall be no cause for regret, and one does not harbor expectations. Thus, one is able to teach others with impartiality.

For one who thus recollects the precepts, ignorance, evil intentions, and the habit of anger are all eliminated, and a joyful mind arises spontaneously. One delights in the precepts and governs their practice;

it is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is removed, its brilliance shines forth. Such is the purity of one who recollects the precepts through the observance of the fast; when the multitude sees them, they are struck with wonder.
There is no one who does not delight in faith.
Regarding the Buddha’s precepts, there are differences between the seven assemblies and the nine assemblies, as well as between the two gates of the Great and Small Vehicles.

When it is now said that one "receives the Buddha's precepts," this refers specifically to the eightfold precepts observed for a single day and night; it concerns precisely these eightfold rules of training.

Because it fully encompasses the precepts associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sāṃvṛti-śīla*), those associated with the Path (*mārga-sāṃvṛti-śīla*), as well as the three groups and the five branches of morality, it is collectively admonished:
"Hold [it] with a single mind. Not being deficient and not transgressing refers to the *prātimokṣa* precepts; being immovable refers to the precepts associated with meditative concentration;

and not forgetting refers to the precepts associated with the Path. Furthermore, not being deficient, not transgressing, and being immovable constitute the precept of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*); not forgetting is...

To have no regrets later is the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*śīla-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*). To be able to teach others with equanimity and without expectation is the precept of gathering sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).
Furthermore, not to be deficient means to protect and uphold the four grave offenses (*catur-mūlāpatti*) such that the root is never impaired;

this is the precept of purity in fundamental action (*mūlakarma-viśuddhi-śīla*). Not to transgress refers to the remaining four branches of the precepts, as well as the preparatory means (*prayoga*) that flow from the roots.
They are entirely without transgression. Thus, their preceding and succeeding retinues and remaining pure precepts remain unshakable;

that is to say, they are not moved by the coarse and base five sensory objects (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) of the desire realm. This is the awakening to pure precepts, which is free from all evil thoughts. They do not forget;

that is to say, because right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) is present before them, they are able to skillfully establish themselves, exercising vigilance and protection. Even if they possess wisdom...
Regarding what such a person raises as questions: they act according to what they preach, and preach according to how they act; later, they have no cause for regret.

They thus maintain right mindfulness and recollect the pure precepts without expectation—that is, they do not seek for themselves the blessings and rewards of humans or devas, nor the stages of the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, or the provisional vehicles.
They are able to teach others with equanimity, relying solely upon the Supreme Vehicle (Ekayāna).
Having realized the bodhicitta, one vows that all sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm may simultaneously attain unsurpassed enlightenment.

This is then dedicated toward the fulfillment of the unsurpassed precepts of the Path. Taking this very one day and one night of the eightfold fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa) as the object of focus, one fully possesses within it the three aggregates and five branches associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-samprayukta*) and the Path (*mārga-samprayukta*), without deficiency or excess.
This constitutes the fulfillment of all Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, a treasury of immeasurable merit.
The fast and precepts (*upavāsa-śīla*) are the dharma-realm; all dharmas tend toward the fast and precepts, and do not transcend them. This is called mindfulness of the precepts (*śīlānusmṛti*).

If even a single day and night of fasting and precepts, encompassing all things both horizontally and vertically, is already like this, how much more so for the five precepts observed throughout one's entire life? How much more so...

If even the śrāmaṇera precepts are thus, how much more so the bhikṣu precepts? Those in the world who hold the precepts in contempt and seek a separate, perfect, and wondrous state do not reflect deeply enough.
For those who delight in upholding the precepts, the maintenance of the Triple Gem depends upon the precepts for its existence;

the realization of the Triple Gem as one essence depends upon the precepts for its attainment. Thus, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: "Fully and completely receive and uphold the precepts of dignified conduct."
It can cause the lineage of the Three Jewels to remain unbroken; therefore, it is called the "governing karma. The metaphor of the bright mirror refers to the Three Jewels as a single essence:
the Buddha is the head, the Dharma is the body, and the Sangha is the clothing. Only through the precepts can one clearly perceive them.

Therefore, the *Prātimokṣa* says: "It is like a person looking at their own reflection in a mirror; beauty and ugliness give rise to joy and sorrow. It further says: "The precepts are like a true jewel-mirror;
they reflect all phenomena without exception."

Fifth, one should be mindful of the heavens: first, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings; second, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; third, the Yāma Heaven; fourth, the Tuṣita Heaven; fifth, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven;
and sixth, the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven. One should reflect: "Because I possess faith, possess ethical discipline, possess learning, and possess generosity..."
The wise one who is mindful of the devas completely eliminates ignorance, malice, and the habit of anger; a joyful mind arises spontaneously.
Their delight in the work of the celestial realm is like a precious gem, always polished and clear. Such is the purity of one who observes the fast while being mindful of the devas.
The retribution of karma arises spontaneously without being contrived; this is called "heaven" (*deva*). The Four Heavenly Kings are:
Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the east, Virūḍhaka in the south, Virūpākṣa in the west, and Vaiśravaṇa in the north.

These guardians of the four continents dwell upon the terraces of Mount Sumeru, forty thousand *yojanas* above the earth. The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven—translated here as the "Thirty-three Heavens"—[is situated there].
He dwells upon the summit of Mount Sumeru. In each of the four directions there are eight heavens, with Śakra at their center, who governs the four continents.

It is eighty thousand *yojanas* above the earth. This is the Salt Heaven (*Lavana-deva*), also called the Flame Heaven (*Jvālā-deva*) or the Yāma Heaven; this translates as "Time-Portion" (*Kāla-bhāga*).
This means that because the light of the sun and moon cannot reach it from above, the beings possess their own radiance, which manifests through the blooming of lotuses.
Because these combined constitute day and night, sixteen thousand *yojanas* above the earth, there exists in the void a ground like a cloud, resting clearly and stably.

The Tuṣita Heaven—also called Dōushè and Dǔshì—is translated here as "Contentment," meaning that its inhabitants are fully aware of contentment regarding the five desires. It is situated thirty-two thousand *yojanas* above the earth.

*Abhāsvara* (Not-Exultant), also called *Nirmāṇarati* (Delighting in Emanations). This refers to those who, according to their will, emanate various pleasant objects while remaining free from arrogance and indulgence.
It is situated sixty-four hundred thousand *yojanas* above the earth. *Paranirmita-vaśavartin* (Mastery over Others' Emanations), also called *Tāvatīṃsa* (Others’ Emanations at Will).

This refers to those for whom the objects of enjoyment appear spontaneously and effortlessly, without requiring deliberate mental effort. It is situated one hundred and twenty [thousand *yojanas*] above the earth.

It is eighty thousand *yojanas*. As for not mentioning the form and formless realms, this is because, based on the merit of observing the precepts for a single day and night, one can induce the retributive fruits of these six heavens;
therefore, it is explained briefly by focusing on what is proximate. This is the fruit of mindfulness (*smṛti-phala*).
Next, "I possess faith and so forth" refers to the causes of mindfulness (*smṛti-hetu*), arising from faith in the Three Jewels and the precepts.

Because they uphold the precepts of the fast without violating them; because they have heard this Dharma-gate of the Great Mantra; because they are able to universally dedicate their merit to all sentient beings;
and because they possess correct wisdom that is clear and free from inversion—they are born among these six heavens, where they experience supreme and wondrous bliss, and gradually attain *nirvāṇa*.
While many sutras extensively clarify the "six recollections," here [the text] emphasizes the recollection of giving.

This is included within the mindfulness of the devas (*devānusmṛti*). Furthermore, regarding this dharma-gate of the mindfulness of the devas, the Āgamas clarify the mindfulness of the six heavens, meaning that one is mindful that birth in heaven results from the ten wholesome paths of action, and that even the heavens are characterized by suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self.

The *Avataṃsaka* clarifies the mindfulness of the merit of the Great Beings (*mahāsattva*) in the Tuṣita Heaven who are destined for rebirth in a single lifetime (*ekajātipratibaddha*). The *Nirvāṇa* Sūtra clarifies the mindfulness of the ultimate heaven (*paramārthadeva*). Now...
The matters of the sūtras are the same as those of the Āgamas. Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka* clarifies that the ten wholesome actions serve as the foundation for the five vehicles;
this is why celestial karma governs all things. By means of the adornment of merit and virtue, celestial karma is elucidated, and thus it is like a precious jewel.
When the ten kinds of precious jewels are polished and refined, they can cause rainfalls of treasure upon the four continents.

Through the repeated cultivation of mindfulness in celestial karma, one can assist the supramundane roots of goodness of the three vehicles (the five vehicles—Buddha, Bodhisattva, Pratyekabuddha, Śrāvaka, and Hīnayāna; or alternatively, humans, devas, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas are also called the five vehicles).
One should uphold the eight precepts and practice the five reflections. This constitutes the fast of the Buddha-dharma, whereby one’s virtue becomes equal to that of the devas.

By extinguishing evil and promoting good, one will be reborn in the heavens and ultimately attain nirvana. Therefore, the wise person exerts themselves through personal effort and extends their mind to cultivate merit.
One who does not fall into the views of craving is called a wise person. One who does not rely on others is called one who practices through self-exertion.
One whose inner and outer states are as one is called one who produces merit from the heart. If one does not practice with exertion, one is like a cowherd.
If one does not produce it from the heart, one values the letter while disparaging the substance; such a person is the same as the Nirgranthas. Examine this carefully.
In this way, Vaira, the merit and blessings of the fast are far-reaching and its renown is vast.

Suppose there were the sixteen great kingdoms of this world, and these sixteen kingdoms were filled with various treasures beyond measure; yet this would not equal the merit of observing the Buddhist fast for a single day.
If one were to compare their merit, the sixteen kingdoms would be like a single bean.

(This text is incomplete; it should read: "If these sixteen kingdoms were filled to capacity with such grains and used for almsgiving, the merit obtained would not equal the merit of observing the fast for a single day. [The merit of] bestowing rare treasures is merely... [the latter].

The cause of worldly fortune and happiness is the one-day and one-night fast (*upoṣadha*); it is definitively the cause for transcending the world. Furthermore, precious jewels are merely the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*);
whereas the complete observance of the fast and precepts constitutes the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*) and the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*).
The heavens above are vast and far-reaching, beyond all description. What constitutes fifty years among humans today is but one day and one night in the first heaven.
The lifespan in that first heaven of the Four Great Kings is five hundred years, which corresponds to nine million years among humans.
Regarding those who observe the Buddhist Dharma fast, they shall be reborn in this celestial realm.
This heaven is vast and far-reaching, beyond description; this serves as a general indication of the superior retribution of the six heavens.

First, the characteristics of the first heaven, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*), are presented, briefly citing the longevity of its inhabitants to manifest the excellence of their merit. Other sutras clarify the highest grade [of this merit].
The ten wholesome actions lead to rebirth in this heaven. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* clarifies that by virtue of the merit of refraining from killing, one attains rebirth in this heaven.

Now it is clarified that through the Buddhist fast (*upoṣadha*), one attains rebirth in this heaven. The ten wholesome actions constitute the mundane true dharma (*saddharma*) of the wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*).
Abstaining from killing is a lifelong precept for a one-factored *upāsaka*. The Buddhist fast (*upoṣadha*) is a merit of diligent practice for one day and one night;
both can induce this retribution. However, the retribution of the fasting ritual does not stop at this alone, as will be explained in detail below.

A hundred years among humans constitutes one day and night for the Trāyastriṃśa devas. The lifespan of the Trāyastriṃśa devas is one thousand years, which corresponds to thirty-six million years among humans.
Other sutras clarify that by cultivating the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*) to a superior degree, one attains birth in this heaven.

The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* clarifies that through the merit of refraining from killing and stealing, one attains birth in this heaven. Now, it is further clarified here that through the Buddhist fast (*upoṣadha*), one attains birth [in this heaven].

Two hundred human years constitute one day and one night in the Heaven of Salt (Saudharma). The lifespan in the Heaven of Salt is two thousand celestial years, which corresponds to one hundred and fifty-two million human years.
Other sutras clarify that by practicing the ten wholesome actions of the highest grade and additionally training in seated meditation, one attains birth in this heaven.
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* clarifies that through the merit of not killing, not stealing, and not engaging in sexual misconduct, one attains birth in this heaven.

Now, it is further clarified here that one attains birth [in this heaven] through the Buddhist fast (*upoṣadha*). It should be stated as one hundred million plus forty-four million years; I suspect the translator...
This is either due to an incorrect local dialect or an error in transcription.
Four hundred years among humans constitute one day and one night in the Tuṣita Heaven.
The lifespan in the Tuṣita Heaven is four thousand years, which corresponds to six hundred and eighty million years among humans.

Other sutras clarify that by practicing the ten wholesome actions of the highest grade (*adhimātra*) together with seated meditation (*dhyāna*), one attains the subtle abiding (*sūkṣma-vihāra*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and is thereby born in this heaven.
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* clarifies that by the merit of the three bodily and four verbal wholesome actions, one is born in this heaven.
Now, it is further clarified here that through the Buddhist fast (*upoṣadha*) one may also be born there. It should be stated: fifty million, seventy-six million years.
Eight hundred human years constitute one day and night for the gods of the Heaven of No More Excessive Joy (Atapa).
The lifespan of the gods of the Heaven of No More Excessive Joy is eight thousand celestial years, which corresponds to twenty-three billion four hundred million human years.

Other sutras clarify that one is born in this heaven by practicing the ten wholesome actions of the highest grade while concurrently cultivating the preparatory stage of concentration (anāgamya-samādhi).
Now, it is further clarified here that one may also be born there through the Buddhist fast (upavāsa); the lifespan should be stated as twenty-three million times ten million plus four million years.
One thousand six hundred years among humans constitutes one day and one night in the Heaven of the Transformation of Response (Nirmāṇarati).
The lifespan in the Heaven of the Transformation of Response is sixteen thousand years, which corresponds to nine billion two hundred and sixteen million years among humans.

Other sutras clarify that one is born in this heaven by practicing the ten wholesome actions of the highest grade while also attaining the concentration of the "not-yet-reached" stage (*anāgamya-samādhi*).

Now, it is further clarified here that one may also be born there through the Buddhist Dharma fast (*uposatha*); the duration should be stated as ninety-two million times ten million, plus one hundred and six million years.

If a person possesses faith, possesses precepts, possesses learning, possesses generosity, and possesses wisdom, and observes the Buddhist fast (upoṣadha), then at the time their life ends, that person’s spirit will be reborn in these six heavens above, where they will dwell in peace, security, and joy, and experience manifold goodness.
I have spoken but briefly; whenever ordinary people practice good deeds, their souls ascend to heaven and receive immeasurable blessings.
"Relaxation" (*yī*) means tranquility (*praśrabdhi*).
Having heard the Buddha’s words, Viyaya said with joy, "Excellent, excellent, World-Honored One! The merit of the fast is most refreshing and immeasurable.
I pray that you accept my observance of the Buddha's precepts; from this day forward, on the six days of the fast each month, I shall exert all my strength to cultivate merit until death."
"The exhaustion of the life-span is called death.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, they all joyfully accepted the teaching.
They rejoiced because the speaker was pure; they rejoiced because the Dharma taught was pure. Having heard the Dharma, they attained [realization].
Because it brings supreme benefit, one rejoices. Through present merit and happiness, one will be reborn in a good realm in future lives, ultimately attaining Great Nirvāṇa.
*The Sūtra on the Fasting Observance* (concluded). Appendix:

The Method for Receiving the Eightfold Uposatha Precepts (*In various sūtras and śāstras, the method for receiving the eightfold uposatha precepts is fully detailed. Generally speaking, the five precepts are the cause for birth as a human or a deva; this [one day]*...

The night-precept fast (*rātri-śīla-upavāsa*) is precisely the cause for transcending the world. Therefore, regardless of whether one has already received the five precepts or not, or has even reached the stage of receiving the bodhisattva *upāsaka* precepts, all may receive and maintain it according to their inclination.

Whether on the six fasting days (*ṣaḍ-upavāsa-dina*), one’s birthday, the anniversary of one’s death, or on days when performing various meritorious deeds, one should resolve to receive it by formally undertaking [the rite]. Although this sūtra consolidates these into eight branches, there is no fault in reciting them as nine branches at the time of formal reception;

for while the phrasing may be expanded or condensed, the meaning neither increases nor decreases. This follows the *Vibhāṣā* and other texts, as it makes the formal declaration easier to perform. (To receive this method of fasting, one must have a monastic—regardless of whether they belong to the Great or Small Vehicle—act as a witness.)

One may rely on the fivefold assembly; however, if one can simply ensure that no one in the world eats at improper times, one may act as a teacher. Should such a person be found to be entirely absent within even a few li, one may instead take the vow before a scripture or an image.

Taking the abstention from eating at improper times as the essence of the fast (*upavāsa*), the remaining branches serve as its support. Regarding the primary causes of birth and death, nothing surpasses sexual desire; regarding the most powerful conditions for increasing birth and death, nothing surpasses food and drink.

Therefore, a sutra says: "All sentient beings depend upon sexual desire to establish their very life and nature. It further says: "All sentient beings depend upon food to abide. Since those who live at home cannot yet permanently abandon their worldly occupations and the entanglements of kin, they are required to receive these Eight Precepts of the *Upavāsa* on the six fasting days.
For one day and one night (the causal condition for planting the seeds of eternal deliverance in future lives), one should first instruct them in the ritual of taking the Three Refuges:
"I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha; I take refuge in the Dharma; I take refuge in the Sangha. For one day and one night, I am a practitioner of pure conduct (*śīlavant*)."
"Venerable Upāsaka (or Upāsikā), the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is my World-Honored One" (recite three times).
"I, [Name], have completed taking refuge in the Buddha; I have completed taking refuge in the Dharma; I have completed taking refuge in the Saṅgha.
For one day and one night, [Name] is a pure-practice Upāsaka (or Upāsikā). The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is my World-Honored One" (recite three times).

Next, one should instruct them in the method for receiving the precepts and the fast (the eight branches, such as non-killing, are called "precepts"; abstaining from eating at improper times is called the "fast"; thus it is named the Eightfold Precept-Fast).
(According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, following the conclusion of the Three Refuges, one should say:

"I, [Name], whether through unwholesome physical karma, unwholesome verbal karma, or unwholesome mental karma, and due to greed, hatred, and delusion, have committed such offenses in this life or in previous lives. Today, with a sincere heart, I repent."

I repent. My body is pure; my speech is pure; my mind is pure. I shall receive and practice the eight precepts. (Having made this declaration, one then says: "As all Buddhas [have done]," and so forth.)
By the merit of these eight precepts of the *upavāsa* fast, I now repay the four debts of gratitude in their entirety and provide sustenance for all beings within the three realms of existence.

May it be shared universally with all sentient beings so that we may together be born in the Pure Land (or, if there are individual aspirations, they may all be included in the dedication; however, one must not depart from the Buddha-Dharma).
The *Sarvāstivāda-vibhāṣā* states: "When receiving the eight precepts of the fast (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*), one should say, 'For one day and one night, I shall refrain from taking life,' and so forth.
This is intended to ensure that the words are definitive and distinct, so as not to be confused with lifelong precepts.

The Buddha originally prescribed [the duration] as one day and one night; it must not exceed this limit. If one has the capacity to receive them for longer, once the first day has passed, one may proceed in succession."

One may receive [the precepts] again, according to one's capacity, without regard for the number of days. Regarding the method for receiving the *zhāi* (fasting/precepts), it must necessarily be received from another, specifically from among the five assemblies (*pañca-saṃgha*).
The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states: "If one first sends a messenger intending to execute someone..."
The messenger was slow and had not yet arrived. The man subsequently resolved his mind and received the *upavāsa* (fasting) precepts.

At the very moment he was about to receive the fast, the messenger arrived and he killed [the victim]. Although it was at a later time, because of the power of the precepts, he did not incur the sin of killing.

If there are those of noble rank who habitually command the commission of evil, if they wish to receive the fast, they must first issue a command to cease their previous evils; only then can they achieve success. If...
If one accepts the fast without first having issued a prohibition, it is not called attaining the fast. One who wishes to accept the fast should first issue a proclamation throughout their domain:
"I wish to observe the fast; on this day of fasting, all evil deeds and matters of punishment or execution shall be suspended."
