Chapter Ten: Contemplating the Mind.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, and bared one shoulder.
With his right shoulder bared, his right knee touching the ground, and his body bowed as he joined his palms, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, as the Buddha has instructed Miao-de and the five hundred elders, I shall expound for you all the subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground.
Now, within this place of enlightenment, the immeasurable and boundless assembly of humans and devas has all conceived a deep longing and yearning; I now submit this request on their behalf."

I ask the Tathāgata: what is the mind? What is the earth? I pray that the World-Honored One, with unconditional great kindness and unimpeded great compassion, will analyze and explain this for the sake of all sentient beings, so that those who have not yet escaped suffering may escape it;

those who have not yet attained peace and happiness may attain peace and happiness; those who have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment may resolve to do so; and those who have not yet realized the fruit may realize it.
They attain the realization of the fruit; being identical in the One Path, they attain nirvāṇa.

At that time, the Bhagavān, with the Great Seal of Wondrous Wisdom—the pure and definitive supreme Dharma obtained through his cultivation of all merit and knowledge over immeasurable kalpas—sealed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! You are now truly the Mother of the Buddhas of the three periods of time. All Tathāgatas..."
Throughout the stages of practice, he has always guided those who first give rise to faith.
For this reason, in the lands of the ten directions, all those who attain perfect enlightenment take Mañjuśrī as their mother.

Yet now, by the power of his original vow, you manifest in the form of a bodhisattva and inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the inconceivable Dharma. Listen attentively, listen attentively; reflect upon it well. I—
"Please explain this in detail for the sake of all. Yes, World-Honored One, we joyfully wish to hear it.
At that time, the Bhagavān had perfectly accomplished the supreme sustenance of all Tathāgatas, the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), and various rare and subtle merits.
He had already well attained the definitive and victorious Dharma of all Buddhas, the Mahāyāna Seal of Wisdom (*mahāyānajñānamudrā*).
He has already perfectly and completely realized the supreme, wondrous wisdom of the vajra secrets of all Tathāgatas;

he is already able to abide in unimpeded great compassion, spontaneously rescuing and gathering sentient beings throughout the ten directions; and he has already perfectly fulfilled the wisdom of wondrous observation.
"Without observing, one observes; without speaking, one speaks. This is the Bhagavān. He addressed the Mother of all Buddhas, the Great Holy Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying:

"O son of good family, this Dharma is named the 'Dharma-Gate of the Most Victorious Secret Mind-Ground of the Tathāgatas of the Ten Directions. This Dharma is named 'The Entry of All Ordinary Beings into Suchness'..."

This is the Dharma-gate of sudden enlightenment upon arrival at the stage [of Buddhahood]. This Dharma is called the true and correct path by which all Bodhisattvas proceed toward Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
This Dharma is called the subtle and wondrous jeweled palace where the Buddhas of the three periods of time enjoy the bliss of the Dharma for themselves.
This Dharma is called the inexhaustible treasury that benefits all sentient beings. This Dharma is able to lead forth the multitudes of Bodhisattvas.
It reaches the stage of sovereign wisdom at the pinnacle of form (*akaniṣṭha*). This Dharma can lead one to the foot of the Bodhi tree.
For the Bodhisattva in their final birth, this Dharma is the true guide; like a *maṇi* jewel, it rains down mundane and supramundane wealth, fulfilling the aspirations of sentient beings.
This Dharma can give rise to the source of the merits of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
This Dharma can dissolve all the fruits of evil karma of all sentient beings. This Dharma can bestow the seal of fulfillment upon all the aspirations sought by all sentient beings.
This Dharma can ferry all sentient beings across the perilous difficulties of birth and death.
This Dharma can quell the waves of the ocean of suffering for all sentient beings. This Dharma can rescue suffering and distressed sentient beings during times of urgent calamity.
This Dharma can exhaust the ocean of old age, sickness, and death for all sentient beings. This Dharma is well able to produce the seeds of the causal conditions for all Buddhas.
This Dharma can serve as a great torch of wisdom for the long night of birth and death.
This Dharma can act as armor to shatter the hosts of the four Māras. This Dharma is the banner of victory for the army of true valor.
This Dharma is the unsurpassed wheel of the Dharma of all Buddhas. This Dharma is the most supreme banner of the Dharma. This Dharma is...
This Dharma is the beating of the great Dharma-drum; this Dharma is the blowing of the great Dharma-conch; this Dharma is the Great Lion King;
this Dharma is the Great Lion’s Roar; this Dharma is like a great holy king of a nation, who is well able to govern with righteousness.
If one complies with the King’s transformation [of the people], one obtains great peace and happiness; if one violates the King’s transformation, one will immediately be executed and destroyed.
Good son, within the three realms, the mind is the sovereign. Those who can contemplate the mind attain ultimate liberation; those who cannot contemplate it remain forever bound in entanglement.
Just as all things arise from the earth, so too do the dharmas of the mind give rise to the virtues of both the mundane and supramundane worlds.
The five evil destinies; those in training and those beyond training; pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas—by these causes and conditions, the three realms are mind-only.
Mind is called the ground. All ordinary beings who associate with virtuous friends, hear the Dharma of the ground of mind, investigate it according to principle, and practice as taught;
who act for themselves and instruct others, and who praise, encourage, and comfort them—such persons are able to...
They sever the two obstacles, swiftly perfect all practices, and rapidly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, the Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, it is only the mental dharma (*citta-dharma*) that serves as the sovereign of the three realms.
Since the fundamental source of the mental dharma is unstained by defilement, how can the mental dharma become stained by greed and anger?"
Ignorance. Regarding the phenomena of the three periods of time, who says that these are the mind? The past mind has already ceased;

the future mind has not yet arrived; the present mind does not abide. Within all phenomena, their intrinsic nature cannot be apprehended; outside of all phenomena, their characteristics cannot be apprehended.
In the midst of all phenomena, nothing at all can be apprehended. The mental factors are originally without form;
the mental factors are originally without a place of abiding. Even all Tathāgatas do not perceive the mind, let alone other people being able to perceive mental factors.
"All dharmas arise from false conceptualization. For what reason and by what causal conditions does the World-Honored One now teach the great assembly that the three realms are mind-only?
We pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will explain this according to reality. At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"So it is, so it is, son of good family! It is just as you have asked. The nature of the mind and mental factors is..."

Emptiness and stillness. I shall employ various analogies to clarify this meaning. Noble son, the mind is like an illusory phenomenon, arising from pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) because it experiences pleasure and pain through various mental conceptions.
The mind is like the flow of water, arising and ceasing in every moment, for it does not abide even for an instant across past and future lives.
The mind is like a great wind, traversing all directions in a single kṣaṇa. The mind is like a lamp...
The mind is like a flame, for it arises through the convergence of various conditions. The mind is like a flash of lightning, for it does not abide for even a moment.

The mind is like space, for it is obscured and covered by adventitious afflictions (*kleśa*). The mind is like a monkey, for it roams among the trees of the five desires and does not dwell there even briefly.
The mind is like a painter, for it can paint the various colors of the world. The mind is like a servant...
The mind is like a servant, for it is driven and employed by the various afflictions (*kleśa*). The mind is like one traveling alone, for it has no second.
The mind is like a king, for it initiates all manner of activities with sovereign mastery. The mind is like an enemy, for it causes one's own self to undergo great suffering.
The mind is like dust, for it defiles itself by producing impurities. The mind is like a reflection, for in its impermanence...

Because one clings to phenomena as being permanent, the mind is like a phantom or a dream. Because one clings to the characteristics of self and phenomena as being a self, the mind is like a yakṣa, for it can devour all manner of meritorious qualities.
Because it delights in filth and evil, the mind is like a blue fly. Because it can harm the body, the mind is like a murderer.
Because it constantly watches for faults, the mind is like an adversary. Because it steals away merit, the mind is like a thief.
Therefore, the mind is like a great drum, for it gives rise to battle. The mind is like a moth, for it craves the color of the lamp.
The mind is like a wild deer, for it pursues false sounds. The mind is like a herd of pigs, for it delights in filth. The mind is like a swarm of bees, for it gathers the flavor of honey.
The mind is like a drunken elephant, for it is infatuated with the touch of the female. Son of good family, such are the mental states and mental factors as they have been described.
It has no interior, no exterior, and no middle. Among all phenomena, it cannot be found when sought; it cannot be found in the past, future, or present.
It transcends the three periods of time; it is neither existent nor non-existent. Yet, constantly harboring defiled attachment, it manifests from delusive conditions.
Conditions lack intrinsic nature because the nature of the mind is empty. Such emptiness is neither arising nor ceasing; it neither comes nor goes; it is neither identical nor different;
it is neither annihilated nor eternal. It has no place of origin and no place of cessation, nor is it something that can be separated from.

It is not that they are not far removed from one another. Thus, the mind and its attributes are not different from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the essence of the unconditioned is not different from the mind and its attributes.
The essence of mental phenomena (*cittadharma*) is fundamentally inexpressible; even that which is not a mental phenomenon is likewise inexpressible. Why is this?

If the unconditioned were the mind, it would be called the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*); if it were separate from the mental phenomena, it would be called the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*). It is forever free from these two characteristics.
Not clinging to the two extremes—those who awaken in this way are said to see the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Those who awaken to the ultimate truth are called noble ones (*ārya*).

The nature of all noble ones is fundamentally empty and quiescent; within the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), there is neither the upholding nor the violating of precepts, nor is there any distinction between great and small.
There is no mind-king (*citta-rāja*), nor any mental factors (*caitta-dharma*). There is neither suffering nor pleasure.

Such is the *dharmadhātu*, whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is stainless and devoid of the characteristics of superior, middling, or inferior distinctions. Why is this? Because it is an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma, and its nature is equal.
It is like the waters of many rivers that, upon entering the ocean, all become of one single taste, as they lack distinct characteristics. This stainless nature is not...
It is truly not false; this stainless nature is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). It possesses the characteristic of being inexhaustible and non-extinguished;
its essence is fundamentally unarisen. This stainless nature is eternally abiding and immutable; it is the most supreme *nirvāṇa*, for it is pure as my own self.
This stainless nature is far removed from all equality and inequality, because its essence is without differentiation. If there be any son or daughter of good family...
Those who seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should, with single-mindedness, practice this Dharma of Contemplating the Mind-Ground.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Mañjuśrī, Mother of Awakening throughout the Three Times, I now ask the Tathāgata for the Dharma of the Mind-Ground.
Within this great assembly, I shall now expound The gateway to the contemplative practice for attaining Buddhahood.
This Dharma is rarer to encounter than the udumbara flower; All the world should look toward it with longing.
The Buddhas of the ten directions who have realized great enlightenment, There are none who did not achieve it by cultivating this Dharma.
I am the Unsurpassed Teacher and Tamer of Men; Turning the wheel of the True Dharma throughout the world, I transform and deliver immeasurable sentient beings.
One should know that this is attained through awakening to the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground.
When all sentient beings hear this Dharma, they joyfully aspire to Bodhi and receive their predictions.
All those with the karmic affinity to receive the prediction who practice this gateway of contemplation shall become Buddhas.
The Buddhas themselves enjoy the great bliss of the Dharma, dwelling in the wondrous jewel palace of the Mind-Ground Contemplation.
Bodhisattvas who have received their office awaken to non-arising; By contemplating the gate of the mind-ground, they pervade the entire dharma-realm.
Bodhisattvas in their final birth sit beneath the tree of enlightenment; Entering this contemplative practice, they realize bodhi.
This Dharma can rain down the seven noble riches, A mani-jewel that fulfills the aspirations of sentient beings.
This Dharma is named the Mother of the Buddhas, Giving birth to the bodies of the three Buddhas of the three times.
This Dharma is named the Vajra Armor, Able to withstand the demonic armies of the four assemblies.
This Dharma can act as a great ship, Causing one to cross the middle of the stream and reach the place of jewels.
This Dharma is the most supreme great Dharma-drum; This Dharma is the lofty and eminent great Dharma-banner;
This Dharma is the adamantine great Dharma-conch; This Dharma is the illuminating great Dharma-torch that lights the world.
This Dharma is like a great holy sovereign, Rewarding merit and punishing transgression in accordance with the human heart.
This Dharma is like a fertile and moist field, Where growth and development depend upon the seasons.
I have used various analogies to clarify the meaning of emptiness; Thus one knows that the triple world is but the single mind.
The mind possesses great power, giving rise to the world, And is sovereignly able to act as the master of transformations.
Evil thoughts and wholesome minds are further accumulated; they are the causes and conditions for birth and death in the past, present, and future.
Relying on deluded karma, there is this world; the fruits of the desirable and undesirable perpetually succeed one another.
The mind is like a flowing stream that does not pause for a moment; the mind is like a whirling wind passing over lands.
It is like a monkey playing upon a tree, And like illusory phenomena produced by illusion.
Like birds flying through the sky without hindrance, Or people rushing toward an empty village—
Thus the dharmas of the mind are fundamentally non-existent, Yet ordinary beings, clinging in delusion, claim they are not non-existent.
If one can contemplate that the essence and nature of the mind are empty, afflictions and hindrances will not arise, and one shall be liberated.
At that time, the Tathāgata gave rise to great compassion for all sentient beings, just as parents cherish and care for an only child.
In order to extinguish the powerful wrong views of the world and to bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings, he proclaimed the *Cittāvalokana-dhāraṇī*, saying:
Oṃ (1) śitha (2) para (3) ti (4) veḍa (5) kalomi (6) (Note: The transliteration provided follows the standard Sanskrit phonetic conventions for the given characters.)
At that time, after the Tathāgata had spoken the mantra, he addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī:

"This divine spell possesses great majestic power. If there be a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, when holding this mantra, raises their pure hands and interlaces the ten fingers of both left and right, pressing the left over the right and gripping them together upright as if in a bond—"
Forming this shape is called the Vajra-Bandha Mudrā. Once this mudrā has been formed, practice the aforementioned mantra for one full recitation;

the merit obtained will surpass that of reading and studying the twelve divisions of the scriptures, being immeasurable and without limit, such that until the attainment of bodhi, one shall never again fall back.
Chapter Eleven: The Arousing of the Bodhicitta.
At that time, the Bhagavān had already successfully obtained the precious crown of the empowerment of all Tathāgatas; he had transcended the triple world;
he had attained perfect mastery over dhāraṇīs; and he had excellently and perfectly realized mastery over samādhis. Sublime...
It brings to full maturity the knowledge of all modes and the knowledge of all aspects, and is capable of producing the various distinctions among sentient beings.
After the Bhagavān had thus proclaimed this sublime gateway of contemplating the mind for the sake of all living beings, he addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"O Great Son of Good Family, I have already taught the Mind-Ground for the sake of sentient beings, and I shall likewise [teach]..."

The Great Dharani for Arousing the Bodhicitta was spoken, so that all sentient beings might arouse the mind of *anuttara-samyak-sambodhi* and swiftly perfect the sublime fruit. At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, the past has already ceased, the future has not yet arrived, and the present does not abide. Regarding these three periods of time..."
"All mental phenomena are by their very nature empty. As for that bodhicitta, what is meant by its 'arising'? Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will explain this for us, severing the web of all doubts and causing us to advance toward Bodhi.

The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, "Good son, among all mental phenomena, various false views arise. It is in order to eliminate these sixty-two views and their manifold varieties [that bodhicitta is spoken of]."
Because they are seen, I declare that the mind and mental factors are empty.
Such views are without any basis, like a dense and lush forest where lions, white elephants, tigers, wolves, and other fierce beasts dwell in concealment;

when their venom is unleashed, it harms people, and all traces of passage are cut off. At that time, there is a wise person who burns the forest with fire; because the forest has been emptied, the great [beasts]... [are revealed].
Just as there are no evil beasts left remaining, so too is it when the mind is empty and views are extinguished.
Furthermore, son of good family, for what reason is the meaning of emptiness established? It is because afflictions arise from the deluded mind that one speaks of this emptiness.

Son of good family, if one clings to the principle of emptiness as being ultimately existent, then the nature of emptiness itself is also empty; even the attachment to emptiness must be eliminated as a sickness.
[The Buddha] said: "Dismiss it. Why? If one clings to the meaning of emptiness as the ultimate, then all phenomena would be without cause and without effect;

what difference would there be from the Lokāyatika [materialists]? Good son, it is like the agada medicine, which can cure all illnesses. If there is a sick person who takes it, they will surely recover.
Once the illness has been cured, the medicine is eliminated along with the illness. To take the medicine when one is not ill—[the medicine would be useless]."

It results in illness once again. Good son, originally the medicine of emptiness was prescribed to eliminate the disease of existence; yet to cling to existence is a disease, and to cling to emptiness is likewise so.
What wise person would take medicine and thereby contract the disease? Good son, if the view of existence arises, it is better than the arising of the view of emptiness.
Emptiness is the medicine that cures the disease of existence, but there is no medicine to cure emptiness itself. Good son, for these reasons, one takes the medicine of emptiness.
Having eliminated false views, one awakens the mind oneself and is able to give rise to bodhicitta.
This awakened mind is itself bodhicitta; there are no two distinct characteristics. Good son, the mind that awakens oneself has four meanings. What are these four? They are:
ordinary beings have two kinds of minds, and Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have two kinds of minds. Good son, as for ordinary beings...

There are two types of mind. What are their characteristics? First, from visual consciousness up to mental consciousness, that which takes its own respective objects as conditions is called the "mind of self-awakening.
Second, apart from the five sense faculties, the mind and mental factors that take objects through a combination of conditions is called the "mind of self-awakening."
“Good son, these two minds can give rise to bodhicitta. Good son, what are the characteristics of the two minds of the noble ones?
The first is the wisdom that contemplates the principle of ultimate reality; the second is the wisdom that contemplates all objects.
Good son, these four kinds are called the mind of self-awakening. At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One...”

The mind has no form or appearance, nor does it have a place of abiding. When an ordinary practitioner first gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), upon what basis do they contemplate what kind of sign? The Buddha said:

"Good son, the sign of the *bodhicitta* contemplated by ordinary beings is like a pure and full lunar disc, abiding brightly within the chest. If one wishes to swiftly attain the stage of non-retrogression..."
One who dwells in an araṇya or an empty, silent chamber, with body upright and mindfulness correct, binds the aforementioned Vajra-bond mudrā of the Tathāgata.
With eyes closed, one observes the bright moon within the chest and reflects thus: "This full lunar disc is fifty yojanas in extent;
it is stainless, luminous, and pure, transparent both inside and out, and most supremely cool. The moon is the mind, and the mind is the moon."
Like the moon, unstained by the dust of defilements and free from the arising of false conceptualizations,

it is able to purify the bodies and minds of sentient beings and cause the great bodhicitta to be firm and non-regressive. Form this mudrā and recite while contemplating these subtle and wondrous verses on the great bodhicitta—
the mantra of the pure initial resolve of all Bodhisattvas.
Oṃ (1) bodhi (2) śita (3) mucipa (4) dhāye (5) mi. This dhāraṇī possesses great majestic power and can cause the practitioner never again to regress.
All Bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present, while on the ground of practice at the time of their first resolve, all single-mindedly contemplate and uphold this mantra.
One enters the stage of non-retrogression and swiftly perfects right awakening. Good son, at that time, the practitioner sits with body upright and right mindfulness, remaining entirely unmoving.
Binding the mind upon the lunar disc, one matures through contemplation; this is called the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of the bodhicitta and the samādhi of attaining Buddhahood.
If there are ordinary persons who practice this contemplation, whatever five heinous crimes, four grave offenses, or ten evil deeds they may have committed—
All such sins as those of the icchantikas are completely extinguished, and one immediately attains five kinds of samādhi gates.
What are these five? First is the kṣaṇa-samādhi; second is the paramāṇu-samādhi; third is the sitasūtra-samādhi;
fourth is the uccanīca-samādhi; and fifth is the supratiṣṭhita-samādhi. What is meant by the name "kṣaṇa-samādhi"?
"Dullness" refers to dwelling upon the mental recollection of a full moon for a brief moment. It is like a monkey that has something tied to its body;
it cannot go far, nor can it remain still nearby, but only stays momentarily, exhausted by hunger and thirst. The ordinary person’s contemplation of the mind is also like this:
attaining samādhi for a brief instant is called a "momentary" (kṣaṇa) samādhi. What is meant by "dust-like" (rajas) samādhi? It refers to [the state] regarding the three...
Faintly; it is partially associated. For example, suppose there is a person who constantly eats bitter things and has never tasted sweetness.
At one time, they obtain a drop of honey that reaches their tongue, causing them to experience superior joy and redoubled exultation, such that they seek out even more honey.
In this way, the practitioner, having consumed various bitter flavors throughout long kalpas, now attains the association with the three sweet [tastes].
It is faint; being associated with only a small portion, it is called the "dust-like" samādhi. What is meant by the "white thread" samādhi?

It means that for an ordinary person, from beginningless time until the end of the future, having now attained this concentration—just as when dyeing black, one sees a single white thread amidst a great deal of black—one such practitioner, amidst the dark night of many births and deaths, has only now [attained it].
One attains the White-Purity Samādhi (*śukla-viśuddha-samādhi*), which is called "the thread. What is meant by the Rising-and-Falling Samādhi?
It refers to when a practitioner observes that the mind is not yet mature; it may be well-established or not well-established.

Such a samādhi, being like a scale tilting up and down, is called "rising and falling. What is meant by the Abiding Samādhi? By cultivating the four preceding concentrations, the mind attains stability.

Abiding, one is well able to guard oneself and remains unstained by any defilements. It is like a person who, during the summer, travels far across sandy deserts and endures the full heat and toxicity, their mind parched with thirst until they can hardly endure it;
yet suddenly obtaining the sweet water of the Snowy Mountains or celestial *sudhā*, they instantly eliminate all feverish distress, and both body and mind become tranquil and at ease.
For this reason, this *samādhi* is called "Peaceful Abiding. Upon entering this concentration...
Thus, having distanced themselves from the obstacles of affliction, they sprout the seed of unsurpassed bodhi and swiftly ascend the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of a bodhisattva’s merit.

At that time, within the assembly, immeasurable humans and devas, having heard this profound mother of all bodhisattvas—the inconceivable great *dhāraṇī*—ninety-eight thousand bodhisattvas and others realized the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). Immeasurable...
Chapter Twelve: The Attainment of Buddhahood by Sentient Beings Who Have Resolved upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Bhagavat was perfectly established in the pure dharma-dhātu, which is equal throughout the three periods of time, without beginning and without end.
It is ultimate; immovable and serene, it is eternally without cessation or exhaustion. The radiance of great wisdom universally illumines the worlds.
Through skillful means, he manifests supernatural powers, transforming the lands of the ten directions so that there is nowhere they do not pervade.
This Bhagavān addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, saying: "After the practitioner of yoga has visualized the lunar disc, they should visualize three kinds [of things]."
The Great Secret Dharma. What are the three? First, the secret of mind; second, the secret of speech; third, the secret of body.

What is called the secret dharma of mind? The practitioner of yoga visualizes within a full moon the emergence of a five-pronged golden vajra, its radiance brilliant like molten gold, emitting countless great [rays].
White light. Observing by means of this is called the secret of the mind. What is meant by the secret of speech?
Oṃ (1) jñāna (2) vīra (2). This dhāraṇī possesses great power;
it is the mantra for all Bodhisattvas to attain Buddhahood. Therefore, it is so named.

The Secret of Speech. What is called the secret of the body? Within the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), with the body upright and right mindfulness established, one forms with the hands the foremost mudrā that guides one toward unsurpassed bodhi, placing it within the moon-disc at the heart-center.
"Good son, I shall now describe its seal-form (*mudrā*) for you. First, insert both thumbs into the palms of their respective hands.
Then, with the index, middle, and fourth fingers of each hand, firmly grasp the thumbs to form fists;
this is the Seal of the Firm Vajra Fist. Next, without altering the fists, extend—"
Extend the left index finger straight upward toward the void. Place the left fist at the heart. With the little finger of the right fist, firmly grasp the first joint of the left index finger.
Then, with the tip of the right index finger, point to the first joint of the right thumb, also placing it before the heart.
This is called the First Wisdom Seal for Guiding to Unsurpassed Bodhi. It is also...
It is named the Great Radiant Seal that Can Extinguish the Darkness of Ignorance.
By the power of empowerment through the binding of this seal, the Buddhas of the ten directions touch the crown of the practitioner’s head and bestow the supreme, definitive prophecy of Great Bodhi.
This is the Great Wondrous Wisdom Seal of the immeasurable mass of merit of the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana. At that time, once the practitioner has bound this seal, immediately—
Perform this visualization: All sentient beings together form this mudrā and recite the mantra.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there shall be no suffering from the three evil realms or the eight difficulties; all shall equally enjoy the supreme, pure bliss of the Dharma.
Upon my head now is a celestial jewel crown, within which the five Tathāgatas sit in the full lotus posture. I am Vairocana.
That Tathāgata is fully endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs;
he emits great radiance that illuminates the worlds of the ten directions, benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
To observe in this manner is called the Supreme Samādhi of the Eight Vairocana Tathāgatas. It is like a person who awakens to the subtle contemplation gate of Kālu and practices it themselves.
This is the visualization: "My body is that of the King of the Garuḍas; my mind and speech are likewise so.
By the power of this visualization, one can neutralize poisonous medicines; no evil poisons whatsoever shall be able to cause harm.

The practitioner who is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) should likewise perform the *vajraparyaṅka* posture, remain motionless in body, bind the *jñānamudrā* with the hands, and silently recite the mantra while the mind enters [into concentration].
This contemplation can extinguish the three poisons and eliminate karmic obstructions; it increases merit and wisdom, causing mundane and supramundane aspirations to be swiftly fulfilled.
The eighty-four thousand afflictive obstructions cannot manifest, and the heavy obstructions of the cognizable realm, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are gradually extinguished.
The great untainted wisdom, capable of severing with the diamond-like *prajñāpāramitā*, manifests.
[The preceding] is fulfilled; one will swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: "It is rare, World-Honored One! It is rare, Sugata! The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is rarer than the *udumbara* flower.
Even if he were to appear in the world, it would be difficult to preach such a Dharma as this—the ground of the mind, the threefold secret, and the unsurpassed Dharma."
The Wheel truly brings benefit and happiness to all sentient beings; it is the true and correct path for entering the stage of the Tathāgata and the stage of the Bodhisattva.
If there are sentient beings who do not begrudge their own bodies or lives and practice this Dharma, they will swiftly realize Bodhi.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: "If there are good sons or good daughters who wish to cultivate and practice..."

The wondrous gateway to attaining Buddhahood through the three secrets: those who would swiftly obtain the Tathāgata’s body of merit should don the thirty-two kinds of great adamantine armor of a Bodhisattva and cultivate this sublime contemplation; they will certainly realize the Tathāgata’s pure Dharmakāya.
What are the thirty-two armors? First, for the sake of sentient beings throughout immeasurable kalpas, not wearying of birth and death, this is the great armor of undergoing suffering.
Second, vowing to deliver immeasurable sentient beings, down to the level of ants, without ever abandoning it, this is the great armor.
Third, awakening sentient beings from the long dream of birth and death and establishing them in the three kinds of secrets, this is the great armor.
Fourth, the great armor of protecting the Buddha-dharma, which at all times responds like an echo.
Fifth, the adamantine great armor that forever extinguishes all afflictions and the dualistic views of existence and non-existence.

Sixth, the great armor of renunciation, whereby one can give away one’s head, eyes, marrow, and brain, as well as wife, children, and precious treasures, to anyone who comes to seek them. Seventh, [the armor regarding] what is received within the household.
Eighth, they are able to maintain the bodhisattva’s threefold pure precepts (*tri-koṭi-śīla*) and never abandon them;
this is the great armor of ascetic practices (*dhūta*). Ninth, they wear the garment of patience (*kṣānti-vastra*), even when encountering adverse conditions.
10. To not retaliate when reviled, abused, or whipped is the great armor of the tenth [vow]. 11.
To teach and transform all pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas, causing them to enter the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna) and turn their minds toward the Great [Vehicle], is the great armor of the eleventh [vow].

12. To have the body and mind free from strife and the mouth free from transgressions, while practicing with diligence day and night without ceasing—like a great wind—is the great armor of the twelfth [vow].
The thirteenth is the Great Armor of the Samādhi of Exposition: regarding birth-and-death and nirvāṇa as being without dualistic views, one benefits sentient beings with equanimity.
The fourteenth is the Great Armor of Unconditioned Great Compassion: benefiting all classes of beings, one never tires of or abandons them.
15. The Great Armor of Unobstructed Great Compassion, which rescues and gathers all beings without limit.

The Buddha said: "Because the body and its fundamental nature are essentially empty in substance, to speak of them as either 'existent' or 'non-existent' constitutes two separate dharmas. [The Buddha] explained that the matter pervades both the internal and external, yet its original nature is not seen.
The non-Buddhist said, "Great Man, if that original nature cannot be seen, how could one see it with my physical eyes? Or could it be seen with the divine eye?

"Great Sage, you speak falsely. If those things do not exist, why is it that we directly perceive such occurrences as weeping and laughing, frolicking and playing, anger and rage, hatred and love, and double-tongued speech?

This establishes two meanings. Furthermore, it was said: "O Great Being, if one cannot say whether something exists or does not exist, how can you say that there is attachment or that there is non-attachment?

Emptiness is not something to which anything corresponds, because its essence is ungraspable. The non-Buddhist said: "If this is the case, then why laugh and cry?"

Regarding matters such as playfulness, anger, hatred, love, and double-tongued speech, what should one perceive them to be? The Buddha said: "They are like a dream, like an illusion, like a transformation, and like a reflected image.
The non-Buddhists asked: "What is the nature of a dream? What is the nature of an illusion or a transformation? What is the nature of a reflected image? The Buddha said:

Regarding painful sensation: those sentient beings who are deluded and attached to that painful sensation fail to see the path to liberation through the avoidance of evil.

Their wandering in saṃsāra is like weaving a web; using thread, they move from one place to another, going and coming again and again. It is also like the two luminaries, the sun and the moon.
Whether moving through day and night, or appearing and disappearing, all worldly conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and will soon be destroyed.
The cycle of birth and death, with its coming and going, is likewise so. Yet the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is beyond the realm of ornamental descriptions.
