A householder disciple—that is, a lay bodhisattva—may likewise maintain one kind of disciple, namely a lay disciple.
Since such a person serves as a model for their teacher, they are by no means comparable to ordinary upāsakas; thus, how could the prohibitions and difficulties not be strictly observed?
Furthermore, within the teachings of this realm, supporting ritual practice is of primary urgency; therefore, the objects and circumstances of that practice must necessarily be [pure].
Only after [the obstacles] have been diminished can the principles of the Truth be brought forth. As for the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, it is a teaching outside the boundaries [of our own tradition];

because its scope for gathering disciples is broad, it excludes only those with the seven transgressions (*saptāvaraṇa*) and does not otherwise discriminate against others. However, what is called "understanding the words of the Dharma Master" is not something easy to achieve.
As the Sūtra says: "The great assembly must believe with their whole hearts: you are one who shall become a Buddha; I am one who has already become a Buddha."
One should always maintain such faith. When the category of precepts is fully perfected, one who possesses this faith is then able to understand the words of the Dharma Master;
thus, it appears easy but is in reality difficult.
3. Question: If one says they are unable to receive them, one should further say to them: "Good son, the Upāsaka precepts are extremely difficult to maintain. Why is this?
Because these precepts can serve as the basis for the Śrāmaṇera precepts, the Mahābhikṣu precepts, the Bodhisattva precepts, and even [the precepts of] the Arhat..."
Taking *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* as their foundation, those who wholeheartedly receive and uphold the upāsaka precepts will be able to obtain such precepts and immeasurable benefits.
If there are those who violate or break these precepts, [they shall suffer accordingly].
"Throughout immeasurable and boundless worlds, you have dwelt in the three evil realms and undergone great suffering and affliction.
Now that you desire to obtain immeasurable benefit, can you receive this with a sincere heart?"
One who receives this precept may likewise leave the household life to become a śrāmaṇera; may likewise leave the household life to become a bhikṣu;
may likewise advance to receive the Brahma-net precepts; and may likewise attain unexcelled bodhi. It is like the saying: "When the foundation is established, the Way arises."
Therefore, one obtains immeasurable benefit; yet if one violates it, the transgression is likewise immeasurable.

Fourth: When asked if one can take refuge in the Three Jewels, if they say they can, one should further say: "The Upāsaka precepts are extremely difficult to observe. Once you have taken refuge in the Buddha..."

"Even at the cost of one's own life, one shall never rely upon Īśvara or other such deities. Once having taken refuge in the Dharma, even at the cost of one's own life, one shall never rely upon the scriptures of non-Buddhist paths.
Once having taken refuge in the Saṅgha, even at the cost of one's own life, one shall never rely upon the heterodox assemblies of non-Buddhists.
Are you able to thus take refuge in the Triple Gem with a sincere heart?"
Question: The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states that a bodhisattva may even listen to the heterodox doctrines of outsiders (*tīrthika*).
It further states that if one daily devotes two parts of one's study to Buddhist scriptures and one part to non-Buddhist texts, this is called "non-offense. What is the meaning of this?
Furthermore, in temples nowadays, it is common to adorn images of deities and perform prostrations before them morning and evening. Why is this done?
"Is there no transgression? He replied: "One may study non-Buddhist texts for the purpose of subduing outsiders; it is not for the sake of practicing according to those non-Buddhist texts.
It is reasonable to adorn and maintain the temple deities, yet bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras must certainly not prostrate to them.
The recent debased customs of the monasteries are not worth mentioning; one should simply practice in accordance with the Vinaya. Tian.
The deity will naturally rejoice. Even if it be Maheśvara, who protects the True Dharma, it is likewise not an obstacle for an upāsaka to pay him homage.
He too has taken refuge in the Triple Gem; he is no different from a brother in the Dharma-gate.
5. Question: If one says they are able to bestow fearlessness, one should further say: "Good son, the Upāsaka precepts are extremely difficult to fulfill.
If a person takes refuge in the Three Jewels, that person has already bestowed fearlessness upon all sentient beings. If...

If a person can bestow fearlessness upon others, that person shall obtain the upāsaka precepts, up to and including anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Are you able to thus bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings?
Six. Explaining the Faults of Violating the Precepts (divided into two parts). First, the introduction:
If one says they are capable, one should further say: "A person has five things which, in the present life, cannot increase their wealth or lifespan."
What are the five? First, taking pleasure in killing; second, stealing; third, sexual misconduct; fourth, false speech;
and fifth, drinking intoxicants.
Next, the explanation [of these] (further divided into six): first, the transgression of killing living beings.
Because all sentient beings kill, they obtain in the present life an ugly appearance, weak strength, an evil reputation, a short lifespan,
the depletion of wealth and possessions, separation from their kin, rebuke by the noble and holy ones, lack of trust from others, and the commission of offenses against others.

To suffer calamity by encountering it unexpectedly is called the fruit of evil karma in the present life. After casting off this body, one shall fall into hell and undergo much suffering and affliction;
with long lifespans of hunger and thirst, along with such things as an ugly appearance, weak strength, and an ill reputation—this is called the fruit of evil karma in future lives.
Even if one obtains a human body, one will again experience an ugly appearance, a short lifespan, and poverty; such is this evil person.
By the power of these causes and conditions, all external five grains, fruits, and melons shall all diminish. The calamity of this person flows out to affect the entire world.
The "five grains" are millet, beans, hemp, wheat, and rice; "fruits" are the produce of trees; "melons" are the produce of vines. Question: What of the evil of a single person?
"Karma—what does it have to do with the world? If it is through the mutual resonance of shared karma, why is the blame placed upon one person alone?
If the evil karma of a single person is so powerful, then those who commit evil today are beyond counting; how then could the world remain established? The answer is:
"Indeed, when sandalwood is moved, its fragrance is smelled from afar; yet when a latrine is disturbed, its stench spreads in all directions."
It is understood that the power of good and evil karma is likewise so. Although those who now commit evil are many, those who cultivate goodness are also by no means few;
this is why the world is characterized by a mixture of suffering and happiness.
If it were not for the causal power of evil people, it would become a pure land; if it were not for the causal power of good people, the evil realms would be filled.
2. The Fault of Stealing, O Good Son.
If a person delights in stealing, that person will also obtain an ugly appearance, weak strength, an evil reputation, a short life, the depletion of wealth, and separation from kinsmen.
When others lose their property, suspicion arises toward oneself; even though one associates with people, they—
Not being seen with faith, one is constantly rebuked by the worthy and the noble; this is called the fruit of evil karma in the present life.
After casting off this body, one falls into hell and receives an ugly appearance, weak strength, and an evil reputation, suffering from hunger and thirst for a long duration of life;
this is called the fruit of evil karma in future lives. Even if one obtains a human body, one will be poor in wealth and property. Although...
They lose what they gain; they are not loved or cherished by their parents, brothers, wives, or children. Their bodies constantly suffer pain, and their minds harbor grief and affliction.
Because of the causal power of this evil person, all the people, in whatever they eat and drink, do not obtain physical vigor or strength.
This is the evil fruit of that person; the calamity flows out to the myriad commoners.
3. The Fault of False Speech, O son of good family:
If there is a person who delights in false speech, that person will in this present life obtain harsh words and an ugly appearance;
even though what they say is true, people will not believe or accept it, and the multitude will all detest them and take no pleasure in seeing them. This is called the evil of the present life.
As for the retribution of karma: after discarding this body, one enters hell and undergoes great suffering, tormented by hunger, thirst, and heat.
This is called the retribution of evil karma in future lives. If one obtains a human body, one's mouth will be incomplete;

though what one says is true, people do not believe or accept it, and those who see one find no pleasure in it. Even when one preaches the True Dharma, people take no delight in hearing it. This is the cause of being such a wicked person.
Due to the power of these conditions, all external objects and assets diminish.

Fourth: Regarding the fault of drinking alcohol, noble son, if there is a person who delights in drinking alcohol, that person in this present life will be prone to losing their wealth and property. Body...
The mind becomes frequently afflicted by illness; one constantly delights in strife and contention; a foul reputation spreads far and wide;
wisdom is lost; the mind lacks shame and remorse; one obtains an ugly complexion and feeble strength; one is constantly reviled by all; people take no pleasure in seeing one;

and one is unable to cultivate goodness. These are called the present evil retributions for drinking alcohol. After casting off this body, one dwells in hell, where one suffers from hunger, thirst, and the like. No...

One should measure this suffering; it is called the retribution for evil karma in future lives. Even if one obtains a human body, the mind will be constantly deranged and unable to maintain mindfulness or contemplate wholesome dharmas.
Due to the causal power of such an evil person, all external objects and assets will rot and decay.
5. The Faults of Sexual Misconduct, O Son of Good Family.
Furthermore, if there is a person who delights in sexual misconduct, that person is unable to protect their own body or the bodies of others.
All sentient beings who see them will give rise to doubt. Whatever they do is preceded by false speech, and at all times, they are constantly...
One experiences suffering and affliction; the mind is constantly distracted and unable to cultivate virtue; one is prone to losing wealth and property;
even toward one's own wife and children, the heart feels no affection; and one’s lifespan is short. These are called the evil fruits of sexual misconduct in the present life.

After casting off this body, one dwells in hell, experiencing wretched physical form and strength, enduring hunger, thirst, and a long life of immeasurable suffering and affliction. These are called the evils of the future life.
Regarding the retribution of karma: if one obtains a human body, one will have an ugly appearance and foul speech;

people will take no pleasure in seeing one, and one will be unable to protect one's wife, concubines, sons, or daughters. Due to the causal power of being such an evil person, one will lack mastery over all external things.

6. Question: Son of good family, regarding these six unwholesome dharmas that you have distanced yourself from, are you now truly able to remain far removed from them? If you say you are able, one should further say to him:
"Son of good family, there are four matters concerning the Upāsaka precepts that one must not perform. What are they?"
These four constitute the causes and conditions for greed; one should not speak falsely for their sake. They are the causes and conditions for hatred, delusion, and fear;
one should not speak falsely for their sake. These are the four improper dharmas. Are you able to abstain from them?
Greed, anger, fear, and delusion are the seeds of these four dharmas; only an Arhat is able to eradicate them completely.
Nevertheless, as soon as one receives the precepts, one must subdue and sever them. One should not, on account of these causes and conditions, engage in false or deceptive actions.

7. Question: Regarding the renunciation of the five [prohibitions] and wandering [in the world], if one says they are capable, one should further say: "Good son, there are five places where one receives the Upāsaka precepts."
There are places where one should not frequent: the houses of butchers, prostitutes, taverns, kings, and *caṇḍālas*.
Can you avoid these five locations?
*Caṇḍāla*. This translates as "butcher" (*túzhě*). Alternatively, it translates as "adorned with insignia" (*yánzhì*), meaning that one adorns oneself with evil karma.
When traveling, they shake bells and carry bamboo poles as their identifying marks; these are the same as those who beat dogs today, executioners, and their like.
Question: It may be appropriate not to frequent the dwellings of butchers, prostitutes, taverns, or *caṇḍālas*;
however, one should likewise not frequent the residences of kings. Is it then that an *upāsaka* is not permitted to hold public office? Answer:
Since the *upāsaka* precepts of a Bodhisattva are received from an assembly of twenty monks, he ought by principle to dwell in purity, delighting in the Way and forgetting worldly power.
How could you go on wandering among kings like those who run toward the heat and cling to power?

Among the Confucian scholars of antiquity, there were also those who did not serve princes or lords, holding their own aspirations in high esteem—such as Zisi, Mencius, Duan Gan, Xue, Liu, and others, of whom there were many.
Having already received the Bodhisattva Upāsaka precepts, you ought naturally to act in this manner.

8. Question: If one says that it is permissible to abstain from the five [prohibitions], one should further say: "Good son, there are five things that must not be done by one who has received the Upāsaka precepts:
first, not selling living beings; second, not selling swords or blades; third, not selling poison."
Medicine. Fourth, do not sell liquor. Fifth, do not press liquor. Regarding these five matters, are you able to abstain from them? To sell living beings is to wound compassion;
to sell swords, blades, and poisons is to draw near to the karma of killing; to sell liquor is to summon and entice those whose natures are disordered and souls are deluded.
Furthermore, in the Western Regions, the pressing of oil also causes great harm to the lives of insects. Therefore—
All these are termed "unwholesome restraint" (*akuśala-saṃvara*). In this region, when pressing oil, if one does not allow the insects to emerge first, there is no offense.

Nine. Question: Regarding the three abstentions from non-action, if one says they are capable [of observing them], one should further say: "Good son, in receiving the Upāsaka precepts, there are another three matters."
There are three things that should not be done: first, making nets; second, dying with indigo;
third, tanning hides. Can you refrain from these three activities?
In the Western lands, indigo dyeing also involves the killing of many insects; this is termed an "unwholesome discipline" (*akuśala-saṃvara*).
In this land, it is not so, and thus there should likewise be no fault. As for tanning leather, the hide is processed with saltpeter before it can be used.
Since this both harms compassion and results in foul odors and impurities, one should not do it.
10. Question: Regarding the two matters that must be avoided, if one says they can [abide by them], one should further say: "Good son, in receiving the Upāsaka precepts, there are again two matters."
There are two things that one ought not to do: first, games such as *chūpú*, *wéiqí*, and *liùbó*; second, various forms of singing, dancing, and musical performance.
Are you able to abstain from these two matters?
All of these belong to the category of indeterminate distraction and wrong karma; they obstruct and cause one to abandon the Right Path, and therefore should not be performed.

(11) Question: If it is said that one is capable after having distanced oneself from the four types of persons, one should further say: "Good son, there are four kinds of persons who receive the Upāsaka precepts."
"You should not associate with these four types of people: first, those who play chess and gambling; second, those who drink alcohol; third, those who practice deception;
and fourth, those who sell liquor. Are you able to distance yourself from such people?"

12. Question: Regarding the renunciation of negligence, if one says they are capable, one should further say: "Good son, in receiving the Upāsaka precepts, there are dharmas that constitute negligence."
What should not be done? What constitutes negligence? It is during times of cold, heat, hunger, thirst, or when one is full from overeating; at dawn or dusk;

when one is anxious (the character *qù* is pronounced *jù*, meaning fear or timidity, or a racing heart; it may also be pronounced *jù*, meaning shame and dread); while working; or at the very moment one first intends to work.
At times of loss, at times of gain, at times of fear, at times of joy, during times of banditry, famine, or illness; during the suffering of youth, middle age, or old age;
at times of wealth, at times of poverty; and for the sake of life or property—during such times as these, failing to cultivate wholesome dharmas is called negligence (*pramāda*).
Are you able to remain free from it?
13. Question: If one says they are capable of performing worldly affairs, one should further say to them: "Good son, before receiving the Upāsaka precepts, you must first study worldly affairs."
Once one has mastered the learning and sought wealth in accordance with the Dharma, upon obtaining such wealth, one should divide it into four parts.

One part should be used for supporting one's parents, oneself, wife, children, and dependents; two parts should be used for lawful trade and investment; and the remaining one part should be set aside.
"Accumulate and store it for future use. Regarding these four matters, are you able to do so?
(14) If he says he is able, one should further say: "Good son, wealth should not be entrusted to four places. First..."
First, an elderly person; second, one who is far away; third, a wicked person; fourth, one who possesses great power. These are the four types of persons to whom one should not entrust anything.
Are you able to avoid these?

15. Question: If one says they are able to distance themselves from the four types of evil persons, one should further say: "Good son, there are four kinds of evil persons regarding the reception of the Upāsaka precepts."

You should always distance yourself from these: first, those who delight in speaking of others' faults; second, those who delight in speaking of false views; third, those whose speech is gentle but whose hearts are evil;
fourth, those who do little but speak much. Are you able to distance yourself from these four types of evil people?
Question: A bodhisattva should exhort and transform all evil persons, causing them all to cultivate goodness. Now, you instruct one to distance oneself from four kinds of evil persons;
does this not perhaps contradict or cause one to lose the bodhicitta? Answer: Those who have long cultivated the path as great beings possess the power to transform others.
However, a bodhisattva at the initial stage of mind should first protect themselves. If one does not distance oneself from evil friends, one will inevitably fall under their influence.
Once the habitual taints have been removed, one causes the bodhicitta to be cultivated and increased; thus, one will not suffer from the inability to transform and deliver these beings.
Sixteenth: When both assemblies of monks are complete.
If it is said that he is capable, one should have this person attend upon and serve a wise renunciant for a full six months.

The wise person, in turn, should with a sincere mind observe the four modes of deportment of his body; if they know that this person is able to act according to the instructions, [they may ordain him].
After six months have passed, when the assembly of monks has gathered in harmony and consists of at least twenty persons, they perform the *jñapti-karman*.
"Jñapti" refers to the formal motion; "karman" is translated as "action" (*karma*), also as "that which is performed," and also as "the accomplishment of a matter."
There is also the method of performing the ritual through proclamation, which refers to performing the ritual before the assembly to accomplish the undertaking of receiving the precepts.
Question: When an outsider seeks to leave the household life, one merely prescribes four months of communal residence;

when a śrāmaṇera receives full ordination, only three masters and seven witnesses are required. Now, this virtuous person wishes to receive the upāsaka precepts—why must he necessarily complete [the period of probation]?

On the sixteenth day of the sixth month, one observes the four modes of deportment; only when one is able to act according to the instructions may one perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*) and confer the precepts before a community of twenty monks.
Is it not the case that leaving the household life is still easy, while this [process] is difficult by contrast?

Furthermore, if there are other circumstances such that the six-month period is not fulfilled or the twenty monks are not available, may one still receive them? Answer: This refers to a specific type of bodhisattva upāsaka.

This layperson is a leader among the laity; as one who assists the bhikṣus both internally and externally to together promote the Buddha-dharma, the transmission of the Dharma to him is treated with particular solemnity.
Since there are no other circumstances that permit it, I fear it would be difficult to grant permission lightly.
One may only confer the five general precepts, along with the precepts from the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* (which refers to the "Cultivation of the Mind" chapter) and the *Bodhisattva-bhūmi-śīla-sūtra*.
17. The formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) for the pure white [action]:

Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This person, so-and-so, now requests from the Saṃgha to receive the Upāsaka precepts for a full period of six months, maintaining the four dignified postures with a sincere mind and purifying the ground of adornment. This person is a man, endowed with masculinity.
"Body. If the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha remain silent; if it does not permit, let it speak.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) itself. Because the Saṃgha remains silent, they collectively grant permission for that person to become an upāsaka.
From this moment, he attains the status of an upāsaka; therefore, it is said that "the task is accomplished."
18. Encouraging the Acceptance of the Refuges and Precepts for the Sangha:
If they grant permission, the wise person should further speak as follows: "Good son, listen attentively, listen attentively!
The Sangha is already in harmony and grants you permission to maintain the Upāsaka precepts. These precepts are the very root of all wholesome dharmas."
Fundamentally, if there is one who accomplishes such precepts, they shall attain the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), up to and including the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
If one breaks these precepts, at the end of life, one shall fall into the three evil realms. Good son, this is the Upāsaka-precept.

It is inconceivable. Why is this? Having received these precepts, even while experiencing the five desires, one is able not to obstruct the fruit of a stream-enterer up to the fruit of a non-returner; therefore, it is called inconceivable.
Will you, out of compassion for all sentient beings, receive these precepts? If you say you can receive them, then at that time the wise person should next explain them to you.
The formula for taking refuge in the Dharma is recited a second and third time in the same manner. Having received the three refuges, one is called an upāsaka. Question:
Although the enjoyment of the five desires does not obstruct the noble fruit, how does this differ from the evil and false view which claims that sexual misconduct does not obstruct the Path?
Answer: The Buddha prohibited sexual desire for those who have left the household life; yet those [who hold the false view] falsely claim that sexual misconduct does not obstruct the Path.
Because it obstructs the Path, it is called "evil wrong view. Now, for laypeople, the Buddha has merely prohibited sexual misconduct;

he does not prohibit eating at improper times or consuming leftover food from the previous day. Nevertheless, if one upholds the precepts according to these practices and cultivates the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), one can realize the first, second, or third fruits of the path.
Therefore, it is said that although one may experience the five desires, they do not obstruct the attainment of the first fruit.
It is the same. However, if one establishes the realization of the fruit of *anāgāmin*, then sexual misconduct must also be permanently abandoned.
How could this be the heterodox claim that sexual misconduct does not obstruct the Path? Question: Why does a lay follower (*upāsaka*) not realize the fourth fruit, that of the *arhat*? Answer:
Because they still dwell at home and have not yet abandoned the remnants of stored food, they do not fulfill the qualities of a Worthy One (*arhat*).
Question: Since a śrāmaṇera also does not have the precept against consuming leftover food from the previous night, why is it possible for him to realize the four fruits? Answer:
Although a śrāmaṇera has not yet received the precept against leftover food, because he dwells within the saṃghārāma, he is able to abstain from such food;

therefore, he may also realize the four fruits. Once the four fruits are realized, the untainted precepts (anāsrava-śīla) arise together with the discipline precepts (saṃvara-śīla), whereby he immediately attains [the state of a bhikṣu].

He is called a bhikṣu. Question: Having already received the three refuges and the usual five precepts, and having now completed the six months, one undergoes the formal ritual of *jñapti-karman* before a community of twenty monks; why is it necessary to receive the three refuges again?
Answer: The three refuges are the fundamental source of all precepts; therefore, all precepts arise from the three refuges.
It is attained simply because the respective intentions are distinct; thus, the non-informative action (*avijñapti*) produced is likewise different for each.
Now, it is precisely by relying on these three refuges that one receives the name of a Bodhisattva Upāsaka.
19. Questioning what is maintained by meditative concentration:
At that time, the wise one should further say to him, "Good son, listen attentively, listen attentively!
The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, has spoken of upāsakas as being of one part, or half a part, or no part, or many parts."

There are those who fulfill the requirements. If an upāsaka has received the three refuges but has not yet received the five precepts, he is called an upāsaka [specifically, an upāsaka bodhisattva by the three refuges alone].
If, having received the three refuges, he undertakes and maintains one precept, he is called "one part" [an upāsaka bodhisattva with one-part precepts].

Having received the three refuges, if he undertakes and maintains two precepts, he is called "a small portion" [an upāsaka bodhisattva with a small-portion precepts]. Furthermore, there are those who receive three precepts...

Such a person is called a "half-part" (*ardhabhāga*) bodhisattva upāsaka. Since the "half-part" was already indicated previously, it is not repeated here; however, because they purify only three of the [five] bodily precepts, they are merely termed "half.

If one has received the Three Refuges and maintains two precepts, yet breaks one precept, this is called "without part" (*abhāga*). (If one breaks a single precept after receiving only one precept, this is also called "without part";

likewise, if one breaks a single precept after receiving three, four, or five precepts, this is also called "without part"—this is omitted here but can be understood by analogy). If one receives the Three Refuges and undertakes and maintains four precepts, this is called "many-part" (*bahubhāga*). If one receives the Three...
"Return home and receive and uphold the five precepts; this is called being 'complete. Do you now wish to be a one-part upāsaka, or a complete one?
Speak according to your inclination. At that time, the wise teacher should grant the precepts according to the disciple's inclination.
Question: Regarding the bodhisattva upāsaka precepts, how can there be differences ranging from one part to full completion?

Since there are such differences from one part to full completion, why is it that after the precepts have been conferred, the dharma of the six grave and twenty-eight light precepts is further explained?
Answer: This meaning shall now be clarified. In the Buddha’s True Dharma, emphasis is placed on the verification of actual practice.

He did not value empty fame. Although he was a layperson, he was able to give rise to the unsurpassed mind of great bodhicitta and maintained the four dignified postures (*īryāpatha*) purely for six months, thereby pleasing the assembly of monks.

Consequently, before an assembly of twenty monks, a formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) was made, and he received the three refuges. At that moment, he was designated as a *bodhisattva-upāsaka*. Even if...
Upon receiving the five precepts, one must also certainly train in and uphold these six grave and twenty-eight light rules.

However, although the five pure precepts appear coarse, they are actually subtle; they seem easy but are in truth difficult. Therefore, the teaching commands that one should reflect with careful scrutiny:
it is better to receive fewer and uphold more than to receive many and uphold few. If one does not receive them, that is one thing; but once received, they must be upheld.

If one upholds them, one must necessarily fulfill the categories and exhaust the ultimate meaning of righteousness. Only by reaching the utmost refinement can one be called a "one-part" *upāsaka* and so forth.

One should know that from the *upāsaka* who does not receive the five precepts, through the one-part *upāsaka*, up to the full-part *upāsaka*, all should collectively study and uphold the six grave and twenty-eight light precepts.
Regarding the Dharma of the precepts: even if one has not transgressed any of the six grave or twenty-eight light offenses, it is merely called "complete.
Even down to a single fraction [of the precepts], it is extremely difficult to seek out that which is subtle and without deficiency, because of this very nature of the precepts.
Therefore, each individual precept encompasses the six grave and twenty-eight light offenses.
Each individual precept can enable one to realize the first, second, or third fruits of the path, and even lead one to gradually ascend to unsurpassed *bodhi*.

Only a Buddha is able to fully perfect the merits of non-killing, non-stealing, non-sexual misconduct, non-falsehood, and non-intoxication; only a Buddha is designated as having reached the ultimate consummation of all things.

From the ultimate stage of the two parts up to the ultimate stage of the full parts of the precepts: even if one does not realize the fruit in this very life, by merely taking the three refuges, one will certainly be reborn among human beings;
with one part of the precepts, one will certainly be reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings; with two parts of the precepts, one will certainly be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
with three parts of the precepts, one will certainly be reborn in the Yāma Heaven; and with four parts of the precepts, one will certainly be reborn in...

Those who possess the full precepts will certainly be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven; those with partial precepts and so forth will certainly be reborn in the Nirmāṇarati or Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heavens.
If one takes these same three refuges and partial precepts and dedicates them toward the Pure Land, one will certainly be reborn in the World of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī).

According to the depth or shallowness of one's spiritual power, one is divided into the nine grades of lotus flowers. When distinguishing the fruit based on the cause, there is not even a hair’s breadth of confusion between them—not merely that.
It is like a mirror reflecting an image. May those who receive and uphold [this precept] contemplate this actual benefit and not cling to empty fame.
Twenty. Having formally conferred the six fundamental precepts, one further says: "The upāsaka has six fundamental dharmas."
That is to say, from the upāsaka who has merely taken the three refuges up to one who has fulfilled all requirements, all possess these six grave rules.
Twenty-one: the first minor precept, that of not killing living beings.
Good son, regarding the upāsaka precepts, even for the sake of one’s own life, one must not kill any living being down to an ant. If...
Once the precepts have been received, if one instructs by word or commits suicide by bodily act, that person immediately loses the upāsaka-precepts.
Such a person cannot even attain the stage of *uṣmagata* (warmth), much less the stages from *srotāpanna* up to *anāgāmin*.
This is called a precept-breaking upāsaka, a foul-smelling upāsaka, a caṇḍāla upāsaka, a defiled upāsaka, and a fettered upāsaka.
This is called the first weighty case.

Although it is for the sake of one’s own body and life, the heavy is cited by way of analogy with the light: if one should not kill even for the sake of one’s own body and life, how much less for other matters?
Even down to an ant—this is citing the light to illustrate the heavy: since an ant is extremely minute, it still should not be killed.

If one kills for the sake of one's own body or life, how much more so for the sake of other things? According to the *Wujie xiang jing* (Sūtra on the Characteristics of the Five Precepts), killing a human being constitutes an irredeemable offense (*anivārya-āpatti*), whereby one immediately loses the Upāsaka precepts.
Killing a non-human (*amanuṣya*) constitutes a middling redeemable offense; killing an animal constitutes a minor redeemable offense. These are not termed "losing the precepts.
If one repents, the guilt of the transgression is extinguished, though the inherent nature of the offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) is not extinguished. If one does not repent, [the guilt remains].

Thus, even if one commits a minor offense, one will still fall into the three miserable realms. Examining the present text closely, it appears that even killing an ant would result in the immediate loss of the precepts;

this should be further distinguished. If one has merely received the Three Refuges, or has received a portion—whether one or two parts—of the precepts against stealing and so forth, one should determine the gravity of the offense according to the *Wujiexiang jing* (Sutra on the Characteristics of the Five Precepts). If one has formally received this specific portion regarding killing...
Regarding the precepts: whether one observes them partially along with other factors, or receives them in their entirety, they are defined and adjudicated according to this sutra.

As for the "Heat" (ūṣmagata) stage: it is the initial position among the four roots of goodness of the internal ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). From the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one gives rise to a corresponding wisdom and attains the wholesome, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) five aggregates (*skandha*).
It subdues the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *vicikitsā-kleśa*). It is like drilling wood for fire, where one first perceives the sign of warmth; therefore, it is so named.
This is called the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*). Relying upon pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), one cultivates the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*);

through the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), one cultivates the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), thereby attaining the Dharma of Heat and proceeding up to the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), thus ascending to the state of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*).

If one violates pure ethical discipline, all the wisdom of the foundations of mindfulness and so forth will not be accomplished; it is like a tree without roots that does not produce sprouts or stems, or like a house [without a foundation].

There is no foundation; they do not establish the ancestral hall or its structures. The vessel for the path of pure conduct, which was received through the unconditioned precepts (*asaṃskṛta-śīla*), is now utterly destroyed;
therefore, it is called "broken morality. Like a corpse, it possesses no fragrance anymore; therefore, it is called "stench. One falls into a base and lowly lineage;
therefore, one is called a *caṇḍāla*. One remains far removed from the pure path; therefore, one is called "defilement."

Because liberation is difficult to attain, they are called *saṃyojana* (fetters). Question: If one is able to be without concealment and sincerely reveals [one's faults], can one universally perform repentance?
If universal repentance is possible, what is the ritual procedure? Answer: This sūtra contains no method for repentance.
Should one wish to repent, one must rely upon the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, or the *Vaipulya* (fangděng) sūtras, or the *Ākāśagarbha-bodhisattva-sūtra*. It is occupied by these.
Examine the various Mahāyāna teachings, such as the sūtras and so forth; then, select a single method from among them and practice it with total dedication.

Only by maintaining an extremely reverent mind and an exceedingly earnest commitment can one achieve success; this is by no means a matter for casual or perfunctory treatment. The following five examples should be understood accordingly.
The second is the Upāsaka precept against stealing:
even for the sake of one's life, one must not steal, not even a single coin. If one breaks this precept, [one fails in their vows].

Such a person immediately loses the upāsaka precepts. This person cannot even attain the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata), much less the stages from Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) up to Non-returner (anāgāmin).
Such a person is called a precept-breaking upāsaka, a foul outcaste (caṇḍāla), and an upāsaka defiled by fetters.
This is called the second grade of gravity.
For one who does not receive this portion of the precepts, stealing five *kārsāpaṇas* constitutes an irredeemable offense; four *kārsāpaṇas* or less constitutes a middling redeemable offense;
and one *kārsāpaṇa* constitutes a minor redeemable offense. For one who does receive this portion of the precepts, even one *kārsāpaṇa* is irredeemable.
Confession. The remainder is to be understood according to the examples in the preceding text.
Third, regarding the precept of not speaking falsely:
as an upāsaka, one must not speak falsely even for the sake of one's life. One may not say, "I have attained the contemplation of impurity," or "I have reached the stage of anāgāmin."
[The Buddha] said: "If one breaks these precepts, that person immediately loses the upāsaka-precepts.

Such a person cannot even attain the stage of 'Heat' (uṣmagata), much less the stages from Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) up to Non-returner (anāgāmin). This is called a precept-breaking upāsaka, a foul-casting caṇḍāla."
An upāsaka with defiled fetters is said to have committed the third grave offense.

Whether this precept was formally received or not, the gravity of the transgression is equal. Even for one who did not receive it, if they were driven to utter a false statement out of desperation for the sake of their own life or livelihood, it remains a middling offense that must be confessed and repented.

The fourth is the Upāsaka precept of refraining from sexual misconduct. Even for the sake of one's life, one must not engage in sexual misconduct. If one breaks this precept, that person immediately loses the Upāsaka precepts;
such a person cannot even attain the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata), much less the stages from Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) up to Non-returner (anāgāmin).
Such a person is called a precept-breaking upāsaka, a foul-candāla, and a defiled upāsaka. These are known as the four grave offenses;

whether one has received these precepts or not, the transgression is equal. Even for one who has not received them, if they yield to an evil woman out of necessity for their own life or body, being coerced by her threats of death, it remains a middling offense that can be repented.
The fifth is the Upāsaka precept of not speaking of the faults of the fourfold assembly:
even for the sake of one’s own life, one must not proclaim the faults of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, or upāsakas.
Upāsikā, regarding all transgressions: if one violates these precepts, that person immediately loses the upāsaka-precepts.
Such a person cannot even attain the stage of "warmth" (uṣmagata), much less the stages from Srotāpanna up to Anāgāmin.
This is called a precept-breaking upāsaka, a foul-candāla, and a defiled-upāsaka. These are known as the five grave offenses.
To proclaim the faults of others is like spitting out maggots; it is already the karma of harsh speech and double-tonguedness.
How much more so to proclaim the faults and transgressions of the Tathāgata’s fourfold assembly? Is this not the most grievous form of harsh speech?

Regardless of whether the fault is real or unreal, if one speaks with a mind intent on causing another to fall into punishment, one will certainly lose their precepts. However, if it is done with a mind of encouragement...
If one recites the precepts on behalf of others as appointed by the Saṃgha, it is called "not an offense. However, if one does so with a mind of anger, one commits a minor transgression.
Sixth, not selling alcohol: (The first half of the heavy precepts is concluded).
According to the Upāsaka-śīla, even for the sake of one's own life, one must not sell alcohol. If one breaks this precept, that person immediately loses [the status of a lay follower].
As for the Upāsaka precepts, such a person cannot even attain the stage of "Heat" (ūṣmagata), much less the stages from Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) up to Non-returner (anāgāmin).
This is called a precept-breaking Upāsaka, a foul Caṇḍāla, and a defiled Upāsaka. These are known as the six grave [offenses].
Question: Regarding the single act of selling liquor, which is a livelihood-generating occupation, why is it considered more serious if one does not greedily desire it nor drink it oneself?

Conversely, if one greedily desires and drinks alcohol, severing the seeds of wisdom and becoming a person of delusion, why is this considered less serious? Answer: Drinking alcohol merely causes confusion for oneself;
selling alcohol causes confusion for all beings. Therefore, the offense is more serious. As for livelihood-generating occupations, there are indeed proper ones. The [occupation of selling liquor]...
This refers to merchants who seek profit according to the Dharma; one should not engage in such evil conduct.
Whether it be merely the three refuges or the full precepts, if one violates this, one loses the Bodhisattva Upāsaka precepts.
Twenty-two. Regarding the binding of the heavy and the arising of the light:
Good son, if one receives such Upāsaka precepts and is able to maintain them with a sincere heart without violating them, then one shall obtain the fruits of such precepts.
Good son, the Upāsaka precepts are called an "ornament" (mālā) and are called...
It is magnificent; its fragrance is subtle and wondrous, pervading everywhere it reaches. It wards off unwholesome dharmas and serves as the wholesome Dharma and Vinaya.
It is a treasury of unsurpassed, sublime jewels, a noble lineage, and a place of great tranquility. It is the flavor of ambrosia and the ground for the arising of wholesome dharmas.
If merely by giving rise to this thought one obtains such immeasurable benefits, how much more so for one who single-mindedly upholds it!
"Not disparaging" refers to the praise of the merit of receiving and upholding [the precepts]. "Adorned with necklaces" is said in contrast to breaking the precepts;
for one who breaks the precepts lacks shame and remorse, and is thus like one who is naked. "Pervaded by exquisite fragrance" is said in contrast to foul odors, serving to exclude them.
Virtuous dharmas, up to and including noble lineage—compared to a *caṇḍāla*, the *caṇḍāla* is called one of evil discipline, a repository of sinful karma, and of low birth.
Now, by receiving the precepts, one spontaneously ceases evil and practices good;
the wondrous jewel of unsurpassed *bodhi* is produced, and one becomes capable of succeeding to the lineage of all Buddhas. Great Tranquility.
Regarding the "abode": in contrast to defilements (*mala*), it is the flavor of ambrosia (*amṛta*); in contrast to fetters (*saṃyojana*), it is the ground for the arising of wholesome dharmas.
This collectively praises the precepts as level ground. Furthermore, being adorned with necklaces is the quality of bliss; fragrance warding off the unwholesome is the quality of purity;
belonging to a noble lineage and tranquility are the quality of self; and ambrosia, which is non-death, is the quality of permanence. This is the initial arousal of bodhicitta.
At the moment of receiving the precepts, one immediately attains such a non-active (wu-wei) precept-body endowed with these four virtues.

To receive and uphold them in every thought-moment is to be fully possessed of the benefits of these four virtues in every thought-moment. (The six grave precepts have been explained above; below are the twenty-eight light precepts.)
Twenty-three. First, the minor precept on failing to provide support for one’s parents, teachers, and elders:

A virtuous son, as the Buddha has said, if an upāsaka, having received and maintained the precepts, is unable to provide support for his parents, teachers, and elders, this upāsaka incurs the offense of negligence (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*);
it does not constitute a formal downfall (*pārājika*), yet it is an impure transgression.
The following twenty-eight types of offenses involving the loss of mindfulness are also called "offenses of transgression against non-action" (*avijñapti*) and "impure action.
Should one commit even a single one of these, one must immediately perform repentance. If one does not repent, all such acts can lead to a fall into the three miserable realms (*trāya*).
This applies regardless of whether one is merely a lay follower who has taken the Three Refuges, or a bodhisattva upāsaka, whether partial or complete in their observance; there is no exception.
It is not so. Although worldly people who do not take refuge in the Triple Gem as upāsakas must still make offerings to their parents, teachers, and elders;
if they fail to do so, they will certainly incur sin. How much more so for a bodhisattva upāsaka?
As for the phrase "losing one's mind," it means losing the correct mental attention toward bodhi, as well as losing wholesome mental attention toward the world.
As for the term "not arising": to reform one's errors and renew oneself is called "arising. If one arises [in this way], one will not fall; if one does not arise [in this way], one shall fall.
Regarding the phrase "impure conditioned action" (*sābhisaṃskāra-akuśala*): both good and evil are discussed in terms of both unconditioned and conditioned action.
Since this is a conditioned evil, it is termed "impure conditioned action. Prior to receiving the precepts... [untranslated fragment].
When one attains the essence of non-informative precepts (*avijñapti-śīla*), then "good" is termed "informative" (*vijñapti*).

Once the precepts have been received and the essence of non-informative precepts has already been attained, even if one commits an offense through loss of mindfulness, it is merely termed "informative impurity. This is by analogy with one who has not yet received the evil precepts.
Before the unmanifest (avijñapti) non-restraint of evil has arisen, the evil is merely manifest (vijñapti). Once one has received the evil precepts, the unmanifest has already arisen;
thus, even if at times one encounters living beings and refrains from killing, or encounters objects and refrains from stealing, these are designated merely as manifest good.
At the very moment one first receives the precepts, the wondrous unmanifest precept arises, and all its merits are present in every thought-moment.

Because it is immeasurable, even if one should occasionally commit any of the twenty-eight kinds of offenses that cause loss of mindfulness, these merely contravene non-action (*avijñapti*) and are termed "action" (*vijñapti*).
This is like a person who falls ill by chance: if they take medicine, they will recover; however, if they do not take medicine, the illness may become severe or even lead to death.

Likewise, if one does not receive the precepts, even if they generate the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), it is as if they have never done so during the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Having received this body, by what practice does one cultivate the path to bodhi and perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas?
Second, regarding the indulgence in drinking alcohol:
if an upāsaka, having already undertaken and maintained the precepts, nevertheless indulges in drinking alcohol, that upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence.

If one does not give rise to the thought of falling [into transgression], and there is no impure intentional action, even if a full measure of wine enters the mouth of a Bodhisattva who has reached the stage of perfection (*pūrṇa-bhūmi*), it does not constitute an offense of loss of mindfulness (*smṛti-pramoṣa*).

Only when less than a quarter-measure is consumed for the sake of indulgence does it become an offense of loss of mindfulness. If wine is used as medicine or applied to a wound, these are both termed non-offenses.
Third: A person with a malicious mind cannot attend to the suffering of illness.
If an upāsaka, having received and maintained the precepts, has a malicious mind and does not attend to the suffering of illness, he is such an upāsaka.
One incurs the offense of a transgression of mind if one fails to arise [in resolve], falls away, acts with impurity, or harbors an evil mind;
thus one incurs the offense. However, if one possesses a compassionate mind but lacks the capacity to act, there is no violation.
Fourth: If there is a beggar and one does not give to them—
specifically, if an upāsaka who has received and maintains the precepts, upon seeing a beggar, is unable to give a portion according to their means,

whether it be much or little (the term *gai* meaning to beg or to solicit), and thus sends them away empty-handed— this upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) and falls from his resolve.
Falling [into impurity]. Performing an act while impure.
Begging for what is inappropriate. Or, if one truly lacks this object and has nothing with which to respond, there is no offense.
Fifth: Seeing the fourfold assembly and being unable to go forward to greet them, bow to them, or inquire after their well-being.
If an upāsaka, having received and maintained the precepts, sees a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, an elder, a senior,
an upāsaka, or an upāsikā, and fails to rise to greet them, pay homage, or inquire after their well-being, this upāsaka incurs a transgression of negligence (manas-kṛta-āpatti).
He does not fall [from the precepts], yet his conduct is impure.
If one has a serious illness, or is among a gathering where the Dharma is being preached, or is sitting in meditation and absorbed in *samādhi*, there is no offense.
Sixth: seeing that the fourfold assembly violates the precepts, one gives rise to arrogance;
or if a lay follower (*upāsaka*), having received and upheld the precepts, [sees] a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, an upāsaka, or an [upāsikā]...

If he disparages the precepts he has received, giving rise to arrogance in his mind and saying, "I am superior to them; they are not my equal," this upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence (manasikāra-doṣa).
It does not constitute a formal fall (pārājika), yet it is an impure transgression.
Seeing others violating the precepts, one should give rise to great compassion and reflect upon oneself: "How can I give rise to arrogance?

Seventh: Regarding the six monthly fast days (*upoṣadha*), if one does not additionally undertake the eight precepts, even if one makes offerings to the Triple Gem as a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who has already received and maintains the precepts, one will be unable to observe the eight precepts on those six days throughout the month.
If an upāsaka makes offerings to the Triple Gem and incurs the offense of "loss of intention" (*manasikāra-apatti*), he does not fall into a state of formal transgression (*pārājika*).

However, if he acts impurely, fails to show respect, or neglects the proper time [for practice], his wholesome dharmas will decline; therefore, there is an offense. This does not constitute a transgression in the case of serious illness.
Eighth: Not going to listen to the Dharma.
If a lay follower (upāsaka), having received and upheld the precepts, is unable to go to a place where the Dharma is being preached within a distance of forty li.
Such an upāsaka incurs the offense of negligence (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), yet he does not fall into a state of defeat (*pārājika*). His conduct remains impure due to his actions;
however, there is no transgression if he does not go because he is personally engaged in superior practice, suffers from a grave illness, or if the other person is preaching the Dharma erroneously.
Ninth: Receiving items for communal use by the Saṃgha.

If a lay follower (upāsaka), having undertaken the precepts, receives bedding and furniture belonging to the *cātuddisa-saṃgha* (here translated as "the Saṃgha of the four quarters"; it is also rendered as "donations for separate rooms").

Regarding beds and seats: if an upāsaka uses them, he incurs an offense of negligence (āpatti-pratikṣepaṇa), though it does not constitute a formal falling away (pārājika) or an impure formal act (saṃghāvaśeṣa).
Since he has not yet entered the number of the Saṃgha, he should not receive [these items]. However, if he uses them temporarily within a monastery, there is no offense.
Tenth: Regarding the drinking of water containing insects—if an upāsaka, having undertaken the precepts, drinks water while suspecting that it contains insects, this upāsaka [commits an offense].
If one commits an offense through loss of mindfulness, it does not lead to falling away; yet there is impurity in such action.
If there is doubt, one should inspect carefully. One should use a water-strainer, or drink only after careful inspection confirms that no insects are present. Only then may it be used for drinking.
Eleventh: Regarding traveling alone through dangerous places.
If an upāsaka, having received and maintained the precepts, travels alone through a dangerous place without a companion, that upāsaka—

To incur an offense through loss of mindfulness, to fail to rise when falling, to engage in impure acts, or to travel heedlessly into danger—these are not the ways of the wise who preserve themselves.
Or, if there was initially no peril but sudden danger arises midway, there is no offense. Or, if one travels with companions and a companion suddenly passes away, there is no offense.
If one does not avoid dangerous obstacles for the sake of the Buddha-dharma, or for the sake of one's parents, teachers, or elders, it is not an offense.
Twelve. Regarding staying alone in a nunnery:
if an upāsaka, having received and maintained the precepts, stays alone in a nunnery, that upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence (āpatti).
One shall not fall into negligence, nor engage in impure actions;
this is to prevent transgressions and avoid suspicion. Should there be unavoidable circumstances, one must have a suitable companion to stay with; in such a case, it does not constitute an offense.
Thirteen: Striking others for the sake of wealth.
If a lay follower (*upāsaka*), having received and upheld the precepts, strikes, reviles, or scolds their own slaves, servants, or outsiders for the sake of wealth or livelihood.
Such an upāsaka incurs the offense of negligence; he does not fall into ruin, yet his actions remain impure.
When dealing with slaves and servants, one should transform them through virtue, possessing both kindness and authority. What need is there for beating or scolding?
Even if they act without principle, one should subdue them according to the Dharma; it is improper to impulsively move the body or utter harsh words.
14. Regarding the giving of leftover food to the Saṃgha or to an upāsaka:

If an upāsaka who has received and maintains the precepts gives leftover food to a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, an upāsaka, or an upāsikā, that upāsaka incurs a *duṣkṛta* (fault of wrong intention). It does not constitute a *pārājika* (falling offense), but it is an impurity.

The *zuo* (beggar-monk) relies on alms for his physical sustenance; although he does not exercise discrimination, when a person of good faith provides an offering, it is only right that he be sincere and devout.
If one gives leftover food to the fourfold assembly, one treats this excellent field of merit with contempt and will thus invite for oneself an unfavorable retribution.
Fifteen: Regarding the keeping of cats or mongooses.
If an upāsaka, having received and maintained the precepts, keeps a cat or a mongoose, that upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence.
It does not constitute a formal downfall, nor is it an impure formal act.
It harms the species of mice and contravenes compassion; although it does not result in the loss of the precepts, the nature-offense (prakṛti-sāvadya) is not slight.

Sixteenth: Regarding the keeping of cattle, sheep, and so forth—if an upāsaka, having undertaken and maintained the precepts, keeps elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, camels, donkeys, or any other domesticated animals.

If one does not perform the ritual of pure giving (*viśuddha-dāna*) for a seeker of ordination, that upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence (*duṣkṛta*), though it does not constitute a formal fall (*pārājika*).
This constitutes an impure act.
Question: Since bhikṣus beg for food from all four directions, they must not keep slaves, servants, or livestock. Now, however, the upāsaka has not yet abandoned his household affairs;
why then is it not permitted for him to keep elephants, horses, and the like? Furthermore, how should the method of "pure giving" (śuddha-dāna) be performed? Answer:
Although this bodhisattva-upāsaka still resides in the household life, he has already become a banner of distinction for humans and devas.

Therefore, all animals must be given as pure gifts (*śuddha-dāna*). Although the method for pure gifting has not been explicitly detailed in the sutras, it may be inferred through reasoning that it should be conducted in the same manner as the pure gifting of wealth and treasures by *bhikṣus*.

Even though one does not personally keep them, one is still permitted to perform the ritual and make use of them (meaning that objects such as elephants and horses are all treated with the intention of entrusting them to a close friend, who then looks after, raises, and uses them on one's behalf).
Seventeen: Regarding the non-storing of the three robes, bowl, and staff.

If an upāsaka, having received and maintained the precepts, does not store the saṃghāṭī robe, bowl, and mendicant’s staff, that upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence (duṣkṛta), though it does not constitute a downfall (pārājika); it is an impure act.
*Saṃghāṭī*. This is translated as "repeated-layered robe" (*chóngfù yī*) and also as "great robe" (*dàyī*). Question: Since its storage and accumulation are permitted, is its wearing also permitted?
If its wearing is permitted, how does it differ from that of a *bhikṣu*? Is it because the regulations for the robes are different, and if so, how should it be constructed?
Or is there a difference in the manner of wearing, and if so, at what time? Answer: The three robes, the alms bowl, and the staff are originally...
Regarding the requisites for renunciation, this sutra speaks only of storing them, not of wearing them.

Only the Vaipulya Dhāraṇī Sūtra prescribes that the two assemblies of lay followers, when entering the maṇḍala to practice the Way, should wear the seamless triple robe (*tricīvara*). "Seamless" means...
This refers specifically to the uncut strips of cloth and differs from those that have been cut and pieced together; it is worn when entering the maṇḍala, but not at all other times.
(18) Regarding the field: it must have pure water.
If an upāsaka, having received and maintained the precepts, must work in a field for the sake of his body and life, he need not seek out pure water.
Regarding those things that grow on land: such an upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence (āpatti-prayoga), yet does not fall into a formal transgression (pārājika).
Whether seeking pure water free of insects, or seeking things grown on land where water is not required, he must not harm living beings in any way.
Nineteen: Regarding the regulation of commodity prices.

If a lay follower (*upāsaka*), having received and maintained the precepts, engages in market transactions for the sake of his own livelihood, such as selling goods by measure or weight; [he must ensure fairness].

Once the price has been stated, one must not move forward or retreat; one should abandon the cheap and proceed toward the expensive. When measuring goods with bushels or scales, one should allow them to be used as they are leveled.
If they are not level, one should speak so as to have them leveled. If one does not act in this manner, that upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence.
20. Not falling away through impure intentional action:
If an upāsaka, having undertaken the precepts, engages in sexual desire at an improper place or time, that upāsaka [falls].
One incurs the offense of a transgression of mind. One must not engage in sexual intercourse if it leads to a downfall or if it is impure.
Even with one’s own wife or concubine, one must not do so in an improper place or at an improper time. A bedchamber is defined as an improper place;
likewise, the middle of the day, or the period before and after childbirth, are all considered improper times.
Twenty-one: Stealing government taxes.
If an upāsaka, having received and maintained the precepts, engages in trade and commerce but fails to pay government taxes, instead concealing them and departing, [he commits this offense].
This upāsaka incurs the offense of "loss of intent" (*duṣkṛta*), which does not constitute a downfall (*pārājika*) or impure action (*aśuddha-karman*).
According to the *Wǔjièxiāng jīng* (Sūtra on the Characteristics of the Five Precepts), if one evades taxes by five coins, one commits an offense that cannot be rectified (*anivartya-āpatti*).
This is said because it may be an ordinary sale of goods in the marketplace, unlike the act of stealing across a customs post or ferry; or perhaps [it applies] even to a bodhisattva upāsaka.
[The offense is] obstructed. Because he has not yet received this portion of the precepts, it is slightly lighter.
Twenty-two: Violating National Laws.
If an upāsaka, having already received and maintained the precepts, violates national laws, that upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence (manasāpatti).
Do not fall into transgression; do not engage in impure actions.
When entering a country, one must inquire about its prohibitions. Such is the case even with worldly laws, let alone for the disciples of the Buddha—how could they fail to exercise self-restraint?
Twenty-three. Regarding new food:

if an upāsaka who has received and maintains the precepts obtains new grain, fruits, gourds, vegetables (the character *ru* means "like the root of *mao* grass," or alternatively, dried vegetables), and does not first offer them in worship to the Three Jewels before consuming them himself, that upāsaka incurs the fault of losing his resolve.
24. Offense: To act impurely or perform prohibited acts.

If a lay follower (*upāsaka*) has received and maintains the precepts, yet the Sangha does not permit him to preach the Dharma or offer praise, and he nevertheless does so on his own authority, it is an offense.
This upāsaka incurs the offense of negligence, yet he does not fall into a state of defeat or impurity in his practice.
Whenever the householder Anāthapiṇḍada teaches or recites the Dharma for newly ordained bhikṣus, he always first prostrates at the bhikṣus' feet before transmitting the teachings;
he does not presume to assume the status of a teacher. Furthermore, he is permitted by the Saṃgha to provide instruction.
Only then may one dare to do so; one must not dare to act on one's own initiative.
Twenty-five: If one is not on a road, one should yield to a monk, whether he be a *śrāmaṇera* or an *upāsaka*.
Once one has received and upheld the precepts, if one is on a road, one must walk behind a *bhikṣu* or a *śrāmaṇera*. This is for an *upāsaka*.
26. Upāsaka: One incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) for failing to rise [to greet], for falling into negligence, or for performing impure actions.

When food is distributed among the Saṃgha without equal sharing, if an upāsaka has already received and maintained the precepts, and the food is being served within the Saṃgha, he should not selectively choose the finest portions for his own teacher.
If one gives excessively, that upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence; he does not fall into a grave transgression, yet his action is impure.
Since the teacher and the community of monks ought to be equal, to show partiality or to give disproportionately more is to entrap the teacher in unrighteousness.
27. Regarding the raising of silkworms:
if an upāsaka, having received and upheld the precepts, raises silkworms, that upāsaka incurs an offense of negligence.
Not causing a fall; impure acts;
raising silkworms—these are skillful means for killing, and are therefore categorized as light offenses. If one boils cocoons and harms life, then it is categorized as a heavy offense.
Twenty-eight: Encountering the Sick on the Road and Failing to Visit (The Minor Precepts of the Upper Section Concluded).
If a lay follower (*upāsaka*), having received and upheld the precepts, encounters a sick person while traveling and fails to go and visit them.
If one provides the necessary means and entrusts [the teaching] to its proper location, yet then departs, such a lay follower (upāsaka) incurs the offense of negligence;
he does not fall into ruin, yet his actions remain impure.
If one has the leisure, one should go to visit; if one lacks the leisure, one should employ skillful means, or having entrusted [the matter] to another, one may then depart.

Or he may have an illness himself; or he may lack strength; or he may have the strength himself and have an attendant to care for him.

Because it benefits both oneself and others, it is the genuine treasure. Its heroic and fierce power is able to triumph over...
Because they have abandoned afflictions, they are called "great men" (puruṣa).

it is extremely difficult, O son of good family, as the Buddha has said, that there are two kinds of bodhisattvas: first, those who live at home; second, those who have gone forth. Those who have gone forth...

(From the mere three refuges up to the full precepts, one should respectively uphold these six grave and twenty-eight light offenses.
For an ordained bodhisattva to uphold the monastic precepts is not difficult; for a lay bodhisattva to uphold the lay precepts is indeed difficult. Why is this?
Because those who live at home are entangled by many adverse conditions.

thus, this Upāsaka precept is likely not yet fit to be received. For now, I shall briefly explain it to manifest the True Dharma.

Having completed the essential annotations for the "Chapter on Receiving the Precepts," I shall next briefly outline the general meaning of the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*.
According to the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*, it was compiled by sages and worthies of the Western Land (India) and should properly be included within the Abhidharma Piṭaka. Now, furthermore...
Regarding the title of this sutra: because it was established by the Buddha’s decree, the term "precepts" (*śīla*) mentioned within the text should properly be referred to as the *vinaya*.

However, the current designation "Dignified Conduct" (*airyāpathika*) is used because the preceding sections contain the six grave and twenty-eight light offenses, as well as the Brahma Net Bodhisattva Precepts;
thus, this [section] is specifically intended for laypeople who must observe the precepts of restraint and maintenance (*saṃvara-ādhāra*). The first half of this sutra is for the Bodhisattva Upāsaka.

The first half [of the precepts] concerns the ethical discipline and decorum of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) characterized by heedfulness; the latter half concerns the ethical discipline and decorum for the sake of renouncing desire.

To summarize: taking the arousal of the bodhicitta as the foundation, even if one is able to strictly maintain pure precepts without having aroused the bodhicitta, they are merely termed "worldly precepts.
In this context, it is stated that abandoning the Bodhisattva vow constitutes a loss of the precepts; therefore...

Regarding the rules of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha-vinaya*), they should be maintained in conjunction with the *Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa-sūtra* (The Sutra of Contemplating the Mind-Ground); then all rules of discipline will be pure.
The opening verse praises the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; this is the standard practice for most works compiled from the Buddhist teachings.
At the beginning of the main text, the phrase "all the virtuous ones" (*sarva-bhadanta*) is used; this is a term of address for those who read.

This sutra, as well as those who receive and uphold this dharma of precepts, trace their origin back to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, stating that these precepts were not created by oneself, nor are they the teaching of a single Buddha or a single Bodhisattva alone. Therefore, it says:
"I now wish to speak of the merits achieved by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time in benefiting all sentient beings."
Regarding the precepts: herein, the four *pārājika* offenses are explained first because they are the most grievous defiling sins;
thus, they are presented collectively at the outset. Master Ouyi stated: "The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* fully elucidates the ten grave prohibitions, yet here only the latter four are listed.
There are three reasons for this: first, killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying are termed the 'fundamental precepts' (*mūla-śīla*)."

Whether one is a layperson or a monastic, those who wish to receive the bodhisattva precepts must have already previously received the five precepts, the ten precepts, the full precepts (*upasaṃpadā*), and so forth;
what need is there to labor over explaining this further? Here, we shall merely clarify the superior discipline (*adhiśīla*) of exalting those above and transforming those below.
Second, regarding the fundamental rules of conduct: even if members of the seven assemblies should violate them, they do not [qualify for the bodhisattva vows].
Regarding confession: although the Mahāyāna permits confession, it requires that one see auspicious signs (*lakṣaṇa*).

As for these four precepts, if they are violated through bonds (*paryavasthāna*) of weak or middling intensity, only confession and purification are permitted; however, if they are violated through bonds of superior intensity, re-ordination remains permissible.

Therefore, these cannot be conflated with the four root precepts. Thirdly, regarding the conduct of a bodhisattva, there are many skillful means—whether following or contrary to conventional norms—and thus there may be occasions for permitting or prohibiting acts such as killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying.
However, these four specific precepts must not be transgressed under any circumstances, in any location, or within any realm of existence; therefore, they alone [are treated as absolute].
To clarify: the relative gravity of the forty minor precepts and their exceptions are self-evident in the scriptural text and do not require further commentary.
