Homage and Praise to the Triple Gem (This sutra was compiled by the sages and worthies of the Western Regions; therefore, one first offers homage and praise to the Triple Gem to seek their transformative protection.
The Buddha is the Honored One among all sages; His supernormal powers and responses are sovereign and free. He assumes physical forms according to the various classes of beings.
The sound is likewise so; those who see or hear it obtain peace and security. May none fail to have faith and devotion in their hearts;
therefore, I take refuge. May all be like the World-Honored One! The merit of the profound Bodhisattva precepts is inconceivable;
those who receive them obtain peace and security, and virtue and wisdom arise day and night.
Constantly protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas, The myriad practices gradually reach full completion.
With the intent of the six perfections and four immeasurables, one universally delivers the masses of the blind; One’s hands and feet never commit transgressions at the outset.

Restraining speech and acting in accordance with one's conduct, one always delights in dwelling within meditative concentration. Such a person is called a true bhikṣu— Upright and straightforward, free from flattery and crookedness.
Always dwelling together with the worthy and holy, loving the multitude as one nurtures oneself—this is called the True Bodhisattva Precepts.

Section Two: The Four Matters of Abandonment (*Catur-pārājika*; in this land, *pārājika* is translated as "abandonment," meaning that if these four matters are transgressed, one must be abandoned outside the Buddha-dharma).
All you virtuous ones, listen attentively and listen attentively; reflect upon them well. I now wish to speak of the [precepts] of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Buddhas and Bodhisattvas achieve the precepts of merit that benefit all sentient beings. For one who thus abides in the Bodhisattva precepts, there are four *pārājika* dharmas.
What are these four? If a bodhisattva, for the sake of gain and honor, praises themselves and disparages others, this is called a bodhisattva *pārājika*.
If a bodhisattva possesses abundant wealth and property, yet [does not share it with] a person in poverty and suffering...
When someone comes to beg, the bodhisattva is stingy and greedy, lacking any heart of compassion, such that they do not bestow even a single coin.
When there is one who seeks the Dharma, they do not speak even a single verse for them. This is called a bodhisattva’s *pārājika*.

If a bodhisattva becomes angry with another person, reviling and insulting them with harsh words, and further strikes them with their hands, or with sticks and stones, and their mind remains [thus]...

It does not cease. If the other person seeks repentance and offers sincere words of apology, yet the Bodhisattva remains angry and their resentment is not resolved, this is called a Bodhisattva *pārājika*.
If a Bodhisattva slanders the Dharma-treasury of the Bodhisattvas themselves, or seeing others slandering it, approves of those words;
having no faith in it themselves, they instead assist the speech of others; whether through their own understanding or by receiving it from another—this is called [a *pārājika*].
The Bodhisattva’s *pāramitās*. Thus, regarding these four *pāramitās* of a bodhisattva, a bodhisattva should not transgress even one;
how much less should they transgress them all? If there is one who transgresses, they are not called a bodhisattva;

in their present body, they cannot adorn *bodhi*, nor can they bring the mind to tranquility. Such a person is a counterfeit bodhisattva, not a true bodhisattva. There are three types of transgressions.

There are three grades: soft, medium, and superior. If one commits an offense with a soft or medium state of mind, it is not termed a loss. If one commits an offense with a superior state of mind, it is termed a loss.
What constitutes the superior grade? It is when one commits the four superior offenses, repeatedly delights in committing them, and has no sense of shame or remorse.

If one does not feel remorse or reproach oneself, this is called a supreme transgression (*āpatti*). Although a bodhisattva may commit these four supreme offenses, they do not immediately and permanently lose [their status].
This is unlike a bhikṣu, who, upon committing the four [parājikas], is immediately and permanently discarded. Why is this? Because when a bhikṣu commits the four...
There is no further way to receive it. Although a Bodhisattva may commit a transgression, they can still receive [the precepts] again;

therefore, this case is not the same. Briefly, there are two matters by which one loses the Bodhisattva precepts: first, abandoning the vow for enlightenment; second, the arising of an intensified evil mind.
Aside from these two matters, even if one discards this body, the precepts are never lost. From this point forward, in every place of rebirth, one will always possess these precepts. If not...
Recall that even if one encounters a virtuous friend and receives [the precepts] again, it is not called "newly obtained.

In this same way, a bodhisattva who possesses the precepts should recognize the matters of transgression and non-transgression, as well as the characteristics of their lightness or heaviness, and their distinctions as soft, middling, or superior.
Section Three: On the Distinction Between Light and Heavy, and Permissible and Prohibited [Acts] (Containing Forty Items). First:
Regarding those who abide thus in the Bodhisattva precepts, they should daily make offerings to the Buddhas—whether to stupas or images.

Next, they should make offerings to the Dharma—whether to those who practice the Dharma or to the Mahāyāna sūtras of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. They should also make offerings to the Saṃgha and to those in the ten directions.

Those bodhisattvas dwelling on the earth should, throughout the day and night, make offerings to the Triple Gem according to their capacity—ranging from a single thought-moment or a single prostration to the recitation of a single four-line verse—and offer them with faith without allowing such practice to cease.

If one fails to show reverence due to a mind of pride or indolence, one commits a grave secondary offense (gòu-zuì). If it is due to forgetfulness or error, one commits a minor secondary offense. Not...

Regarding those who commit an offense: if one is ill, insane, possesses a pure mind, has attained the stage of a bodhisattva, or—like a srotāpanna—has attained the indestructible pure mind and is able to constantly make offerings to the Triple Gem without interruption, this is called non-offense.

2. If a Bodhisattva who has eliminated greed and practices contentment becomes insatiable, becoming greedily attached to gain and offerings and failing to restrain the mind, he commits a grave defiled offense.

There is no offense if, although he is greedy for gain and offerings, he constantly gives rise to a sense of regret, thinking: "I shall apply myself with diligence to sever this intention and exercise extreme self-restraint."
If, while greed still arises, one takes a small benefit to assist in severing great greed, this is called non-offense.
Third: regarding respect for elders, when a Bodhisattva encounters an elder, a senior, one of long-standing virtue, a fellow teacher, or a fellow student, and gives rise to a mind of arrogance...
If, with a mind of anger and malice, one does not rise to welcome or pay homage, avoids their seat, or, when they speak, does not listen to their conversation;
or if, when questioned, one does not answer truthfully, one commits a grave defiling offense (*gurutara-mala-āpatti*). This is provided that there is no intention of pride, anger, or delusion.

To commit this offense through mere indolence, mental indifference (*avyākṛta*), or a distracted mind constitutes a minor transgression (*āpatti*). There is no offense in the following cases: if one is ill; if one is insane; if one is asleep;
if one is listening to or preaching the Dharma; if one has previously been engaged in conversation with another; if it is for the purpose of subduing others, eliminating evil, or increasing goodness;
or if there are restrictions from the Saṃgha or if one is protecting the feelings of many people. These are called non-offenses.
4. Regarding receiving offerings according to an invitation:

when a Bodhisattva is invited by a donor to their own home or within a monastery, and the donor provides whatever is required, if the Bodhisattva—out of pride, anger, or contempt—does not go to receive it, they commit a grave defiled offense. If they do not go out of laziness, they commit [a secondary offense].
Minor Offenses. There is no offense if one is ill; if one is insane; if one is far away; if the path is dangerous and difficult;

if it is for the purpose of subduing others to eliminate evil and increase goodness; if the invitation was lost; if it is for the sake of cultivating virtue; if it is to hear what has not been heard before; if one knows that the host intends to cause harassment;
or if there are restrictions from the Sangha or one protects the intentions of many people. These are called non-offenses.
5. Regarding taking objects to give them away in turn to Bodhisattvas:
from others, one may obtain gold, silver, lapis lazuli, various miscellaneous jewels, necessary items, as well as treasures hidden in the earth and ownerless property;
all these should be taken with the thought that they shall be given away in turn. However, if one acts with an evil mind or anger...

Therefore, to refuse [a gift] constitutes a grave offense of defilement (*gurutara-āpatti*). If one thinks, "I will not act as a causal condition for others," or if it is out of a mind of indolence, one commits a light offense of defilement (*laghu-āpatti*).
There is no offense in the following cases: if one is deranged; if it is for the purpose of subduing [the recipient] to eliminate evil and increase goodness;
if one knows that once received, the recipient will certainly give rise to attachment; if one knows that once given, the donor will feel regret; or if one knows the [recipient's] disposition.
If the donor has gone mad; if one considers that the donor will fall into poverty and suffering after giving; if one knows that the object given belongs to the Triple Gem;

if one knows that the object was obtained through robbery or theft; or if one knows that upon receiving it, the recipient will suffer greatly—namely, facing calamities from the king, bandits, death, imprisonment, the spread of a bad reputation, or being banished from the territory—this is called not committing an offense.

Sixth: When a Bodhisattva is requested by another to teach the Dharma according to their needs, if they refuse to teach due to a mind of anger, malice, or envy toward that person, they commit a grave secondary offense (gurutara-āpatti).
If they refuse to teach due to a mind of laziness, they commit a minor secondary offense (laghu-āpatti). There is no offense if [the requester] is a non-Buddhist (tīrthika).

One seeks the Dharma while considering that one might otherwise be subject to ridicule. This applies if [the listener] is ill or insane; if it is for the purpose of subduing them, extinguishing evil, and increasing goodness;
if one knows the person before does not understand its meaning; if the person before is disrespectful or acts contrary to the Dharma; or if the person before has dull faculties.

If one knows that the person does not understand the profound Dharma and fears they will give rise to wrong views; or if one knows that upon hearing it, they will destroy their original resolve and cause the extinction of the True Dharma;
or if one knows that upon hearing it, they will certainly proclaim the matter to those who are not suitable vessels—these are called cases where there is no offense.
7. With a compassionate mind, a bodhisattva instructs a sentient being who sees that person committing evil, violating precepts and prohibitions, and performing various sinful deeds.

If the bodhisattva knows they can be transformed into goodness, yet out of an evil mind or a mind of anger abandons them and fails to instruct them, they commit a grave defiled offense. Why is this? Because the bodhisattva...
One does not give rise to a mind of compassion toward those who maintain the precepts purely in body, speech, and mind.

Rather, if one sees an evil person who violates the precepts, breaks the prohibitions, and commits various sinful acts, one gives rise to the utmost compassion. Therefore, there are cases where there is an offense and cases where there is no offense.

There is no offense if one is insane; if it is for the purpose of subduing others to eliminate evil and increase goodness; if there is a restriction by the Sangha; or if it is to protect the feelings of many people. These are called non-offenses.

8. When a bodhisattva who accepts benefits expediently follows the *prātimokṣa* and the formulated *vinaya* as prescribed by the Buddha, desiring to cause those without faith to believe and those already possessing faith to increase, these śrāvaka precepts and bodhisattva precepts are equal and without difference. Why is this?

If even a śrāvaka, who acts primarily for his own sake, still desires to study so as to cause those without faith to believe and those with faith to increase, how much more so for a bodhisattva whose practice and study are always for the sake of sentient beings—how could he not be able to do this? Therefore, their names are the same, and there is no transgression.
As prescribed by the Buddha, those who are śrāvakas should have few desires and engage in few causes and conditions. A bodhisattva is not like this.
Why? Because seeking one's own benefit in accordance with their own inclination, rather than for the sake of others, is the way of a śrāvaka.
If a bodhisattva were thus, they would not be called a bodhisattva. For the sake of others, the robes they may receive—even numbering in the hundreds or thousands—from those who are not relatives...
Brahmins and householders will exhaust all their efforts in seeking [wealth], just as they do for robes and bowls.
For the sake of others, they will beg for thread and instruct weavers to weave it; they will store *kauśeya* silk garments and accept gold and silver, even in amounts reaching hundreds of thousands.

Such matters differ from those of the śrāvakas. If a bodhisattva, who originally acts for the sake of sentient beings, gives rise to a mind of anger or malice, abandons sentient beings due to minor causes or conditions, and dwells alone in his own place, he commits a grave defiling offense (gurutara-āpatti).
If, however, he dwells in his own place due to a mind of indolence, having few desires and few concerns, he commits a light defiling offense (laghu-āpatti).

Nine. Regarding the precepts that pacify the five matters, there are five unrighteous practices for a bodhisattva: first, flattery; second, ostentation; third, seeking signs; fourth, seeking profit through profit; and fifth, wrong livelihood.
When these five matters exist, one feels no shame. One who neither restrains nor ceases [the offense] commits a grave defiled transgression.
One who does not commit it is one who recognizes this as unrighteous and constantly desires to restrain it; this is called "not committing."

Tenth: If a Bodhisattva, out of self-importance regarding their deportment, engages in frivolous play, distraction, or loud shouting and speech that constitutes improper conduct, causing others to laugh and being held in contempt by the assembly, they commit a grave secondary offense (*gaurava-āpatti*).
If, however, it is due to long-standing habituation or committed through forgetfulness or error, they commit a minor secondary offense. Not so [if it is unintentional].
Regarding those who commit an offense: if one recognizes it as contrary to the Dharma and constantly seeks to restrain it; or if an outsider is angry and one acts out of a desire to subdue them;
or if a person is suffering and one acts to bring them joy; or if one wishes to engage in playful banter to win someone over;
or if two people are disputing and one acts to reconcile them—these are called non-offenses.
Eleventh: The speech must be definitive.

A bodhisattva who sees thus and speaks thus should not delight in nirvāṇa, should not turn away from nirvāṇa, should not fear the afflictions (kleśas), and should not extinguish the afflictions. Why is this? Because for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas...
Because they wander through birth and death, one who speaks in such a manner commits a grave defiled offense. Why is this?
If one were to compare a Bodhisattva’s delight in *nirvāṇa* and dread of afflictions (*kleśa*) to that of a *śrāvaka*, it would not even be comparable by a factor of ten million.
Why is this? Because *śrāvakas* act for their own sake alone, whereas Bodhisattvas always act for the sake of all sentient beings. Thus, the Bodhisattva...

12. Although dwelling amidst the outflows (*sāsrava*), he attains mastery over the cessation of afflictions; thus he surpasses those Arhats who dwell in the state of being without outflows (*anāsrava*).
13. He guards his own body and speech.
If a bodhisattva gives rise to physical or verbal karma, they should personally guard themselves so as not to cause others to fall into the fault of arrogance.

If one intentionally fails to guard oneself and causes another to fall into a fault, one commits a heavy defiled offense (*gurutara-mala-āpatti*). If one fails to guard oneself through lack of attention and, by being negligent in one's actions, causes another to commit a fault, one commits a light defiled offense (*laghu-mala-āpatti*).
There is no offense if [the other] is a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*) or one who has followed [the bodhisattva] into the monastic life.
Acting in accordance with the Dharma: if one encounters a person who is excessively wrathful and malicious, this is called non-offense.
(Thirteen) Regarding the expedient administration of punishment:

if a Bodhisattva perceives that sentient beings before them must be subjected to the pain of a staff in order to subsequently benefit from it, yet fails to treat them out of self-protection, this constitutes an offense.
Minor Offenses. There is no offense if there is little benefit and much suffering; this is called non-offense.

Fourteen: If a Bodhisattva repays an insult with an insult, anger with anger, a blow with a blow, or a pulling and dragging with a pulling and dragging in order to take revenge, he commits a grave offense.
Fifteenth: The Offense of Quarreling.
If a Bodhisattva quarrels with another, or harbors mutual resentment, with a mind of malice, anger, or arrogance, he fails to repent.

Regarding the offense of failing to repent: if one commits a grave secondary offense (*gurutara-āpatti*) and, out of indolence or negligence, does not seek repentance, one commits a light secondary offense (*laghu-āpatti*).
There is no offense if it is for the purpose of subduing oneself, extinguishing evil, and increasing goodness; or if those externalists insist upon performing what is contrary to the Dharma.

If that person delights in quarreling, their enmity will increase further; if one knows that the other person will ultimately not accept an apology, or if offering an apology toward them would give rise to grave arrogance in them, this is called no offense.

Sixteen: If a Bodhisattva harbors resentment toward another and, when that other person seeks forgiveness in accordance with the Dharma, refuses to accept it out of a malicious intent to cause them distress, they commit a grave secondary offense (*gurutara-āpatti*).
If they refuse to accept the other's apology without a mind of malice, they commit a minor secondary offense (*laghu-āpatti*). There is no offense in the following cases: [list of exemptions].
If it is for the purpose of subduing [the opponent], extinguishing evil, and increasing goodness; or if the other person is wicked or unrighteous—this is called no offense.
(17) Regarding the cultivation of patience and the absence of anger:
if a bodhisattva becomes angry with another, and that anger does not cease, he commits a heavy defiled offense. There is no offense if: [if...]
He constantly restrains himself, yet the mind of anger still arises; this is called non-offense.
(18) A bodhisattva who temporarily maintains a retinue does so only to provide service, as well as food and clothing; this is called non-offense.

Nineteen: A bodhisattva who diligently guards the precepts may give rise to thoughts of indolence, taking pleasure in eating at improper times, or becoming greedily attached to sleep, whether leaning or lying down.
One commits a grave offense of defilement. There is no offense if one is ill; or if one has committed [the act] but lacks skillful means; or if one is exhausted from traveling on a road;
or if it was done as a constant restraint. These are called cases where there is no offense.
Twenty: It is a grave defiled offense for a Bodhisattva, with a mind of attachment, to speak of worldly pleasures; however, there is no offense if one speaks out of forgetfulness or error.

This constitutes the offense of a minor defilement. There is no offense if someone asks a question and one answers with few words while maintaining a correct mind; or if one discusses extraordinary news;
or if one discusses matters concerning the Dharma. These are called non-offenses.

21. If a Bodhisattva who desires to practice dhyāna for the sake of the Dharma knows that another possesses the Dharma, yet, out of anger or pride, is unable to humble their mind and seek to receive the Dharma from them, they commit a grave secondary offense (gurutara-āpatti).
If, however, it is due to a mind of indolence that they do not seek to receive it, they commit a light secondary offense (laghu-āpatti).
There is no offense if one is ill; or if one lacks skillful means; or if one knows that the person does not comply with the teachings of the Dharma;
or if one possesses skillful means oneself, is learned, and has mastered their own mind. These are called non-offenses.

Twenty-two: If a bodhisattva gives rise to desire belonging to the desire realm and fails to apply the antidote of diligent contemplation, thereby failing to swiftly eliminate it, they commit a grave defiled offense.

There is no offense if they constantly strive with diligence to extinguish it, yet the mind of desire still arises; this is called no offense. As it is with desire, so it is with the remaining hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
Twenty-three. Not being attached to meditative concentration:
if a bodhisattva craves the flavor of dhyāna and becomes attached to its merits, they commit a grave defiled offense.
There is no offense if they constantly desire to abandon attachment, yet an attachment-mind still arises; this is called no offense.
24. The Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging perceived thus and spoke thus: "A bodhisattva should not listen to, accept, recite, or study the scriptural collection of the śrāvakas."
For a bodhisattva, this is precisely what they should study. To speak such words is to commit a grave offense of defilement. Why is this?

A bodhisattva should study even the scriptures of non-Buddhists, let alone the words of the Buddha. There is no offense, however, for one who does so with the desire to discipline śrāvakas and lead them into the Mahāyāna; this is called being without offense.

Twenty-five: To fail to study the Dharma-piṭaka of the Bodhisattvas of the Two Vehicles, but instead to exclusively set it aside and greedily study and recite the sūtras of the Śrāvakas, constitutes a minor offense.

26. If a Bodhisattva who possesses the treasury of the Buddha’s sūtras does not diligently study them, but instead diligently studies the secular texts of non-Buddhists, they commit a grave defiling offense.

There is no offense if their faculties are extremely sharp such that they can retain [the teaching] upon hearing it once; or if they take up [non-Buddhist texts] to assist those that accord with the Buddha’s word.

Transformation: If one uses those sublime words to assist in clarifying the Buddha-dharma, and one’s mind remains unshaken regarding the Buddha-dharma and the meaning of the Buddhist scriptures, this is called non-offense.

If a bodhisattva wishes to study the scriptures of external paths, they should study them as described above; however, if they should receive [the teachings] therein, [they must apply the same criteria].
To give rise to a mind of attachment is not like taking bitter medicine; it constitutes a grave defiled offense.

Twenty-seven: Not slandering the profound meaning—should a bodhisattva hear the Dharma-treasury of bodhisattvas, including its most profound secrets, the supreme ultimate truth, and inconceivable matters.

This is exclusively the realm of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Within this meaning, to give rise to a mind of slanderous denial, saying that this meaning is useless, was not spoken by the Buddha, and cannot benefit or assist all sentient beings—to commit such slander is to incur a grave defiled offense (*gurv-āpatti*).
There is no offense in the following cases: if one is contemplating the definitive meaning; if one speaks for the sake of skillful means; or if a Bodhisattva hears this profound meaning.
At that time, if one does not give rise to faith, one should, with a mind free from deceit and for the sake of generating faith, reflect as follows:
"I ought not to act thus; I am like one who is blind, lacking the eye of wisdom. How could I slander what has been spoken from the Buddha’s own mouth?
In this way, the bodhisattva reproaches himself for his delusion, thinking: "This is the domain of the Buddha; it is not within my reach. If one can act in this manner, it is considered correct.
If one acts in this way, yet their mind does not understand and they do not give rise to slander, this is called "no offense.
(28) It is a heavy defiled offense for a Bodhisattva, out of a hateful and evil mind and for the sake of food and drink, to praise themselves and disparage others; it is no offense [otherwise].

If it is for the purpose of subduing non-Buddhists, or subduing arrogance, or increasing the Buddha-dharma; or for the sake of inspiring faith in those who do not yet believe, or increasing the faith of those who already believe—this is called not committing an offense.
Twenty-nine: Regarding the Bodhisattva who listens to the Dharma as appropriate.

If there is a household where the Dharma is being taught, or a place where the Vinaya is being recited, or a great assembly for the Dharma, should one fail to go and listen due to a mind of anger, envy, or pride, one commits a grave defiled offense (*gurutara-mala-āpatti*).
If one fails to go and listen due to a mind of indolence, one commits a light defiled offense (*laghu-mala-āpatti*). Not [to do so]... [is not an offense].
Regarding the transgression: if one does not hear it oneself; if no one calls out; if one is ill; if one lacks skillful means;

if one knows that the teaching being given does not accord with the principles of meaning; if one knows that the speaker will pose difficulties for oneself; if one knows that there is nothing further to be heard beyond what has been said;
if one has attained *dhāraṇī*; if one is naturally of great learning; or if one is diligently cultivating roots of goodness—these are called non-transgressions.
Thirty. Regarding the entrustment of tasks to act together as a bodhisattva:
if someone comes to request assistance, one should say, "I have certain matters to attend to; I shall manage the arrangements for you. This refers to going together and returning together.
To manage various affairs; having managed them to completion; to guard wealth and property; to reconcile disputes; to prepare food and drink;
and to cultivate meritorious deeds—should one fail to perform even one or two of these matters, one commits a grave impurity offense (*gurutara-āpatti*).

If one fails to do so out of laziness, one commits a light impurity offense (*laghu-āpatti*). There is no offense if one is ill, lacks skillful means, has personal business, or [if it is] that person...

It is not an offense if one is able to accomplish it oneself; if there is no one to request assistance; if it is a matter of no benefit; if it is for the purpose of subduing others, extinguishing evil, and increasing goodness;

if there is no other person requesting assistance; if it is in return for work done by another; if one is diligently cultivating roots of goodness; if one is personally dull-witted and fears losing the sequence of tasks;
or if there is a restriction from the Sangha for the sake of protecting the sentiments of many people. This is called "not an offense."
31. Regarding the compassionate care of the sick:
if a bodhisattva, upon seeing a sick sentient being, fails to provide care due to an evil mind or a mind of anger, they commit a grave defiled offense.
If one fails to provide care due to laziness, one commits a minor offense (light defilement). There is no offense if one is personally ill; or if one lacks skillful means;

or if one has requested another to attend to them; or if the patient already has their own relatives; or if one knows that the patient is capable of providing for themselves through their own efforts.
If one is chronically ill; or if a person is still able to rise and sit up; or if one wishes to diligently cultivate superior roots of goodness;

or if one is so extremely dull-witted that one fears losing one's place in the assembly; or if one fears being deprived of nursing care—just as in the case of illness, the same applies to other sufferings such as poverty.
These are called non-offenses.

Thirty-two: If a Bodhisattva perceives sentient beings before them for whom it would be beneficial to provide instruction according to their needs, yet fails to initiate such instruction due to a malicious mind or a mind of anger, they commit a grave defiled offense. If they fail to instruct out of laziness, they commit a minor defiled offense.
It is an offense. There is no offense if one lacks the means; or if one causes another to instruct him; or if he already has a virtuous friend of his own;

or if it is for the purpose of subduing him, extinguishing evil, and increasing goodness; or if, after showing him the proper means, he becomes even more angry and perverse, lacking any heart of respect or affection, and acts willfully and obstinately—these are called cases of no offense.
Thirty-three: The Bodhisattva Recalling the Debt of Gratitude for Gifts.
When sentient beings provide what one requires, one should remember their kindness.

If, with an evil mind or a mind of anger, one fails to acknowledge or repay that kindness, one commits a grave secondary offense (*gaurava-āpatti*). If one fails to repay it due to laziness, one commits a minor secondary offense. There is no offense if—
If one lacks the power; if one lacks skillful means; if it is for the sake of subduing [the recipient], extinguishing evil, and increasing goodness;
or if one wishes to repay the kindness but the donor does not accept it—these are called non-offenses.
34. Consoling those who have suffered loss:

If one sees that a relative has died, or that someone has lost their wealth, and encounters various forms of grief and suffering, yet out of a malicious or angry mind does not go to offer consolation, one commits a grave defiled offense. There is no offense in cases such as those previously mentioned regarding the bodhisattva acting as a messenger.
It is said:
Thirty-five. When a bodhisattva is asked for something, they must give it.

If someone asks for food, drink, or other necessities, and the bodhisattva does not give them, they commit a grave offense of defilement (*gurutara-āpatti*). There is no offense in the following cases:
If one lacks the object oneself; if one requests an impure object; if it is for the purpose of subduing others, extinguishing evil, or increasing goodness;
if it is prohibited by the king; or if it is restricted by the Sangha—these are called non-offenses.
Thirty-six. Regarding the instruction of disciple-bodhisattvas:
a teacher should instruct them at the appropriate times. If a disciple lacks necessities, the teacher should exhort a person of sincere faith to provide for them.
If, out of a malicious mind or a mind of anger, one fails to instruct or provide for them, one commits a grave defiled offense.
If, out of a lazy mind, one does not instruct [the disciple] on how to provide offerings, one commits a minor offense (light impurity). There is no offense in the following cases:
if it is for the purpose of subduing [the disciple], extinguishing evil, and increasing goodness; if it is to protect the boundaries of the Sangha; if one is ill; if one lacks skillful means;

if one has entrusted the instruction to another person; if the disciple’s merit is sufficient to obtain offerings; or if the disciple was originally a non-Buddhist and lacks a wholesome, virtuous mind. This is called [no offense].
Offense.

Thirty-seven. A Bodhisattva who protects others with a mind of loving-kindness commits a grave defiled offense if, out of anger or an evil mind, they fail to protect the intentions of others. If they are lazy or negligent...

To be negligent and fail to protect the feelings of others constitutes a minor secondary offense (*laghu-pāyantika*). It is not an offense in the following cases: if it concerns an unlawful matter; if one is ill; if there is a restriction by the Sangha;
if one is protecting the feelings of many people; if the person is a non-Buddhist; or if it is for the purpose of subduing them to eliminate evil and increase goodness. These are called non-offenses.
38. A bodhisattva who praises the goodness of others:
when seeing the virtuous conduct of another, they are unable to praise it, and instead conceal that person's goodness with an evil mind or a mind of anger.
If one commits a grave offense of defilement: if one is indolent and negligent, and does not praise the virtues of others, one commits a minor offense of defilement.

There is no offense if one knows that the person does not delight in being praised; or if one is ill; or if one lacks skillful means; or if it is for the purpose of subduing them to eliminate evil and increase goodness;
or if it is to protect the boundaries of the Sangha; or if one knows that hearing praise would cause them to give rise to further arrogance; or if they possess no genuine virtue.

If one says something appears to be wholesome when it actually lacks the meaning of wholesomeness; or if one is acting as a non-Buddhist teacher; or if one is praising someone at an inappropriate time—these are called non-offenses.
Thirty-nine. Governing the assembly according to the Dharma.
A Bodhisattva who serves as a leader for many people, upon seeing that their followers are engaged in unrighteous activities, ought to reprimand or expel them.
If, out of a mind of anger or malice, they neglect to reprimand or discipline them, they commit a grave secondary offense (gurutara-āpatti).

If, due to laziness or negligence, they fail to instruct or reprimand them, they commit a light secondary offense (laghu-āpatti). There is no offense if they know that the person is of an evil nature and prone to violent anger, and thus will not accept instruction.

If one waits for the proper time to admonish; if one fears it would cause a schism in the Saṃgha; or if one knows that the person is upright by nature, has little habitual shame, and delights in repenting after repeatedly committing offenses—these are called non-offenses.

Forty. Bodhisattvas who manifest according to circumstances possess supernatural powers and transformations; they manifest in accordance with sentient beings at all times, sometimes using skillful means to inspire awe.
One should cause them to give rise to faith. If, out of fear of offerings given in faith, one does not manifest transformations, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

There is no offense if the person is deeply attached to evil dharmas and false views; or if they are a non-Buddhist (tīrthika); or if they revile the worthy and holy ones; or if they are clinging to false views.
If one is insane or suffering from pain, this is called non-offense.
This concludes the fourth section on the benefits of upholding the precepts:
the accomplishment of the bodhisattva precept-aggregate. It possesses immeasurable and wondrous fruits; by the power of the causal conditions of this precept-aggregate, [these results are attained].

They are fully endowed with the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*). Although the recipient has not yet attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, by virtue of attaining these five meritorious qualities, they are: first, constantly protected and remembered by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
second, receiving constant pure bliss; third, having no regrets at the time of death; and fourth, upon casting off the body, attaining rebirth in the worlds of the Buddhas.

The realms. Fifth, it adorns *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. A bodhisattva who upholds the bodhisattva precepts does not do so for their own sake, but solely for the benefit of others and to adorn *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
These bodhisattva precepts are all those of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
This is what is accomplished by Bodhisattvas; even the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions are likewise so.

The Bodhisattva’s vast compassion extends its universal grace to sentient beings throughout the six realms. Regarding the suffering and afflictions of the three miserable paths and the eight difficulties, there is nowhere in the ten directions that does not receive benefit.
Their merit is incalculable; their fortune and wisdom are like space. Having briefly explained these essentials, they joyfully prostrate and practice accordingly.
They universally give rise to the bodhicitta; through this, their fortune, wisdom, and life are perfected.
Compassion grows within men and women, and through successive acts of joy and relinquishment, all shall attain the path to Buddhahood.

Forever exhausted, with nothing remaining; may the ten directions share in this vow. To the Exalted One of Infinite Majesty, who is self-enlightened without a teacher—this is the fifth section on receiving the precepts for oneself.
If one wishes to become a bodhisattva upāsaka, yet is negligent regarding the five precepts and proper conduct, and has no teacher from whom to receive them:
At that time, if there is no preceptor, the recipient should, before an image of the Buddha, personally vow to receive the observances of a Bodhisattva Upāsaka.
They should perform the prostrations in this manner: baring the right shoulder, kneeling on the right knee with palms joined, they should speak as follows:
"I, [Name], inform the Buddhas of the ten directions and all the Bodhisattvas dwelling upon the Great Grounds: now, in the presence of all the Buddhas, I desire..."
I receive all precepts. I train in all bodhisattva precepts: the five lay precepts (*upāsaka-śīla*) and their dignified conduct;
the bodhisattva precepts that encompass all wholesome dharmas; and the precepts for the benefit of sentient beings.

These precepts were studied by all bodhisattvas of the past, will be studied by all bodhisattvas of the future, and are being studied by all bodhisattvas of the present. I, too, shall study them in this same way. Second.
The third [section] concludes with the same explanation. As for the remaining matters, they should be explained in detail as previously stated.

Regarding the sixth section on the lay follower (*upāsaka*) who has abandoned desire and possesses the fivefold division of abstention: he fully observes the five precepts and remains far removed from the four physical evils. First is killing; second is stealing.
Third is sexual misconduct; fourth is drinking intoxicants. One should distance oneself from the five evils of speech: first, lying; second, harsh speech;
third, divisive speech; fourth, idle chatter; and fifth, frivolous talk. One should distance oneself from the five wrong livelihoods:
first, selling meat; second, selling alcohol; third, selling poison; fourth, selling living beings; and fifth, selling weapons.
One should distance oneself from five matters of adornment: first, incense; second, flowers; third, necklaces and ornaments;
fourth, anointing the body with fragrant oils; and fifth, perfuming one's clothing. One should distance oneself from five matters of indulgence: first, singing; second, dancing; third, playing music;
fourth, decorating musical instruments; and fifth, going to watch or listen to them. These five precepts should be observed according to one’s capacity.
Regarding what is capable of being maintained: if one is able to fully observe the five precepts for the duration of one's life, that is best.

If one cannot, then according to how many years, months, days, or nights one can maintain them—even for a mere moment—one may still maintain them briefly. It is not only as when the Buddha, at the time of his parinirvāṇa, maintained them in their entirety.
The Buddha commanded the four great śrāvakas and the six arhats: "After my parinirvāṇa, within this True Dharma,
if there are those of the two groups of renunciants who purely uphold the prohibitive precepts, or those of the two groups of learners who, according to their respective capacities,
maintain the higher precepts with a focused mind, and provide dwellings, bedding, clothing, food, drink, and all other requisites for the livelihood that accords with the Path— "

These requisites are to be bestowed upon the Sangha of the four quarters and upon all the worthy sages. You all should accept these invitations; if you do not accept them, you will incur transgression.
Viewed from this perspective, the worthy sages are not far away; they respond when their presence is invoked.

If you wish to perform meritorious deeds, you should first exert yourself to uphold the supreme precepts, and thereafter, with a sincere heart, invite the Sangha of the four quarters and all the worthy sages. If you do not...

It is best if one can do so for a lifetime; even for a single day and night is excellent. If one cannot, one should accept the offerings at the time they are set forth and cease once they are concluded.
All these worthies and sages will come to receive the invitation.
Chapter Seven: Repentance According to the Dharma.
If there is anything transgressed, one must immediately repent according to the Dharma. All these bodhisattvas, having committed an offense, incur a *duṣkṛta* (minor) offense.
They should repent according to the Dharma before those who can explain the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna and are capable of receiving their confession. If a bodhisattva...
Regarding those who commit an offense involving a *pārājika* matter due to intense afflictions (*adhimātra-kleśa*), they lose their vows of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*) and must receive them again.

If one commits an offense involving a *pārājika* matter due to middling afflictions (*madhya-kleśa*), one should confess the *duṣkṛta* offense before three persons, or more than three, by kneeling with palms joined.
If the offenses committed are numerous, one should speak thus: "Venerable sirs, please bear this in mind."
I, [Name], having abandoned the Bodhisattva Vinaya, have committed a *duṣkṛta* offense regarding the matter as described.

The remainder is as explained in the method for repenting a *duṣkṛta* offense of a *bhikṣu*. If one commits an offense involving the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) that constitutes a *pārājika* offense, or any other offense, one shall repent before a single person.

Below this are the rituals for paying homage to the Triple Gem, the arousal of the bodhicitta and the making of vows, the procedures for worshipping the Buddhas of the Four Directions, the method for receiving the corded seat (*śayanāsana*), the method for receiving the mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*), and the methods for concluding the session, moving to another location, and receiving food.
These are supplementary texts outside the core precepts and have not been recorded here; they may be fully understood by consulting the Tripitaka.
Appendix: Five Points of Discussion 1. Discussion on Receiving the Precepts:

According to the various Vinaya sections, the precepts are divided into seven classes of practitioners (*saptasaṃgha*), each with its own distinct name and status. Laypeople and monastics differ in their respective order of precedence.
The five groups of those who have left the household life may all serve as preceptors for receiving the precepts from laypeople. There are two principles regarding this:
first, it is because when one resolves to take the precepts, there is concern that a full assembly of monks (*bhikṣu*) might be difficult to encounter, leading to a loss of benefit.

If there is a *bhikṣu*, one should seek to receive them from him; if there is no *bhikṣu*, one should seek to receive them before a *bhikṣuṇī*; and if neither of the two assemblies of monks is present, [one should proceed accordingly].
One should receive it from a śikṣamāṇā; if there is no śikṣamāṇā, one should receive it before a śrāmaṇera.
If none of the four higher assemblies are present, one should receive it before a śrāmaṇerī. This refers to the allowance for receiving [the precepts] according to the appropriate occasion. Second.
That is to say, even if there is a bhikṣu who does not maintain the precepts, one may receive [the precepts] from a bhikṣuṇī who maintains them;
or even if there is a bhikṣuṇī, should she not maintain the precepts with purity, one may receive them from a śrāmaṇerikā who maintains the precepts.

This, then, opens the way for those who follow [the lay community]. If there is a bhikṣu who, while maintaining the precepts, separately seeks to receive the precepts from another group, this is not permitted;

it must be received from the *mahāsāṃghika* (great assembly of monks) to be considered valid. As it is with the five precepts, so it is with the eightfold fast-precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa-śīla*), and even up to the Bodhisattva Great Precepts, which are received by Bodhisattvas among the five groups of the ordained; this serves as the precedent.

This may be inferred. Furthermore, there are two types of Bodhisattva precepts: first, those of the Brahma Net (Brahmajāla), and second, those of the specific school (mūla). One should receive one or the other according to what is appropriate.

Second, regarding the distinction between the titles used for prostration: the seven assemblies within the Buddha-dharma correspond to the nine ranks within the Confucian bureaucracy. Although they are equally subjects, [the distinctions remain].
That the distinction between the honorable and the humble does not lose its proper order is the great etiquette for abiding in the world; it must not be disordered.

Lately, however, among both the monastic and the lay, titles and ranks have not been distinguished. People falsely claim kinship with the Dharma, whether by having once taken refuge under a name or having once received the precepts, and thus erroneously consider themselves of the same lineage as ordained monks.
Consequently, they address one another as "teacher," "brother," or "sister," even down to those of the lowest station, calling them...
You, my disciples and nephews, not only violate the regulations regarding monastics and laypeople, but you even demand that they pay you homage; you go so far as to engage in insults and the like.
According to the *Daśacakra-kṣitigarbha-sūtra*, regarding those who have gone forth within my Dharma, if they are vessels of the Dharma:
If one who is not a vessel for the Dharma shaves off their hair and beard, dons the *kāṣāya*, and yet fails to show respect toward those disciples,
instead harassing, reviling, or even inflicting physical punishment upon them, or imprisoning them, or even taking their lives—
this constitutes a grave offense against the Buddhas of the three periods of time. It severs one's roots of goodness and will lead inevitably to rebirth in the city of the Avīci Hell.
Investigating the origins and developments of this situation, it is seen that they all stem from the fact that those who act as preceptors often harbor personal attachments;

by pursuing gain and sustenance at the expense of the Dharma, they cause householders to fail to heed strict instructions and to treat the Sangha with arrogance due to their pride in wealth and status. Alas!

The winds of Māra blow daily, and the path of the Dharma declines. I hope that both monastics and laypeople will reverently observe the Buddha’s regulations and diligently maintain the order of the Sangha.

Third, regarding the regulations for robes according to the Vinaya: for laymen and laywomen who have received the *upāsaka* and *upāsikā* precepts, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* permits the possession of one robe for performing prostrations and repentance, called a *pāṭa* (in Sanskrit;
in the language of Tang, this means "plain strips"). "Plain" (*man*) refers to being without patterns; it is a single piece of woven wool.

It differs from secular dress only in that it is dyed a "ruined color" (kasāya). Unlike monastic robes, which are made by cutting and sewing pieces to represent the appearance of a field, this is made of plain strips.

As for what is called a "repentance robe," it may be worn for any single act—such as paying homage to the Triple Gem, circumambulating halls or stupas, reciting scriptures, or practicing the methods of repentance—and each such activity permits its use. Once the virtuous task is completed, one should immediately discard it.
Whether at home for meals or wandering through the marketplace, it is not permitted to wear [the robe] at any time.

Lately, those who receive the precepts while living as householders have mostly remained in their secular appearance, yet they indiscriminately don the field-robe (*kṣetrapaṭa*) as they enter and exit cities and travel to and from monasteries.
This ruins the outward manifestation of the *saṃgha* and violates the regulations and decorum of the Dharma King. How can wearing it in such a manner not be a transgression?

Those who practice erroneously still return to the teacher’s home. If one follows the clear regulations of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, there is no mention at all of the three robes, alms bowl, or staff for lay bodhisattvas of the two assemblies.
If one relies on the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, it merely states that one may store away the *saṃghāṭī* robe, alms bowl, and mendicant’s staff;
it likewise says nothing of actually wearing them (this is likely intended as preparation for giving to the Sangha; once given, one immediately fashions new ones to store). I hope that all...

O Benevolent One, seeing that your family resides among those of virtuous faith, if there are those who wish to receive the precepts, you should first take this monastic robe and provide them with earnest instruction,
so that they may reverently follow the Buddha’s command and gloriously establish the True Dharma.

Regarding the fourth section on the confession and recitation according to the Vinaya: when members of the two lay assemblies (*upāsaka* and *upāsikā*) have violated their precepts, they should go before the Saṃgha for confession during the first watch of the night on the fourteenth or the twenty-ninth day of the month.
This applies to both the dark and light fortnights (the thirty days of the month are called the "dark fortnight," while the fifteen days [of the waxing moon] are called the "light fortnight").
On the day of the *poṣadha* (the term *poṣadha* is translated here as "recitation of the precepts"), one should recite the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.

As for those of the Hīnayāna who remain in their own homes, they should recite the *Pañcaśīla-lakṣaṇa-sūtra* and the *Śīla-vipatti-praśamana-sūtra*. Regarding the two assemblies of lay followers in the Mahāyāna, the characteristics of the precepts they receive differ:
one is the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* with its ten grave and forty-eight light precepts; these are common to all seven classes of practitioners, whether monastic or lay bodhisattvas.

Regarding the reception [of precepts]: there is the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*, which consists of six grave and twenty-eight light offenses. This only encompasses those living as householders and does not include those who have left the home life.
This was the World-Honored One’s regulation applied according to the capacity of his audience; the bestowal of the Dharma depends upon the individual.

If one receives the ten grave and forty-eight light offenses, one should attend the fortnightly *poṣadha* ceremony at a place where there is a community of Bodhisattvas to hear and recite them. Should there happen to be no such community nearby...

In a monastic dwelling or one’s own private Buddha hall, it is permitted to recite [the precepts] oneself. However, if one has received the six grave and twenty-eight light offenses, one must only kneel and recite them before a Buddha image in one’s own residence;
even if a monastic dwelling is nearby, one must not listen to the recitation because the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*) differ.
The characteristics of the precepts in both scriptures are already fully contained in my previous compilation; they are not recorded here.
Regarding the five points concerning erroneous claims:
according to the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma Piṭakas of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles, among the lay precepts, only the two assemblies of upāsakas and upāsikās are mentioned;
I have not yet seen any instance of a *kumārī* (an unmarried girl) receiving the precepts and immediately being designated as a *śikṣamāṇā*. Now...

In the transmission of the precepts at that time, there were many errors; regarding the *śikṣamāṇā* in particular, the errors were especially grave, and thus they must now be corrected. In Sanskrit, *śikṣamāṇā* means "a woman training in the precepts.
She is a female novice (*śrāmaṇerī*) who, upon receiving these precepts, may train in the full precepts of a *bhikṣuṇī*. According to accounts from the Buddha’s lifetime, various nuns...

They would immediately ordain people, allowing them to leave the household life and receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). Because they did not know the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*), these individuals committed unlawful acts. The Buddha said:

"One should grant them the ritual procedure for training in the precepts for two years (two years means two full years), so that they may first practice and study, and only thereafter receive full ordination."

All the major precepts for bhikṣuṇīs should be studied. With the exception of taking food with one's own hands and giving food to others, the sequence of the five groups of renunciants in various sūtras, vinayas, śāstras, and manuals of confession places the śikṣamāṇā above the śrāmaṇera, because she fully trains in the major precepts of a bhikṣuṇī.
These are: bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, and [śrāmaṇerī].

This refers to the śrāmaṇerikā. When the assembly gathers, because the ritual protocols were inconvenient, even the mahābhikṣuṇīs were ranked after the śrāmaṇerīs, and the śikṣamāṇās were ranked after the mahābhikṣuṇīs.
Thus, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "They sit below the bhikṣuṇīs and above the śrāmaṇerīs.
From the mid-Imperial period onward, the ordination platform (*śīla-maṇḍala*) was closed off, and the rules for the precepts (*śīla*) fell into disuse.
It is almost beyond hearing. Not only has the method for training in the precepts long been abandoned, but even the name and meaning of *śikṣamāṇā* have become unknown.

It has come to the point that those who claim an untonsured maiden seeking to receive the five precepts is a *śikṣamāṇā* have passed down this error from one generation to the next, unchanged until today.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, during the time of the Buddha, there was the wife of a certain elder.

She was unaware that she was pregnant when she left the household life and received full ordination (*upasampadā*). Later, as her body grew large and became visible, the elders (*gṛhapati*) criticized and disparaged her.

Consequently, the Bhikṣuṇīs established the rule that there must be a two-year period of training in the precepts; only after receiving the six rules (*ṣaḍ-dharma*) may one then receive full ordination.
Based on this textual evidence, it follows that a married woman may also become a *śikṣamāṇā*, and the term does not refer exclusively to a maiden.
Furthermore, the treatise states: "There are two types of śikṣamāṇās: first, those who are eighteen-year-old maidens who receive the six rules;
second, those who are ten years old in their husband's family and may receive the six rules. This text refers specifically to the maiden;

as for the phrase "ten years old in her husband's family," commentators explain that this may be due to the mother’s death, or because the maternal family is poor and suffering and thus unable to provide protection and support, whereby the girl is [taken] young...

A woman who has returned to her husband’s home and lived there for ten years finds that the aperture of emotion gradually opens; moreover, while living with a husband, it is difficult to remain free from desire.
Furthermore, as for the eighteen young maidens, although they have not yet married, their years are already advanced; therefore, one must take precautions.
However, it need not be discussed whether she is a maiden or a wife; if she is one who has already left the household life, then there is no doubt regarding her reaching that state.

They are placed above the śrāmaṇeras and below the bhikṣuṇīs because, although they have left the household life with the aspiration to attain full ordination, they are temporarily delayed for two years due to considerations of interference and suspicion; this serves as a period for training in the precepts.

This is not comparable to the śrāmaṇeras and others, who do not yet possess the aspiration for full ordination. Furthermore, these śikṣamāṇās are not the same as the upāsikās regarding what they receive.
Regarding the characteristics of the precepts, there are separate rules for the training of *śikṣamāṇās*, which will not be detailed here.
According to the Vinaya regulations, a *śikṣamāṇā* is specifically a renunciant nun (*pravrajitā bhikṣuṇī*), and not a lay girl observing the precepts. According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
The youth Sudhana went to the great city of the royal capital of Sthira, wishing to visit the laywoman Acalā, but he did not know her location.
Countless crowds of people all told him: "The laywoman Acalā is a maiden living within her own home, protected by her parents," and so forth.
According to this, it can be seen that a maiden may also be called an upāsikā (laywoman).
Yet another clear proof.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty.

Qingpingyao Zhenji Houxue Yirun, Reprint of the *Expounded by the Great Master Tiantai Zhizhe*:
"The Bodhisattva Precepts are the opening chapter for mobilizing goodness and the vanguard for repelling evil.
By returning directly to the Way, the source of birth can be exhausted."
The Master Yunqi Lianchi’s *Fayi* (Revealing the Hidden Meaning): "The source of birth can be exhausted.

That one has undergone births throughout kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, flowing on without end, is truly because of practicing erroneous deeds and following deviant paths, being deluded and turning one's back on the way home.
Now, by adhering to these precepts, ceasing evil and practicing good, one follows the path of rectitude, stilling delusions and returning to the Truth."
Indeed, how could one not dry up the flowing currents of the river of craving and parch the vast expanse of the ocean of suffering,
thereby realizing and attesting to non-arising?

If even those of the Śrāvaka’s minor practices cherish and revere the *vinaya*, how much more so should a Bodhisattva, possessing a comprehensive heart, not maintain the precepts with meticulous care?
Both the internal and external factions alike venerate and uphold [the teaching]. The common people of the royal house submit themselves with reverent devotion;
surrendering their persons as pledges, they turn toward it with single-minded submission.
This is indeed the supreme cause for hastening toward the ultimate fruit and the wondrous practice for establishing the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

Since Buddhahood is attained through the precepts, they are called the supreme cause for the ultimate fruit; they function as the vehicle for directing wholesome intentions and rely upon the precepts to subdue demons.
Therefore, it is called the "Sublime Practice of the Site of Enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa), which serves to repel evil intentions.
The scripture is titled the *Brahmajāla* because it seeks to clarify that the Buddha-dharma teachings are diverse, just like the mesh of the net of the Brahma King.

Regarding the term "ground of the mind" (*cittabhūmi*) in this chapter: the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline (*saṃvara*) universally guards the three types of action (*trikarma*). Mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*) are one in essence and differ only in name.

Among the three types of action, mental action (*manaskarma*) is primary, while bodily and vocal actions are secondary. This is discussed from the perspective of what is most preeminent; therefore, it is called the "ground of the mind."

Regarding "the substance is one while the names differ": initially, there is only the single substance of true suchness, quiescent and still. It receives the name "mind" (*citta*) due to its accumulation and origination;
it receives the name "thought" (*manas*) due to its deliberation and measurement; it receives the name "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) due to its discernment and differentiation.
When its fundamental source is investigated, these are not two distinct substances.
*Bodhisattva* is translated as "One who accomplishes sentient beings through the mind of the Great Way. This title is established because their mental activity is vast and universal.

From the initial generation of the resolve for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) until the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), all are called *bodhisattvas*. The term for "Dharma" (*dharma*) carries the meaning of "precept" (*śīla*).
In the Sanskrit language, it is *śīla*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that in the language of Qin, it means "innate goodness" and is also called "coolness," because it can...
It is called "Pratimokṣa" (Discipline) because it stops the heat and affliction of violating the precepts;
it is also translated as "Preserving Liberation," meaning that by maintaining the three karmas, one is freed from all bonds.
It is also called "pure livelihood," meaning one sustains oneself with purity;
it is also said to mean "accomplishing dignified deportment."
Its majesty is awe-inspiring and its ritual protocols are exemplary.

In future births, one will avoid the three evil realms; taking form in a pure land, one prevents transgressions and ceases evil. Thus, it is also said that "precept" (*śīla*) refers to the meaning of restraint.
To bind oneself by vows and not indulge in license.
"Instruction" (xùn) means teaching and admonition.
Furthermore, it is said that "le" (勒) signifies restraint and "jin" (禁) signifies prohibition.
Just as a horse accepts its bridle, or as one obeys the prohibitions and edicts of a king, daring not to transgress them—both of these are names established according to their respective meanings.

Now, regarding what is called "precept" (*śīla*), there is the precept of discipline (*saṃvara-śīla*), the precept coexistent with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahaja-śīla*), and the precept coexistent with the Path (*mārga-sahaja-śīla*).
Precepts (*śīla*) are prohibitions; ritual decorum (*vṛtta*) refers to physical deportment, which can restrain various evils of the body. Concentration (*samādhi*) is stillness and withdrawal;

at the time of entering meditative absorption, one naturally becomes disciplined and wholesome, preventing all evils. The Path (*mārga*) is that which enables penetration; after the realization of truth, there is naturally no transgression.
At the stage of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), when plowing a field, insects remain four inches away—this is the power inherent in the Path. These two [precepts and concentration]...

The dharma of precepts is a superior function of the mind; its power can give rise to the precepts. Because the path (*mārga*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) arise simultaneously with the restraint (*saṃvara*), they are called "concomitant.
Regarding "concomitant with concentration": when the mind is tranquil, all evils do not manifest. Regarding "concomitant with the path": when the mind is luminous, the multitude of delusions [cease].

It ceases of its own accord; one merely cultivates meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and the precepts are thereby perfected. Hence it is said that they arise simultaneously with the restraint (*saṃvara*).

As for the three categories of restraint—restraint of the person, restraint of wholesome dharmas, and restraint for the sake of sentient beings—these three clusters of precepts are named after the *Śrī-mahāyāna-saṃgraha-vaipulya-bhūmi-śīla-sūtra* (the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*) and do not pertain to the Tripiṭaka.
This bodhisattva restraint encompasses the cessation of the three types of action; here, it is presented through the manifestation of body and speech.
All are termed "restraint" (*saṃvara*).
Precepts encompass the three types of action. That restraint now appears to belong primarily to body and speech is because it is defined by its manifest characteristics.
Regarding the "gathering of virtue": based upon restraint, one gives rise to the mind of great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*), which is able to cease all non-cultivation of virtue.
Regarding the matter: one diligently cultivates all manner of goodness to fulfill the vow for bodhi.
While the meaning of *śīla* (precepts) is the cessation of evil, it is called "gathering goodness" because one practices all virtues precisely where evil is ceased.
Thus, it is said that from the foundation of the *vinaya* (discipline), one gives rise to the bodhicitta.
Regarding "gathering [beings] for their welfare": there are eleven matters by which a bodhisattva benefits sentient beings.
First, performing acts of benefit for sentient beings by always engaging in the same activities as them; second, tending to the sick; third, preaching the Dharma; fourth, repaying kindness;
fifth, rescuing them from suffering and hardship and dispelling their grief and affliction; sixth, providing for the poor; seventh, gathering a community through virtue; eighth...
1. To comfort sentient beings; 2. To praise those with virtue; 3. To censure faults and evils so that they may reform; 4.
To manifest faults and evils through supernatural powers (ṛddhi) so that people will fear and avoid them.
The *vinaya* (discipline) enables the mind to abide; it gathers what is wholesome to spontaneously fulfill the Buddha-dharma, and it gathers sentient beings to bring them to maturity.
These three encompass all the precepts of a Mahāsattva. In the "Chapter on Precepts" of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, ten kinds of precepts are enumerated: first, the unimpaired (*avikala*).
"Deficient" refers to that which is already completely abandoned or destroyed; it belongs to the *pārājika* (defeats).
Second, "unbroken" refers to that which is damaged but not yet destroyed; it belongs to the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meetings)."
3. Not pierced. As for "pierced":
if it is leaking but not yet damaged, it constitutes a pāyattika offense. 4. Not mixed.
When both body and mind are fully integrated, it is called "unmixed"; thus, one avoids all three faults. Five: Following the Path.

By conforming to the principle of the Truths (satya), one is able to destroy the delusions of views. Six: Non-attachment. Having seen the Truth and become a sage, one is free from any defiled attachment toward the delusions of thought.
These two points concern the observance of the precepts according to the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya). Seven: Praised by the Wise.
8. Sovereignty (*vaśitā*): With respect to a bodhisattva’s transformation of others, they attain sovereignty amidst the world while being praised by the Buddhas;

this refers to the observance of precepts according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). 9. Accordance with meditative concentration (*samādhi*): Without arising from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), they manifest all modes of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*).

Manifesting the images of the ten realms to guide and benefit sentient beings, their majestic deportment and movements are spontaneously and eternally pure; therefore, it is called the "precept of following meditative concentration" (*anupādiśamatha-śīla*).

When manifesting from the cessation of concentration, they are the conventional within the ultimate; when their movements are eternally pure, they are the ultimate within the conventional—spontaneously so.
"Zhe" (者) means "spontaneously" or "naturally.
As for the "tenfold fulfillment": the various precepts and disciplines previously mentioned that involve restraint are termed "incomplete," whereas the precepts of the Middle Way [are complete].

There is no precept that is not fully provided; therefore, it is called "complete. By employing the wisdom of the Middle Way, one universally enters into all phenomena; therefore, it is called "complete.
This is the upholding of the precepts of the ultimate truth of the Middle Way.
Such precepts encompass all precepts and further enter into all precepts. Commentary:
Just as the Indra’s net of the Great Brahmā King possesses a thousand layers of variegated patterns that do not obstruct one another, so too are the gateways of the Buddhas’ teachings;
they adorn the Brahma-body without any obstruction. This name is established based on this analogy. In summary:
The metaphors throughout this treatise are diverse and not uniform, like the net of Brahmā. The title of the chapter, "Mind-Ground" (*cittabhūmi*), is also a metaphorical name.
What is elucidated within this chapter—the essential functions of the Mahāsattva—is like the heart within a human body;
it can coordinate all affairs, produce supreme fruits, and serves as the basis for the Mahāsattva. In terms of its meaning, it is like the earth.
*Fayi*: "Indra" is here called the Heavenly Emperor (*Tiandi*), and is also termed the "Red Jewel" (*chizhu*).

This refers to the red-jewel net of the Great Brahmā Heavenly King, wherein crimson rays radiate back and forth and jewel colors intermingle in brilliance, forming a thousand layers of intricate patterns."
There is no mutual obstruction. Citing this to clarify the worlds of the ten directions, their infinite establishment is likewise so.
The gateways of the teachings of the Buddhas of the ten directions, their infinite arrangements, are likewise so.
The various practices and realizations of the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions who rely on these teachings, their infinite diversity, are likewise so. Their adornments—
As for the Brahma-body (Brahmakāya): it is the essence of the pure mind, the source of all Buddhas, which is named the Brahma-body.

Arrayed, it constitutes immeasurable worlds; unfolded, it constitutes immeasurable gates of teaching; and manifested through transformation and guidance, it constitutes immeasurable practices and realizations.
Thus, the adornment of this body is like that of the Brahma King, who uses nets of pearls as floral ornaments.
"Mind-ground" (cittabhūmi) is also a metaphor. It means that when the hundred skeletal members of a human body are assembled together, there must necessarily be a governing mind.
When a Bodhisattva cultivates the manifold virtues, there must necessarily be a vital and subtle function.
This vital function is precisely the precept of the essential substance of the source-mind. All matters are presided over by it, just as the earth supports all things.

The arising of the causes for the supreme fruit is like the earth’s nurturing of all things. As for the reason the sutra is titled *Brahmajāla* and the chapter is titled "Mind-Ground" (*Cittabhūmi*), it is because:

the inherent purity of self-nature is called "Brahma" (*brahma*), and its encompassing of the realms of dust and worlds is called "Net" (*jāla*). —Master Ouyi of Lingfeng, Combined Commentary. Self-nature is fundamentally pure, hence it is named "Brahma.
It contains and encompasses the realms of dust and worlds, hence it is named "Net."

At that time, Vairocana Buddha, for the sake of this great assembly, briefly opened up a portion of the Ground of the Mind (*cittabhūmi*) from among the inexpressible Dharma-gates as numerous as the sands of hundreds of thousands of Ganges Rivers— just as much as the tip of a hair.
Commentary: Vairocana is translated as "Pure and Perfect. It is called "Pure" because all afflictions have been completely exhausted;
it is called "Perfect" because all virtues are fully realized.
*Fayi*: When all afflictions are exhausted, there is no delusion that is not eliminated; this is the fruit of ceasing evil.
When all virtues are perfected, there is no excellence that is not gathered; this is the fruit of practicing good. This "great assembly" refers to the Buddhas upon the thousand petals.
"Even as much as a hair-tip: by using the small to illustrate the great, this speaks to the extreme vastness of the Dharma-gate.
This has been taught by all Buddhas of the past, will be taught by the Buddhas of the future, and is being taught now by the Buddhas of the present.
Bodhisattvas of the three periods have studied, will study, and are now studying it. I have cultivated this 'Mind-Ground' for a hundred kalpas; therefore, they call me [the Tathāgata]."
Vairocana, you Buddhas transmit what I have spoken to all sentient beings, opening the path of the mind-ground for them.
This has been transmitted by the ten thousand sages without differing words, and received by the thousands of worthies as a non-dual Dharma.
It is also the perfected Dharma already tested by myself; it should be clearly followed and trusted. To "transmit" means to pass on the Buddha’s words.
And regarding sentient beings: as for opening the path of the mind-ground, the original mind-ground is level, upright, empty, and penetrating.
Since beginningless time, deluded emotions have congested and obstructed it. By restraining oneself with the precepts (*śīla*), these congestions depart and obstructions are removed;
it becomes vast, level, and upright, and expansive, empty, and penetrating. This is the essential purport of this sutra. Question: "To collect the mind is the precept. What does this mean?

What is meant by "opening"? The answer is: the precepts of the Hīnayāna merely involve restraint and self-preservation, whereas the precepts of the Mahāyāna additionally involve opening up and benefiting sentient beings.
Thus, the meaning of "restraint" is narrow, while the meaning of "opening" is broad.
At that time, in the Lotus Treasury World (Padmagarbhalokadhātu), amidst a brilliant celestial radiance, upon the lion throne, Vairocana Buddha emitted light.
This light addressed the Buddhas upon the thousand petals of the lotus, saying: "Take this 'Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground' and depart.
He then further transformed into the billions of Śākyamunis and taught this "Chapter on the Supreme Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground" in succession to all sentient beings.
"You all should receive, uphold, read, and recite [this], and practice it with single-minded devotion.
"The manifestation" refers to the Lotus Treasury World (*padmagarbha-lokadhātu*), which is the Flower Treasury World (*puspagarbha-lokadhātu*).

"Proclaiming light" means that [the Buddhas] such as those on the Cloud Terrace (*meghaprāsāda*) and others all preach the Dharma. Regarding "a thousand times ten million": in the Western Regions, there are four types of "ten million" (*koṭi*); the first is... (ten).

Ten million, ten billion, ten trillion, ten quadrillion; now [it is] a hundred thousand times ten billion. This means that there are a hundred billion upon each of the thousand petals, taking "ten million" (qianwan) as "one hundred million" (yi).
This refers to the number of the Great Trichiliocosm. The phrase is then turned to connect with the following sentence, stating that it also includes all Buddhas and sentient beings.
According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Śākyamuni is identical to Vairocana, though they are distinguished by their respective superior and inferior aspects.
They are not one, for they fuse the fundamental and the manifested; yet they are not different, for they now follow capacities and conditions within the gateway of transformation and salvation.
In principle, this should open the ears [of the listener]. Combined Commentary: Regarding "emitting light to announce universally," this reveals the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground.
Whether fundamental or manifested, whether cause or fruit, there is nothing that does not take wisdom as its precursor. Thus, it is explained in the upper fascicle.
Kāśyapa initiated [the assembly] by emitting light; the Bodhisattvas gathered the multitude by emitting light; now Śākyamuni emits light to entrust [the teaching];
and subsequently, Śākyamuni again emits light to recite the precepts.
At that time, the Buddhas upon the thousand-petaled lotuses—the hundreds of billions of Śākyamunis—rose from their majestic lion thrones within the World of the Lotus Treasury.
Each withdrew in turn, and from every part of their bodies they emitted inconceivable rays of light.
These lights all transformed into immeasurable Buddhas, who simultaneously offered infinite flowers of blue, yellow, red, and white to Vairocana Buddha, receiving and upholding [his teaching].
The "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground" has been concluded. Each [of the Buddhas] then vanished from this Lotus-Womb Treasury World.
Having vanished, they entered the Samādhi of the Flower-Light of Essential Nature Space and returned to their original source world, beneath the Bodhi tree in Jambudvīpa.
Emerging from the Samādhi of the Flower-Light of Essential Nature Space, they then sat upon a thousandfold vajra...
At the Radiant King’s throne and in the Hall of Sublime Light, he taught the ten oceans of worlds. Rising from his seat again, he went to the palace of Śakra and taught the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Rising from his seat again, he went among the Yāma devas and taught the ten practices (*caryā*). Rising from his seat again, he went to the fourth heaven (*Tuṣita*) and taught the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*).
Rising from his seat again, he went to the Nirmāṇarati devas and taught the ten meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*). Rising from his seat again...
