however, there is no such restriction regarding the withholding of material wealth. Furthermore, within the first two years of ordination, a nun shall not be given material wealth.

Regarding the Dharma: to fail to give [the precepts] after two years constitutes an offense of the third category (pārājika). To fail to give within two years constitutes an offense of the seventh group (sthūlātyaya).
"To conceal" means that within two years—that is, while still less than two years since first going forth—one has not yet attained self-reliance;

at the initial stage of going forth, one is unable to stand on one's own, and thus the bestowal of both material wealth and the Dharma is appropriate and urgent. Once two years have passed, one is gradually able to stand on one's own; [at this point,] one may either give or...

It may be relaxed. For Śrāvakas, not giving wealth is not subject to a formal rule of restraint. As for the double rule for Bhikṣuṇīs, it is because the method by which women request wealth is such that neither [party] can easily change their course;
therefore, in addition to the censure, each instance is separately defined according to the specific matter, and they do not combine to form a single grave offense.

*Fayi*: Regarding the two matters of stinginess (*mātsarya*) and disparagement (*nindā*), they do not combine to form a single grave offense; rather, it is stated that each constitutes a distinct transgression. This differs from the analogy of praise and disparagement.

If, O Son of the Buddha, one is stingy oneself, teaches others to be stingy, or [engages in] the causes of stinginess, the conditions of stinginess, the methods of stinginess, or the karmic actions of stinginess—yet the Bodhisattva sees...
When any impoverished person comes to beg, the Bodhisattva should give them whatever they require;
yet, if with a malicious mind or a hateful mind, they do not bestow even a single coin, a single needle, or a single blade of grass;

or if there is one who seeks the Dharma, they do not explain even a single word, a single verse, or a portion of the Dharma as small as a mote of dust, but instead revile and insult them—such a person is a Bodhisattva [in name only].
A *pārājika* offense. [Combined commentary:
"With a mind of ill-will" means being stingy, parsimonious, and mean-spirited. "With a mind of anger" means not being pleased with that person.

This does not refer to subduing by discerning the [disciple's] capacity. This also involves both natural (*prakṛti*) and proscribed (*pratikṣepa*) karma. Five conditions constitute the gravity [of the offense]: first, the assembly...
First, birth; second, the perception of a sentient being; third, a mind of stinginess and disparagement; fourth, manifesting the signs of stinginess and disparagement;

fifth, the other person’s acceptance [of these signs]. Regarding "sentient beings": those in the upper and middle realms, as well as those in the lower realm who possess precepts, all constitute grave offenses; others are minor.
The six phrases regarding the perception of sentient beings consist of three heavy and three light cases, as explained above. Regarding "a mind of stinginess and disparagement":
this refers to being maliciously resentful and begrudging with respect to wealth or the Dharma, wishing to strike, revile, or refuse others; such acts constitute an offense.

However, if it would be inappropriate for them to hear the Dharma or receive wealth, or if they ought to be rebuked and humiliated, there is no offense. To manifest the signs of stinginess and disparagement means either to conceal or evade [the teaching].
If one does not give wealth or the Dharma; or says there is none at all; or drives the person away with a staff;
or addresses them with harsh words and abuse; or does it oneself; or causes another to strike or revile them—all these constitute grave offenses.

If the other person accepts [the refusal], perceiving my signs of stinginess and receiving my blows and insults, a grave offense is incurred in accordance with each specific act and word. If they... [are sent away]... [the offense is likewise grave].

If one is asked by a messenger to seek wealth or request the Dharma, yet acts with stinginess toward that messenger, speaking reproaches from afar—since this is not face-to-face, the harm and affliction are somewhat slight;
in all such cases, no grave offense is incurred, or even if grave, the precept is not lost. There is no transgression in the following cases:
The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states: "If one does not possess [the object] oneself; if one seeks an object that is not lawful; if the object would not benefit the recipient;
if one employs skillful means to subdue the recipient; if the recipient has violated the king's law and one acts to protect the king's mind;
or if one acts to uphold the monastic regulations—these clarify that withholding wealth in such cases does not constitute an offense. It further states: "If a non-Buddhist seeks to find fault..."
If they are gravely ill; if they are insane; if one knows that by not speaking [the truth] one will bring them to discipline; if the Dharma one practices has not yet been mastered;
if one knows that the person before one is incapable of respectful compliance or lacks proper decorum; or if they are of dull faculties.
If, upon hearing the profound and subtle Dharma, one gives rise to a mind of fear; or if one knows that having heard it will increase wrong views, lead to disparagement, or cause regression;
or if that person intends to speak of what they have heard to evil people—this clarifies that not giving [the teaching] to such a person does not constitute an offense.
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: "If a petitioner comes three times and one does not give, this is called a grave transgression.
There is no transgression if one uses skillful means and kind words to console them, ensuring that the petitioner does not give rise to resentment.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva gathers a following of disciples, they should protect and sustain them through two matters, namely:

Regarding the Dharma, as well as food and clothing, one should likewise observe this precept while concurrently applying its prohibitions and allowances. As for the distinction between what is prohibited and what is permitted, the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states:

"If one observes that sentient beings can be benefited through skillful means by using harsh words, yet refrains from doing so out of fear that they will become distressed or sorrowful, this constitutes an offense that arises from non-affliction.
There is no offense if, upon observing them, one perceives that [the harsh words] would result in little benefit in the present..."
Benefit. As for the retribution of frequently giving rise to sorrow and affliction: the sin of stinginess and disparagement likewise leads to the three miserable realms (*trāya*).

Furthermore, as a residual retribution for stinginess regarding wealth, one is born impoverished life after life; as a residual retribution for stinginess regarding the Dharma, one is dull-witted and ignorant birth after birth.

[The text] clarifies that those who are physically poor beg for wealth, while those who are mentally poor beg for the Dharma; therefore, one should provide them with whatever they require. Thus it is said.
It is said: "All. The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states: "Upon seeing a beggar, one should give according to one's means, whether much or little.
To send them away empty-handed constitutes an offense. According to this, if even a lay bodhisattva acts thus, how much more so should an ordained bodhisattva who studies great compassion?
Question: "If my own understanding is not yet clear, and I have no Dharma to instruct others, what should I do? Answer:
This rule prohibits withholding [confession] when it exists; if there were no such rule, one should naturally face the matter with sincerity.
One must not speak falsely or delude others, for doing so will instead incur severe retribution.
○ Ninth: The Precept Against Refusing Confession Out of a Mind of Anger.

Commentary: To refuse to accept an apology violates the way of engaging with others; this offense is common to all seven assemblies. However, the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna do not agree entirely on its gravity.

For a Bodhisattva, whose primary purpose is to embrace sentient beings, to harbor anger and create a barrier constitutes a grave offense (pārājika). For a Śrāvaka, who seeks his own benefit, it constitutes an offense of the seventh category (dūṣaṇa-saṃghāvaśeṣa).

If a disciple of the Buddha becomes angry themselves, teaches others to become angry, or engages in the causes of anger, the conditions for anger, the methods of anger, or the karmic actions of anger—
then a Bodhisattva ought to cultivate roots of goodness and non-contention toward all sentient beings and constantly give rise to a mind of compassion and a mind of filial obedience;
yet instead, they further revile and insult all sentient beings, even including those who are not sentient beings, with harsh speech.
Furthermore, if one strikes with the hand, or uses knives and staves, and the intent still does not cease— even when the other person seeks reconciliation and offers apologies with kind words—
if one’s anger remains unresolved, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.

Combined Commentary: As for the "cause," it is a mind of resentment and alienation. As for the "condition," it is the expedient means of hostile anger. As for the "dharma," it is the manifestation of signs and the utterance of words.
As for the "action," it is when the other person understands and knows that they will not accept [the teaching], yet one inflicts the suffering of physical and verbal oppression upon them;
the gravity of the offense is determined by the extent of these physical and verbal actions. As for "non-sentient beings," this refers to transformed or illusory persons.
And so forth. Although those [objects] are insentient, if one perceives them as sentient beings and acts with anger or contempt, one also commits a light offense.

This also involves both natural and prohibitive karma. Five conditions constitute a grave offense: first, a sentient being; second, the perception of them as a sentient being; third, [the intent to harm]; fourth, [the performance of the act]; and fifth, [the completion of the act].
The mind is obstructed by anger. Fourth, showing the sign of not accepting [the apology]. Fifth, the other person understands and accepts it. Regarding "sentient beings":

those who are superior or middling in status constitute a heavy object; those who are inferior constitute a light object. Alternatively, one who possesses precepts is also a heavy object, provided they have not lost their precepts.
The six permutations regarding the perception of sentient beings are as explained above. "The mind is obstructed by anger" means harboring resentment and being unwilling to reconcile.

This refers precisely to the owner of the property. Regarding the demonstration of not accepting [the confession]: it may involve closing the gate to create a separation, or speaking aloud that one will not accept it.
As for what constitutes no offense, the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states: "If one employs skillful means to bring the other person to discipline;

or if the other person does not repent according to the Dharma and their mind is not impartial, then not accepting their confession involves no fault. It further states: "If [the offender] is not remorseful..."
Hatred: if one’s nature does not accept repentance, this is an offense arising from non-affliction.

Furthermore, it is said that if a bodhisattva offends another, or even if they have not committed an offense but cause others to suspect them, they should immediately repent and apologize; likewise for harboring resentment, contempt, or arrogance.

If one does not perform the ritual confession and apology according to the Dharma, it is an offense arising from defilement (*kliṣṭa*). If it is due to laziness or indolence, it is an offense arising from non-defilement (*akliṣṭa*).
This applies unless one employs skillful means to subdue the other person, or unless that person intends to commit an unwholesome act.

Subsequently, if the recipient does not apologize, there is no offense. If one knows that the other person’s nature is prone to quarreling and litigation, and if one were to offer an apology, it would only increase their anger;
or if one knows that the other person is harmonious and patient, free from resentment, yet fears they might feel ashamed or humiliated—if in such cases one does not apologize, there is no offense.
The commentary states: This is a minor defiling offense (*āpatti*), and it should also be governed by this precept as well.

Regarding "opening and prohibiting": The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states that if one encounters sentient beings who ought to be rebuked, subdued, or penalized and expelled, yet—due to a defiled mind—one does not rebuke them; or if one rebukes them but does not subdue them;

or if one subdues them but does not penalize and expel them, this constitutes an offense arising from defilement (*kliṣṭa-āpatti*). If it is due to indolence or laziness, it constitutes an offense [of non-defilement].
It is not an unwholesome arising. One does not commit an offense in the following cases: if the person is incurable; if they are unfit for conversation;
if they are difficult to instruct; if they frequently give rise to resentment; if, upon observation, one fears that because of them a dispute, conflict, or contradiction will arise;
if there is litigation; if there is a dispute within the Saṃgha; if there is schism in the Saṃgha; or if the person is not deceitful and possesses a sense of shame and remorse.

He gradually repented of his own accord. It is further said: "If a bodhisattva has accomplished various supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), he should terrify those who ought to be terrified and attract those who ought to be attracted. This is because he wishes to cause sentient beings to consume their offerings of faith.
If he does not use supernormal powers to terrify or attract them, this constitutes an offense that arises from non-afflictive causes."

Furthermore, the Chinese translation of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states: "Moreover, when a bodhisattva sees sentient beings whose conduct has strayed from the path, who act unreasonably, and who utter coarse and evil speech, he may sternly rebuke and expel them through skillful means in order to lead them out of unwholesome states and establish them in wholesome states.
In this way, with a mind intent on benefiting them, the bodhisattva [acts] toward all sentient beings."
Uttering harsh words does not constitute an offense; rather, it generates much merit. The commentary explains:
since this is done with a mind intent on benefiting others, it is clear that there is no intervening mind of anger. Regarding the karmic retribution:
the sin of harboring resentment also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms. If they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, they are constantly...
Others seek out one's faults. Second, one is constantly afflicted by others' harm.
The Chapter on Pure Precepts (*Śīlaskandha*) states that for one who is free from ill-will (*vyāpāda*), there are likewise four kinds of retribution:

first, in this present life, the six sense faculties are sharp and keen, one’s appearance is dignified and pleasing, and one is trusted and attached to by others; second, the mind is free from ill-will toward all afflictions.
Harm, beating, abuse, and reprimands—none of these arose at all. It was as if someone were holding the *garuḍa* mantra;
no poison whatsoever could harm them. Because they were free from anger, their heart of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) increased.
Through this mantra of loving-kindness, thirty-six *koṭis* of devas, ghosts, and spirits were all subdued and compelled to pay homage to loving-kindness.

The mantra shall cause no harm. Third, in future ages, by means of the ladder of a compassionate mind, one shall ascend to be born in the Brahma world and dwell in peace and happiness for one kalpa, causing all sentient beings to sever evil and cultivate goodness.
Fourth, one shall gradually attain unsurpassed bodhi, fully endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
Blazing and brilliantly manifest, immeasurable merits are accumulated within his body.

○ The tenth precept, the Precept Against Slandering the Triple Gem, is also called the Precept Against Slandering the Dharma of Bodhisattvas, or the Precept Against False Views and False Teachings. "Slander" refers to being in opposition [to the truth].
[This is] the name. In general, any interpretation that does not accord with principle, any speech that is not careful or truthful, and any divergent explanation are all termed "slander.

[From] *Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden): "An interpretation that does not accord with principle" refers to a heterodox and deviant view—a mistaken explanation that does not conform to the correct principle. Speech...
To speak falsely regarding matters that are doubtful or ambiguous without investigating the truth; to propound heterodox views;
and to formulate a separate doctrine contrary to the unchanging, settled conclusions of the sages and worthies of the outside world.

The seven classes of followers commit this offense equally; it is proscribed for both the Great and the Small Vehicles. For a Bodhisattva, whose primary responsibility is to transform others, to allow heterodox teachings to confuse the orthodox constitutes a grave offense.
Śrāvakas differ from this: if they do not desist after three admonitions, they commit an offense of the third category.
If a Buddha’s disciple personally slanders the Triple Gem, teaches others to slander the Triple Gem, or slanders its causes, conditions, teachings, or karma; and if that Bodhisattva,

upon seeing a non-Buddhist or an evil person utter even a single word of slander against the Buddha, feels as though three hundred spears are piercing his heart— let alone when they slander with their own mouths—
and yet fails to give rise to a mind of faith and filial obedience, instead further assisting those evil people in their depravity.
To see someone slandering [the Dharma] constitutes a *pārājika* offense for this bodhisattva.

(Combined note: As for the "cause," it is the mind of wrong view; as for the "condition," it is the expedient means of false speech; as for the "dharma," it refers to matters such as verbal expression and written composition;
as for the "action," it is the understanding and comprehension by the person before one. This also consists of both natural (*prakṛti*) and proscribed (*pratikṣepa*) karma, and is [an act of] evil.
Seeing is the root; furthermore, it is compounded by verbal transgression. Five conditions constitute a grave offense: first, the sentient being;
second, the perception of that being as such; third, the intention to speak; fourth, the actual utterance; fifth, the recipient’s understanding. Regarding the sentient being:

if one slanders those in the higher or middle realms, it is grave; if toward those in the lower realms, it is light. There are six permutations regarding the perception of the sentient being, as previously described.
This can be understood. To speak of those who harbor such views means that, driven by false perspectives, they conceptualize and insist: "Only this is real; all else is false.
Since their minds are fixed upon erroneous interpretations, they delight in proclaiming them to others. Although false views are numerous, there are four primary categories:
first, superior; second, middling; third, inferior; and fourth, miscellaneous. As for the superior, it consists of the denial of cause and effect, as follows:

Regarding icchantikas and others: the "intermediate" refers to those who consider the Three Jewels to be inferior to non-Buddhists. If this is established through mental calculation, one loses the precepts.
However, if the mind recognizes that the Three Jewels are superior while the mouth says they are not, and one has not yet turned back [to the Lesser Vehicle], the essence of the precepts is not lost;

yet for every such utterance, a grave offense is incurred. The "inferior" refers to those who abandon the Great [Vehicle] to take up the Small. If this is established through calculation, one loses the Bodhisattva precepts. Calculation...
If it has not yet been accomplished, one commits a minor offense; this is subsumed under the category of mental opposition to the Mahāyāna precepts mentioned below. Regarding "mixed" [offenses]:
these may involve biased attachment, mixed faith, fixing the mind on the Hīnayāna, or erroneous reflection on the meaning. There are two types of biased attachment.

1. To hold exclusively to the Mahāyāna while slandering the Hīnayāna constitutes a transgression arising from defilement (*kliṣṭa*). 2. To slander a single division [of the teachings] also constitutes a minor offense (*laghu-mala*).
Regarding those with mixed faith: they do not reject cause and effect, nor the Three Jewels or the Mahāyāna;

however, they merely claim that non-Buddhist spirits and deities also possess awesome power, or they petition documents to exorcise spirits, or further encourage others to do so—all such acts constitute minor offenses. [End of section on] Binding.

Regarding those who contemplate the Hīnayāna: although they know the Mahāyāna to be sublime and superior, they wish first to attain the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle and subsequently cultivate the Great Vehicle.
This is called "contemplating retreat" (念退); it constitutes a minor offense (輕垢) and is also subsumed under the transgression of temporarily violating the Bodhicitta precepts as described below.

Regarding those whose reflections on the meaning are biased and erroneous: if it is as people today do, where their understanding of the meaning is shallow and they provide interpretations based on only three or five schools because their intellectual power is insufficient, this should not be considered a transgression.

However, if one carelessly adopts or rejects [the teachings], or if one knows that another’s interpretation is correct yet stubbornly wishes to establish a different view, both constitute a minor offense (light defilement).
Furthermore, there are those who preach "similar-dharma" (pseudo-teachings), as stated in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*: "If..."
The bodhisattva perceives in this way and speaks thus: "A bodhisattva should not delight in nirvāṇa; rather, they should turn away from nirvāṇa.
They should not fear the afflictions (kleśa), nor should they be exclusively weary of them. Why is this?
Because a bodhisattva must undergo birth and death for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas in order to seek great enlightenment (mahābodhi). Having made this [resolution]...

To speak [of it] constitutes a defiled transgression. Why? Because the śrāvaka’s deep delight in nirvāṇa and his dread and aversion toward afflictions do not equal those of a bodhisattva by even a hundred-thousand-millionfold. His cultivation of the undefiled mind surpasses that of an arhat.
Regarding the actual speaking: whether one speaks of it oneself, or instructs another to proclaim it, or acts [upon it].
Regarding written works, commentaries, and the like: if one accepts the erroneous words of a predecessor who has already understood them, one incurs an offense for every word spoken.
If one reads the text and develops understanding through it, one likewise incurs an offense for every word spoken. *Only prohibitions are not exempted.* As for the karmic retribution:
The sin of wrong views also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms. If they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, being born into a family of wrong views; second, having a mind that is deceitful and crooked.

To give rise to such hidden thoughts and seek the Dharma outside [of oneself] are all termed "non-Buddhists" (tīrthika); it does not necessarily mean they are extremely perverse. To abandon the Mahāyāna in one's heart is all termed...
An "evil person" does not necessarily refer to one who commits great evils.
You virtuous students, you should train yourselves in these ten *prātimokṣa* precepts of a bodhisattva.

Within them, you must not commit even a single transgression so small as a speck of dust, much less violate all ten precepts in their entirety. If there is anyone who violates them, [they shall not...]
Though they have manifested the bodhicitta in this present body, they shall lose their status as a king, as well as their status as a *cakravartin* wheel-turning monarch;

they shall also lose their status as a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, and they shall lose the ten stages of setting forth (*prasthāna*), the ten stages of nurturing (*puṣṭi*), the ten vajra-stages, the ten bhūmis, and the wondrous fruit of the eternally abiding Buddha-nature.
They lose everything and fall into the three evil realms, where for two or three kalpas they shall not hear the names of their parents.
Regarding the names of the Three Jewels, for this reason you must not transgress each one individually.

You all, O Bodhisattvas—those who are now training, those who shall train, and those who have already trained—should train in these ten precepts in this manner; you should respectfully uphold them. The eighty thousand categories of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*) shall be explained in detail.
*Fayi* (Unveiling the Hidden): "The Benevolent One" (*renzhe*) possesses compassion, filial piety, and a heart devoted to benefiting others;
this is precisely the title for one who studies the precepts well. It is like what the world calls a person of profound virtue (*houtu*).
*Prātimokṣa* means "preserving liberation. Liberation is the fruit, while the precepts are the cause; thus, the fruit is spoken of within the context of the cause. To uphold the precepts is like...
The level ground is the fruit of Buddhahood; the bodhicitta is the sprout. If the precepts of the mind-ground are deficient, although the seed of the Buddha exists, the sprout will not grow.
Even a Wheel-Turning King, the most honored and noble in the world, also attains this status through the precepts.
Because the mind-ground is upright and majestic, he is fundamentally noble. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*...

The *Mojing* (Commentary on the Vinaya) states: "To commit a *pārājika* offense is called 'destroying the root. Just as when a stone is split or life is severed, how could it ever be restored to its former wholeness?
Although the Mahāyāna repentance rites speak of their eradication, such individuals will forever lack the functional capacity of a monk within the fundamental Dharma.

Since this is a primary prohibition unlike other transgressions, one must be especially diligent and self-disciplined, even to the point of sacrificing one's body, to maintain firm protection. This applies to all ordinary sentiments."
It is easy to arise [in transgression], yet the objects of perception may allow for deficiency. If there is not even a single thought of concealment, the Vinaya permits repentance;

this can only purify the karmic offense of the violation, but how could it ever involve the Dharma of the Sangha? Since one has already studied and is now upholding [the precepts], why offer further exhortation?
It is truly because the mind-ground is inexhaustible; the Bodhisattva studies the Dharma-gate of the mind-ground.
It is likewise inexhaustible. Since the Buddha himself recited it every half-month, how much more so the Bodhisattvas? [Combined Note:

Regarding the statement that one cannot resolve to attain bodhicitta in this life, this refers specifically to the present existence. Furthermore, as for the loss of royal status and the like, this refers to the present life.
Now that its meaning has already been lost in the present, it will surely lose its name as well in the future. Question:
If one violates the first four precepts, then the entire essence of the precepts is lost; if one violates the latter six precepts, one merely loses the Bodhisattva-dharma.
Why is it said that one also loses the status of both bhikṣu and bhikṣuṇī? The answer is: this is a statement made from a general perspective based on the momentum of the situation.
Furthermore, it is like falling from a high place; by the very nature of things, one reaches the bottom without stopping midway.
Thus, the fact that Śāriputra regressed from the sixth mind yet continued to transmigrate through the five realms of existence serves as proof of this principle.

Commentary: The eighty thousand chapters on majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*) shall be explained in detail; this is a pre-emptive reference to the latter section of the Great Text (*Mahāvaipulya-sūtra*), where the eighty thousand chapters on majestic deportment are to be expounded.
*Fayin*: The "Great Text" refers to the original version consisting of one hundred and twenty fascicles.
○ Regarding the Forty-eight Minor Precepts:
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, "I have finished expounding the ten *pratimokṣa* precepts; I shall now expound the forty-eight minor precepts."
*Fayi*: It is not merely called the ten *pārājikas*, but rather the *mokṣa* (liberation). For if one violates them, it is the ultimate evil;
yet if one relies upon them, one attains liberation.
Commentary on the First Precept: Not Respecting Teachers and Friends.

Arrogance must not be allowed to grow, as it hinders progress toward goodness; therefore, this precept was established. It is a violation for all seven classes of practitioners and is regulated by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.
Combined Commentary: Only prohibitions are not permitted; however, if one employs skillful means to bring about subduing, this may also be termed "permission.
O Sons of the Buddha, when one desires to receive the position of a king, the position of a Wheel-Turning King, or when officials receive their positions—
One should first receive the Bodhisattva precepts. All ghosts and spirits will protect the person of the king and the persons of his officials;
all Buddhas will rejoice. Having received the precepts, one should give rise to a heart of filial obedience and a heart of reverence.

Upon seeing elders, preceptors (*upādhyāya*), instructors (*ācārya*), those of great virtue, fellow students, those of the same view, or those of the same practice, one should rise to welcome them, prostrate, and inquire after their well-being. And as for the Bodhi...

Śakra, on the contrary, gave rise to a mind of arrogance, conceit, delusion, and anger; he did not rise to welcome him or prostrate before him, nor did he provide each with offerings according to the Dharma.
Instead, he offered his own body, his kingdom, cities, men and women, the seven treasures, and all manner of goods as provisions for him.
If one does not do so, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
[Commentary on the Hidden Meaning: The Great Precepts apply equally to both monastics and laypeople; why, then, does the text single out kings and officials?

This is because for those who have left the household life, teachers and friends serve as fathers and elder brothers, and it is a matter of natural principle that they should be revered without the need for further explanation. Furthermore, regarding monks and nuns...
There is no fixed position [for the teacher]. Arrogance is difficult to produce; for when kings and officials possess power, pride and haughtiness easily arise.
Thus, while the intention is universal, the expression is partial. A teacher gives birth to my Dharma-body; therein lies the way of a father, and one should therefore be filial and obedient.
A friend assists me in my cultivation; therein lies the way of an elder brother, and one should therefore be respectful. Furthermore, teachers and friends must not be opposed.
One must not be arrogant, for all should practice filial piety and reverence. Passages such as "selling one's body" and so forth speak of the ultimate limit of sincerity and respect;

they describe sacrificing one’s own person for the sake of the Dharma, and one’s resolve ought to be thus. However, this is not necessarily required in every case. [Combined Note: There are three types of *sthavira* (elders):
first, the *sthavira* by years, whose seniority in the precept-ordination (*kaṭhina*) is prior; second, the *sthavira* by merit, who is esteemed by the assembly...
I pay my respects. Third, the Venerable Upādhyāya Dharmatā has entered the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*).

*Upādhyāya* is translated here as "Preceptor" (*qīnjiàoshī*) or "One who gives birth by power" (*lìshēng*), because it is through this person's power that one is born into the body of untainted, wondrous precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*).

*Ācārya* is translated as "Master of Discipline" (*guǐfànshī*), meaning one who instructs in dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) and demonstrates the proper rules and models to me; this refers to the passage below.
This refers to the Dharma teacher who provides instruction. "Virtuous One" (*bhadanta*) is a general praise for one who possesses great merit.

"Fellow student" (*sabrahmacārin*) means one who follows the same teacher. "One of the same view" (*samadṛṣṭi*) means one whose mind shares the same understanding. "One of the same practice" (*samacaryā*) means one whose body performs the same actions.
"Arrogance" (*mada*) is to exalt oneself; "conceit" (*māna*) is to disregard others; "delusion" (*moha*) is not knowing the noble ones (*ārya*); and "anger" (*dveṣa*) is the state of the mind...
Regarding the passage "conceiving anger and selling one's own body," this cites a grave case to illustrate a lighter one;
it means that if one should still perform such offerings, how much more so should one not fail to perform the rites of welcoming and prostrating? These are the forty-eight minor precepts.
According to the ten grave rules (*daśa-guru-dharma*), there must likewise be causes, conditions, dharmas, karmic actions, and so forth;
however, because these minor stains (*laghu-āpatti*) are collectively designated as "wrongdoing" (*duṣkṛta*)—whether they have been completed or not—they are not explained in detail here.

These also consist of both natural (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and proscribed (*prajñapti-sāvadya*) karmas, which become grave through four conditions: first, the teacher or companion, namely the *sthavira* (elder) and fellow practitioners.
2. Regarding the six phrases concerning the perception of [others] as teachers or friends: two are grave, two are light, and two are non-offenses. 3.
As for the lack of a respectful mind—such as failing to rise to greet or prostrate due to arrogance, anger, or resentment—this constitutes a defiled offense (*kliṣṭāpatti*).

If one fails to do so due to laziness, indolence, a neutral state of mind (*avyākṛtacitta*), or forgetfulness, the offense arises from a non-defiled motivation (*akliṣṭāpatti*). There is no offense if [the other person] is heavy... [text truncated].
If one is ill; if the mind is distracted; if one is asleep and unaware; if one is listening to the Dharma; if one is preaching the Dharma;
if one is among the assembly hearing the Dharma and protects the speaker’s mind; if one uses skillful means to bring another into subjection; if one protects the monastic regulations;

or if one protects the sentiments of many people—these four cases constitute a completed act [of non-offense], such as not going to welcome someone when one should have welcomed them, or not providing offerings when one should have provided them.

The offenses are determined according to the specific circumstances; they are strictly prohibited and not permitted. However, if one employs skillful means to bring about subduing [of the transgressor], this may also be termed "permission.
Regarding the karmic fruit: teachers, friends, and spiritual mentors are the great causes and conditions for attaining the Way and constitute the entirety of the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
If one does not respect them, one will forever lose the benefits of the Dharma and be possessed by Māra. If one respects them, one will constantly encounter virtuous conditions.
To accomplish the Buddha-dharma.
○ Second, the Commentary on the Precept Against Drinking Alcohol:

Because alcohol opens the door to negligence, it is proscribed. It is an offense for all seven assemblies; it is regulated by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. It constitutes a violation with every swallow.
"Light defilement.
"Revealing what was hidden. "Swallowing by swallow": each swallow constitutes one light defilement.
O Sons of the Buddha, if you intentionally drink alcohol, the transgressions arising from alcohol are immeasurable. If you pass a vessel of alcohol through your own hands...
One who provides alcohol for others to drink shall have no hands for five hundred lifetimes; how much more so if one drinks it oneself?
Furthermore, one must not teach any person to drink, nor cause any sentient being to drink alcohol—how much less so if one drinks it oneself? No kind of alcohol whatsoever may be drunk.
If one intentionally drinks it oneself or teaches others to drink it, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
[Combined Commentary. Therefore, "one who drinks" clarifies that it is not a case of drinking through ignorance. "All sentient beings" refers to those of various species.
This constitutes a prohibitive karma (*vāritakarma*). A transgression is established through four conditions: first, it must be alcohol—that is, something which, when drunk, causes intoxication.
2. Regarding the six cases concerning the perception of alcohol: (1) each swallow constitutes an offense; (2) minor impurities; (3) no offense.
(3) Having the intention to drink; (4) it enters the mouth; each swallow constitutes an offense. If one instructs another to drink, both are guilty of an offense for every swallow.
There is no offense in cases where a disease cannot be cured except by alcohol. Exceptions include, for example, the case of Mallikā’s husband.
As for the retribution for the sin of drinking alcohol, there are five sets of five hundred karmic fruits.

For the first five hundred lifetimes, one dwells in the Hell of Saline Dregs; for the second five hundred, in the Hell of Boiling Excrement; and for the third five hundred, in the Hell of Curled Worms.
Four hundred and five [lifetimes] were spent among flies and gnats; five hundred and five [lifetimes] were spent among insects of delusion, fever, and ignorance.

The text states that for five hundred lifetimes he had no hands, though this may simply be citing the final five hundred. *Fayin* asks: For those who are immersed in vice, it is logically consistent that they should have no hands.
Why, then, does one incur such calamity merely by passing a vessel? Furthermore, as for [the gravity of offenses against] a sovereign or a parent...
"Longevity! When a minister or son presents a cup of wine [in celebration], how could such a heart of sincerity and reverence result in an evil retribution? Answer:
"Generally speaking, when we speak of 'offenses,' it refers specifically to those who possess the Bodhisattva precepts.

To resolve upon the Great Mind (bodhicitta) and realize the Great Fruit is precisely what ensures longevity for one's sovereign and parents. As for the reverence shown with a cup of wine, that is but a minor form of respect."
However, the response from those without hands is not something felt by this class of people.

Those who receive such retribution are surely those who habitually hold the vessel of delusion, constantly store the medicine of delusion, entice and lead deluded people, and thereby accomplish deluded karma.

How can they be compared to those who present cups of wine to their sovereign or parents? Although it may not be called "great reverence," they nonetheless do not fail to maintain a heart of sincere respect.
As for the retribution for those without hands, it is certainly not applied to such as these; therefore, I have set this forth.
○ Third, the Commentary on the Precept Against Eating Meat:
Eating meat cuts off the heart of great compassion. A Mahāsattva takes compassion as his fundamental principle; thus, he must renounce it entirely. As for the Śrāvakas—

Regarding the gradual teaching: initially, three kinds of pure meat and so forth were permitted; later, all such meats were also prohibited. If one suffers from a serious illness that can be cured by drinking medicine, according to the Vinaya, it is permissible to consume it.
Alternatively, this was not prohibited due to specific circumstances.
*Fayi*: "Serious illness" excludes minor ailments. In the *Three Piṭaka Enumeration*, the Vinaya permits [eating meat] only in three cases:
not seeing, not hearing, and not suspecting [the animal was killed for oneself]. The *Essential Explanation of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra* adds "naturally dead" and "left over by birds" to make five kinds.
To the [three types of pure meat] previously mentioned, one adds "not for oneself" and so forth, making nine types of pure meat in total: first, not seeing the killing;
second, not hearing of the killing—meaning that one's ears do not hear of the killing, nor does one hear people say, "I killed this for your sake."
3. Not suspecting it was killed for oneself; 4. Not killed for oneself; 5. Naturally deceased; 6. Left over by birds; 7.
Dried while alive—meaning that after death, it dried naturally over time; 8.
Encountered unexpectedly—meaning meeting by chance without prior appointment or agreement; 9. Previously killed—meaning not killed at the present moment.
I have killed; this is indeed one who was already killed previously. [Combined Note:

Knowing that water contains insects, or suspecting it contains insects, to use it without inspecting or straining it is prohibited for both monastics of large and small status. Furthermore, silk from silkworms is prohibited for both large and small status.
However, for the sake of sentient beings, those of the Mahāyāna are permitted to possess *kauśeya* (silk) and the like, though not for their own personal use.
Regarding the use [of animal hair]: the Lesser Vehicle does not prohibit it, nor does the Greater Vehicle have any specific prohibition.
Nevertheless, the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-sūtra* also addresses this matter; therefore, it is most excellent not to use it.
If a disciple of the Buddha intentionally eats meat, they must not eat the flesh of any sentient being.
Indeed, those who eat meat sever the seed of great compassion and the Buddha-nature; all sentient beings will see them and depart. Therefore, all Bodhisattvas—
One must not eat the flesh of any sentient being. To eat meat incurs immeasurable sin. If one eats it intentionally, one commits a minor offense (light defilement). [Commentary:
"To eat meat intentionally" clarifies that this does not refer to accidental consumption; it specifically points to the transgression. Upon seeing [meat], one should abandon it and depart.
It is like the seagull that departed from the old man’s artifice. Question:
The sutras state that when a person who eats meat enters a mountain forest, tigers, wolves, and lions all come to assemble there. Why, then, do you say they depart? Answer:
"Departing" means they are startled by his murderous intent and distance themselves; "assembling" means they are drawn by the scent of their own kind.
They seek one another; whether departing or arriving, these are all conditions of evil. Question: When Guṇavarman responded to the Song Emperor, he said:
"What Your Majesty cultivates differs from that of a commoner. To utter a single virtuous word, and the officials and commoners all rejoice;
to disseminate a single benevolent policy, and both spirits and humans are harmonious. Punishments do not shorten lifespans, and labor does not [oppress the people]..."
If labor is applied, wind and rain will be timely and the hundred grains will flourish. To observe the fast in such a manner—where the fast itself is so great—is it not sufficient?
Why must one first cease eating for half a day or spare the life of a single bird before it can be considered a grand salvation?

These words and the precepts seem, at first glance, to be inconsistent. Answer: This is to follow conditions and accord with capacities, adapting and transforming without stagnation. It is precisely...
This is the very essence of a Great Being (*mahāsattva*). Therefore, when encountering a sovereign who honors the Way, one will comply with and promote his excellence.
When circumstances do not permit such action, then what Ananda spoke was a subtle expedient of indirect and circuitous application—a marvelous art of silent guidance and latent transformation.
In the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the Buddha told Mahāmati: "There are immeasurable causes."
For these reasons, one should not eat meat. As it is said: sentient beings, upon smelling its odor, all give rise to terror, just as dogs are startled and bark at a *caṇḍāla*.
Because compassion does not arise; because incantations do not succeed; because one is abandoned by the devas; because there are many evil dreams at night;
and because tigers and wolves smell the scent. [The scriptural passages] are numerous and not recorded here in full. From the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
Yan also said: "Even if those who eat meat should attain an opening of the mind that resembles *samādhi*, they are all great *rākṣasas*.
Question: "The harm caused by silkworms is also cruel; why is it that while eating meat is prohibited, wearing silk is not? Answer: "..."
Because these textual accounts are seen cross-referenced with one another: boiling cocoons involves the taking of life and is subsumed under the ten grave precepts against killing;

the cauldron of boiling water and the silk-winding machine are subsumed among the instruments of slaughter; by analogy with the raising of domestic livestock, it is subsumed under the category of harming sentient beings;

and for the sake of profit and bodily sustenance, it is subsumed under the category of maintaining oneself through wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*). Furthermore, since the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* also prohibits silk and fine cloth, we know that [these matters] concern the monastic community.
As for the patched-robed practitioners (*śramaṇa*), they are called "plain-clothed scholars" (*bùyī*); there is no need to discuss them further.

As for kings and ministers, however, they detest coarse clothing and value the beauty of the *fùmiǎn* (sacrificial robes and ceremonial caps); this is because the established teachings of the ancients exist to that effect. [Combined Note:
All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and are of the same substance as myself; yet now we eat their flesh, which is an act of extreme cruelty. Therefore—
It is said that this severs the seeds of great compassion and the Buddha-nature. The *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra* states:

"If silk, cotton, or fine cloth has been passed down through successive hands and is separated from the hands of a killer, yet is offered to a bhikṣu, it should not be accepted. One who accepts it lacks compassion.
This constitutes a prohibited action (*pratiṣiddha-karma*) wherein guilt is established through four conditions: first, it must be meat; specifically, the flesh of a sentient being.

The parts of the body: (1) flesh; (2) two types—those considered heavy and those considered light; (3) two cases where there is no offense; (4) when there is the intention to eat, this constitutes the primary act of ownership;
(5) upon entering the mouth, for every swallow, an offense is incurred. Regarding what is permitted or prohibited:

if antlers of deer, tiger bones, or the like are processed and incorporated into medicine, this should not constitute an offense. However, if one harms a living being for the sake of medicine, one incurs the same [offense].
Regarding the retribution for the sin of killing, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "To kill sentient beings for profit, or to purchase various meats with wealth—both are evil karmas;
upon death, one falls into the Raurava Hell. The *Buddhottama-śikhara Sūtra* states: "From death to death and from birth to birth, they will prey upon one another;
these evil karmas arise together, persisting until the end of the future."
○ Fourth, the Precept Against Consuming the Five Pungent Roots (wuxin).

Foul-smelling foods obstruct the Dharma; therefore, they are prohibited. For the seven classes of practitioners, great and small, the rules are as previously stated. For Bodhisattvas, it is particularly grave because it causes the complexion to change.
*Fayi*: The vapors of pungent and acrid foods can arouse various desires within the physical body; "slight emphasis" means to place a small degree of emphasis.
If you are a disciple of the Buddha, you must not eat the five pungent roots: garlic, leeks, *chimi*, *lanshi*, and *xingqu*. These are the five pungent roots;
they must not be eaten among any types of food. If you should eat them intentionally, you commit a minor offense (*qinggou-zui*).
Combined Commentary: *Gṛñjanaka* is leek; *laśuna* is garlic; *mūlaka* is small onion. *Hiṅgu* is not found in this region.
If any of these pungent substances are mixed into any food, it may not be eaten; it is not merely a prohibition against eating them alone.
This constitutes a prohibited action (*pratikṣepa-karman*), for their foul stench obstructs pure dharmas; therefore, they are forbidden. It is established by four conditions.

Regarding the transgression [of the rule]: as with the precept against eating meat, concerning what is permitted and what is prohibited—if an illness cannot be cured by anything other than garlic and the like, one must eat it in a secluded room away from others.
One must not enter a Buddhist stūpa or a monastic hall, nor may one enter the monastic bathhouse.
One must not enter the upper latrine. One should wait until seven days after ceasing the consumption of these foods have passed and the foul odor has completely vanished;

then, having bathed and washed one’s clothes, one may enter the assembly after being perfumed with incense, as clearly explained in the Vinaya. Regarding the karmic retribution, the *Buddhottama-sūtra* states:
"These five kinds of pungent plants, when eaten cooked, arouse lust; when eaten raw, they increase anger. Even if one is able to proclaim the Ten [Precepts]..."
The deities of the two classes of sutras and the celestial immortals of the ten directions will loathe its foul stench and all depart from it.
Various hungry ghosts will lick its lips and mouth; its merit and virtue will diminish daily, and it will long be without benefit.

When practicing *samādhi*, virtuous spirits will not protect them, and the Demon King will find an opportunity. At the end of their lives, they will naturally become members of the Demon King’s retinue and receive demonic blessings.
[If one violates this precept] to its full extent, one falls into the Avīci Hell.
○ Fifth, the Precept Against Failing to Instruct Others to Repent Their Offenses:

This was established because those who rely on evil allow their transgressions to grow. Thus, the two monastic orders (bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs) commit a full offense; the remaining three orders as well as lay followers [commit a partial offense].

Even if there is no formal monastic assembly or material offerings [to provide for them], if one sees another commit a transgression and does not cause them to repent, one also commits a minor offense (laghu-pāyattika).

This regulation applies equally to both major and minor precepts. If, O disciples of the Buddha, you see any sentient beings violate the eight precepts, the five precepts, or the ten precepts; break the prohibitions; or commit the seven heinous acts (saptānantarya) or the eight...
It is difficult. If there are those who have committed offenses of violating the precepts, one should instruct them to repent.

Yet, if a Bodhisattva continues to dwell with them, shares the same monastic requisites and offerings, and performs the *poṣadha* together with them—reciting the precepts as part of the same assembly—without exposing their offenses or instructing them to repent, they commit a minor offense of defilement.
Combined Commentary: The "Eight Precepts" refers to the Eightfold Abstinence (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa). Furthermore, the "Eight Grave [Precepts]" refers to those in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
The "Five Precepts" are those received by laymen and laywomen of pure faith (*upāsaka* and *upāsikā*). The "Ten Precepts" refer to the Ten Wholesome Precepts and the Ten Precepts of the Śrāmaṇera.

Moreover, the "Ten Grave [Offenses]" of this sutra—regarding "violation of prohibitions"—comprehensively clarifies the transgression of all precepts; that is, it destroys the clarity of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.

Prohibitions. The seven reversals are detailed below. The eight difficulties are the retributive fruits of violating the precepts: first, hell; second, the animal realm; third, the realm of hungry ghosts;
fourth, being deprived of the sense faculties, such as being blind, deaf, or mute; fifth, being born into a family of wrong views and possessing worldly wisdom and eloquence;
sixth, living before or after a Buddha; seventh, the northern continent (Uttarakuru); eighth, the heaven of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñisattva*). One.
Regarding all offenses of violating the precepts—whether great or small, heavy or light, whether cause or effect—one should instruct them all to perform repentance (*pratideśanā*).

To instruct in repentance means to bring forth the matter by means of the three bases: what has been seen, heard, or suspected, thereby causing one to reform the past and cultivate the future, abandoning faults and transforming toward goodness.
The Sanskrit term *kṣamāpana* is, in this land, translated as "requesting forbearance" or "requesting pardon."
This is the intended meaning. "To manifest the removal of past transgressions" means that "repentance" (*kaukṛtya*) is a term from this region [of China]; its meaning is called "evil-doing.
This refers to retrospectively condemning what was previously done as evil, and resolutely resolving to change one's path and alter one's course;

it thus manifests the cultivation of future goodness. "Living together and sharing benefits" refers to the common taste of food. "The *poṣadha* and the recitation of the precepts" refer to the common Dharma.
Regarding the "flavor" (artha): in principle, one should expose faults in accordance with the Dharma. Therefore, one who neither exposes nor instructs commits an offense.
*Fayi* (Unveiling the Hidden) states: *Poṣadha* means "speaking face-to-face. Every half-month, one exposes faults and performs repentance.

Those who abide in this manner constitute a "pure assembly," hence it is called "Pure Abiding" (*śucivihāra*). *Hezhu* (Combined Commentary) states: This is a prohibitive act (*pratikṣepa-karma*). An offense is established through four conditions. First:
1. There is an offense. 2. There is the perception of an offense; if one actually says there is no offense, it is not an offense. 3. Absence of the intent to instruct. The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states:
"To fail to admonish out of anger is a defiled offense (*kliṣṭāpatti*); to fail to do so out of indolence or laziness is a non-defiled offense. 4.
To dwell together in silence without instructing [the offender] to repent is one offense; to partake of food with them is another.

[These are] offenses. They share the same flavor of the Dharma. Furthermore, there is one offense [for each] act, with a separate determination for each instance. Regarding those who do not commit an offense, the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states: "If one is insane;
if one knows [the truth] but does not speak it in order to subdue that person; if one protects the mind of another; or if one protects the regulations of the Saṃgha."

Furthermore, it is said: To see sentient beings creating unwholesome karma for this life and future lives, and out of a heart of resentment not to provide them with the correct teaching, constitutes an afflicted offense (*kliṣṭa-āpatti*).
There is no offense in the following cases: if one lacks wisdom oneself; if one lacks the power;
if one causes someone who has the power to speak; if the person themselves has the power; or if the person themselves has a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); or if... [the text continues].
One should employ skillful means to bring them under control. If one were to preach the Dharma correctly [to such a person], they would harbor hatred toward me;

or they might utter harsh words, or act with perversion, or lack affection and respect. Furthermore, if that person’s nature is wicked and perverse, and moreover does not repent their own faults, this precept should also concurrently prohibit instructing them to repent; it is merely an action of prohibition (*vāraṇa-karman*).

Not repenting of one's own transgressions constitutes a violation of one's nature-karma (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). Regarding the seven classes of followers (*saptanikāya*), they do not all share the same status.
A bhikṣu may point out the offenses of all seven classes; a bhikṣuṇī may point out the offenses of six classes, but she may not point out the offenses of a bhikṣu.
If one privately exhorts and admonishes a bhikṣu who is a relative or an acquaintance, there is no offense.
A śikṣamāṇā may expose the offenses of the five assemblies, but she may not expose the offenses of bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs.
A śrāmaṇera may expose the offenses of the four assemblies, but he may not expose the offenses of the three higher categories. A śrāmaṇerī may expose the offenses of the three assemblies.

One may not expose the offenses of the four assemblies of the ordained. The two assemblies of the laity may expose offenses among their own respective classes, but they may not expose the offenses of the five assemblies of the ordained.
If there are close friends or acquaintances who privately exhort and admonish one another, there is no offense whatsoever.

Furthermore, for the two assemblies of the laity, there is no matter of sharing communal offerings; they are only prohibited from failing to expose [offenses] and from sharing the distribution [of robes].
Regarding the two transgressions of the *Sāṃghika-vinaya* concerning what is permitted and what is prohibited, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If that person is violent and fierce, or if by the power of a king, the power of a high minister, or the power of violent men, there arises a cause for taking life or harming one who practices the holy life (*brahmacarya*), one should form this thought:
'The karmic retribution for his sinful actions will surely come to him of its own accord; he himself should know this.'"
At that time, if one merely guards the sense faculties, there is no offense. Furthermore, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"There are five internal qualities by which one should exhort another: [exhorting] at the proper time, not at an improper time; with truth, not with falsehood;
for the benefit [of the other], not for their detriment; with gentleness, not with harshness; and with a compassionate heart, not with anger. As for the karmic fruit:

The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "If a virtuous bhikṣu sees one who destroys the Dharma and remains indifferent, failing to reprimand, expel, or remove them from their position, that person is an enemy within the Buddha-dharma.
If one is able to reprimand and expel such a person, know that they shall obtain immeasurable merit, beyond all calculation.
The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: "Cāṇḍālas and the like, as well as butchers..."
"Child, although one may commit evil deeds, they cannot destroy the True Dharma of the Tathāgata, nor will they necessarily fall into the three evil realms.
However, if a teacher fails to instruct and admonish their disciples, they thereby destroy the Buddha-dharma and will certainly fall into hell.
The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states: "It would be better to accept evil precepts than to take the life of countless beings within a single day."
Root. He shall never keep base and evil disciples who cannot be tamed. Why is this?
Such evil discipline brings calamity only upon oneself. To keep evil disciples whom one cannot instruct leads countless sentient beings to commit evil;
it allows them to slander immeasurable, sublime, and virtuous dharmas, and to destroy the harmony of the Saṃgha, causing many...

Sentient beings who commit the five deeds of immediate retribution (ānantarya) are therefore more grievous than those who violate the precepts of non-restraint (*akuśala-saṃvara*). [This is] the manifestation of their hidden [intent]. Question:

If one is instructed but does not reform, should they be exempt from punishment? Answer: Among the scholars of the world, there is a saying: "If instruction is not strict, it is the teacher’s negligence;
if learning achieves no success, it is the student’s fault. If one is instructed yet does not reform, what blame can be attributed to the instructor?
[End of section].
○ Sixth, the precept against failing to provide for those who request the Dharma.

Since this deprives one of the benefit of the resources that sustain the spirit, it is established that all seven assemblies commit this offense equally; however, the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna do not fully share in its provisions.

Combined Commentary: If one has not yet completed five summer retreats (*varṣa*) in the Hīnayāna and is not yet familiar with the Vinaya Piṭaka, one should invite any person who comes who holds the Vinaya;
all others are not so enjoined. In the Mahāyāna, one seeks the Dharma without satiety; therefore, one should invite everyone.
If, O sons of the Buddha, you see a Mahāyāna Dharma Master, a fellow student of the Mahāyāna, or one who shares the same views and practices,
coming to a monastery, a private residence, or a city— whether they have come from a hundred *li* or a thousand *li* away— you must immediately rise to welcome them and see them off,

prostrate before them, and make offerings. You should provide for them three times each day, offering daily meals worth three *liang* of gold, food and drink of a hundred flavors, bedding and seats, and medicine.

One should serve the Dharma Master by providing all that is required. One should constantly invite the Dharma Master to preach the Dharma during the three periods of the day, prostrating at each of the three times daily, and never giving rise to anger or a mind of resentment. One should be willing to sacrifice one's own body for the sake of the Dharma and request the Dharma without weariness.
If one does not act thus, one commits a minor offense.
Commentary: The phrase "those of the Mahāyāna who share the same view and the same practice" distinguishes them from those of the Hīnayāna.
*Fayi*: A "Dharma Master" does not necessarily refer to one who lectures on sūtras and śāstras; rather, anyone who has attained thorough mastery of the Mahāyāna Dharma is such a master.
Regarding "those who study the Mahāyāna together," first the Mahāyāna masters are mentioned, followed by [the students].
"Friends who ride together should all be invited to provide offerings. [Combined Note: Regarding the phrase "daily consuming three *liang* of gold," this is an expression of extreme intensity.
"Three times" refers to before noon, after noon, and during the first watch of the night. "With a mind of anger" means feeling resentment toward that Dharma Master.
"Afflicted by distress" means fearing one's own excessive expenditure. "Willing to sacrifice one's body for the sake of the Dharma" uses a heavy case to illustrate a light one. This is a prohibition.

The karma is established through four conditions for the commission of an offense: first, the person is a Dharma teacher; second, the perception that they are a Dharma teacher (if one does not know this, there is no offense);
third, the absence of a request from them, whether out of anger or vexation—which constitutes a defiled offense—or through negligence, forgetfulness, or error—which constitutes a non-defiled offense;
fourth, passing the time in indifference, whereby the offense is determined according to the specific circumstances. Furthermore, it includes failing to receive the teacher’s instruction.
This precept should also be understood as encompassing these [faults]. The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states:

"To seek a concentrated mind while harboring resentment or pride, and thus refusing to accept the teacher’s instruction, constitutes an afflicted offense (*kliṣṭāpatti*). To do so out of laziness or indolence constitutes a non-afflicted offense (*akliṣṭāpatti*).
There is no offense if one is ill, if one lacks physical strength, if one knows that the person is speaking erroneously, or if one is oneself [overwhelmed by] excessive..."

There is power in hearing [the Dharma]. If one has previously received the teachings regarding what is permitted and what is prohibited, and knows that [the teacher] will not request [instruction], yet acts so as to bring them to discipline, the karmic fruit is this:
by not requesting, one loses the benefit of the熏 (xūn, perfuming) of hearing and obstructs the seeds of wisdom;
by requesting, one is able to remain constantly inseparable from the True Dharma.
○ The seventh precept: not going to hear the Dharma.

The intent of its formulation is the same as before; however, whereas the previous case concerned the Bodhisattva coming to me and my requesting him to preach the Dharma, this present case concerns the Bodhisattva being there and my going to hear the Dharma from him.

If, O sons of the Buddha, there is the preaching of the Dharma, the Vinaya, the Sutras, or the Shastras anywhere—whether in a great residence or wherever else the Dharma is being preached—a newly initiated Bodhisattva should take the volumes of the Sutras and Vinaya and go to the place where the Dharma Master resides to listen, receive, and inquire about them.

Whether it be in mountain forests, beneath trees, on monastic grounds, or within rooms, they should go to all such places where the Dharma is preached to listen and receive it; if they do not go, [they commit an offense].
If one listens to, receives, or inquires about [this] while committing a minor offense, one incurs a light defilement sin.
The commentary states: "The *Vinaya* sutras and precepts" refers to the Mahāyāna *vinaya* sutras and precepts, not the *vinaya* within the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*).
Because Mahāyāna sutras possess the meaning of extinguishing evil, they are called *vinaya*.
*Fayi*: When both the Sūtras and the Vinaya refer to *vinaya*, it is because the power of Mahāyāna sūtras is able to extinguish evil, which is identical in meaning to the Vinaya.
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śīla-sūtra* does not distinguish between distant and near; whereas for the *Upāsaka*, it allows for non-offenses within a *yojana*.

Thus we know that the regulations for those who have left the household life apply to the distant, while the regulations for those remaining at home apply to the near. This is because those who have left the household life take hearing the Dharma as their primary task.
To refrain from going because of the distance is due to contempt for the Dharma. As for those living at home, their bodies are constrained by worldly affairs;
thus, they are unable to listen from afar, yet this is not out of contempt. [Combined Commentary. "In all places" refers generally to both monastic quarters and secular lands.
"Great houses" specifically refers to secular lands, while "mountains, forests, and so forth" specifically refers to monastic grounds. *Dharmavinaya Sūtra*.

Regarding "Vinaya": *dharma* means "guiding and upholding," while *vinaya* means "extinction. These terms refer to that which is explained. The two characters "Sūtra" and "Vinaya" refer to that which explains.
Thus, *vinaya* is correctly translated as "Vinaya," while *sūtra* is also glossed as "Dharma" and "Constant.
Although the wording appears redundant, the meaning is clear. This Dharma-Vinaya is equally upheld by both the Great and Small Vehicles, and is shared by all seven classes of followers.

This practice is not restricted solely to Śrāvakas. This constitutes an obstructive karma (*vāraṇa-karman*). A transgression is established through four conditions: first, it is the teaching of the Dharma and Vinaya;

second, the perception that it is the teaching of the Dharma and Vinaya; third, the absence of the intention to go—whether due to anger, pride, or the like, which constitutes a defiled offense, or due to indolence, which constitutes a non-defiled offense;
fourth, the failure to go and listen. A daily offense is incurred for each day [one fails to attend]. — *Śīlasamuccaya* (Susheng).
In the Sūtras, it is prescribed that one must go within forty *li*. This case should be treated likewise. There is no offense in the following circumstances:
if one does not understand; if one is ill; if one lacks strength; if the other person speaks erroneously; if one protects the mind of the speaker;

if one has heard it repeatedly, already mastered it, and understood its meaning; or if one is practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and does not wish to interrupt it even for a moment—in all these cases, there is no offense.
Regarding transgressions, permissions, and prohibitions, the *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* states:
"If a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma while intermingling it with the doctrines of non-Buddhists, any virtuous bhikṣu who diligently seeks the Way should depart from his seat.
If he does not depart, he is not a virtuous bhikṣu, nor can he be called one who follows the Buddha’s teachings. Regarding the karmic retribution, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi Sūtra* states:

When a bodhisattva listens to and receives the Dharma from a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), they should listen with a pure mind and single-minded attention, without dwelling upon five points regarding the person who preaches the Dharma. First, one should not dwell upon their broken precepts;

that is, one should not think, "This person has violated the disciplinary code (vinaya-saṃvara); I should not receive the Dharma from them. Second, one should not dwell upon their lowly nature; that is to say...

First, one does not think: "I will not receive the teachings of the sūtras from that person of low birth. Second, one does not think: "I will not receive the teachings of the sūtras from that person of evil conduct.
Third, one does not dwell on their ugliness; that is, one does not think: "I will not receive the teachings of the sūtras from this ugly person.
Fourth, one does not dwell on their impaired speech; that is, one does not think: "I will not [receive the teachings] from that person of improper speech."
When listening to and receiving the teachings of the sūtras, one should rely solely on the meaning and not on the phrasing. Fifth, one does not dwell on disparaging speech;
that is, one does not think: "I will not listen to or receive the teachings of the sūtras from a person who speaks with coarse words."

If one does not maintain mindfulness regarding these five points, that bodhisattva is diligently upholding the true Dharma and does not give rise to thoughts of aversion toward the teacher of the Dharma.

If a bodhisattva of inferior capacity gives rise to thoughts of another's faults and withdraws from delighting in hearing the Dharma, it should be known that this bodhisattva is unable to deliver themselves; their wisdom has declined and diminished due to the fault of not listening.

Furthermore, if one can listen with a sincere heart, then even as a novice monk who playfully tossed [a flower], one is capable of realizing the four fruits of the path; how much more so for one who truly expounds the True Dharma!
○ The eighth precept: Turning away from the Great and turning toward the Small.

*Fayi*: Whether one has turned away from or remains oriented toward [the Dharma] is not yet determined; this still belongs to the minor offenses. Once turning away or remaining oriented has become established, one loses the Bodhisattva precepts.

Furthermore, when turning away or remaining oriented resides within the mind, the loss pertains only to oneself. When it is manifested externally through speech, the harm extends to others, constituting the tenth grave offense.

If a disciple of the Buddha, in their heart, rejects the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas that abide eternally, claiming they were not spoken by the Buddha, yet instead accepts and upholds the teachings of the two vehicles of the śrāvakas,
the evil views of external paths, and all the prohibitive precepts and heterodox sūtras and vinayas, they commit a minor offense of defilement.
*Fayi*: To turn one's back on the Mahāyāna and claim it is not the word of the Buddha is a grave offense. Why, then, is this categorized as a "light defilement"?
It is because the mind turns away while the mouth has not yet proclaimed these words; these characters represent an internal deliberation.

If there were a sound of slander, it would belong to the tenth heavy offense. [Combined Note]: The phrase "claiming it is not the word of the Buddha" refers to conceptualization through mental intention.

"Speculative reckoning" (*vitarka*) refers to the intention to accept and uphold [a view]. This possesses both the karma of nature (*svabhāva-karman*) and the karma of prohibition (*pratiṣedha-karman*).

To reckon the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*) involves only the karma of prohibition; to reckon the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) involves both the karma of nature and the karma of prohibition, because their views are heterodox.
It directly restrains those who are hesitant and undecided; this is the preliminary means for the two lower types of heterodox views, as their reckoning still [persists].
It is not yet accomplished; therefore, for the time being, a light offense is incurred. If it were calculated as accomplished, one would lose the Bodhisattva precepts.

This applies equally to the seven assemblies [of the Sangha], though the Mahayana and Hinayana do not fully coincide. Since the Hinayana is one's original practice, it is not an offense; however, calculating it as external, one incurs a *rekhā* (guilt of mental reproach).
If one resolves to go there, a sin corresponding to each step taken must be confessed. Upon hearing the teachings of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), one does not enter [into their system].
If one’s mind regrets [the offense] and returns [to the path], it is still permitted to perform repentance and co-reside with the community.
However, if even a single word enters the heart and one follows that [erroneous] teaching—even to the extent of plucking out a single hair—one loses the bhikṣu precepts and incurs a grave impediment;

in this present life, one is no longer permitted to be counted among the Saṃgha. This is a prohibition that is never lifted. As for the karmic retribution, if one calculates it externally, it constitutes a false view.
Falling into the three miserable realms, they regard the Lesser Vehicle as sufficient and obstruct Great Bodhi, thereby concealing their true potential.

Formerly, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu composed five hundred treatises elucidating the Lesser Vehicle and disparaging the Greater; later, upon meeting Asaṅga, he repented his errors and intended to cut out his own tongue.
Asaṅga instructed him to use his tongue to praise the Mahāyāna once more. Vasubandhu received these instructions and resolved his mind toward the Great Vehicle;
he propagated it widely and extensively, ultimately attaining the fruit of sainthood. To reform one's errors without hesitation is truly a law for all ages.
The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: "Reading secular texts, prose, verse, commentaries, or sub-commentaries does not constitute an offense."
It is for the purpose of destroying false views; for the purpose of knowing that external scriptures are false and illusory while the Buddha-dharma is true and real;
and for the purpose of understanding worldly affairs so as not to be treated with contempt by worldly people.
○ Ninth Precept: Not Tending to the Sick.
This was established because failing to do so violates compassion; thus, it is an offense for all seven assemblies. However, the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna do not fully coincide on this point.

A Bodhisattva (Mahāsattva) should tend to everyone, whereas for a Śrāvaka, the duty is limited to teachers, friends, fellow residents, those sharing a room, and other monks and nuns; beyond these, no such rule is prescribed.
Because they fundamentally do not involve themselves with external things.
O Sons of the Buddha: whenever you see anyone who is ill, you should always provide for them and make offerings to them as if they were no different from the Buddha himself.

Among the eight fields of merit, the field of merit consisting of nursing the sick is the foremost field of merit. This applies whether it be one's parents, teachers, monastics, or disciples who are ill, or even those whose faculties...

They suffer from a hundred kinds of ailments and afflictions, all of which he should provide for so as to cure them; yet the bodhisattva, out of a mind of anger and resentment, does not look upon them.
Even within monasteries, cities, towns, wildernesses, mountain forests, or on the roads, if he sees the sick and does not provide relief, [he commits an offense].
[This constitutes] the offense of a light stain.

The Commentary states: "To provide for a sick person as one would for the Buddha" is said to mean practicing the utmost reverence. This clarifies that it is the intention (*citta*) that matters, not the field of merit (*kṣetra*).
For example, when Ānanda divided his rice and gave it to a starving dog, because this intention was pure, it was equal to [giving to] the Buddha. Bodhi...
A bodhisattva, seeing all who are ill, should attend to them all according to their own capacity.

In this text, the mention of parents, teachers, disciples, and so forth begins with those closest at hand; it concludes by stating that whether in cities or wildernesses, one must rescue all who are sick.
This should be understood as applying to all cases. If one sets [the matter] aside with a mind of anger, one incurs a light secondary offense (*āpatti*) according to the person involved.
If one lacks the capacity [to resolve it], there is no offense provided one gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness.
*Fayi*: Among the eight fields of merit, the Buddhas are most venerable. Why, then, is caring for the sick ranked first?

This is because the Buddha represents the field of reverence (*gurutā-kṣetra*), which does not inherently encompass compassion (*karuṇā*). It is precisely regarding these sick people that the Buddha entrusted me with this duty after his parinirvāṇa.
One should provide excellent offerings to them, for they contain many Buddhas and worthy sages; thus they are the Field of Reverence (*gurutā-kṣetra*).

Furthermore, when the hundred limbs suffer in pain and one requires others for the sake of life, they are the Field of Compassion (*karuṇā-kṣetra*). How much more so, then, since all Buddhas and beings of the human and heavenly realms universally make offerings [to the sick];
