this is translated as "garment of intermediate colors," which refers to robes of dyed (debased) colors. This name is established based on the color; it is also called "removing impurity" and "detachment."

Furthermore, regarding the mention of "emaciated clothing" and so forth, these names are established based on their underlying meaning. The phrase "all difficult circumstances" serves as an inclusive illustration for other cases as well.
○ The thirty-eighth precept: Violating the order of seniority and subordination.

Commentary: Because disorder and confusion lead to the loss of proper decorum, this rule was established. It applies equally to all seven assemblies; it is prescribed for both the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna.
If you, O sons of the Buddha, sit according to the Dharma in proper sequence: those who received the precepts earlier shall sit in front, and those who received them later shall sit behind.
This does not depend on age—whether old or young—and applies to bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, nobles, kings, princes, and so forth.
Eunuchs and slaves should all sit first according to the order in which they received the precepts; those who received them later should sit in successive order.
Do not be like the foolish outsiders, whether old or young, who sit without precedence or sequence, following the manner of soldiers or slaves.
In my Buddha-dharma, those who came first sit first, and those who came later sit later; thus it is with the Bodhisattva.
First, regarding sitting out of the proper order: one commits a minor offense (light defilement). [Combined Note:

There are two ways in which sitting is "in accordance with the Dharma" (*yathādharma*): first, generally for all seven classes of practitioners; second, specifically according to the sequence of the precepts.

There are two times for sitting: first, during the recitation of the precepts; second, at ordinary times. In both cases, disorder must not occur. This does not depend on whether [the offender] is questioned.
The categories of "old" and "young" also have two meanings: first, the general sense concerning the seven classes of practitioners; second, the specific sense concerning the sequence of precepts.
Regarding the general sense: even a bhikṣuṇī with a hundred years of seniority may not sit before a bhikṣu who has only recently entered the summer retreat.
This remains the case even if that bhikṣuṇī has received the bodhisattva precepts and likewise possesses a hundred years of seniority.
In early summer, one may sit before a Śrāvaka bhikṣu; how much more so before a bodhisattva bhikṣu? This is because the bhikṣu belongs to the highest assembly.

Therefore, even if a śikṣamāṇā has reached a hundred years of age, or a bodhisattva precept-holder has already completed a hundred *varṣas* (years of ordination), neither may sit before a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī of either the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna. This is because...
Because they have not yet entered the number of the Saṃgha, a śrāmaṇera— even if he is a hundred years old by birth,
or has already observed the Bodhisattva precepts for a hundred *la*— is not permitted to sit before a Śrāvaka *śikṣamāṇā*.
Likewise, a śrāmaṇerī— even if she is a hundred years old by birth, or has also observed the Bodhisattva precepts for a hundred *la*— is not permitted to [sit before one].

A śrāvaka śrāmaṇera sits before [a lay practitioner]. Even if an upāsaka is a hundred years of age and has received the bodhisattva precepts for a hundred *la* (years of ordination), he must not sit before a śrāvaka śrāmaṇerī who drives away crows;
how much less so before a śrāmaṇera or a bhikṣu. Thus, the *Śīlasamuccaya-sūtra* states: "If an upāsaka..."

If one walks ahead of a bhikṣu or a śrāmaṇera, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*. It should be understood that this is an offense regarding walking (*caryā-saṃvara*). One also incurs an offense when sitting;
this is an offense regarding sitting (*niṣadyā-saṃvara*), yet there is likewise an offense regarding walking. Regarding the two distinct cases:
as with the assemblies of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, one must discuss both the Great and Small Precepts together. When [the assembly] is large...
If it is great, it remains great; if it is small, it remains small. By no means may the great usurp the place of the small.
Thus, when Mañjuśrī accepted King Ajātaśatru’s invitation, he still had to firmly defer to Kāśyapa before temporarily taking precedence over him.

This clearly demonstrates that, in ordinary circumstances, the order of the precepts must not be disturbed. As for the other five assemblies, they should each discuss the Bodhisattva precepts among themselves alone.

Next, it need not be determined by age; this is easily understood. Regarding the mention of "bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, nobles, and so forth," it means that one first enumerates the fixed hierarchy of the seven assemblies from highest to lowest, and subsequently, each group enumerates its own sequence of precepts according to its respective class.
Once the bhikṣus have finished enumerating their sequence of precepts, the bhikṣuṇīs then enumerate theirs; others are not mentioned.

Regarding the "three groups," this is merely an abbreviation of the text. "Noble persons" refers generally to kings, princes, and the like, spoken of in contrast to eunuchs, slaves, and those of low status.
Although these are likewise termed the two groups of householders, they must each be categorized according to their own kind.
For instance, although a prince may have received the bodhisattva mahāśīla, he has not yet left the household life.
The family [lineage] still cannot take precedence over that of one's sovereign or father; thus, it also constitutes a distinct category.
The term "even unto" (*nai-ji*) is a word of abbreviation, intended to indicate that elders, officials, Brahmins, householders, and so forth, each form their own separate category.
This is because, within the conventions of worldly law, these individuals are ranked according to their rank, age, or virtue.
Since there is originally no fixed rule, we shall now simply set forth the precepts. However, there are also kings in the Western Regions who serve as disciples to Brahmins;

this must be discussed separately. For now, we shall provide a general summary for those who have not yet left the household life, and it is certainly not permissible to confuse the titles and positions of ruler and subject. This applies whether it concerns a prince of this country or someone from another country.

As for kings, they act as teachers and friends to one another; or when a prince has not yet ascended the throne, he likewise acts as teacher and friend to brahmins, elders, householders, and others—all of which shall be discussed separately. As for eunuchs and slaves...
Furthermore, they must necessarily form their own distinct class and may not be intermingled with the ranks of the noble.

For eunuchs (*pandaka*), according to the Dharma of renunciation, fall under the category of "grave obstacles" (*gurudharma*); they are absolutely prohibited from entering the ranks of *bhikṣus* or *śrāmaṇeras*.

As for slaves, they fall under the category of "light impediments" (*mṛdu-pratibandha*); if their master grants them a surname, they are permitted to receive the precepts of a *bhikṣu*, a *śrāmaṇera*, and so forth.

Upon entering the ranks of the bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras, one sits before the king; yet even now, though one has received the great bodhisattva precepts, one has not yet escaped the status of a slave or servant.
Therefore, it is necessary to establish them as a distinct category, so that the distinctions between master and servant, noble and base, shall not be confounded.
Question: Since sovereign and subject, father and son, and master and servant all receive [the precepts] together...
The Bodhisattva precepts must likewise each be established for their own specific category.

Why is it that in the Vinaya, when a minister receives full ordination first and a king receives it later, the minister becomes the junior seat-holder; or when a son receives full ordination first and a father receives it later, the son becomes the junior seat-holder;
or when a servant receives full ordination first and a master receives it later, the servant becomes the junior seat-holder? Answer: This concerns the Bhikṣu precepts.
The Dharma manifests supramundane characteristics and is not subsumed under worldly dharmas. Therefore, if a ruler does not grant permission, a subject cannot leave the household life;
if parents do not grant permission, a child cannot leave the household life; and if a master does not grant permission...

Then a slave may not go forth [into the religious life]. Once a ruler, father, or master has granted permission to go forth, at the very moment of going forth, one permanently relinquishes the status and titles of a subject, son, or servant.
Therefore, if the ruler, father, or master later undergoes full ordination (*upasampadā*), that person [the former slave] shall be appointed as the *upādhyāya* (preceptor).
Even if the ruler, father, or king remains a householder, he likewise regards that person as his superior.

They are fields of merit. Therefore, according to the laws of the five regions of India, when renunciants see their sovereigns, fathers, or hosts, they all uniformly address them as *dānapati* (donors), and there is no custom of returning a salutation.
As for the Bodhisattva precepts, they encompass both the mundane and the supramundane; they do not subvert conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Thus, a sovereign remains a sovereign, a subject remains a subject, and the relationships of father and son, or master and servant, remain as they were.
It is likewise so. If one were to remove their titles and ranks while enumerating the sequence of the precepts, then the worldly dharmas would not be established as they are.
Question: If, upon leaving the household life once and for all, one forever relinquishes the titles and ranks of minister, son, or slave...

Is it not the case that one who has neither father nor sovereign is precisely what the Confucianists criticize? Answer: One merely abandons name and status, but does not abandon affection and righteousness.
Therefore, the Vinaya regulations stipulate that a bhikṣu should exert his whole heart and all his strength to provide filial support for his parents.
If he fails to provide such support, he incurs a grave offense. Even when the Buddha’s mother entered nirvana, the Buddha personally lifted her with his own hands.
Furthermore, when a bhikṣu dwells in the mountains and forests, he lacks the ritual protocols for serving a sovereign.

Nevertheless, if he receives the king’s offerings or becomes intimate with the king, he must likewise offer loyal counsel according to the circumstances; in this way, he does not abandon worldly loyalty and filial piety.
How much more so for those who practice according to the Dharma and propagate the sublime teachings, causing devas and nāgas to rejoice, protecting the state and the people,
and enabling their parents of the past and present to together leave the ocean of suffering— this further accomplishes supramundane loyalty and filial piety.
That being so, who could surpass those who have left the household life in terms of great loyalty and great filial piety?

Since such a supreme purpose exists, there can certainly be no further discussion of trivial, empty fame or empty positions. In sum, when discussing that which is vast and great, nothing compares to the Bodhisattva precepts;
therefore, even those remaining at home may receive them upon their heads, yet they are not permitted to disrupt worldly names and positions. Thus it is said:

In terms of respect, nothing compares to the monastic discipline (*vinaya*). It is indeed the banner of the sages and worthies, the fragrant emblem of world-transcendence, that which binds the wheel of the Saṃgha, and that upon which the Buddha-dharma depends. Regarding the rules of what is permitted and what is prohibited:
when Mañjuśrī and Kāśyapa responded to King Aśoka’s invitation, Mañjuśrī initially yielded to Kāśyapa, not daring to contravene the constant regulations of the ancient Buddhas.

Kāśyapa ultimately yielded to Mañjuśrī; thus he followed the original intention of the presiding host. Furthermore, when those such as junior monks or śrāmaṇeras preach the Dharma, they ascend the Dharma seat.
Regarding karmic retribution: if one does not respect the precepts, one distances oneself from the True Dharma;
whereas by respecting the formal aspects of the precepts, one gives rise to superior benefits, as in the ancient cases of the young monkey and the elephant.
The causes and conditions are fully contained within the sutras and vinayas.
○ The thirty-ninth [precept]: The Commentary on the Precept of Not Cultivating Merit and Wisdom.
The two adornments of merit and wisdom are like the two wings of a bird; they must be cultivated. They constitute the essential path for descending [into the world]; therefore—
The prohibitions apply equally to the seven assemblies, yet the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna do not entirely coincide. A Bodhisattva should cultivate all that is wholesome;
a Śrāvaka, during the summer retreat, should make a self-vow to cultivate meritorious deeds, while at other times no such prohibition is established.
*Fayi* (Uncovering the Hidden): The path that leads to transcendence consists in the dual cultivation of merit and wisdom; it is the swift and essential way to escape birth and death.
If merit is slight, one will constantly encounter obstructive conditions; if wisdom is shallow, one will frequently stray onto wrong paths.

Therefore, it is said that such a state deviates from the path of transcendence. Regarding the "self-vow during the summer retreat": when one sits in retreat, one practices; yet, such practice is limited by its duration.
It is not like the Bodhisattva, who never ceases to practice.
O Disciples of the Buddha, you should constantly teach and transform all sentient beings; you should establish monasteries, mountain forests, gardens, and fields;
you should construct Buddha-stūpas and places for winter and summer retreats and for sitting in meditation. You should establish all such sites for the practice of the Way.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should expound the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya for the sake of all sentient beings.
Whether it be during times of illness, national calamities, or threats from bandits; on the day of the passing of one's parents, siblings, upādhyāya, or ācārya;

or during the third, fourth, fifth, or even the seventh seven-day period following their death—one should likewise expound the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya at all such assemblies for the observance of fasts (poṣadha).
Whether seeking blessings, traveling for business, or engaged in livelihood; when burned by great fires, swept away by great floods, or when their ships are driven by black winds;

or when facing the perils of rākṣasas upon rivers, lakes, and the great ocean—if one reads, recites, and expounds this sutra and vinaya, then even all karmic retributions for sins, the three evil realms, the eight difficulties, the seven heinous offenses, being bound by cangues, shackles, and pillories, as well as excessive lust and excessive anger [shall be extinguished].

There are many who are ignorant and many who are afflicted by illness; all such persons should be taught this sutra and its vinaya. If a newly initiated bodhisattva does not do so, they commit a minor offense of defilement.
Commentary: Regarding the cultivation of merit—whether performed by oneself or taught to others—the text briefly enumerates seven matters:
first, monasteries; second, mountain forests; third, gardens; fourth, fields; fifth, stupas; sixth, places for winter and summer meditation and retreat;
seventh, all places for the practice of the Way. All such categories as these should be established. If one’s strength is insufficient, there is no offense. Regarding the cultivation of wisdom:

"Also performing it oneself and teaching others to do so" means to reveal what was hidden. "Performing it oneself and teaching others" refers to performing these seven matters oneself and simultaneously teaching and transforming sentient beings, causing them to perform these seven matters as well.
According to the tenth fascicle of the *Yaoji* (Essential Compendium), the Buddha said: "At that time, the monastics and the laity were practicing [these rites] in a corrupt manner..."
On their behalf, they compete to promote vegetarian feasts and lectures, forcibly suppressing others to seek wealth and construct pagodas and temples.

This is contrary to the scriptures and instead incurs prior offenses. This refers to those who, through irrational solicitation, falsely associate themselves with the construction of temples to use public funds for private gain.
To deceive oneself regarding causes while remaining ignorant of their effects means that while the heavenly realms have not yet been achieved, hell has already been established.
Cultivating merit in such a manner is not as good as avoiding transgressions; thus, students must clearly discern this. [Combined Commentary:
To establish monasteries and the like is a regulation intended to cultivate merit; to lecture on the Mahāyāna and the like is a regulation intended to cultivate wisdom. This is...

Regarding prohibitive actions (*vārita-karman*): one should practice according to one's capacity. If one encounters conditions that require action but fails to act, one incurs an offense for each instance, except in cases where one lacks the physical strength to do so;
in such cases, there is no offense. This corresponds to what is called "dwelling in little benefit, doing little, and having little application" in the *Pratimokṣa-sūtra*.
If it is done with a mind of resentment or malice, it is a defiled offense (*kliṣṭāpatti*); if it is due to laziness or indolence, it is not a defiled offense.
Regarding transgressions, there is no distinction between major and minor offenses for both [the Bodhisattva and the Śrāvaka]. During the summer retreat (varṣā), the Śrāvaka should repair dwellings;
at other times, this is not prescribed. For the Mahāsattva, however, one should perform meritorious deeds at all times. This is the distinction between what is permitted and what is prohibited.
Alternatively, there are those who constantly cultivate all superior activities such as meditation and recitation, having no leisure for other pursuits. As for their karmic fruition:
if they do not cultivate [these practices], they lose the two kinds of adornment; if they do cultivate them, the provisions for enlightenment increase spontaneously.
These nine precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent mind. They shall be explained in detail in the Chapter on the Brahma-Maṇḍala.
[Combined Commentary. This concludes the summary of the nine precepts of the fourth section.
○ Forty: The Commentary on the Discernment of Receiving the Precepts.

If there are those whose hearts delight in receiving [the precepts], they should all be granted them. If one were to reject them with anger or malice, it would contradict the spirit of encouragement and exhortation;

therefore, this was established as a regulation. This applies equally to both monastic orders (the two assemblies). As for others who lack a teacher or model, it has not yet been established; thus, the Great and Small Vehicles do not fully coincide in this regard.

A Bodhisattva fundamentally acts for the sake of others. If a Śrāvaka agrees to [bestow] the precepts but later regrets it, this constitutes a transgression; if they do not agree, there is no transgression.
O Disciples of the Buddha, when conferring the precepts upon others, one must not engage in discrimination; this includes all kings, princes, and great ministers.

The hundred officials, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, laymen, laywomen, lustful men, lustful women, the eighteen Brahmā heavens, the sons of the six heavens of desire, those without sexual organs, those with dual organs, eunuchs, slaves, and all ghosts and spirits—all may receive the precepts.
They should be taught that the robes they wear must all be dyed in "ruined colors" (kāṣāya) to accord with the Way; they should be dyed blue, yellow, or red.
Dark purple. All dyed robes, even down to bedding, must be entirely of a discolored hue. The robes worn on the body must all be dyed [in such colors].
In whatever country one resides, the robes worn by a bhikṣu must differ from the secular clothing of the people of that land.
When one wishes to receive the precepts, the preceptor should ask: "In this present life, will you not commit the seven..."

Regarding the offense of inversion: a Bodhisattva Dharma Master may not bestow the precepts upon those who have committed the seven heinous offenses in their present body. The seven heinous offenses are:

shedding the blood of a Buddha, killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing one's Upādhyāya (Preceptor), killing one's Ācārya (Teacher), destroying the Saṃgha that performs the *karmavācanā* or turns the wheel of the Dharma, and killing an Arhat.
If one possesses all seven heinous offenses, they shall not receive the precepts in their present body; as for all other people, [they may].
One may receive the precepts. According to the dharma of those who have left the household life, one does not prostrate before kings, nor does one prostrate before parents;

one does not show reverence to the six types of relatives, nor offer salutations to ghosts or spirits. However, if there are those who come from as far as a hundred or a thousand *li* to seek the Dharma, and they understand the words of the Dharma Master, yet the Bodhisattva Dharma Master, out of an evil mind or a mind of anger, does not immediately bestow the precepts upon all such sentient beings.
Precept: To commit this light offense of defilement.
[Combined Note: "One must not make discriminations" means that one should not discriminate among categories.

That is to say, from kings down to ghosts and spirits, all possess Buddha-nature; all may practice the Bodhisattva path according to their respective types. Therefore, all are permitted to receive [the precepts].
This concerns the precepts. Furthermore, there are two matters that should be examined: first, physical appearance; second, karmic obstacles.

Regarding the instruction to teach [the candidate] about the robes worn on the body and so forth, this is intended to instruct them to examine their physical appearance. "Kāṣāya" is the Sanskrit term for these robes.
This is called "dyed clothing," also known as "altered color" (*kāsāya*) or "reclining requisites. It is the general name for the robes of those who have left the household life.
The Vinaya prescribes three types of altered colors—namely blue, black, and madder—but the current regulation establishes five types.
These must all differ from the attire of laypeople. This primarily clarifies the essential nature of *bhikṣus* and *bhikṣuṇīs*.
This is the Saṃgha Jewel; therefore, three types of field-robes (kṣetra-vastra) have been specifically prescribed for them, forever distinguishing them from the laity.
As for the five groups beginning with the śikṣamāṇā, they need only wear dyed (prakṛti-varṇa-virakta) robes and must not be confused with the bhikṣus.

Regarding the instruction to inquire whether one has committed the seven heinous crimes (*saptānantarya-karma*) in this present life, it is intended to cause one to discern their karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*). [The] seven heinous karmas...
It is established that one will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell. Therefore, this directly obstructs the category of the precepts (*śīla-skandha*).
Since it cannot be known whether such an event occurred in a previous life, nor does it act as an obstruction to the precepts in that regard, the question concerns only the present existence.

Regarding the *upādhyāya* (preceptor), there are two types of bhikṣus: first, the *śrāmaṇera-upādhyāya*; second, the *upasampadā-upādhyāya*. There are three types of bhikṣuṇīs: first... [text continues]
1. The precept-mother (*upādhyāyī*) for the ten precepts; 2. The precept-mother for a *śikṣamāṇā* receiving the six rules;
3. The precept-mother for full ordination (*upasampadā*). None of these may be performed by a *bhikṣu*. There are two types of *śikṣamāṇā*:
first, those with a precept-mother for the ten precepts; second, those with a precept-mother for the six rules. [The same applies to] *śrāmaṇeras* and *śrāmaṇerīs*.
All are of one kind; that is, those to whom the ten precepts are conferred. Regarding the *ācārya*, there are five types of bhikṣus: first, the *ācārya* of the ten precepts;
second, the *ācārya* who instructs at the time of receiving full ordination; third, the *ācārya* who performs the *karmavācanā* at the time of receiving full ordination;
fourth, the *ācārya* of dependence (*niśraya*), even for as little as a single night of dependence; and fifth...
The *ācārya* who teaches recitation, up to and including receiving from them even a single four-line verse or explaining its meaning.
There are seven kinds of *bhikṣuṇīs*: [the six types mentioned previously] plus, at the time of receiving full ordination, the *karmācārya* within the *bhikṣu* saṃgha and the *ṣaḍdharmācāryā*.
There are three kinds of *śikṣamāṇās*: first, the *daśaśīlācāryā*; second, the *ṣaḍdharma*... [text fragmentary].
The *dharmācārya* (preceptor of the Dharma); the *pāṭhācārya* (preceptor of reading and recitation). For *śrāmaṇeras* and *śrāmaṇerīs*, there are two types each:

first, the preceptor for the ten precepts; second, the preceptor for reading and recitation. For *upāsakas* and *upāsikās*, there are three types each: first, the *ācārya* for receiving the five precepts;
second, the *ācārya* for receiving the eightfold fast (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa-saṃvara*); third, the *ācārya* for reading and recitation. Furthermore, if one includes...
When receiving the Bodhisattva precepts from an ācārya, each of the seven assemblies of disciples adds one further category.
Regarding the schism of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), it requires at least eight persons residing together, all of whom are bhikṣus;

four persons form one faction and four persons form another, and within a single great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), they separately recite the *prātimokṣa* and separately perform various *karmas*, thereby effecting a schism.
Regarding the Sangha that breaks the Wheel of Dharma: it requires at least nine persons. One person claims to be the Buddha and entices four bhikṣus to follow his separate teaching.
The remaining four bhikṣus maintain the correct doctrine and do not comply. Thus, they are divided into two factions.
Whether within or outside a formal boundary (sīmā), as long as they cause what is non-Dharmic to be proclaimed as Dharma—as in the case of Devadatta and others—it is called a schism.
Regarding the Wheel of the Dharma: "Sages" refers to those who have attained the four fruits of the Hīnayāna, as well as those of the Mahāyāna path and above.
Now, one who does not bow to parents or kings, nor show reverence to the six kin or spirits, yet comes from a hundred or a thousand *li* away—how earnest must their desire for the Dharma be!
To refuse to transmit it to such a person would be to fail the one who is ready for it; would this not be far too severe?
"Ah! As for 'evil mind' and 'hate-mind,' this clarifies that they are not minds that perceive the opportune moment to benefit sentient beings.
Regarding the 'precepts for all sentient beings,' this clarifies that these great precepts are fundamentally intended to be received equally by all sentient beings;

they do not resemble the *bhikṣu* or *śrāmaṇera* precepts, which must be conferred upon specific categories of individuals after selection. This is the fourth [point], concerning obstructive karma (*vāraṇīya-karma*).

The offense is established based on the following conditions: 1. Being a fit vessel for receiving the precepts; that is, not having committed one of the seven heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*), and possessing a physical appearance and demeanor in accordance with the Dharma.

2. Possessing the intention to receive [the precepts]. There are six permutations: two cases of grave offenses, two cases of light offenses, and two cases of non-offenses. 3. Having a discriminatory mind;

that is, perhaps despising them for being low-born, or feeling anger toward them for being impoverished, and so forth—[this applies when they are] precisely the owners of the property. 4. Causing [them] to be unable [to receive the precepts].
Receiving [the precepts]. One incurs an offense according to the person who refuses [to grant them]. If one knows that the person is incapable of receiving them, there is no offense.

The *Bodhisattva-śīla-karman* states: "When a bodhisattva wishes to receive the bodhisattva precepts, they should first be taught the Bodhisattva-piṭaka-mātṛkā, the bodhisattva training rules (*śikṣāpada*), and the characteristics of the points of transgression, so as to..."

Listen and receive [the precepts]. Examine them with wisdom; having the personal inclination and the capacity for discernment, one should receive the bodhisattva precepts, not merely because of another’s exhortation, nor for the sake of surpassing others.
It should be known that such a person is called a firm bodhisattva, capable of receiving the pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, it is said: "One who lacks pure faith should not receive them from [another]; that is to say,"
One should not receive such pure ethical discipline from one who initially lacks faith and understanding and is thus unable to enter into it;

from one who engages in improper reflection; from one who possesses stinginess and greed; from one who is obscured by stinginess and greed; from one who has great desires; from one who lacks contentment;
from one who violates pure ethical discipline; or from one who lacks reverence for the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) regarding the restraint of the precepts (*śīlasaṃvara*).
One should not receive [the precepts] from one who is arrogant and lax;
nor from one who is resentful and hateful, who lacks much forbearance, or who is unable to endure the transgressions of others; nor from one who is indolent or lazy.
One who is largely attached to sensual pleasures; one who sleeps day and night; one who delights in reclining, lying down, and associating with crowds;

and one who delights in idle chatter—one should not receive [the teaching] from such a person. One whose mind is distracted—even for as little as the time it takes to milk a cow—cannot abide in the cultivation of a virtuous mind focused on a single object;
one should not receive [the teaching] from such a person. One who is obscure and dull-witted... [is foolish].

Regarding those who belong to the class of delusion and those whose minds are extremely inferior, one should not receive the precepts from them if they disparage the Bodhisattva Sūtra-piṭaka and the Mātṛkā.
The explanation states: these are all excluded as being unfit vessels for the Dharma. How could it be said that there is no selection at all?
Furthermore, if the person before one originally does not wish to receive them, yet one forces them to receive the precepts, this also constitutes an offense.

Regarding the light defilement of "opening and closing" (discriminating between what is permitted and forbidden): when one perceives the capacity and benefit [of a recipient], one does not first bestow [the teaching].
Although this may appear as great anger, it is neither an evil mind nor a mind of malice. This is like the case of Dharmakṣema regarding the śramaṇa Dàojìn. As for the retribution:
if one discriminates falsely, one incurs the sin of being stingy with the Dharma and loses both [self-]benefit and [benefit for others]. If one discriminates skillfully...
Thus, the retinue is adorned and the Dharma-gate is made radiant and manifest. Within this ground of mind, there is neither noble nor base;
neither monastic nor lay; neither male nor female; neither defiled nor pure; neither celestial nor human;
neither whole nor incomplete; neither superior nor inferior; neither manifest nor obscure. It is of a single flavor and equal, without duality.
It is distinct. What is there to be rejected or accepted that gives rise to such discrimination? All are stained by the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of blue, yellow, and so forth.
Paramārtha states: "Blue" refers to verdigris; "black" refers to mixed mud. The *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* says:
"The Mahāsāṃghika school diligently studies the various sūtras and proclaims their meanings. Their dwelling place is situated in the center, and they should wear yellow robes."
The Dharmaguptaka school thoroughly understands profound principles and meanings; its manifestation of the Dharma is preeminent, and they should wear red robes.

The Sarvāstivāda school is broadly learned, quick-witted, and adept at guiding others through transformation; they should wear black robes. The Kāśyapīya school is courageous and protects living beings;
they should wear madder-colored robes. The Mahīśāsaka school practices meditative contemplation to enter the profound, thoroughly investigating and elucidating [the truth].
Regarding "dark and secret," one should wear blue. Based on this, the five colors are established. How, then, can these be called "defiled" (or "ruined") colors?

However, within that text, there are phrases such as "blue that is not the blue of the eastern direction," from which we know that within the category of defiled colors, there are five distinct varieties used to represent the five schools (*nikāya*), rather than the five beautiful colors of the mundane world. This is as with the aforementioned blue and yellow.
As for colors such as red or black, it is not necessary to distinguish them with strict certainty; it is sufficient that they differ from secular clothing.

When both monastics and laity receive the precepts, they must all wear dyed (ruined-color) robes. In cases where it is permissible to dye them ruined-color, both monks and laypeople should do so together.
In cases where it is not permissible to dye them ruined-color, the laity may follow their convenience, whereas monks must invariably wear ruined-color robes. Not...
That which may be dyed refers to those colors that are not locally approved. The *Dharmakṣaya-sūtra* states:
"When the Dharma is about to perish, the kāṣāya robes will naturally turn white. One should know that the whiteness of the robes is a sign of the extinction of the Dharma.

In this context, the prohibition against laypeople occupying high seats establishes the distinction between the monastic community (the black-robed) and the laity (the white-robed); one must therefore be cautious.
Furthermore, those who perform the *karmavācanā* and turn the Wheel of Dharma assemble the community for the *poṣadha*, acting as the Buddha’s representatives to propagate the transformation.
This is precisely what is meant by the "harmonious Saṃgha. To destroy such people is to extinguish the Buddha-Dharma; how could this not constitute a grave offense?
It is not merely a matter of living together in a crowd with mutual affinities that one may falsely assume the name of "harmony. Moreover, anyone capable of propagating the Dharma...
Benefiting sentient beings is all termed "turning the wheel of the Dharma. In the sutras, the two terms "grave offense" (*zhòng*) and "parricide" (*nì*) have distinct meanings.
There are those who commit grave offenses but do not commit parricide; there are those who commit both grave offenses and parricide.

When a *śrāvaka* harms his teacher, he has already committed a grave offense, yet specifically it is not called parricide. This is because parricide is a grave offense upon which an additional crime of parricide is further added. Question:
For a subordinate to kill a superior is in every case a transgression. Why, then, is it that for a *śrāvaka* to harm his teacher is not a transgression? Answer:
Within the Buddha-dharma, what is grave is weighed against the transgressions of worldly law; the transgressions within the Buddha-dharma are one degree greater than those of worldly law.

While for a *śrāvaka* to harm his teacher constitutes a grave offense that already qualifies as a worldly crime of transgression (*ānantarya-karma*), that which is called a transgression for a Bodhisattva is even further [grave].
It is more serious. Therefore, the commentary states: "The gravity for a Bodhisattva is greater than the gravity for a Śrāvaka.

Regarding those who do not pay respect to rulers, parents, the heavens, the earth, and so forth: this means that according to the dharma of renunciation, one has already ceased practicing worldly etiquette and reverence toward kings, parents, six types of relatives, ghosts, and spirits; thus, when receiving the precepts today, [one must not act in such a manner].
Furthermore, one asks whether they are noble or lowly, close or distant, human or divine; it depends solely on observing whether their intention is sincere.

Since you have come from afar to seek the Dharma, your sincerity can be known. With the exception of those who have committed the seven heinous offenses, if anyone else understands the words of the Dharma Master, you should immediately bestow the precepts upon them. Why then do you give rise to evil thoughts and anger? Do not...
If one gives [the teachings] and then refuses them, saying "I will not give," or delays them, saying "I will not give immediately"— if such is the case,
it is either because they seek profit and sell the Buddha-dharma, or else they lack compassion and seek only their own self-benefit.

For this reason, one incurs offense. If you examine their intention and find it not yet sincere, yet do not immediately grant [the teaching] because you wish to bring them to fulfillment—just as Wuchen was in his progress toward the Way—then this is a great expedient of transformative guidance, whose merit is immeasurable;

do not regard such cases with indifference. Question: Setting aside for the moment the ghosts and spirits of the six relations, why is it that one does not pay ritual homage to the sovereign and father?
I respectfully reply: For one who has left the household life, prostrating before a sovereign or a father is not an act of reverence. Why is this?
Even Śakra Devānām Indra does not desire those who observe the five precepts to prostrate to him, for he fears it might diminish their merit.

Therefore, those who have left the household life should repay the kindness of their sovereign and parents by practicing the Path with diligent application; they should not do so by kneeling, bowing low, or crawling on the ground.
Small courtesy is for the sake of reverence. This is precisely what a loyal minister and a filial son do:
they love their sovereign and father yet do not prostrate; this is called "great reverence. How could this be called arrogance? Question:
Since a śrāmaṇera who has not yet received the bhikṣu precepts may not receive the bodhisattva precepts, does it then follow that a śrāmaṇera is inferior to ghosts and animals? And...
[Question: Is it for the two groups of householders? Why is it that they are permitted to receive [the bodhisattva precepts] there, yet here they are not permitted to do so? [Answer:

The institutional frameworks of householders and monastics are inherently distinct, yet their underlying intent is roughly the same. For a householder, one must first receive the five precepts before being permitted to receive the bodhisattva precepts.
For one who has left the home life and shaved their head, one must first receive the bhikṣu precepts before being permitted to receive them.
Regarding the Bodhisattva precepts: those such as male and female ghosts and animals who are able to receive them are already those who possess the five precepts.
Now, the names of the Triple Gem are established because of the Bhikṣu precepts; a Śrāmaṇera has not yet entered the stream of the Triple Gem.
If a Śrāmaṇera were to directly receive the full precepts [without the intermediate stage], then the Bhikṣu precepts would be abolished, and the Saṃgha...
The Treasures are abandoned; the Three Jewels are deficient. How can the magnitude of such loss be described? Question: The sutras speak of "lustful men and lustful women.
Does this not refer to laypeople who do not receive the five precepts, but instead receive [the bodhisattva precepts] directly? Answer:

Even in such cases, it must be that during the course of a single assembly, they first receive the five precepts and subsequently receive the bodhisattva precepts. Thus, while the sequence may be bypassed, it is nonetheless incomplete.
This has not been arranged in sequential order.
Regarding the forty-first precept, the "Precept Against Acting as a Teacher for the Sake of Profit":
if one lacks internal realization while externally acting out of desire for fame and profit, and thus rashly presumes to teach, there is the fault of misleading others. Therefore—

The regulation applies equally to the two groups of monastics; however, it is not applied to the minor precepts for both groups together. For the three groups of novices and laypeople, as they lack the status of being formal teachers, it is not applied.
If, O Son of the Buddha, when teaching others to arouse faith, a Bodhisattva acts as a teacher and instructor for another person...
When one sees a person who wishes to receive the precepts, they should instruct them to request two masters—the Upādhyāya and the Ācārya. These two masters should ask:
"Do you have any of the seven obstructing offenses (*saptāvaraṇa*)? If the candidate currently has any of the seven obstructing offenses, the masters should not confer the precepts upon them.
If they do not have the seven obstructing offenses, they may confer the precepts. If there are those who have violated the ten precepts, they should be instructed to perform repentance.
Before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva, one should recite the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts during the six periods of the day and night.
With utmost sincerity, one should prostrate before the thousand Buddhas of the three periods of time until a "good sign" is obtained. This may take one week, two or three weeks, or even up to a year;
one must see a good sign. A "good sign" refers to the Buddha coming to stroke one’s head, or seeing light, flowers, and various other extraordinary phenomena.
If auspicious signs appear, one’s transgressions will be extinguished. If no such good signs occur, although one performs repentance, it is of no benefit;

such a person will not obtain the precepts in their present life, yet they will gain increased merit through the act of receiving them. If one has violated any of the forty-eight minor precepts, one may repent before another person (pratimukha-vinaya), and the transgression will be extinguished.
This is not the same as the case of the seven grave prohibitions (*saptāvaraṇa*). Furthermore, the instructor in this Dharma must understand each of these matters thoroughly. If...
They do not understand the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas, nor the characteristics of what is light or heavy, or what is right and wrong.

They do not understand the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the nature of the lineage of practice (*śikṣāgotra*), the nature of growth (*vivardhanagotra*), the nature of the lineage of essence (*dharmatāgotra*), the unbreakable nature (*abhedyagotra*), the nature of the lineage of the path (*mārgagotra*), or the nature of the true dharma (*saddharmagotra*).

Furthermore, they fail to attain each of these dharmas regarding the various degrees of meditative practice and its emergence and entry, the ten factors of dhyāna (*daśa-dhyānāṅga*), and all methods of cultivation.
This is acceptable. However, if a Bodhisattva, for the sake of gain and fame, seeks and covets excessively, greedily desiring disciples,
and falsely pretends to understand all the sutras and vinayas for the sake of offerings— thus deceiving themselves and deceiving others—
then one who bestows the precepts upon such a person commits a minor offense (light defilement).
Combined Commentary: The "Dharma Master who provides instruction" refers to the *śikṣācārya* (preceptor). Regarding the *bhikṣu* precepts, they are received within the Saṅgha;
therefore, both the *upādhyāya* and the *karmavācanā-ācārya* must be present *bhikṣus* who perform these roles.
Regarding the Bodhisattva precepts, they are received before the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions; therefore, the present [method...]
The Master said: "One may only receive the title of *śāstrī-upādhyāya*. Regarding the instruction to request two masters:

this refers to requesting the Honored One Buddha as the *upādhyāya*—in this land, that is Śākyamuni—and requesting the Bodhisattva who is next in succession as the *ācārya*—at this time, that is Maitreya. These are called the two masters. In the text, regarding the *upādhyāya*...
The phrase "the two masters, the ācārya and the upādhyāya" refers to those who should be questioned; that is, the preceptor (śāstṛ) should ask.
This means that before requesting the two masters, one must first inquire regarding the obstructing impediments (antarāyika-dharma), ensuring that the seven types of impediments are absent.
This is merely to formally request the two masters. Thus, the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: "May the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and virtuous ones of the ten directions listen.

Now, at the time when [the name] 'So-and-so' has been recited three times, one has received the bodhisattva precepts from the Buddhas and the Sangha of Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions. The speaker is I; the recipient is So-and-so. I am for the sake of..."
Regarding the witnesses: the "Great Master" refers to the immeasurable Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Saṅghas of the ten directions; the "Junior Master" refers to my own person.

Furthermore, having received the Bodhisattva precepts, since one takes the primordial Buddha as the Upādhyāya (Preceptor) and the Buddha of the Successive Stage as the Ācārya (Instructor), one likewise takes the Buddhas of the ten directions as the venerable witnesses of the same ritual platform. The Bodhisattvas of the ten directions...

Sā was a virtuous friend and fellow student. That he does not now request [the Buddha] to bear witness as his fellow student is because it is like the ordination of a bhikṣu, which requests only two masters.
Although other sūtras also provide for the invitation of five types of holy masters, they differ because they are expanded or abbreviated according to the capacity of the practitioner.
Regarding the violation of the ten precepts, this refers to one who has previously received these bodhisattva [precepts].

If one has received the Bodhisattva Great Precepts and yet violates them; or if one has previously received the Bhikṣu, Śrāmaṇera, or Five Precepts and has damaged their fundamental roots—then it is necessary to perceive auspicious signs (*lakṣaṇa*).

However, if one committed acts such as killing or stealing before receiving the precepts, these constitute merely worldly natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and are not termed "violations of the precepts"; thus, there is no need to inquire [about such matters].
It is only regarding the seven heinous offenses that one must inquire; for even in this present life, one shall not receive the precepts.

This means that re-receiving the full ordination (*mahāśīla*) is not permitted. However, one may obtain the benefit of receiving the precepts by creating superior causes for receiving them in a future life.

As for "confession before another" (*pratimukha-pratideśanā*), it means confessing one's own transgressions before a pure assembly of Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna practitioners, vowing not [to commit them again].
To perform it again is what is called the ritual repentance (*dharmaparyāya-kṣamaṇa*). Regarding the characteristics of offenses, whether light or heavy, right or wrong:
those that are light are easy to repent for; those that are heavy are difficult to repent for. What is an offense must be repented of; what is not an offense need not be repented of.

If one describes a light offense as heavy, or a heavy offense as light; if one claims that what constitutes an offense is not an offense, or that what is not an offense is an offense, one will be unable to resolve others' doubts or bring them out of transgression.
The First Noble Truth (paramārtha-satya) is the very essence of the precepts;
it is the primary cause for the ground of the mind, the ultimate fruit of eternal abiding, and the nurturing of the nature of the cultivated seeds.

"Nature" (*prakṛti*) refers to the gradual growth of the practice of the contemplation of emptiness; it is the ten stages of the "mind of setting forth" (*prasthānacitta*), which is the indestructible nature of the innate lineage (*prakṛtisthagotra*).
It is "indestructible" because it is established as conventional truth through the discernment of its provisional nature;

it is the ten stages of the "mind of nurturing" (*puṣṭicitta*). "The lineage of the path" (*mārgagotra*) refers to the Middle Way that is able to penetrate; it is the ten stages of the "gold-like mind" (*suvarṇacitta*).

The "adamantine mind" refers to the true nature of the Dharma, which means entering and realizing the stages of the noble ones—namely, the ten bhūmis as well as the two awakenings of Equal and Wondrous.

Regarding the "entering and exiting of various contemplative practices": when setting out on the path, one enters emptiness from the conventional; when nurturing [the practice], one enters the conventional from emptiness;
with the vajra-like samādhi, one turns away from the two extremes to enter the Middle Way; and at the ten bhūmis, one proceeds from...

Regarding all those who enter the state of sainthood (*ārya*): for those of the nature of the lineage of practice (*śikṣamāṇagotra*), the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) is still slight; for those of the nature of growth (*anugata-gotra*), the contemplation of emptiness is abundant.

For those of the nature of the lineage of nature (*prakṛti-gotra*), the contemplation of the provisional (*upādāya-prajñapti-vipaśyanā*) is still slight; for those of the nature of the unbreakable (*abhedyagotra*), the contemplation of the provisional is abundant.

For those of the nature of the lineage of the path (*mārgagotra*), the contemplation of the middle way (*madhyama-vipaśyanā*) is still slight; for those of the nature of the true dharma (*saddharmagotra*), the contemplation of the middle way is abundant. Furthermore,
If one practices the three contemplations sequentially, the cultivation is slight; if one practices them within a single moment of mind, the cultivation is extensive.
Regarding the ten factors of dhyāna (*dhyānāṅga*): these are the ten factors, such as joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*), employed in the four dhyānas.

If one does not understand what is light or heavy, right or wrong, one is obscured regarding the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*). If one does not understand the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one is obscured regarding the principle of the precepts (*śīla-naya*).

If one does not understand the nature of the lineage of practice and so forth, one will be obscured regarding the various distinctions between the concentration associated with the Path and the concentration associated with the Dharma.

If one is obscured regarding the characteristics of the precepts, one will be unable to resolve doubts or emerge from transgressions. If one is obscured regarding the principle of the precepts, one will be unable to inspire genuine faith and genuine understanding.
If one is obscured regarding the distinctions between the Path and concentration, one will be unable to lead others toward cultivation, realization, and entry. Is this not so?
This refers to "one blind man leading a multitude of blind men. This constitutes a prohibitive offense (*pratiṣedha-karman*) that severely undermines the transformation through the Dharma.
Two conditions constitute the transgression: first, the intention for gain; second, the act of gathering disciples. The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states:
"To maintain a retinue out of greed for service and offerings is a defiled offense (*kliṣṭāpatti*). This [rule] also concurrently governs the aforementioned [case of] non-existence.
Regarding the master who performs the ordination ceremony: the fault of the former lay in his love for fame; now, the fault lies precisely in his love for profit.

Both fame and profit are the root of birth and death and constitute great obstacles to Bodhi; their transgressions are equal. Therefore, both cases conclude by stating that he deceives himself and deceives others.
Yet for those who act for the sake of profit, their minds become increasingly base and inferior. As for the other five assemblies, there is no matter of receiving precepts;
however, if one causes them to gather a following for the sake of profit, they likewise commit an offense. This is strictly prohibited and not permitted.
Regarding the karmic retribution, such destruction of the Dharma gate is more severe than the offenses of the evil codes of conduct (*akuśala-vinaya*).
Section Forty-Two: Prohibiting the Preaching of the Precepts to Evil Persons.

The "Commentary on the Precepts" states: Generally, those who have not yet received the Bodhisattva precepts are all termed "evil persons. If one were to preach [the precepts] to them in advance, they would be unable to receive them with earnest reverence once they do so later;
therefore, this rule was established. It applies equally to the seven classes of followers and is mandated for both the Mahayana and Hinayana traditions.
*Fayi*: "If one drinks only after becoming thirsty, the sweetness of the water is appreciated; if one lights a lamp only after falling into darkness, the utility of the lamp is revealed.
Therefore it is said that if the teaching is given prematurely, the mind treats it lightly."
If you, O Son of the Buddha, for the sake of profit or sustenance, do not preach these Great Precepts of the Thousand Buddhas before those who have not yet received the Bodhisattva precepts,
nor before non-Buddhists or evil persons, nor even before those with false views— except in the case of a king.
It must not be said of any others; such evil persons do not receive the Buddha's precepts and are called "beasts.
In every place where they are born, they do not see the Triple Gem; like wood or stone, they lack a mind and are called "heretics. These people of false views are no different from wooden stumps.
Yet, if a Bodhisattva preaches the seven teachings and precepts of the Buddha before such evil persons, they commit a minor offense.
[This is] a transgression. [The following is] the combined commentary. Regarding the "recitation of the precepts" (*poṣadha*): it refers to the recitation of the precepts every half-month.

Regarding the exclusion of kings: this is because the Buddha-dharma was entrusted to kings. To live in vain and die aimlessly is why they are called "beasts" (*tiryagyoni*). They are stubborn and utterly lack awakening.
Therefore, like wood or stone, they turn their backs on awakening and unite with the sensory dust; thus they are called non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). This is a prohibitory act.
If one speaks of this in advance to others, the subsequent reception [of the precepts] will not be performed with earnestness;

for this reason, when the *Poṣadha* (confession of precepts) is held every half-month, those who have not yet received the full ordination (*upasampadā*) must first be sent away. A transgression is established through four conditions. First, the person who has not received the precepts, namely—
1. One who has not yet received these Bodhisattva precepts. 2. One who has not yet formed the perception of the person as such. There are six phrases:
two are grave offenses, two are light offenses, and two are non-offenses. 3. Speaking with a specific intention, namely for the sake of gain and so forth.

4. When the other person hears it, from that moment the offense is established. The Sevenfold Assembly commits this equally; however, the Mahayana and Hinayana do not fully coincide. [This applies to] the Hinayana.
At all times, one must not explain the names of the five categories of offenses (*pañcāpatti*) to śrāmaṇeras and others.
This is because if they were to understand the meaning of these five categories, it would constitute the grave offense of stealing the Dharma (*dharmasteya*).

In the Mahāyāna, one must only expel those who have not received the precepts during the fortnightly recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*; at other times, this is not required. As stated in the preceding text:
At all times, one should always lecture upon this sutra and its vinaya. As the subsequent text states:
"Upon seeing any sentient being, one should exhort them to receive the three refuges, the ten precepts, and so forth. Thus, it is known that this is not the same as the Vinaya-piṭaka.
Furthermore, at all times, bodhisattvas—whether bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs—must likewise not [judge others] by means of the offenses categorized under the five groups of transgressions.

To explain this to those who have not yet received full ordination would cause Bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras and others to prematurely learn the names and meanings of the five categories of offenses, thereby creating a grave hindrance that would forever obstruct their receiving full ordination in this life. This is a prohibition that must not be breached;
for regarding the karmic retribution: to speak of it would be to treat the True Dharma with irreverence, while not speaking of it serves as its protection.
